Journalist to be crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
- Published
Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I, who is set to be crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom later, has long been a familiar face in the country.
For many Ugandans, he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller, as a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster.
But Kijanangoma, 56, has now become the subject of media attention himself - his rise to the Tooro throne sparking controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country.
Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it has been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.
Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34.
The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices starting from midnight. The new king then walks about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he is crowned.
A mock fight follows, to signify that kingship does not come easy, and he is then blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, the Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast.
He performs other ceremonies that signifies his assumption of the throne, before he sits on the throne and an actual crown placed on his head to signify his new authority, his new position as the new Tooro king.
But the selection of Kijanangoma as king was far from straightforward.
According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should succeed him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne.
But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma.
The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son.
Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected.
However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions.
The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome.
Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family".
"As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay".
The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute".
"No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X.
But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind".
While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan".
A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources.
Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965.
Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs.
According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.
After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development.
"I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said.
Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead.
The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala.
The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s.
The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty.
Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him.
The date of the coronation was announced by the government and Museveni is scheduled to attend.
The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X.
Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage.
His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum".
The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer.
Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300 km (186 miles) from Kampala.
He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999.
He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation.
The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader.
After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people".
His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition.
"I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC.
She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it."
She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man".

Ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party-led protest in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, and on the day of the protest on October 10, Hindu Rakhsha Dal (HRD) chief Pinky Chaudhary and its members posted a series of videos on social media platforms inciting violence against the demonstrators. Strikingly, several such videos were made in the presence of police.
In the clips, Chaudhary and other HRD members urged “Hindutva supporters” to “set the protesters’ minds right” while using communal and inflammatory rhetoric. He described those planning to demonstrate as “anti-national” and “anti-Hindu”.
Despite reports claiming that Chaudhary was placed under house arrest, he continued to issue calls for HRD members and other “kattar Sanatanis” to reach Jantar Mantar and confront the protesters ahead of Saturday’s protest and on the very day.
Moreover, a video posted by News Capsule on October 10, the day of the protest, showed a group of men dragging, beating and physically assaulting young protesters near Kamla Market. Alt News identified one of the alleged assailants as Ravindra Govinda, a member of Hindu Raksha Dal.
Govinda shatred a clip on his Facebook account in which he declared “support for the Delhi police in treating the protesters” while identifying himself as a member of HRD. “…As we, the Hindu Raksha Dal, had declared, we will stand with Delhi police in treating these cockroaches…,” he says, while continue to issue threats against the agitators.
Govinda was also seen in a video posted by Pinky Chaudhary, claiming that HRD members were fighting against CJP protesters to “protect Sanatanis”.
One of the goon seen beating the kid is Ravindra Govinda. Member of Hindu Raksha Dal. He was detained in the morning. Look how Police is handling the goons. https://t.co/nONEQVhY4f
— Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear) October 10, 2026
‘We Will Beat Them With Sticks’
On October 9, Chaudhary posted a video in which he stood alongside a group of men carrying batons and openly threatened physical violence against protesters expected to assemble at Jantar Mantar the following day.
Chaudhary declared in the video: “Laath bajake inke pichwade thik karne, dimag thik karne jayenge” (We will beat them with sticks and set their minds right). He added: “Jo log iss desh ko Islam meh le jane ki galat fehmi rakhte hai” (Those who are under the misconception that they can turn this country into an Islamic nation.) He said HRD members and staunch Sanatani believers will “handle” all those who have the “insect of secularism” in their head.
View this post on Instagram
Threats Continued Despite Police Intervention
A few hours later on October 9, Chaudhary uploaded another video claiming that police had arrived at his residence and placed him under house arrest. However, even as he stood in front of several police personnel, he continued to issue threats.
In this video, he declared that several members of HRD had already reached Delhi and were prepared to confront the demonstrators. Referring to Jantar Mantar as an “adda of terrorists”, he reiterated that HRD members would use their batons against those he described as opponents of Sanatan Dharma. “Jitne Sanatani virodhi hai, unke pichwade laal karke hi wapas ayenge” (We will return only after making the backsides of all those who oppose Sanatanis red), he said. He further described HRD members as warriors who are “neither afraid to die nor to kill.”
Chaudhary portrayed the outfit as pro-police and pro-nationalist, claiming that its members wanted to teach the protesters a lesson for allegedly misbehaving with police personnel. He also accused CJP supporters of insulting Hindu deities, attempting to establish an Islamic state, and acting against the nation. “India is safe till date, only because Sanatani warriors are here,” he said.
View this post on Instagram
Chaudhary’s Son Joins Calls For Violence
In another video, Harsh Chaudhary, son of Pinki Chaudhary, posted a video appearing alongside several HRD members, including Lalit Sharma. The video was accompanied by the caption: “Hindu raksha dal puri takat k saath cockroach-o ki gaand pitne pohunch raha hai” (Hindu Raksha Dal is arriving in full force to beat the asses of cockroaches).
Dismissing the need for batons, he claimed that he was physically strong enough to pick people up and pin them down himself. “We don’t need lathis; I am tough enough to pick them up and pin them down,” Harsh said.
View this post on Instagram
Threats From Inside Police Station
On October 10, Harsh and his team were detained by the Ghaziabad police. They went on to post a video after recording it while sitting inside the police station and in front of police personnel, where they urged Hindu warriors to “set the mind right” of the protesters. Even as the continued to issue these threats while in police detainment, no cops were seen preventing them from recording the videos or issuing violent threats.
View this post on Instagram
Ravindra Govinda, Other Assailants Held
Prior to his Instagram account becoming unavailable, Govinda had also uploaded several videos in which he expressed support for the Delhi police and BJP government. In these videos, he said HRD members would stand along with the police and participate in “treating” the cockroaches.
Independent journalist Pranav Pradhi, posting a video on X, questioned Delhi police officials regarding the apparent disparity in treatment of protestors and “Sanatani warriors” of HRD.
He pointed out that Govinda and other members of HRD, who had been making inflammatory statements and issuing violent threats, were not detained on October 10, while several other protesters faced prompt detention. Pradhi highlighted that there were at least six people gathered together, which violated Section 163.
Delhi Police is stopping ordinary citizens from gathering or protesting, citing Section 163 of the BNSS. But Hindutva groups are gathering openly and threatening protesters.
They claim the protesters are raising anti-India slogans. I have covered these protests and haven’t witnessed this. And frankly, this is an old tactic. Nothing new here.
So I asked Delhi Police a simple question: if ordinary citizens aren’t allowed to gather, how are these groups allowed to assemble and openly threaten protesters?
They had no answer.
— pranav pradhi (@pranavpradhi1) October 10, 2026
Govinda later uploaded a video indicating that he and his associates had been detained by the police.
On October 11, Sunday, Delhi police arrested the four men seen allegedly assaulting protesters in the video. “Taking suo motu cognizance of a video circulating on social media showing four men allegedly assaulting a male protester, Delhi Police, PS Kamla Market, acted promptly and initiated legal proceedings,” Delhi police said in a statement. The four held include Govinda (35), Raman Saini (50), Vivekanand (32), and Kapil Kumar (27).
‘We Won’t Let India Become Bangladesh’
Ahead of the protest on October 8, Sharma released a video in which he issued threats while brandishing a baton. In the video, he stated that the HRD team would go to Jantar Mantar to “treat” the “anti-nationals.” He also declared, “We won’t let this country become Bangladesh.”
On October 9, Sharma uploaded a video showcasing a baton that resembles a baseball bat. He specifically threatened Dipke and Rathee, saying, “Do not confront HRD members, or this baton will enter through your mouth and come out from your ass.”
He stated that in places where Sanatan Dharma is insulted, where Sita Mata is disrespected, and where slogans against Brahmanwad and Thakurwad are raised, they will wreak havoc at Jantar Mantar on those individuals so that seven generations of theirs will remember it. He further claimed that HRD will take revenge for the mistreatment suffered by the Delhi police.
On live video, he used inflammatory language and expletives, urging Sanatanis to gather at Jantar Mantar in large numbers to confront the protesters. Sharma also uploaded several videos issuing threats of violence at Jantar Mantar against the protesters. In a video posted in the early hours of October 10, Sharma used expletives targeting Dipke, Rathee and their mothers while reiterating that HRD members were prepared to use violence against the demonstrators.
Later, Sharma uploaded another video where several HRD members were seen gathering and raising ‘Jai Sri Ram’ slogans, and other inflammatory slogans in police presence. 
Journalist Rana Ayyub posted a video in which Sharma was identified by Alt News. The video shows Sharma making inflammatory slogans like, “Dipke, Rathee kaha milenge? Rahul k pichwade meh!” in the presence of several police officials. The police officials can be seen asking them to board their cars. In the post, Ayyub said, “They threatened to detain me when I asked if they were facilitating this hate.”
This is Delhi police in all her glory. They threatened to detain me when I asked if they were facilitating this hate https://t.co/5cmHhw3Hke
— Rana Ayyub (@RanaAyyub) October 10, 2026
Notably, there was deployment of a massive contingent of police personnel and army battalions at Jantar Mantar. The authorities invoked Section 163 and detained protesters and journalists, Opposition politicians en masse.
Meanwhile, Indian Express Hindi posted a video showing a group of men adorning saffron scarves brutally assaulting a man at Connaught Place. The assailants were seen wearing metal knuckles, due to which the victim sustained wounds on his back and tore his shirt. The protester ran ahead to safety, where a few policemen were visible standing by the roadside, but none of them came to his rescue, Indian Express reported.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Eight injured in South Korea knife attack
- Published
A man has been arrested after stabbing several people in a shopping centre in Incheon, in a rare knife attack in South Korea.
Eight people were wounded in the incident on Tuesday afternoon, according to local news reports.
The 59-year-old suspect was reported to have carried out the attack at 13:40 local time (05:40 BST) with knives strapped to both of his hands, according to Incheon Namdong Police Station.
Law enforcement is currently investigating the suspect's motives for the attack, which took place in a building housing an outlet of Homeplus, one of South Korea's largest discount supermarket chains.
The suspect reportedly started stabbing people while travelling on an escalator from the floor where Homeplus was located.
Pictures and clips carried by local media show him attacking people at a food court.
The man was subdued by bystanders who used chairs to block his path and was later detained by police officers.
All eight victims - six women and two men - were taken to the hospital.
One of them suffered from "cardiac arrest", while the others had injuries to their back and shoulders.
In response to the casualties, authorities had set up an emergency medical centre on the building's first floor.
According to local reports, the suspect was wearing an electronic monitoring ankle bracelet at the time of the attack.
Reports said he had been previously convicted for attempted murder after he stabbed his ex-wife, and had spent four years in prison.
He had also reportedly been booked by police last month on suspicion of carrying a knife while holding a one-man protest in front of an Incheon hospital over medical treatment he had received.
The attack happened in a country known for its high public safety standards.
South Korea recorded about 0.5 homicides per 100,000 people in 2024, according Statistics Korea. That is about one-tenth of the global average.
However, a series of seemingly random and violent attacks across the country in 2023, which resulted in multiple fatalities and injuries, caused widespread fear.
Such attacks were known as 'Mudjima' or 'Don't Ask Why' crimes, a term used to describe acts of violence targeting strangers conducted by people with no personal link to the victims nor had obvious motives.
In April 2025, a man in his thirties attacked random strangers at a supermarket resulting in the death of a woman in her sixties.

SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for Episode 6 of “Tommy & Tuppence,” now streaming on BritBox.
The finale of “Tommy & Tuppence” finds the Agatha Christie detective duo, played by Josh Dylan and Antonia Thomas, on the verge of a new chapter.
The BritBox Original series brings the classic characters into the modern day, where Tommy and Tuppence are exes instead of a married couple (as Christie originally wrote). A decade after dating at university, they bump into each other at a wedding and soon become embroiled in a murder mystery. The two have an exciting will they-won’t they chemistry as they solve cases around London (with the help of Tommy’s Aunt Ada, played by Imelda Staunton), begin their own private detective business and start getting closer. But there’s just one problem — Tuppence is married to a director back in L.A.
The series’ sixth episode sees Tommy and Tuppence solve a cold case surrounding harrowing child murders in the countryside, just as Tuppence at last acknowledges her feelings for Tommy and decides to divorce her husband. In classic rom-com fashion, just as Tuppence bursts through Tommy’s door with the news, she sees him kissing police detective Draper (Callie Cooke). Then, Tuppence’s sister presents them with their biggest mission yet: helping the U.K. government with a major case.
Popular on Variety
“Finally, it clicks and she realizes — but is she just a bit too late?” Thomas tells Variety over Zoom.
“Much of their relationship is characterized by sliding doors moments and missing each other just by a hair’s breath, which is in part infuriating but also kind of tantalizing,” Dylan adds. “It’s like, when are they going to get it out?!”
Below, Dylan and Thomas break down the finale episode, reveal how they established Tommy and Tuppence’s chemistry and discuss a potential Season 2.
First of all, what made you want to come on board the series?
Dylan: Obviously, Agatha Christie is untouchable in so many ways — incomparable rather, because she’s the Queen of Crime and it’s beloved by people. But when I read the scripts I felt like, here’s an opportunity to do something that I don’t think I’ve seen before, which is blending that cozy crime world, that Agatha Christie world, with an opportunity to make this feel really grounded and naturalistic and real.
Thomas: Tommy and Tuppence are amateurs anyway, so it lends itself really well to the more modern-day idea of being a sleuth and listening to a podcast and trying to figure something out yourself. Like we can all relate to that; I love a true crime podcast. And the way that [Christie] wrote those characters was quite modern actually, for the time. Particularly Tuppence being a pretty outspoken, front-footed woman, she was very modern in the way that she behaved. So that felt like a very easy transfer.
Tommy and Tuppence are married in Christie’s stories, but in this adaptation they’re exes in this sort of will they-won’t they phase. How did you establish that chemistry?
Thomas: Josh and I did a lot of meeting up and trying to work on the relationship and find a colloquial shorthand in and amongst the text. I certainly was quite daunted by the scenes where there’s quite a lot of exposition and they’re going through and trying to figure out the crime. I remember being like, “I don’t know how to do this!” And Josh was like, “I think these are the moments that they’re having the most fun and also when they as characters are connecting the most.” And as soon as you said that, it totally unlocked it for me. Because there’s two things going on, which is really fun about Tommy and Tuppence — the relationship between them and the crimes that they’re solving. So to use the crime-solving as a way to become closer was so fun. And then [writer] Phoebe [Eclair-Powell] was really open with allowing us to be freer with some of those bits to make it feel more modern.
Dylan: Yeah, and moments where it allowed for a little bit of improvisation. They let us get away with some of that, which was kind of them.
What were the conversations you had about Tommy and Tuppence’s history?
	Dylan: We’re still piecing bits together, to be honest. I think the idea is that they met at university and were together and obviously had an amazing connection, but the details, the reason why they split up is still a bit contentious. They get along and they have this care for each other, but you grow up a lot in 10 years. So at the top of the series and throughout, you’re seeing these people that have this core chemistry and connection, but they’re realizing the ways in which they’ve changed and the ways they’re still the same. And that feels really human and real and truthful to me, and was really interesting to play.
Thomas: And also, as much as they have changed, they’re still the same. It’s like that idea of a leopard doesn’t change its spots. The thing that was the problem last time, 10 years ago, is still basically the problem. It’s just, are they more mature? Can they address things differently?
Dylan: But on the flip side, the spark that drew them together in the first place is also still there, in exactly the same way.
What makes them work so well together in a more professional sense, as a detective duo?
Thomas: I think the fact that they’re quite opposites. They’re the yin and yang, they complement each other. Tuppence is pretty impulsive, she’s very instinctual and has often a strong gut feeling about things and is quite ballsy. So she’ll want to attack things head on, and then Tommy is much more thoughtful and precise and forensic often about things, which is really needed. The push and pull between them I think keeps them steady and in the middle.
And I have to ask, what was it like working with Imelda Staunton as Aunt Ada?
	Dylan: What a legend. She’s cool as hell and very twinkly and magical. And seems to kind of be the perfect Aunt Ada.
Thomas: There’s so much fun to her, like she brought such a fun, almost impish, brilliant side to Ada. And working with her and just watching her work, she’s such a seasoned veteran. It was a brilliant.
Let’s get into the final episode. It’s quite intense — you’re hunting down Jane Lancaster, a child murderer who then sets the house you’re all in on fire, and then Tuppence finally confesses her feelings to Tommy while he’s unconscious. What was that like to film?
Dylan: Oh my god, that’s actually a bit triggering. I just got flashbacks to being in that cottage and being in the room with the wonderful actress Alice Krige as Jane Lancaster — being in this tiny little bedroom with her for like, two days. It was so intense.
Thomas: You had to do your big ol’ speech, didn’t you?
Dylan: Absolutely glorious monologue. And then being carried out of the fire, I remember Antonia — she’s an incredible actress anyway, full stop the end, but I remember this particular take where I was a dead weight on the floor like, succumbed to the flames, and she was over my face and then a tear fell in my mouth.
Thomas: [Laughs] And then we were also really tired because that was the end of the shoot. I don’t know if I’ve done a job as intense because we’re basically in every scene, bar a few. And so by the time we got to Episodes 5 and 6, we’d been going for a few months. And then those two episodes just ramped up and it’s just really dark, isn’t it? It’s about child murder and kidnapping and Ada dies and that’s really sad. And then between the two of them as well, they’re not in a good place.
Do you think Tommy heard Tuppence’s confession? At the end, he seems to be moving on with Draper…
	Thomas: No, I don’t think he does. I think that’s what’s sort of sad about it, in a way. And about the ending altogether. Finally, it clicks and she realizes — but is she just a bit too late? 
Dylan: Much of their relationship is characterized by sliding doors moments and kind of missing each other just by a hair’s breath, which is in part infuriating but also kind of tantalizing. And they’re not always the best — shock, horror – at expressing themselves. They clearly feel a huge amount, they’re very sensitive and very compassionate and feeling, but they just keep missing each other. It’s like, when are they going to get it out?!
It’s almost like we need a second season! And the ending sets that up quite well, with an offer for the duo to help the government on a case. What would you want to see from a potential Season 2?
	Thomas: Would love a second season.
Dylan: I would love to do one.
Thomas: Also, can we do it somewhere exotic?
Dylan: Yeah, the Caribbean? We’ll take Spain! No, to be fair, we’d love to do it. These characters have so much scope and potential and range to go on so many more adventures, and we love the creative team. It does feel like Season 1 ends at a very exciting junction, and they grow a lot as well. What I love about this show is that it’s grounded and funny and doesn’t take itself too seriously a lot of the time, but then I do think it has the capacity in moments to go to some darker places and stretch. So I think that would be quite nice, to continue that theme.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) as Britain looks to reaffirm its support for Ukraine, including with the promise of a new package of surface-to-air missiles.
The meeting comes at a difficult time for Mr. Zelenskyy. U.S. President Donald Trump said at the weekend he should be replaced as Ukraine’s leader, days after cutting a deal with Moscow to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
Britain has said it does not support the U.S.-Russia diesel deal, and called for allies to keep up the economic pressure on Moscow.
“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe,” Mr. Burnham said in a statement before the meeting.
Mr. Burnham said backing for Ukraine was vital to keeping people in Britain safe and pledged further military support.
He announced the planned delivery of £45 million ($59.60 million) of surface-to-air missiles used to target jet-powered Russian drones, with £10 million of that package fast-tracked to meet an urgent need in Ukraine.
Mr. Burnham has asked officials to draw up further sanctions, military aid, and fiscal support, and his foreign and finance ministers have been lobbying allies to follow Britain in banning maritime services that support Russian liquefied natural gas exports.

A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people.
An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week.
The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq.
In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports.
After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.”
The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors.
In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday.
The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties.
Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike.
On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.”
On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details.
The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others.
The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued.
“We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X.
Trump said on Saturday night that he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, after the previous attack on the airport.
The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis.
Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit.
It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump is facing the midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home threatening his party’s performance at the polls.
Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children.
Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the past month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier.
The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.
The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.
Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said.
The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.
“Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.”
The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March.
On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom.
The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles.
Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low.
The Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government.
Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US.
Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Around 4,000 registrations were completed under the SVAMITVA scheme after patwaris resumed work on Tuesday, against an overall target of nearly 50 lakh registrations. Work under the scheme had been delayed as patwaris had been on strike since its launch.
They had refused to work as executants in property registrations, fearing that they could face legal complications if someone challenged the registrations in future.
Last Friday, a delegation of patwaris met Chief Minister Mohan Yadav, who assured them of legal protection under the scheme. Following the assurance, it was expected that patwaris would resume work.
However, they did not return to duty, stating that several of their colleagues had either been terminated or suspended. They demanded that the government withdraw the termination and suspension orders before they resumed work under the scheme.
On Tuesday, a delegation of patwaris led by Upendra Baghel met Deputy Chief Minister Rajendra Shukla and raised the issue of disciplinary action against their colleagues. Shukla subsequently spoke to Chief Secretary Ashok Barnwal regarding their demand.
The Chief Secretary informed the Deputy Chief Minister that all disciplinary actions taken against patwaris would be withdrawn by Wednesday. In the meantime, patwaris resumed work under the SVAMITVA scheme on Tuesday.

Jantar Mantar denotification as protest site based on Supreme Court orders: Delhi Police tells high court
The court issued notice on a request to reconsider a protest-permission denial and will hear the case on November 17.
The Delhi Police on Tuesday told the Delhi High Court that they denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site in the Capital following a Supreme Court order earlier this month that nudged authorities to consider alternative, better-equipped spaces where residents could exercise their democratic rights without hindering public safety.
“We denotified Jantar Mantar after Supreme Court’s order dated October 9,” the Delhi Police told the single-judge bench of justice Amit Mahajan.
The submission was made while the court was hearing a petition filed last week by Indian Youth Congress (IYC) president Uday Bhanu Chib against Delhi Police’s denial of permission for a protest at Jantar Mantar.
Deep Dive
Delhi Police was represented by additional solicitor general Chetan Sharma and standing counsels Ashish Dixit and Amit Tiwari.
Also Read | Jantar Mantar’s changing place in Delhi’s protest map
The Supreme Court on October 9 called for a rethink of Delhi’s decades-old arrangement of holding demonstrations at Jantar Mantar, recording that the Delhi Police commissioner and other competent authorities would consider designating an alternative venue with better facilities for peaceful protesters.
A bench comprising chief justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the national capital needed a larger, better-equipped space where citizens could exercise their democratic right to protest without compromising public safety, access to emergency services or the interests of other residents. “It is high time that some other place with amenities for peaceful protestors need to be identified and designated,” the bench said in its order.
Delhi Police on Monday denotified Jantar Mantar as a protest site, ending its 33-year-long designation as one of the country’s demonstration hubs. They designated three alternative venues for protests: Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground in north Delhi, and CBD Ground in east Delhi.

The order, titled “Guidelines for Holding Protests or Demonstrations in Delhi”, said the Union ministry of home affairs constituted a committee to “examine alternative proper venues for citizen’s right for organising protest demonstrations in place of the existing ‘designated site’”.
“Based on the committee’s recommendations, Jantar Mantar as a protest venue has been de-notified,” the order said, adding that three new venues were designated for organising protests and demonstrations.
On Tuesday, Chib’s lawyer Siddharth Luthra urged the court to issue notice in the prayers to reconsider its request by undertaking a fresh, reasoned and individualised assessment. With regard to the prayer against Delhi Police’s October 1 denial to hold a protest at Jantar Mantar, the senior counsel sought time to amend the prayer in view of Monday’s notification.

The law officer opposed notice being issued, saying the petition was infructuous in view of Monday’s notification. He said that all the prayers emanated from Chib’s prayer against the denial.
However, the bench issued notice on the reconsideration prayer and will now hear the case on November 17.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.
Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only.
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

In summer and fall 2026, numerous posts claimed U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr said, "Infertility is genetic. If your parents can't have kids, neither can you."
For example, a meme of Kennedy featuring the purported quote spread widely on Facebook on Oct. 2.
Snopes readers have also reached out to us to verify the authenticity of the alleged remark.
(Facebook user "Truth and Accountability Project")
Though Kennedy has spread incorrect health information many times over the years, there is no evidence he said the above quote. Variations of this quote are on X and in humor books dating back years before he was sworn in as health secretary in 2025. As such, the remark is incorrectly attributed to Kennedy.
Entering variations of the quote in Google, Bing (archived) and DuckDuckGo uncovered no authentic video or reportage indicating that Kennedy ever made such a statement.
Earlier online examples of the quote are not attributed to him at all. One of the earliest variations of the quote on X, from Aug. 14, 2022, reads: "Infertility is genetic, if your parents couldn't have kids you also won't." Other X accounts, including one labeled as a parody account, shared the same quote days later.
Another variant of the quote appears in the 2002 book, "Science Askew: A Lighthearted Look at the Scientific World," by Donald E. Simanek. An even earlier version appears in the 1997 book of humor, "Living, Laughing, and Loving Life," by Dan Miller and Jeanne Zornes. Snopes contacted Zornes to learn if the quote originates from this book. We will update this article if we learn more.
While he didn't originate the quote in question, Kennedy has long been concerned with infertility issues. In May 2026, at a White House event, he raised the alarm on male infertility, saying:
The fertility crisis for women began in 2007; for men in 1970. Men had twice the sperm count as our teenagers do today. This is an existential crisis for our country. We had a series of presidents who were trying to discourage childbirth and motherhood in this country. We now have a president who is trying to encourage it.
In 2025, Kennedy said on Fox News: "We have fertility rates that are just spiraling. A teenager today, an American teenager, has less testosterone than a 68-year-old man. Sperm counts are down 50%." Experts debunked this particular claim, according to an NBC News report.
An analysis by The 19th, a nonprofit newsroom focused on gender and politics, found that while evidence shows sperm counts are lower than decades ago, it is not clear that factor influences the declining birth rate in the United States.
For further reading, Snopes has looked into numerous quotes rightly or wrongly attributed to Kennedy.

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. this week launched an agency-wide effort to study and document any health problems reported after vaccination, the Department of Health and Human Services said on Thursday.
The initiative is the latest step by Kennedy, who spent years questioning vaccine safety and founded an anti-vaccine group before taking office, to reshape federal immunization policy. The American Academy of Pediatrics says childhood vaccines are studied in placebo-controlled and comparison-group trials and monitored for safety after approval.
The federal Vaccine Injury Table lists 14 compensable injuries across 16 vaccine types under the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, a no-fault system in which claimants file against the government, not vaccine makers. Since 1988, it has awarded roughly $5 billion across about 12,300 injury and death claims.
The new moves, which appear to be part of Kennedy’s decades-long efforts to sow skepticism about vaccines, come as he faces legal challenges to his attempts to alter US childhood vaccination schedules and growing concern among public health experts about falling immunisation rates, particularly against measles, which has seen a resurgence in the US since last year. The effort centers on a National Institutes of Health clinic
opened on Monday to treat and study patients reporting health problems after receiving vaccines, HHS said in a statement. Other measures include a proposal by the Centers for
Medicare & Medicaid Services to reimburse physicians for reporting suspected injuries to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS; a CDC effort to update VAERS; and HHS requiring electronic health records to capture vaccine-related adverse events.
Kennedy has said U.S. children receive too many vaccines, falsely claiming repeatedly that kids get up to 90 doses before age 18, which has been echoed by President Donald Trump. Kennedy has long argued that chemicals in vaccines are dangerous, though experts say there is no evidence of harm.
In his first year heading HHS, he fired all 17 independent expert members of the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee and selected new panelists, many of whom shared his anti-vaccine views.
In January, the CDC announced a revamped childhood vaccine schedule that reduced recommended vaccines, dropping universal recommendations for flu, rotavirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B at birth, some forms of meningitis and respiratory syncytial virus.
A federal court issued a preliminary injunction in March blocking key parts of the proposed changes, finding that Kennedy and HHS had violated federal law in reshaping the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunisation Practices. The injunction has prevented ACIP from holding meetings to make recommendations on immunisations often needed for insurance coverage.

The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.
That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.
“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.
“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.
The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded in disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.
“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.
South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”
Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the Prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.
Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.
“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.
“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.
Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Donald Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Monday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

A cluster of Shigella infections linked to a temple festival has put health authorities in Thrissur on alert, with 10 cases reported in the district in the first nine days of October. Seven of the cases, including that of a seven-month-old child, were reported from Tholur among people who had attended a festival at a temple there.
The suspected source of the infection has been traced to a well at the temple, from which water was drawn for rituals. The well has since been chlorinated, District Medical Officer M. Sujatha said.
“The seven Shigella cases reported from Tholur were among people who attended a festival at a temple in Tholur. The source of infection has been identified as the temple well from which water was taken for rituals. The well has been chlorinated,” Dr. Sujatha said.
Health teams are closely monitoring the situation, while hospitals have been instructed to respond immediately if any further cases are detected. Awareness campaigns have also been conducted in the area, with people advised to seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms, she said.
All those who tested positive for Shigella have sought treatment, and most have recovered. The remaining patients are also recovering, according to the DMO.
The other three Shigella cases reported during the nine-day period were from Wadakkanchery, Arimbur and Adat.
The Shigella cluster comes amid a wider surge in fever cases in the district. As many as 4,914 people sought treatment for fever between October 1 and 9. During the period, 39 dengue cases and four cases of leptospirosis were also confirmed.
Dengue cases have been reported from several parts of the district, including Kodakara, Mattathur, Meloor, Thrissur Corporation, Avinissery, Chalakudy municipality, Kaiparamba, Kodassery, Pananchery, Puthukkad, Adat, Alur, Puthur, Mullurkara, Pariyaram, Tholur, Orumanayur, Thalikulam and Choondal.
Leptospirosis cases were reported from Pananchery, Pazhayannur, Porkulam and Kuzhur.
Dengue cases
The DMO said a significant number of dengue cases had been detected in migrant labour camps and among their contacts. “Most of the dengue cases have been reported from migrant labour camps and their contacts. We are keeping a close watch on them and monitoring the situation,” she said.
Health authorities have stepped up surveillance and preventive measures across the district. The DMO urged people with fever to take adequate rest, drink sufficient water and consume nutritious food, while vulnerable people, particularly those with compromised immunity, should take extra precautions and seek medical care when necessary.
With Shigella cases emerging in connection with a common gathering and dengue continuing to surface across multiple locations, health officials are keeping a close watch on possible further transmission and urging the public to maintain strict hygiene and food and water safety.

Regulator would quit over Man City interference
- Published
The head of English football's independent regulator says he will resign if he encounters any political interference over the future of Manchester City.
As chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan has the power to assess the suitability of club owners and executives.
If an independent commission's findings that the club broke Premier League financial rules are upheld, the watchdog would have to decide whether to force a sale.
Last month, the Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owners decided to sell up.
When asked about Burnham's comments, Kogan told BBC Sport: "The Prime Minister is entirely entitled to make his own observations on anything.
"We are independent. That is in the name. I am the chairman of the Independent Football Regulator and independence absolutely runs through everything we're doing.
"And no politician has tried to influence and would try to influence anything we do on that."
When asked what he would do if he did come under political pressure over the case, Kogan replied: "I would resign."
An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations. City insist they are innocent and have appealed.

  - Published3 hours ago
Kogan on next steps on Man City
The prime minister initially told the BBC of his concerns, before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".
However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process.
Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanded all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club are released. The government released these details on Monday.
"As far as we, as the regulator, are concerned, we have a very, very clear course of action that is governed by statute and we are going to follow that course of action and no comment by any politician or indeed any individual is going to affect what we do", said Kogan.
"Process is going to drive what we do. Process will lead us to a conclusion.
"We cannot reach any conclusion at this stage because we don't know the outcome of any appeal and once we do then we will act accordingly."
The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing - which could take months to convene - to decide the punishment.
City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving the club and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.
City's punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or being ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they won in the affected period.
Asked how crucial it is that it was resolved as soon as possible, Kogan said: "I think it's very important."
Kogan added that the case was "raising very serious issues if Manchester City on appeal is found to be guilty of the allegations within those findings".
"We are waiting like everybody else to see what the independent panel will do… and then we will bring in a view in terms of our own investigation and statutory powers if we need to do so.
"Our powers relate to individual owners, directors and senior executives. They refer to whether people are in a position to run a club in a way that is safe, coherent and done with probity, and we will be examining those things."
An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 that led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation.
The commission's report said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".
