Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music
If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
Writer Yiyun Li does not talk about "grief" or the "grieving process." To her, those words make it sound that at some point you emerge from grief. Instead, Li prefers to use the word "abyss," which, she says, is where she expects to be for the remainder of her life.
Li's teenage sons both died by suicide six years apart, Vincent in 2017 at age 16, and James in 2024 at age 19. Her Pulitzer Prize-winning 2025 memoir, Things in Nature Merely Grow, chronicled the loss of her sons and her effort to go on.
"James' death taught me to suffer better," she says. "To say, 'I can do it, and I can live with my pain and sorrow without ever wanting to stop feeling.'"
Li's new novel, Music Against the Night, is set in the late 1700s and early 1800s and centers on two prodigies who are brought together by music, and drawn apart because of their aspirations. The novel focuses on music, which sits outside of words.
"I think I've had the feeling both times after my children's death that words often fall short, and falling short doesn't mean not succeeding, falling short doesn't mean failing," she says. "But when I start a new project, I would like a subject [where] words naturally fall short. So music is that choice."
Li grew up in China and served a year in the Chinese military before coming to the U.S. to study immunology. She eventually left her Ph.D. program to become a writer. Li is now a professor in the creative writing program at Princeton University.
Interview highlights
On the decision to set Music Against the Night in a different time period
I was in the middle of the novel when James died. This is a novel far from my usual interests or concerns, and the reason I think I went back to history is I would like to live again through history, through historical figures, through my characters living in the late 18th and early 19th century. ... I'm making the past into a new now for myself and possibly for my readers.
On how playing piano connects to her grief
I began my piano lessons at the end of 2023, purely to get to know how to play the piano. And James died in February 2024, so two months into my piano lessons he died, and it occurred to me that piano or music is a good way for me to count time — because music is about time. It's about counting the measure, counting the rhythm. And also music is about ... be[ing] engaged with something else. You can sit in your sadness all day long, do nothing, or crying. Or, like me, I could just sit there and just play the same drill again, and again, as a way to know I was, in a way, staying in touch with the world. ...
I'm not a concert pianist, but somehow I find it liberating and healthy to do something that you absolutely love but cannot do well. Every time I go to my piano lesson, I'm so intimidated. I'm sweating because I just can't do it. I can hear other people do it, I cannot do it myself. But I think that's, again, acknowledging the limit of my capacity.
On raising two gifted children
Both my children could be called prodigies, but James, my younger son, especially was extraordinarily odd and brilliant. ... We were greatly baffled. I remember he was 5 or 6, he said, "Mommy, you will never see the world. I see it full of dots and squiggly lines." And that again was a strange perception of the world [that] we adults did not have access to. …
What is the responsibility or the difficulty of bringing up a child [who is] very brilliant? … Some people would say, well, you really have to train him to be the next Einstein, but we did not want him to be the next Einstein, we want him to be a normal, happy boy living in an ordinary life.
On her son Vincent
He was a brilliant painter and we still have all his paintings around the house. He was an oboist and when he wanted to learn the oboe, the oboe teacher said he was a bit young, because he was 8 when he want to learn oboe, but he was certain. ... [He had] started on the piano and he could articulate that piano was not his instrument. He wanted to play the oboe. But mostly, he wrote beautiful poetry. He was a great poet. And he was a greater reader. I wouldn't call him an outlier, as James was, but he was brilliant and fun and interesting.
On struggling with suicidal ideation
Sometimes I think people have all sort of thoughts about or against people who have chosen suicide, and people who've chosen or attempted suicide are often called selfish. But my experience is oftentimes people [are] in great pain, whether it's great mental pain or great physical pain. And sometimes people in deep depression cannot tell the difference between mental pain and physical pain, because everything together is a great kind of suffering. I think it's not that people who experience that kind of suicidal urge, it's not that they want to die or they want [to] use this to hurt other people.
On becoming a writer
I was born with innate curiosity and also sensitivity to things that did not quite make sense. So I grew up in China. And for instance, when I was little, all the adults would say, since you're a child, you have no right to decide who you want to be or what you want to do. And my mother even had a saying, something along the [lines] that an adult decides and the child follows. I was quite young, you know, 4 or 5. I just couldn't make sense of all of these teachings because I thought I was as capable of thinking as the adults, and why did I have to follow them? So I think that sort of sensitivity to things that are very, very nonsensical, I think maybe that's one thing that made me into a writer.

Duane “Keffe D” Davis, the former California gang leader convicted of murder for orchestrating the 1996 fatal shooting of rapper Tupac Shakur, has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.
“For three years, I’ve heard you say some variation of the same thing … ‘Yeah, I was involved in this. But I’m different. I’ve moved on. I got out of Compton. I’m a grandfather now,’” Judge Carli Kierny said Tuesday as she delivered the sentence.
“You don’t get to take a man from his family. You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it,” Kierny continued.
On 7 September 1996, Shakur was gunned down near the Las Vegas strip shortly after a Mike Tyson boxing match. He succumbed to his injuries days later.
For decades, his murder remained unsolved and one of hip-hop’s most enduring mysteries. Davis is the only person to be convicted in connection to Shakur’s murder.
“It was hard sitting, listening over and over and over again to someone describe – bit by bit, how they hunted Tupac Amaru Shakur down,” the rapper’s sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, said on Tuesday minutes before Davis was sentenced.
She described her brother as a father figure. “He was who God trusted to take care of me,” she told the court.
The grief from her brother’s murder led Sekyiwa Shakur to be hospitalized several times for depression, suicidal ideation and PTSD, she said.
She and the rapper’s stepbrother, Maurice Shakur, called for Davis to face the maximum penalty.
“Time to sit down and contemplate what you’ve done to the world, not just to me,” Sekyiwa Shakur said.
Davis stared intently, but appeared stoic as the relatives spoke. He vowed earlier during the hearing to appeal the case.
A confluence of several factors hindered the investigation. The code of silence within street culture made some witnesses averse to police cooperation. Las Vegas police were skeptical about leads from their Compton counterparts, given that the head of security for Shakur’s record label was a former Compton cop.
Orlando Anderson, a gangster and Davis’s nephew, was on law enforcement’s radar as the possible gunman. The night Shakur was killed, the young rap star got into an altercation with Anderson. Las Vegas police interviewed Anderson, but he was never arrested. Anderson later died in 1998.
But then, in 2023, Davis was arrested on a murder charge.
It was Davis’s own media tour, touting his status as one of the last surviving eyewitnesses, and a 2019 “tell-all” memoir that led to the breakthrough.
Davis had felt emboldened by a 2008 backdoor deal he brokered with police. He spoke candidly to investigators about Shakur’s shooting, who had actually been seeking information about the death of Christopher Wallace, known as Biggie Smalls or The Notorious BIG. Under a proffer agreement, Davis was not to face charges for any offenses he shared.
In his memoir, Compton Street Legend, Davis wrote that he and a group of other men targeted Shakur and his entourage, seeking retribution for the scuffle with his nephew.
The memoir and the interview became central to prosecutors’ case. They argued the details amounted to a confession and that his public remarks voided the proffer agreement.
During Davis’s murder trial, his defense team maintained that these details were embellished. They also argued, during the trial, that there was no physical evidence, such as a murder weapon, tying Davis to the Las Vegas slaying.
Ultimately, jurors sided with the state.

During my 10+ years of clinical experience in various States and with numerous patient populations, I have seen that dental anxiety is a constant challenge. I have seen this phenomenon in children clutching their parents’ hands before their first cleaning and in accomplished professionals quietly cancelling appointment after appointment in the hope that the problem will somehow resolve itself.
It doesn’t.
In my experience, the longer you leave a fear unchecked, the greater the clinical and human cost becomes. Dental anxiety is not a moral failing. This is a well-documented psychological response—and one with important, measurable public health consequences.
How severe is it?
Roughly a third of people have significant dental anxiety, and roughly a tenth have a clinical phobia. That’s not a little footnote. That means a lot of the population is actively avoiding or delaying care that could prevent serious disease. The downstream consequences of this avoidance are visible daily in my clinical work: infections tolerated for months, decay advanced far beyond what early intervention would have required, and patients presenting with pain that could have been prevented years ago.
Knowing where it starts
Dental anxiety typically has a definite source. A painful or poorly done procedure in childhood can be a source of dental anxiety. A provider who was in a hurry or didn’t tell the patient what was happening. The specific sensory environment of a dental office—the sounds, the smells, and the physical vulnerability of lying back with your mouth open—can leave powerful imprints, especially in young patients. That memory is not just wiped out; it impacts behaviour for decades. For some, it’s not just one event but an accumulation. Years of avoidance layered on top of embarrassment about how their teeth look now, and a fear of judgment prevents them from asking for help. This cycle of shame avoidance is one of the hardest patterns I see clinically. When these patients do come in, they need much more intervention than if they had come in sooner, and this becomes an instance of the very fear that kept them away.
The health price of avoidance
Research literature teaches us, that oral health is not an island. Untreated dental disease is a chronic inflammatory load on the body. It has been linked to cardiovascular risk, dysregulated blood sugar, and impaired immune function. When a patient avoids dental care for years, it is not just their smile that is at risk; they are carrying a preventable health load that will rise elsewhere in time.
In addition to the system effects, the impact on quality of life is immediate and real. A toothache interferes with sleep. It impacts nutrition, concentration, and the ability to speak with confidence. These are not trivial consequences; they affect how people show up in their professional and personal lives every day.
What works in practice
The most significant change I’ve made in my practice is making communication a priority before any procedure begins. When patients feel informed and in control, it greatly reduces their dental anxiety. A stop signal—a raised hand that stops everything instantly—can alter the psychological dynamic in the room. It shifts the patient from passive recipient to active participant, and that shift matters enormously. I also allow extra time for anxious patients. The problem is not that procedures take longer, but that rushing them increases anxiety. I explain everything before it happens, check in frequently, and never minimise what a patient is feeling. These should not be luxury accommodations; they should be routine parts of effective care.
For patients with more severe anxiety, pharmacological support is appropriate. Nitrous oxide is safe, effective, and rapidly reversible. There are also oral sedation choices if needed. These are clinical tools, not last resorts, and patients should feel comfortable asking about them.
A message to patients
If fear has kept you from the dentist, remember you are not alone, and you are not too far gone to be helped. What I ask of patients in this situation is one small step—not a treatment plan, not a procedure, simply a conversation. Come in and tell us about your nervousness. A good provider is a good listener and will start there. There is no need to be afraid of the dental chair. With the right approach, it can be a place where you take difficult things and make them manageable—and where the relief on the other side is worth it.
(Dr. Sowjanya Gunukula is a U.S.-licensed dentist with international training who focuses on preventive and evidence-based oral healthcare and contributes to advancing community and public health dentistry. sowji.gunukula@gmail.com)

East Bengal FC let a promising start slip through its fingers as it squandered a twice-earned lead before going down 2-3 against Iraqi side Al-Shorta in its second Group D outing of the AFC Champions League Two at the Salt Lake Stadium here on Tuesday.
David Lalhansanga Hmar struck twice in a lively first half to put the host in the driving seat, but Al-Shorta hit back with two quick goals after the break to turn the contest on its head. Despite being reduced to 10 men in the 76th minute, the visitors held firm to leave East Bengal ruing a string of missed chances.
David opened the scoring in the seventh minute with a superb piece of opportunism. The East Bengal forward brought down Hardik Bhatt’s centre while shielding an Al-Shorta defender, swivelled sharply and fired home with a clinical left-footed finish.
The East Bengal lead lasted only seven minutes as Ahmed Yahya rose to meet a corner in the 14th minute and headed home to restore parity. East Bengal had less of the ball but looked dangerous on the counter attacks, troubling the Iraqi side with its direct attacking play. The host registered 10 shots, of which seven were on target, while Al-Shorta managed just one effort on target in the first half.
East Bengal vs Al Shorta - As it happened
The Red and Gold brigade reclaimed the lead four minutes before the break. Daniel Ramirez’s free-kick was parried by goalkeeper Jalal Hassan, but Basim Rashid kept the move alive near the goal line with a clever back-heel. David was on hand to finish from close range, completing his brace and sending the home crowd into celebration.
David had two more opportunities before half-time to complete a hat-trick, but failed to convert either. Those misses would come back to haunt East Bengal after the break.
Al-Shorta emerged with renewed purpose after the restart and levelled the scores through Hussein Al-Saedi in the 51st minute before Kingsley Kuku struck again two minutes later, heading home a corner delivered by Argentine substitute Cristian Barco.
Suddenly, East Bengal was chasing the game. The host came agonisingly close to restoring parity in the 66th minute but Hassan came in the way again as he first saved Ramirez’s effort from inside the box and reacted swiftly to deny Edmund Lalrindika on the rebound. The goalkeeper’s double intervention proved crucial as Al-Shorta clung to the slender advantage.
The visitor was reduced to 10 men in the 76th minute when defender Abdoul Magid Boubacar was sent off after receiving his second yellow card. Gaining the numerical advantage, East Bengal threw men forward in search of an equaliser. However, Al-Shorta’s defence stood its ground, frustrating the home side until the final whistle.

I'm petite, have a small frame, and have never had to struggle with weight issues. 
I regularly went to the gym six days a week, and have done so for years taking a combination of strength training and boot camp-style classes in addition to walking. Despite my efforts, I started adding on weight — just over 10 pounds in about 24 months.
I didn't know why or what to do about about the weight gain. I was working out almost every day, but I felt exhausted and defeated. Others suggested I turn to medication. "Don't stress, just get on a GLP-1, and if your doctor won't give it to you, just grab it online," one friend told me.
My BMI wasn't high enough for my doctor to prescribe medication, and I didn't want to override my provider's advice. But despite all of my effort, I wasn't seeing the results I wanted.
I was bored at the gym
Then, during a gym class, I realized I had become lazy. I was picking up the easiest weights and would go through the motions, never pushing myself too hard during workouts. The repetitive movements were just so boring.
After that class, I tried to think of an activity that might bring me more joy. Wasn't there something else that could be more fun? That's when I decided to take more dance classes, instead of just the one I was already taking on Saturdays.
I was hesitant to dance like I used to years ago
I was a danced into high school, but I had to leave the program because of difficulties at home.
I always felt sadness and disappointment about quitting. I had continued dancing on and off as an adult, but I had never really returned to it in a meaningful way. I thought about how much I loved to dance as a little girl, grinning ear to ear even when I forgot all the steps. Research has shown that the surprising benefits of dance extend beyond physical fitness.
Now I take four to five dance classes a week, a combination of modern, and West African.
It's fun and doesn't feel like the same drag that the gym was to me. And I finally lost those stubborn pounds I had gained. When I take classes every week, I mix up levels to keep challenging myself and track my progress. Dance has also given me a community where we hold one another accountable and empower one another as we cheer one another on.
More on workout routines
Dance was the true exercise I really needed
Returning to dance has helped me shed those few extra pounds, but it has also helped me connect to a part of me that is more accepting of myself and others. I'm happier and healthier than I've been in years, and no longer associate something I love with failure. 
I've learned that the workout that keeps me coming back is the one I enjoy, and it's never too late to try again.

Mariam recently disabled Facebook Messenger. As the administrator of a Facebook group for women in the United Arab Emirates with close to 400,000 members, she’d become accustomed to receiving messages from strangers. But then came a shift in the volume—and nature—of those messages until they were impossible to ignore.
“Being the admin of this group has subjected me to all kinds of harassment,” says Miriam, who asked to be identified only by her first name because she fears online retaliation. They “either want to advise you to be holy and cover up, or they want to sexually harass you—or both.”
Mariam has run the group for more than a year. And even though intended for women, the group’s size and visibility has meant that Miriam also gets a lot of messages from men. She has received a deluge of unsolicited messages telling her how to dress, not to raise her voice or wear makeup, and to cover her hands with gloves so that no skin is visible.
“I couldn’t take it any longer. It was starting to affect my mental well-being,” Miriam says.
Many women who are conspicuous on the internet have been harassed online. That comes in countless forms, even if the same misogyny underlies it. The particular variety Miriam was subjected to stems from a section of the “manosphere” dressed in the clothes of religion—the Muslim manosphere.
At its core, the manosphere is built around male grievance and antifeminist ideology—though whether that’s entirely organic or engineered to sell supplements and other products is up for debate. Regardless, it has no shortage of subcultures to chose from: Incels, pick-up artists, men’s rights activists, and followers of the Red Pill.
Some nuances may make these groups distinct, but they largely share a common worldview: Feminism has destabilized society, women have acquired too much power, and men must reassert control. And the Muslim manosphere is no different. It’s adopted those ideas circulating through the wider manosphere and rebranded them in the language of faith.
Sarah Kaddoura, a feminist researcher and creator of the YouTube channel Haki Nasawi, examined the Arabic-speaking manosphere in a 2025 report. In her study, she describes some of the most prominent influencers, such as Jordanian relationship coach Kareem Atta’i, who posts online as Coach Kareem or Red Pill Arabic.
Atta’i packages his ideas as relationship advice, but his videos frequently frame interactions between men and women as contests for power. Atta’i’s videos, which WIRED Middle East has watched, describe violence as a means of “disciplining” women or retaliating against sexual rejection.
The Arabic manosphere does more than translate Western Red Pill content. Its creators have adapted the ideology to local anxieties around religion, masculinity, marriage, money, and social change.
Kaddoura says influencers use financial insecurity, political instability, religious identity, and fears about declining morality or social cohesion to build their audiences. Misogyny becomes an explanation for a much wider sense of frustration—and women become its most visible target.
The problem is not religious expression online but the use of religious authority—real or claimed—to legitimize misogyny, harassment, and the public surveillance of women. The Muslim manosphere is also not confined to the Arab world. Like the broader manosphere, it crosses borders, languages, and platforms.
Take prominent UK-based creator Ali Dawah, whose channel features street debates and commentary about relationships, gender roles, religion, and Western culture. In one clip, Dawah says he hates Muslim feminists “the most.” In another video, he approaches women in public and challenges them over clothing he describes as immodest.
“Dawah” is not just this YouTuber’s name. In Arabic, it means to make an invitation to someone to learn about Islam. Ali is just one of many influencers often called “Dawah Bros,” and they’re generally known for being more aggressive than offering an invitation when it comes to promoting their manosphere-esque content.
Kaddoura sees the Dawah Bros as a platform-native successor to an older variety of media figure. During the 1990s, Islamic television programs in Egypt and Saudi Arabia regularly featured sheikhs answering callers’ questions about relationships, clothing, and acceptable behavior. However, unlike television preachers, today’s influencers are not limited to scheduled broadcasts, and they aren’t only interacting with people who’ve chosen to call in.
For many Muslim women—especially those who are in prominent places on the internet—these ideas do not remain confined to podcasts or debate videos. They spill into comment sections and private messages, where strangers appoint themselves enforcers of morality.
A 2026 report by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue analyzed nearly 14,000 comments directed at 40 prominent public figures and influencers on Instagram in Jordan over a 12-month period. Among comments classified as hate speech, harassment, or abusive language, 72 percent targeted women, 11 percent were classified as religious or moral harassment, and the vast majority of those comments—85 percent—targeted female influencers.
Additionally, all of the comments classified as sexual harassment were directed at women, underlining the pervasive contradictions in how women are policed on the internet—the same online environment that instructing women to make themselves invisible also subjecting them to unwanted sexual attention. That contradiction is visible in the messages Mariam has received.
The manosphere’s reach is shaped in part by the recommendation systems that determine what users encounter in their feeds. “As soon as you create an account on TikTok, YouTube, X, Instagram, and others as a male, it doesn’t take long for the algorithm to start recommending misogynistic content,” Kaddoura says.
Engagement-based systems can amplify emotionally charged and polarizing content, including manosphere videos. Content blaming women for men’s loneliness or financial insecurity can generate reactions from supporters, critics, and the women being targeted. Those interactions may increase its visibility.
That becomes even thornier when religion enters the picture. The relationship coaches and other men preaching religion online often present personal opinions as religious instruction, Kaddoura says. This can make disagreement appear immoral, and criticism can then be presented as evidence that the creator is defending the faith against hostile forces.
But how exactly a user’s behavior tips over from passively encountering the content to actively engaging with it remains an open question. Researchers can examine publicly available videos and identify influential accounts, but they have limited access to the internal data needed to trace how users move between creators and communities. This leave key questions unanswered, such as whether prolonged exposure changes their behavior.
For women such as Mariam, the technical route behind the harassment may be invisible, but its effects are not. A creator publishes a video. Recommendation systems carry it into other users’ feeds. And then, eventually, users repeat its message in women’s comment sections and inboxes. Repeat ad infinitum.
WIRED Middle East contacted Ali Dawah and Kareem Atta’i for comment. Neither responded by the time of publication.

Srinagar, Oct 13: Kashmir turned colder on Tuesday as a fresh Western Disturbance brought rain to the plains and snowfall to higher reaches, with temperatures dipping further and a wet spell forecast to continue until October 15.
Rain began in parts of North Kashmir late Tuesday afternoon before extending to Central Kashmir by evening.
The Meteorological Department said rainfall activity was likely to intensify in South Kashmir in the coming hours.
Higher reaches, including Afarwat in Gulmarg, Razdan Pass and Tulail in Gurez valley of Bandipora district, Sadhna Top in Kupwara, and Minamarg, Zero Point and Zojila Pass near Sonamarg, witnessed light snowfall, a MeT official said.
Snowfall was also reported from Sinthan Top, Margan Top, and Pir Ki Gali in south Kashmir as well as the PirPanjal range.
The weather shift comes after a relatively warm start to October, with daytime temperatures now falling across Kashmir, the Chenab Valley and the PirPanjal region.
The gloomy conditions and growing chill have prompted people to bring out woollens.
Srinagar recorded a maximum temperature of 20 degrees Celsius on Monday, 2.8 degrees below normal and the lowest maximum temperature in the city so far this month.
Pahalgam recorded a maximum of 14.2 degrees Celsius, 5.4 degrees below normal, while Gulmarg settled at 11.8 degrees, 1.9 degrees below normal. Qazigund recorded 22.2 degrees Celsius, 0.8 degrees below normal, while Kokernag registered 20.4 degrees, within the normal range.
Kupwara recorded 20.4 degrees Celsius, 3.4 degrees below normal.
Cloud cover kept night temperatures relatively high. Srinagar recorded a minimum of 11.2 degrees Celsius, 4.9 degrees above normal.
The minimum temperatures were 9.4 degrees in Qazigund, 10.4 degrees in Kokernag, 8.6 degrees in Kupwara, 6.8 degrees in Pahalgam and 5.4 degrees Celsius in Gulmarg.
In Jammu division, Jammu city recorded a maximum temperature of 30.5 degrees Celsius. Banihal recorded 19.5 degrees, Batote 22.1, Katra 26.6 and Bhadwewah 21 degrees Celsius, all below normal.
Wet spell to continue till October 15
The Meteorological Department has forecast light to moderate rainfall across Kashmir from October 13 to 15, with isolated places likely to receive heavy rain on October 14 and 15.
Higher reaches may receive further snowfall during the three-day period, particularly in Gulmarg, Gurez and parts of the PirPanjal range.
However, the department said there was no indication of very heavy snowfall.
Minimum temperatures are likely to remain near current levels during the wet spell, while maximum temperatures could fall by another one to two degrees Celsius, the official said.
After October 15, weather conditions are expected to remain largely dry.
Minimum temperatures may fall again, while maximum temperatures could rise slightly, he said.
Farmers advised caution
The Meteorological Department has advised farmers to exercise caution while carrying out agricultural activities during the wet spell, particularly paddy harvesting.
“Farmers should exercise some caution with harvesting activities currently under way during these three days. After that, they can resume their work properly,” the official said.
The department said the forecast did not indicate conditions likely to cause major road disruptions or landslides.
However, travellers have been advised to wear adequate warm clothing as temperatures continue to fall.

Creating question papers at the last-minute can curb incentive to leak, says Nadan Nilekani
Nandan Nilekani also suggested expanding the computer-based testing (CBT) infrastructure across the country.
Generating examination papers at the last minute from a “massive question bank” will eliminate the “economic incentive” behind paper leaks, Infosys chairman and head of the high-powered task force (HPTF) on examination reforms Nandan Nilekani said on Tuesday. He also suggested expanding the computer-based testing (CBT) infrastructure across the country.
“The moment you have a question paper then that creates an economic incentive for that to be sold. So the way to do that is to really have a massive bank of questions and only at the last minute generate the question paper for that day and therefore then the question of having a question paper goes away and there is no economic incentive for that,” he said while addressing the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi.
Also Read I Government, NTA officials may not be named in CBI charge sheet over NEET-UG paper leak
To be sure, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), in its first charge sheet filed in a Delhi court in May in the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak case, said question papers for the May 3 examination were sold and purchased by the accused for amounts ranging from ₹25,000 to ₹25 lakh.
Six-member task force
Nilekani added that expanding the network of testing locations was another priority. “We have 150,000 locations (of CBT centres) where a young boy or girl can take a test that needs to be expanded. So I think these are all systemic issues, which we will address in our committee,” he said.
When asked if he could envision a future where AI spontaneously creates examination papers on the actual day of the test, Nilekani responded with affirmation. He further said that using technology and looking at the root causes of exam leaks and irregularities systematically could solve the problem. “They are solvable issues.”
The government-appointed six-member HPTF, constituted on July 27 with a three-month mandate, was set up after the cancellation of NEET-UG 2026 on May 12 by National Testing Agency (NTA). At least 120 questions in a guess paper — a compilation of suggested questions based on previous trends and patterns — were found to match the May 3 examination paper, triggering widespread protests and eventually the resignation of then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan on July 25.
An October 5 affidavit filed by the Department of Personnel and Training in the Supreme Court said the panel had held about 18 meetings and more than 40 consultations including one with Union health ministry on whose behalf NTA conducts the test for admission to UG medical courses, and remained “on track” to submit its report within the prescribed timeframe.
The debate over shifting NEET-UG from pen-and-paper testing (PPT) to CBT has, however, exposed significant infrastructure and policy hurdles.
Also Read I 'Why do we need a question paper': Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani on ways to combat exam leaks in India
More than 2.2 million candidates registered for the 2026 examination currently held in pen and paper mode, requiring question papers to be printed, packed, transported under security, stored in vaults and distributed to examination centres. The lengthy supply chain, involving printers, transporters, storage facilities, centre coordinators and invigilators, creates multiple potential vulnerabilities for paper leak.
In CBT, encrypted questions are electronically distributed to examination infrastructure under strict access controls, reducing dependence on physical transportation. The format is already used for JEE-Main, CUET and UGC-NET.

Kipchoge, 41, breaks course record at Melbourne Marathon
- Published
Two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge says "his body is still peaking" after winning the Melbourne Marathon in a course record time at the age of 41.
The Kenyan crossed the line in two hours nine minutes 10 seconds for his 17th career win over the distance and first since the Berlin Marathon in 2023.
"I believe that my body is still peaking - still able to compete with the next generation," Kipchoge said.
"The oldest athlete is still competing but I am happy to run with the Gen Zs."
The course was partly raced along the Australian Formula One track at Albert Park and finished inside the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).
"On the course, it was really wonderful, I enjoyed seeing people standing, cheering, and shouting my name," added Kipchoge, who slowed down inside the MCG to wave to the fans.
"It was actually different - running on a beautiful course, but also running on the Formula One track, and above all else, finishing on a cricket ground.
"It makes me proud to run with the younger generation and inspire the running community in Melbourne."
Australian Thomas do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35, with compatriot Reece Edwards third.
New Zealand's Camille French won the women's race in 2:28:25, followed by Australian Sinead Diver and Nichola Sheridan of Ireland.
The Melbourne Marathon was the third leg on Kipchoge's world tour, on which he hopes to complete a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica, over two years.
Each marathon will raise funds for the Eliud Kipchoge Foundation, which focuses on education, environmental sustainability and health.
Kipchoge is considered one of the greatest long-distance runners of all time, winning two Olympic marathon golds, plus a silver and bronze over 5000m.
His honours also include a world title, 12 World Marathon Major victories and two official world records.
In 2019 he became the first person to break the two-hour marathon barrier under special conditions in Vienna, clocking an unofficial time of one hour 59 minutes 40 seconds.

Even as the Centre informed the Supreme Court on Monday (October 12, 2026) that it had decided to cap trade margins at 30% for non-scheduled cancer drugs, the court questioned why the benefit of such price regulation should be confined to cancer drugs and not extended to other essential medicines and medical products.
The development comes after a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta expressed concern over stark disparities between the price to retailer (PTR) and the maximum retail price (MRP) of certain medicines, particularly cancer drugs, with mark-ups in some instances soaring to 1,000%. The Bench had flagged that such exorbitant mark-ups constituted “broad daylight dacoity” and placed an enormous financial burden on patients.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre, informed the Bench that the proposed 30% trade-margin cap would cover both patented and non-patented cancer medicines, with an expert committee headed by the Director General of Health Services tasked with identifying the drugs to be brought within its ambit. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) will examine the committee’s recommendations before issuing a price notification to implement the cap.
The Bench, however, said that while the intervention was commendable, it was inadequate, and questioned why other medicines and medical devices could not also be brought within the 16% retailer margin prescribed under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013.
“This is just the tip of the iceberg... this has come around only because of the unduly hard observations we made during earlier hearings. What about other drugs,” the Bench asked.
The top court was hearing petitions filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha seeking stricter enforcement of price controls under the DPCO to curb disproportionate margins across the pharmaceutical supply chain.
Justice Mehta drew attention to steep markups on medical devices and consumables, pointing out that an India-made cardiac stent costing around ₹5,000 was being sold by hospitals for more than ₹25,000. He cited the example of a saline drip line carrying an MRP of ₹11 being sold for ₹270.
“We understand that there are transportation costs, raw material costs, R&D costs and other ancillary costs, but all these are included in the MRP. What is the logic behind allowing them to sell at 400 times the actual cost? How can you allow this? What is the benefit for the patients?” the Bench observed.
‘Balance in pricing’
Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, also appearing for the Centre, cautioned against a uniform cap across medicines, arguing that low-value products often required higher margins to remain commercially viable for retailers. Excessive regulation, she said, could discourage retailers from stocking such medicines and affect their availability, particularly in rural areas.
Ms. Bhati stressed the need to preserve some room for market forces rather than subject the entire pharmaceutical sector to price controls.
“Higher margins in such cases are important for ensuring the availability of such medicines to consumers… Our concern is that there has to be a balance in pricing. There has to be some level of market play available for drugs. We do not want to control the entire ecosystem of drugs. The policy was framed with the outlook that there should be intervention only when necessary,” she submitted.
The Bench, however, was not persuaded, observing that ensuring the availability of price-controlled medicines was the government’s responsibility.
“If the DPCO -approved medicines do not reach customers, then it is the duty of the government to ensure it reaches [sic] the patient. The actual dispute is over which medicines should be on the DPCO-controlled list and which should not,” Justice Mehta observed.
Accordingly, the Bench gave the Centre until October 27 to work out the modalities for capping medicine prices, when the matter will be heard next.
Centre’s affidavit
The Centre, in its 551-page affidavit, said the proposed trade-margin rationalisation (TMR) was expected to reduce the MRP of anti-cancer drugs by 20% to 70%, translating into estimated annual savings of around ₹2,500 crore. It said the measure would reduce patients’ out-of-pocket expenditure and improve the affordability and accessibility of cancer medicines, while retaining a 30% trade margin for the distribution chain.
The Centre cited a similar intervention by the NPPA in 2019, when a 30% trade-margin cap was imposed at the first point of sale on 42 select non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines. The margin was based on an industry-practice assumption of 10% for distributors and 20% for retailers.
The measure, it said, led to a substantial reduction in the MRP of 526 brands and annual savings of around ₹984 crore for patients, based on information furnished by pharmaceutical companies. The Centre said the 2019 exercise provided a policy and operational precedent for extending trade-margin rationalisation to a wider range of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines.
Detailing the existing price-control mechanism, the Centre said the ceiling price of medicines listed in Schedule I of the DPCO is determined by taking the simple average of the price to retailer of brands and generic versions with a market share of at least 1%, and adding a 16% margin.
“The ceiling price so fixed becomes the MRP, i.e., the price above which the drug cannot be sold in the market. However, the manufacturer is at liberty to give an appropriate margin to the wholesaler and the retailer within the ceiling price,” it said, adding that ceiling prices had so far been fixed for 935 formulations.
For non-scheduled formulations, manufacturers are free to determine the initial launch price, subject to the NPPA’s regulation of subsequent price increases. The Centre said competition in the pharmaceutical market generally acted as a restraint against arbitrary pricing.

For the first time in medical and legal history, a prisoner has “survived a complete execution attempt in the U.S.” According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Christa Pike’s failed execution was “the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era (since 1976). There is no precedent.” This game-changing bioethics case may even end lethal injection.
About 7,000 people were executed in the U.S. between 1900 and 1976, and 1,683 people after 1976. Ultimately, since 1900, only 0.6% (55) have been women. Pike is now the second woman on death row the U.S. Supreme Court declined to rescue from a botched execution.
On June 18, 1953, the controversial case of accused spy Ethel Rosenberg, who had two small children, also came before the Supreme Court. It overturned her stay of execution. The following day, on June 19, 1953, the electric chair execution of Rosenberg failed; the settings were not properly adjusted for a woman of Rosenberg’s size, and she did not die after the first round of electrocution.
A doctor examined her and informed the state she was not dead and that they needed to electrocute her a second time. The report from United Press International and The New York Times described the debacle and the role of two physicians involved who “ordered” more electrocution. According to Rosenberg’s biographer, “she was removed from the electric chair after three charges, only for it to be discovered her heart was still beating, so, gruesomely, she had to be strapped back into it.”
Nineteen years later, in 1972, after five more women were executed without incident in the U.S., the Supreme Court of California ruled the death penalty unconstitutional in People v. Anderson, which led to the commutation of all California death sentences to life sentences. This included three of the women involved in the brutal Manson murders — Susan Atkins, Patricia Krenwinkel, and Leslie Van Houten — all scheduled to be gassed. That same year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that capital punishment violated the Eighth Amendment in Furman v. Georgia.
In response to the Furman ruling, states began to explore more humane methods of execution, which is what led to the current lethal injection protocol, originally pioneered by Oklahoma’s state medical examiner at the time, Jay Chapman in 1977, and later adapted by Jack Kevorkian as a method of “medicide” — an early version of what we now call medical assistance in dying.
In 1976, the U.S. Supreme Court sanctioned state executions again in Gregg v. Georgia because it saw lethal injection as a “sanitized, quasi-clinical procedure” upholding the Eighth Amendment. Lethal injection became the norm when executions restarted in 1977; Ronald Reagan compared it to putting an animal to sleep. On June 11, 2001, Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh was executed using the Chapman protocol. It was even broadcast on a closed-circuit system to survivors and affected families.
But over time, due to a variety of systems issues with obtaining certain medications, the lethal injection protocol has deviated from the standard devised by Chapman.
More importantly, since the lethal injection protocol requires an intravenous line insertion, the person administering it has to be competent in IV infusion. But the people facing execution often have veins that are tricky to access. A disturbing report in 2022 found that more than a third of executions are “botched” because of unskilled personnel.
Since the American Medical Association and the American Nurses Association state that it is unethical for medical providers to participate in any way in executions, state prisons struggle to find skilled personnel to handle lethal injection, resulting in many failed attempts. The case of Lee Hamm, another failed attempt at lethal injection, raised numerous questions about the role of health care providers after a botched procedure.
Just prior to Pike’s planned execution, NPR reported that the opaque Tennessee protocol does involve health care providers, and some are willing to cross ethical lines. Physician Mark Fowler, for instance, was involved in the failed execution case of Tony Carruthers in May.
But the Carruthers case created a bioethics chasm where “dozens of Tennessee medical professionals told the governor that health care professionals shouldn’t help with executions, ever. No matter the method.” Fowler reportedly was involved in Pike’s failed execution as well.
The majority of health care providers maintain either the American Medical Association’s code of ethics or the American Nurses Association’s position. A recent Hastings Center Bioethics Forum essay concludes that lethal injection is unethical, while other bioethicists have suggested that the presence of a health care provider would not only be “lending the prestige of medicine to the execution” but also provide the false impression that lethal injection was being supervised by doctors, and therefore more acceptable.
The Pike case is novel not only because it’s the first time in legal history a prisoner has survived a completed execution procedure resulting in dizzying legal repercussions, but because of the “hot mess” clinical ethics case that has emerged.
When Pike remained alive after the failed procedure, she was rushed to the hospital for lifesaving treatment. What were the “goals of care”? To make her medically stable enough for another attempt at execution? (Tennessee’s Prison Commissioner resigned, and the state has paused executions for the remainder of the year, but not indefinitely.) Per national and local news reports on Oct. 7, Pike initially remained intubated and unconscious as her health care team planned to remove life support in the belief that Pike was progressing to brain death. Pike also remained in restraints (handcuffed and shackled to her bed), which complicated her care.
But then she awoke and spoke, raising new questions about her neurological status. Pike first inquired: “Where am I and who are you?” Her attorneys state: “There is still a lot of cognitive confusion. … She is very aware that the state tried to execute. … She is very aware up to a point.”
Any clinical ethicist would advise at this juncture that Pike may fully regain decision-making capacity and is already showing signs of understanding and appreciation. Patients who are inmates and have decision-making capacity can make all medical decisions, including end of life decisions, but the correctional institution may limit options based on costs. In general, correctional officers should not be involved with inmates’ medical decisions, but health care providers do not have the authority to remove restraints; such decisions reside with the correctional facility.
Bioethicists have been actively debating this case, with consensus that if Pike were deemed to be incapacitated, a court-appointed surrogate decision-maker (someone who makes decisions in the best medical interests of a patient who does not have autonomy) would be necessary since the state — even Tennessee’s Adult Protective Services — would have a conflict of interest. Pike’s biological family has provided insight into her childhood that would also raise questions about authentic surrogacy. Because of Ford v. Wainwright, incapacitated prisoners cannot be executed, so if Pike regains capacity, the legal road is unclear.
As of this writing, it’s impossible to predict Pike’s ultimate prognosis or fate, but the legal and medical issues in the Pike case are on a collision course. Pre-Pike, lethal injection was “passing” as a “death with dignity” medical assistance in dying procedure, which, ironically, is illegal in several death penalty states, including Tennessee. Post-Pike, lethal injection will never be the same. Its procedural flaws have been exposed; it’s the emperor with no clothes because it only “pretends to be medicine.” Of course, there are other forms of execution that actually look like one instead of medicine, as in the case of the planned execution by firing squad of the Fort Hood shooter, which may even be streamed live.
For states that want to continue lethal injection, medical expertise at various points in the process — whether it’s training prison staff, providing medical opinions on “candidacy” for lethal injection, or actually participating — will likely become a requirement that most health care providers will find ethically incompatible with clinical ethics principles of practice. If medical expertise becomes a legal requirement for lethal injection, but no reputable health care provider will participate, then the stigma of participation may effectively end lethal injection as we know it.
M. Sara Rosenthal, Ph.D., is professor and founding director of the University of Kentucky Program for Bioethics and Oncology Ethics Program and chair of the UK HealthCare Ethics Committee.

The Africa Cup of Nations could continue to be held every two years, with discussions under way to reverse its proposed switch to a four-year cycle.

Why is everyone saying 'I Am Jane Doe' – and why should you care?
When internet users tried to uncover the identity of a woman accusing seven Cornell University students of sexual assault, social media users responded with “I Am Jane Doe”. The movement has become a viral stand against victim-blaming, with a message that resonates in Singapore too.
What are we talking about? The I Am Jane Doe movement.
Who's Jane Doe? Jane Doe is a pseudonym commonly used to protect the identity of women in legal cases, including victims of sexual assault.
It sounds familiar. A 2017 documentary titled I Am Jane Doe followed a group of American mothers seeking justice for their teenage daughters who were trafficked for commercial sex through the now-defunct classifieds website Backpage.com.
So who does this Jane Doe refer to? She is the woman who has accused seven men of sexually assaulting her in 2024, when she was an undergraduate at Cornell University, an Ivy League institution in the United States.
The men were members of the university's Chi Phi fraternity. According to her lawsuit, she was pressured into taking drugs and sexually assaulted while incapacitated.
In September 2026, the former Cornell student filed a civil lawsuit against the seven men, Cornell University, the Chi Phi fraternity and other parties. The allegations have not been proven in court, and no criminal charges have been filed against the seven men – dubbed the Cornell 7 – as of writing. The criminal investigation was reopened in September.
How did the I Am Jane Doe movement start? Disturbingly, some internet users tried to uncover the victim’s identity. Their efforts led to several women being wrongly identified as Jane Doe, and harassed and threatened as a result.
In response, people – mostly women – began declaring “I Am Jane Doe” across social media. Some men joined in too.
Beyond expressing solidarity with the victim, the movement sought to protect Jane Doe’s anonymity by flooding social media with posts, making it harder for those attempting to identify her through online searches.
Some participants also shared their own experiences of sexual assault and harassment in various spaces, including on school campuses and at home.
But this happened in America. What does it have to do with Singapore? Quite a lot, actually. Sexual violence, harassment and the attitudes that excuse them are not uniquely American problems. Singapore has its own uncomfortable history of such incidents.
Like what? Remember the notorious SG Nasi Lemak Telegram group, which had more than 40,000 members and was used to circulate obscene images and videos of girls and women?
Or the Singapore Sports School case in 2024, when police investigated students creating and circulating deepfake nude images of their female schoolmates?
There were also voyeurism cases involving university students, including the National University of Singapore scandal that prompted a review of the university's disciplinary procedures, and several female private-hire drivers who experienced sexual harassment.
These are different offences with different circumstances. But they touch on similar issues around consent, privacy and the sexual objectification of women and girls – as well as how institutions and communities respond when boundaries are violated.
Why do people still excuse or minimise sexual violence? One explanation is what advocates call rape culture – attitudes and behaviour that normalise, trivialise or excuse sexual violence, or shift responsibility onto the victims.
It can appear in familiar questions and remarks: What was she wearing? Was she leading him on? Why was she out so late? Why was she drinking? Why didn't she fight back? Why did she take so long to report the assault? Surely he didn't mean any harm? Do we really need to ruin his future over one mistake?
The conversation shifts from examining the alleged wrongdoing to questioning whether the person reporting it behaved appropriately.
And these attitudes aren't merely hypothetical. Singapore women's rights organisation AWARE has repeatedly highlighted how such misconceptions, also known as rape myths, can discourage survivors from seeking help or reporting sexual assault.
According to AWARE, only three in 10 clients who approached its Sexual Assault Care Centre between 2018 and 2021 had made a police report.
What happens when the hashtag stops trending? Well, the internet will probably find something else to talk about. But the questions raised by the movement remain: Why does the person reporting an alleged sexual assault sometimes end up facing as much scrutiny as the allegation itself?
What can I do if I know someone who has experienced sexual violence? Listen, respect their privacy and avoid pressuring them to disclose details or take steps they're not ready for.
In Singapore, AWARE's Sexual Assault Care Centre provides support and information to survivors of any gender. The National Anti-Violence and Sexual Harassment Helpline is another avenue for help. SG Her Empowerment (SHE) also has a helpline to support victims of sexual deepfakes and other forms of digital harassment.

The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals.
Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.
The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.
Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs. Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.
The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.
Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China.
On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.
“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.
Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.
Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”
Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.
Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.
The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.
On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

Women account for 43% of the workforce in India’s Ayush services sector, with their representation crossing 50% in several organised segments, including hospitals, day-care centres, educational institutions and wellness establishments, according to a new assessment of the sector released by the Central government on Thursday (October 8, 2026).
The Ayush Services Sector Report, prepared by the Research and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) and released on Ayurveda Day 2026, estimates that the sector supports 1.76 million livelihoods across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services.
Women’s representation is highest in spas and wellness resorts, where it exceeds 60%, followed by educational institutions at 58%, day-care centres at 57% and hospitals at 53%, says the report.
The findings come as the Ayush services economy expands beyond traditional clinical practice into wellness, education, preventive health and medical value travel.
16.91% growth
The sector, comprising Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy, was estimated at $36.92 billion in 2024-25. It has registered a compound annual growth rate of 16.91% since 2022-23.
Standalone clinics remain the largest segment, generating an estimated $16.21 billion, or 43.9% of the sector’s revenue. Day-care centres contribute another $10.13 billion. Together, the two segments account for more than 70% of the sector’s revenue.
“More than one million livelihoods are concentrated in local and standalone clinics, underlining the sector’s employment footprint across urban and rural areas,’’ says the report.
The wellness segment has recorded a 21.29% compound annual growth rate, while yoga centres registered about 75% growth in revenue over two years, according to the assessment.
Ayurveda remains the largest individual Ayush system, accounting for $17.73 billion, or about 48% of the total services revenue.
The sector is also gaining a foothold in medical value travel. Ayush-related medical value travel generated an estimated $1.77 billion in 2024-25. Although international patients account for only around 5% of patient volumes, they contribute an estimated 15-25% of hospital-segment revenue, with therapeutic programmes typically involving stays of five to 11 days.
The assessment projects that the Ayush services economy could expand to between $216 billion and $318 billion by 2047.
Job opportunities
Union Minister of State for Ayush Prataprao Jadhav said the sector’s expansion was creating employment opportunities across healthcare, wellness, education and allied services, while also opening avenues for entrepreneurship and women’s participation.
The report projects further employment opportunities in healthcare delivery, wellness, education, medical travel, research, digital health and allied services as the sector expands.

Frederick G. Banting and John J.R. Macleod were awarded the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery of insulin, a hormone that regulates blood glucose levels. Their work helped establish insulin as a treatment for diabetes, a disease that, in its severe forms, had often been fatal before insulin therapy became available.
The prize was shared equally. Banting and Macleod were recognised “for the discovery of insulin”. The award acknowledged research conducted at the University of Toronto in the early 1920s, when investigators developed pancreatic extracts that could lower blood sugar in diabetic animals and subsequently demonstrated their therapeutic potential in humans. Charles Best, who worked with Banting, and biochemist James Collip, who helped purify insulin for clinical use, also made important contributions to this work.
Research on pancreas and blood sugar
Diabetes had been linked to the pancreas decades before insulin was isolated. In 1889, researchers Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering demonstrated that removing the pancreas from dogs produced diabetes. Subsequent research established the importance of the islets of Langerhans, clusters of cells within the pancreas, in regulating blood sugar.
The challenge was to identify and extract the substance responsible for this effect. Several researchers attempted to prepare pancreatic extracts, but obtaining a preparation that could be used safely and consistently in patients remained difficult.
Frederick G. Banting was a Canadian physician and surgeon whose interest in diabetes led him to investigate the role of the pancreas in regulating blood glucose. After serving in the First World War, he returned to Canada and worked in medical practice before pursuing research.
John J.R. Macleod was a Scottish-born physician and physiologist who had built his career around teaching and research in physiology, including carbohydrate metabolism. By 1920, he was a professor of physiology at the University of Toronto.
Banting approached Macleod in 1921 with a proposal to isolate a substance from the pancreas that could regulate blood glucose. Macleod provided laboratory facilities, scientific guidance and access to experimental animals. Banting began the work with Charles Best, a medical student who assisted with the experiments. Their collaboration brought together Banting’s research hypothesis and Macleod’s experience in physiology, setting the stage for the experiments that led to the development of insulin as a treatment for diabetes.
The researchers tied off the pancreatic ducts of dogs, allowing the enzyme-producing tissue to degenerate while attempting to preserve the islets. They prepared extracts from the pancreas and tested them in dogs whose pancreases had been removed. The extracts lowered blood sugar and improved the animals’ clinical condition.
These experiments provided evidence that an extract from the pancreas could help compensate for the loss of its normal blood sugar-regulating function. However, the early preparations were not suitable for prolonged use in humans because they contained impurities that caused adverse reactions.
Purifying insulin for treatment
In 1922, biochemist James Collip joined the research team to improve the purity of the pancreatic extract. His work helped produce a preparation suitable for clinical testing.
In January 1922, insulin was administered to Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old boy with severe diabetes, at Toronto General Hospital. The first injection produced limited results, and an abscess developed at the injection site. After the preparation was further purified, a second course of treatment produced a marked improvement in his condition, with a substantial reduction in blood glucose and urinary glucose.
Thompson’s response demonstrated that insulin could be used to treat diabetes in humans. The development of more reliable preparations and the expansion of production subsequently allowed treatment to reach more patients.
Insulin did not cure diabetes, but it changed the outlook for people living with the disease. Before its introduction, severe diabetes was often managed through restrictive diets that could prolong life only for a limited period. Insulin enabled patients to use glucose more effectively and helped prevent the severe metabolic disturbances associated with insulin deficiency.
The role of Best and Collip
The Nobel decision remains a significant part of the history of insulin research. Although Banting and Macleod received the prize, the work involved a larger research team.
Banting was unhappy that Best had not been included among the laureates. He shared half of his prize money with Best. Macleod, in turn, shared half of his prize money with Collip, recognising his contribution to the purification of insulin.
Later historical assessments of the discovery acknowledged the importance of contributions made by researchers who were not included in the award.
Laboratory discovery,modern diabetes care
The introduction of insulin marked a turning point in the treatment of diabetes. It allowed many people living with severe insulin deficiency to survive and helped establish hormone replacement as a major approach to treating endocrine disorders.
Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It helps glucose move from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy or stored for later use. When the body produces insufficient insulin, or cannot use it effectively, blood glucose levels can rise.
Insulin remains essential for people with type 1 diabetes, in which the immune system destroys the pancreatic beta cells that produce the hormone. It is also used by some people with type 2 diabetes when other treatments do not adequately control blood glucose.
The treatment has evolved considerably since the first pancreatic extracts were administered. Modern insulin preparations are manufactured under controlled conditions, with different formulations developed to vary how quickly they begin working and how long their effects last.
The Nobel recognition
Banting and Macleod received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for 1923. Banting delivered his Nobel lecture, titled ‘Diabetes and Insulin’, on September 15, 1925, while Macleod’s lecture, ‘The Physiology of Insulin and Its Source in the Animal Body’, followed on May 26, 1925.
The discovery also has a lasting connection to World Diabetes Day, observed on November 14, the birthday of Banting, who was born in 1891. More than a century later, insulin remains a cornerstone of diabetes treatment, changing a condition that was once often fatal into one that can be managed with sustained treatment.

Bouncing back after a poor run of results, defending champion Rajputana Royals registered back-to-back wins with a classy display against high-flying Chero Archers in the Archery Premier League’s season 2 in Hyderabad on Tuesday.
The Royals, who went through a rut with three straight defeats before turning it around on Monday, were in terrific rhythm as they thrashed Chero 6-0 without dropping a set.
The result moved Royals to six points and keeps them firmly in semifinal contention, while Chero also remains on the same tally. The star of the show for Royals was compound world No. 1 Ella Gibson, who scored 60 out of a possible 60.
Chero, who went back to their recurve international archer in Casey Kaufhold ahead of Kumkum Mohod, lost the first set 73-74 after the American started with a costly 7. In the second set, Royals edged ahead 76-75 with Chero paying the price for a couple of 9s from their compound archers.
The third set was tied at 58-58 after six arrows each, after which Atanu Das, who has otherwise been in fine form when selected, hit a rare 8. For Royals, Sangeeta – who was playing her first match in place of Ankita Bhakat – responded with a sensational 10. With an 8 needed to win, Tokyo Olympic champion Mete Gazoz delivered a 9 and brought out his signature celebration and some thigh-fives with his team.
“We didn’t start well over the first four days. I guess everybody misses us because I think the APL needs more energy and more dancing and now we’re giving that,” Gazoz quipped after the win.
Mighty Marathas and Kakatiya Knights seem to be peaking at the right time as they moved clear at the top of the table with eight points each.
Marathas’ recurve star Dhiraj Bommadevara was in terrific form, repeatedly shooting clutch 10s with barely any time left on the clock as the anchor for his side. At the top, ‘Mr. Perfect’ Mike Schloesser set up the sets well and finished with 78 out of the possible 80 points as Marathas’ stunning resurgence continues. They top the table ahead of Knights with only set points difference separating the two sides.
In the final match of the day, the Knights consigned Chola Chiefs to the bottom of the table as Nico Wiener and Neeraj Chauhan were both in terrific form at the start and end of the sets – both registering 59 out of 60 – while Spain’s recurve archer Elia Canales was an able support. In Jyothi Surekha Vennam’s absence, Avneet Kaur also stepped into the lineup admirably for the home franchise.
The scores
Rajputana Royals bt Chero Archers 6-0 (74-73, 76-75, 77-75).
Mighty Marathas bt Prithviraj Yodhas 6-2 (76-74, 77-73, 70-78, 76-75).
Kakatiya Knights bt Chola Chiefs 6-0 (74-73, 79-78, 77-75).

Rubio to visit India October 17–22; Jaishankar says trade talks near 'landing point'
Marco Rubio will visit India and meet senior officials and business leaders. The talks will test efforts to resolve trade differences and deepen strategic ties.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will visit India from October 17 to 22, with stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar, following a visit to Uzbekistan, as New Delhi and Washington seek to strengthen strategic ties amid continuing trade negotiations and disagreements over tariffs.
The US Department of State announced Tuesday that Rubio will first travel to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, to participate in the C5+1 Ministerial with the five Central Asian republics before heading to India for his second official visit to the country this year.
In India, Rubio will meet senior government officials to discuss the bilateral strategic partnership, regional and global developments, and expanded energy cooperation. He will also engage with business leaders to promote investment and economic ties, according to the State Department.
The announcement comes as Indian External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said Tuesday that India-US trade negotiations were moving towards a resolution, even as Washington’s changing trade policies force countries to reassess their economic relationships with the United States.
“My sense is that this is an issue which is heading towards a landing point,” Jaishankar said during a conversation with Bloomberg News Editor-in-Chief John Micklethwait at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi.
Jaishankar said the United States was seeking to rebuild domestic industries and reset the terms on which other countries access its market. He indicated that India was evaluating the proposed agreement in the context of the terms Washington was offering other trading partners.
“The United States has repositioned itself,” Jaishankar said, adding that countries needed to “recalculate and reset” their relationships with Washington as its approach to international engagement changed.
The remarks offer a cautiously optimistic assessment of the trade negotiations, which have faced renewed uncertainty over tariffs, market access and the competitive position of Indian exports.
FROM MAY'S OPTIMISM TO RENEWED TRADE UNCERTAINTY
Rubio’s forthcoming visit follows his four-day trip to India in May, when he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Jaishankar for discussions on trade, energy, defence, maritime security and regional developments.
During his May 24 meeting with Jaishankar, Rubio expressed confidence that the two countries could reach a durable trade agreement. He said the negotiations had made substantial progress and that Washington hoped to conclude an agreement beneficial to both sides.
Jaishankar, meanwhile, called for an early conclusion to the interim trade agreement, describing it as an important step towards a comprehensive bilateral trade deal first envisaged during Modi’s February 2025 visit to Washington.
The May discussions also covered energy diversification, nuclear cooperation, critical minerals, technology and visa-related challenges faced by Indian travellers. Rubio subsequently met Modi, discussing trade and energy, and conveyed an invitation from President Donald Trump for the Indian prime minister to visit the White House.
Rubio’s May visit also included engagement with the Quad, the strategic grouping comprising the United States, India, Japan and Australia, underscoring the wider geopolitical significance of the relationship.
TRADE DEAL REMAINS A KEY TEST
Despite the optimism expressed in May, negotiations have continued amid changes in US tariff policy and disagreements over market access. Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on October 5 that the talks had reached a plateau, with further concessions becoming increasingly difficult for both sides.
The United States has sought to address its trade imbalance and expand access to the Indian market, while New Delhi has sought terms that protect sensitive domestic sectors and keep Indian exporters competitive against rival economies.
Jaishankar’s latest comments suggest that discussions are continuing and that a resolution remains possible. However, his remarks do not amount to an announcement that a final agreement has been concluded.
Rubio’s October visit will therefore provide another opportunity for Washington and New Delhi to advance their economic and strategic partnership, with energy cooperation explicitly identified by the State Department as an important part of the agenda.

At least five people have died after Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel pummelled Mexico’s Pacific coast, causing flooding that downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and inundated homes.
Simon claimed the life of a 71-year-old man who died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo in the southern state of Guerrero, governor Evelyn Salgado said at a press conference.
The storm also damaged infrastructure and homes in the state’s coastal towns, including the major seaport of Acapulco, she said.
Tropical Storm Rachel is blamed for the deaths of four members of one family, including two children, whose bodies were found on the outskirts of the city of Ensenada in Baja California, the state’s prosecutor’s office reported.
Five more people remained missing, while security forces used helicopters to rescue 32 people, prosecutors said. Baja governor Marina del Pilar said officials were helping more than 50 people in temporary shelters.
Simon did not make landfall and, after weakening to category two on the five-point Saffir-Simpson scale, was moving away from the coast, authorities said. A rain alert remained in place.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said heavy rainfall associated with Simon in west-central Mexico over the next few days might still produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Officials warned waves of up to five metres high were still expected in some coastal areas. Flooding and landslides had already hit communities close to rivers and streams in the states of Michoacan and Colima.

Meteorologists say the 2026-27 El Niño, which causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions, is certain to be the biggest ever recorded. Scientists now also think human-caused global heating is making El Niños more intense.
