The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.
The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.
Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.
Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”
“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”
The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination”.
The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates, where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.
Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.
The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.
He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.
“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

The US national parks are incredible, and I understand why so many people flock to these iconic landscapes to see some of the most breathtaking scenery in the country.
However, after traveling solo to all 63 US national parks and all 50 states, I've discovered that some of the most stunning and underrated places aren't part of the national park system — they're state parks.
These hidden gems offer the same beauty, adventure, and solitude, often without the crowds, reservations, or permit hassles that come with national park visits. Here are some of my favorites.
Devil's Lake State Park in Wisconsin has something for everyone.
Despite being Wisconsin's most-visited state park, I find that many people I talk to don't know about Devil's Lake in Baraboo. However, it's my favorite of Wisconsin's 50 state parks.
In my opinion, the park's East and West Bluff trails offer some of the best panoramic views in the Midwest. Additionally, the massive rock formations — like Balanced Rock and Devil's Doorway — make it a favorite for hikers and rock climbers alike.
Beyond the cliffs, the park offers kayaking, swimming, and peaceful lakeside picnic areas, making it a perfect year-round destination.
Coopers Rock State Forest in West Virginia is the perfect place to watch the sunset.
West Virginia is another one of my favorite states for outdoor recreation. Its state park system is full of gems, but I always recommend visiting Coopers Rock State Forest.
I love hiking in this park or simply enjoying a sunset at Coopers Rock Overlook, which offers a panoramic view of the Cheat River Gorge.
The park also has many unique rock formations scattered throughout the forest along the miles of scenic trails.
Letchworth State Park in New York is home to stunning waterfalls.
Often nicknamed the "Grand Canyon of the East," Letchworth State Park is a natural wonder where the Genesee River carves through a deep gorge, creating three stunning waterfalls framed by towering cliffs.
With 66 miles of hiking trails, scenic overlooks, and endless opportunities for outdoor recreation, Letchworth is a paradise for nature lovers.
The park is especially magical in the fall, with its vibrant autumn foliage, making it one of the most spectacular leaf-peeping destinations in the Northeast.
Visiting Utah's Kodachrome Basin State Park feels like stepping into another world.
When visiting Utah, many travelers aim to see one (or all) of the state's "Mighty Five" national parks. However, Utah is also home to 46 state parks — my favorite being Kodachrome Basin.
Just over 20 miles from Bryce Canyon National Park, Kodachrome Basin feels like stepping into another world entirely.
The less-crowded landscape is a stunning mix of red, orange, and yellow hues, and striking "sand pipes" — tall, thin spires of rock that the park is known for.
Hike, camp, or drive through the rock formations of this hidden gem park for a peaceful adventure.
Matthiessen State Park in Illinois feels magical.
Matthiessen State Park is a hidden gem known for its dramatic canyons, cascading waterfalls, and towering forests, creating a stunning, almost magical landscape.
With peaceful trails and fewer crowds than nearby Starved Rock State Park, Matthiessen is a must-visit for nature lovers in the Midwest. I especially love visiting in the fall to enjoy the changing foliage.
Eldorado Canyon is one of my favorite state parks in Colorado.
With four major national parks and over 40 state parks, Colorado is known for outdoor recreation. However, I've found that, outside of the locals, many people don't know about one of my favorite places to visit — Eldorado Canyon State Park.
Just 9 miles outside Boulder, the park is known for its dramatic canyon views, rock climbing, and scenic hiking trails. Its towering golden sandstone cliffs make it one of the top climbing destinations in the US, with over 500 routes.
Visitors can also choose to cross-country ski or snowshoe in the winter months.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

Actor Seth Green—yes, that one—has seen Godzilla Minus Zero and says it’s awesome.
While introducing the New York Comic Con panel for the 39th film in the Godzilla franchise, Green stressed that the filmmakers behind the movie “have created kaiju that feel physically real and, trust me, emotionally terrifying.”
While a lot of that terror came from the work of Oscar-winning visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima, some it came from the shrieking of Godzilla and his three-headed nemesis, King Ghidorah. Those roars were the work of sound designer Natsuko Inoue and her team, who created the monsters’ outsize vocalizations by rolling speakers to the top of an outdoor dam—much to the horror of people nearby.
“There were people having a picnic, maybe people just taking a stroll,” Hisafumi Takeuchi, who also worked on sound for the film, said during the panel. “The person walking their dog, though—they had the worst time, because the dog was freaking out and barking back at us.”
Since the creatures are imaginary, getting their screams to sound realistic is essential to making them seem believable—and genuinely scary—onscreen. At first, Inoue wasn’t sure if the idea of recording at the dam would work. Those fears were quickly put to rest.
“The first time we sent that roar out on the speakers, I could see the relief and confidence in everyone's eyes,” Inoue said. “By using speakers and projecting it into the real world, capturing the reverb, the echo, the reflection of the sound back with the mic, it manifests it in our world.”
For other kaiju sound effects, Inoue’s team took an analog foley approach. To simulate Ghidorah’s dragon-like wings, for example, they flapped a rubber fisherman’s suit and mixed that noise with the sounds of an accordion-like air duct.
Getting two of Toho’s most famous monsters right was a huge undertaking, especially after the success of Zero’s predecessor, Godzilla Minus One, which brought home $114 million worldwide at the box office. Following that 2023 film’s harrowing mix of post–World War II malaise and bracing kaiju destruction will be tough, but a new trailer shown during the film’s panel at NYCC promised a sequel full of aerial dogfights and a punch-’em-up for the ages between Godzilla and Ghidorah.
Like the previous film, Godzilla Minus Zero is directed by Takashi Yamazaki and features visual effects from Tatsuji Nojima, whom Green called “the first Gen Z Oscar-winner” for his work on One.
Nojima began doing visual effects as a hobby while he was still a teenager before joining animation house Shirogumi as a compositor. After Yamazaki noticed a crude animation of waves that Nojima was working on, the director tasked the budding animator with developing the idea. Nojima turned around a fully rendered shot of ocean water over rocks that looked indistinguishable from reality. After that, Nojima recalled, Yamazaki said, “OK, I think you’re ready to animate and do VFX for Godzilla now.”
During the panel, Nojima broke down how he created a shot from the trailer showing Godzilla bursting out of the ocean while chasing a seaplane. “I simulated 200 million particles to get the whitewater effect correct in Godzilla Minus One,” he said. “With this shot in Godzilla Minus Zero, the scale is absolutely different with the new Imax aspect ratio, plus there was no live-action plate, so we're dealing with a lot of CG on screen. We required 2 billion particles.”
Godzilla Minus Zero is set to hit US theaters on November 6 and Japanese theaters on November 3, which has become known as Godzilla’s birthday since it marks the date in 1954 that Ishirō Honda’s original film was released in Japan.

AI video startup Clueso has raised $10 Mn (about ₹95 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by Dharana Capital. The round also saw participation from new investors Founders Future and Neotribe Ventures, alongside existing backers Y Combinator and F7 Ventures. With the latest round, Clueso has raised a total funding of about $12 Mn to date. The startup last raised $1.4 Mn in a seed funding round led by F7 Ventures. Clueso plans to deploy the fresh capital towards expanding its enterprise sales and marketing operations and developing the AI agents powering its platform. It will also improve its video editing capabilities and deepen integrations with systems that store product and company information. Automating Enterprise Video Production Founded in 2023 by IIT Madras batchmates Akash Anand, Prajwal Prakash, and Neel Balar, Clueso helps businesses create and update videos using AI agents. The startup says its platform identifies gaps in existing video content, captures software workflows, and generates videos with scripts, voiceovers, animations, and captions. Users can edit these videos through a browser-based editor and refresh them when products, processes, or brand guidelines change. To support this, Clueso integrates with business tools to access company information and keep video content consistent. Its Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration also enables AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT to create, edit, and manage videos on the platform. “We position ourselves as a dedicated end-to-end platform for enterprises and not a single prompt-to-video tool that consumers or creators use,” Anand told Inc42. Clueso charges a subscription fee based on the volume of videos created and updated, the number of teams using the platform, and the products covered. The startup claims to have over 1,000 paying customers globally, including Atlassian, GitLab, Zendesk, Gainsight, Global Partners, Seismic, and Ironclad. Its Indian customers include PhonePe, Zoho, and MoEngage. According to Clueso, about 65% of its customers are based in the US, 20% in Europe, and around 10-15% in India. More than 70% of the videos created on the platform are customer-facing, including product launch videos and educational content. Other uses include employee training, onboarding, and compliance. Headquartered in San Francisco, Clueso has a 39-member team, including around 35 employees in India, with a significant presence in Bengaluru. Over the next 12-18 months, the startup plans to expand its enterprise integrations and customer base while automating more of the video production process. It also aims to track viewer engagement and use that data to improve video content. Anand said the long-term goal is to turn video into “a living system rather than a one-time asset you produce and forget about”.

A wave of biotech companies is looking to prove that it’s possible to slow down the aging process. Mountain View, California–based Rubedo Life Sciences is starting with the most outwardly visible sign: the skin.
The company’s experimental treatment is showing early promise that it may be able to reduce the appearance of aging, according to data the company presented at the Aging Research and Drug Discovery meeting in Boston earlier this month.
In a small clinical trial, Rubedo tested its topical cream on 11 people with atopic dermatitis, an inflammatory skin condition and the most common type of eczema. The drug targets a mechanism of cellular senescence, a biological state in which damaged or stressed cells permanently stop dividing but do not die. These senescent or “zombie” cells accumulate as people age and can release substances that contribute to inflammation and tissue damage, which contributes to disease.
After four weeks of using the cream, participants lowered the biological age of their skin by about two years, on average. That estimate was based on an aging “clock” designed by a different company, Mitra Bio, which performed an independent analysis on participants’ skin samples. One person in the trial had a reduction of more than 11 years in skin age. Separately, Rubedo found that its treatment was tied to a reduction in inflammation-related markers and a 10 percent increase in a type of collagen associated with skin elasticity and structure.
Biological or epigenetic age is an estimate of how well a person is aging compared to their calendar age. Aging clocks like Mitra’s attempt to calculate this number by looking at patterns of methylations, chemical modifications to DNA that regulate how genes function and can change over time. That metric doesn’t necessarily prove that the body or a particular organ or tissue has become functionally younger, though.
“Our idea is to find ways to change the trajectory of how we age,” says Marco Quarta, Rubedo’s cofounder and chief scientific officer. “Aging is complex. There are many mechanisms, but cellular senescence is one of them.”
Senescent cells are also involved in normal biological processes, such as wound healing and tumor suppression, but their accumulation over time is associated with many age-related conditions. Getting rid of them is one of the leading strategies that anti-aging and longevity companies are pursuing.
Rubedo’s approach aims to clear out senescent cells by targeting a protein known as GPX4, a gatekeeper for cell survival. By transiently turning off GPX4, the drug is designed to make senescent cells more susceptible to ferroptosis, a regulated form of cell death, while reviving stressed, non-senescent cells nearby.
In a separate study, researchers looked at the drug’s effect on actinic keratosis, a skin condition caused by sun damage and produces rough, scaly skin patches and can sometimes progress to skin cancer. In a trial of 18 people, the cream led to a 46 percent reduction in total lesions after a month of use.
Rubedo is studying the same drug for psoriasis and skin with sun damage. Soon, the company will add androgenetic alopecia, a type of hereditary hair loss, to the list. CEO Frederick Beddingfield, previously the chief medical officer at Allergan, where he launched Botox, sees potential in a lower-potency, over-the-counter version for general skin aging, which would compete with retinol. The company is also formulating the drug into a pill to study whether it can be used to treat metabolic conditions associated with aging.
“It's great to see them doing this work,” says Eric Verdin, president and CEO of the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, which has developed several aging clocks. “I would probably be a little circumspect about what these clocks really measure, because right now, there are a proliferation of them.”
Plus, the results that patients will care about is how their skin actually looks and feels, not a result from a biological aging test.
And senescence is just one piece of the aging puzzle, says Anthony Rossi, a dermatologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “Some senescent cells are good because they turn things off, like cancer progression.”
He says the science is novel but the work is still very early-stage, and it will be interesting to see how it affects biological aging in people with healthy skin, not just those with certain skin conditions. “The best anti-aging routine right now is sleep, a good diet, and exercise,” he says. For now, at least.

- To fast travel in Valor Mortis, you need to defeat General Lothaire and reach the Abandoned Church.
- After unlocking it, players can fast travel using the Lantern save points.
- Players can only travel to locations where there is a kindred Lantern.
Valor Mortis is divided into multiple levels, each being in a different area. Each area is quite large and has a ton of hidden secrets that can only be reached after unlocking specific abilities. Some abilities only unlock much later in the game, making it quite tedious to make your way back. Heading back to explore becomes much easier after unlocking fast travel. Here is a quick guide on how to fast travel in Valor Mortis.
How to Unlock Fast Travel in Valor Mortis
Valor Mortis is a soulslike, and like the other games in the genre, this game also has specific safe points. The safe points in Valor Mortis are the Lanterns, where players can also level up. Like other soulslike games, the Lanterns also act as a fast travel beacon. Players can interact with the Lantern and fast travel to any other unlocked Lantern in the game.
However, this feature is not available from the start, and players have to unlock it first. To unlock Fast Travel in Valor Mortis, players simply need to progress the story until they defeat the ‘General Lothair, the Eagle-Bearer’ boss.
Upon defeating this boss, players will be able to enter the Abandoned Church. This place will become the base of operations for players, and reaching there will unlock fast travel in Valor Mortis.
How to Fast Travel in Valor Mortis
After you have unlocked fast travel in Valor Mortis, you can simply use any Kindered Lantern to fast travel in the game. Other than that, every Lantern is also connected to the Abandoned Church, so players can directly head back there to upgrade their weapons. So, here is how you can fast travel in Valor Mortis:
- Interact with any Lantern and select the Fast Travel option.
- Pick the destination you want to reach and select it.
- Next, you will be transported to the new location.
That’s it. Now you know how to fast travel in Valor Mortis. Have any further questions? Ask us in the comment section below.

Just over 10 years after its initial release, space exploration and survival crafting game No Man’s Sky is making its way to the iPhone and iPad, Apple and developer Hello Games announced today.
It will run on devices as far back as the iPhone 11 and the third-generation iPad Air. No Man’s Sky might not have the most cutting-edge AAA graphics (though they’re still strong, and they’ve come a long way since launch via updates), but the game’s uncommon method of generating galaxies of incomprehensible scale on device consistently for all players from a single-seed happening on a phone is remarkable for those of us who remember phones performing far behind consoles or desktop PCs.
This version of the game includes all of the content and systems updates to the game that have been added over the years—the expansions that famously took the game from a rocky launch reception to a widely beloved redemption story.
There are a couple of compromises, though, and it’s similar to what we saw with No Man’s Sky on the Nintendo Switch. Hello Games says the ability to build and explore player-made planetary settlements is limited to the iPhone 15 Pro and later, and multiplayer is not supported on any iOS device. “We are excited to see player feedback on iOS, and will support it appropriately based on how many folks are playing,” the company says, leaving the door open to perhaps not supporting all future content updates if the player base isn’t there to justify it.

NEW DELHI: A 29-year-old driver was allegedly beaten to death by a club manager, his wife and three bouncers in north Delhi’s Sarai Rohilla after a party turned violent in the early hours of Sunday.
The man had gone to the club with friends when he allegedly spilled beer on the manager’s wife, who was celebrating her birthday, triggering an argument. Police held five people, including the club manager, his wife and a bouncer, within hours of the incident. The deceased, Daljeet Singh, a resident of JJ Colony in Raghubir Nagar, visited the club on New Rohtak Road in Inderlok in north Delhi around 3.30 am on Oct 11 with five friends, Pawan, Arbaz Ali, Ashu, Tinu and Gautam.
During the altercation, Daljeet and his friends were allegedly assaulted by the club staff. The group later returned to their respective homes in Raghubir Nagar. After reaching home, Daljeet vomited and went to sleep, police said.
His condition deteriorated around noon Sunday, after which his wife, Puja, took him to Guru Gobind Singh Hospital in Khayala, where doctors pronounced him dead. Later, a PCR call was made around 6.52 pm on Sunday.
Police subsequently received information about the death from the hospital and verified the circumstances surrounding the incident. The alleged assault was captured on CCTV cameras.
Five Arrested
How Minor Collision Ended In Murder
Bouncers Attacked Driver For An Hour: Friend
Police have registered an FIR under multiple sections of BNS including for murder, attempt to murder, voluntarily causing hurt, wrongful confinement, and criminal intimidation involving serious threats. Sections under Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act (COTPA) were also included.
The five arrested accused have been identified as Dilawar alias Hasnain, a guest organiser; Sunny alias Gaurav, the club manager; Sharvan Kumar, who was responsible for checking entries at the main gate; bouncer Vikash Balyan; and Harshita, the manager’s wife, whose birthday was being celebrated at the club, according to police. Investigators alleged that Sharvan assaulted Daljeet while another person was taking him back.
Meanwhile, the in charge of Inderlok police post has been sent to District Lines for alleged dereliction of duty after the club was found operating until the early hours of the morning, police said. Sources said the club had remained open until at least 5 am.
Daljeet worked as a driver and was the sole breadwinner for his family, a friend said. He is survived by his wife, an eight-year-old son and a younger brother.
Tinu, one of Daljeet’s friends who was present at the club, said the group had been enjoying themselves when a minor collision caused beer to spill on the manager’s wife.
Another friend alleged that Daljeet was hit on his stomach, legs and head during the assault. This prompted the group to intervene. The situation soon escalated when bouncers joined the altercation, he claimed. He alleged that she grabbed Daljeet by his hair and attacked him with bottles.
“We were seven people and they were more in number. They thrashed us for nearly an hour,” Tinu alleged. He claimed that three members of the group were locked inside a room and beaten for 30 to 40 minutes. The group was allegedly assaulted with sticks and fists. Tinu also alleged that one of the accused pulled out a pistol and threatened them.

అక్టోబర్ 10న ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద భారీ నిరసన చేపట్టనున్నట్లు కాక్రొచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ప్రకటించింది. ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర ఓటర్ల జాబితా సవరణ (SIR) ప్రక్రియను వెంటనే నిలిపివేయాలని, 2025 జూన్ 25 నుంచి ఓటర్ల జాబితా నుంచి తొలగించిన పేర్లన్నింటినీ తిరిగి చేర్చాలని కూడా CJP డిమాండ్ చేస్తోంది. లెఫ్ట్ వింగ్ విద్యార్థి సంఘాలు కూడా ఈ నిరసనలో పెద్ద సంఖ్యలో పాల్గొంటామని ప్రకటన విడుదల చేశాయి. జంతర్ మంతర్లోకి ప్రవేశించేందుకు ప్రయత్నించిన సీజేపీ (CJP) నేతలను పోలీసులు అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో “జ్ఞానేశ్ కుమార్ రాజీనామ కోరుతూ.. ఢిల్లీలో మిన్నంటిన విద్యార్థుల ఆందోళనలు” అంటూ భారీ సంఖ్యలో ప్రజలు గుమిగూడిన వీడియో ఒకటి సోషల్ మీడియాలో షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). దీని వెనుక ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: సిఈసి జ్ఞానేశ్ కుమార్ రాజీనామ కోరుతూ ఢిల్లీలో విద్యార్థులు ఆందోళనలు చేస్తున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో జూలై 2026లో కోల్కతాలోని సీల్దా రైల్వే స్టేషన్లో ధర్మేంద్ర ప్రధాన్కు వ్యతిరేకంగా జరిగిన నిరసనకు సంబంధించింది. ఢిల్లీకి సంబంధించిన వీడియో కాదు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టిస్తుంది.

Terrorists could use AI to target UK with drones and bioweapons, MI5 chief warns
Sir Ken McCallum said UK was entering ‘new era of national security’ with most threats since the Cold War, as he warned against rising danger from Russia and Iran

Terrorists could exploit artificial intelligence to target Britain with drones or biological weapons, the head of MI5 has warned.
Speaking after his annual speech at MI5 headquarters in London, Sir Ken McCallum said the UK had entered a “new era of national security” and the security service was directing more resources to keeping Britain safe now than in the Cold War, warning that essential services such as banking, flights, and healthcare were at risk of being disrupted by adversaries, including Iran and Russia.
He warned about the growing threat of AI provoking real fear that terrorists could use the technology for warfare, saying “we’ve caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies”.
He said the possibility of AI-enabled drones added “a new twist” for bad actors and warned the greatest concern is “AI's potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons”.
“These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community – MI5, GCHQ, MI6 – is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI security institute to take them on. Part of that means retaining the capability edge against those who mean the UK harm. As they seek to harness AI, we must stay ahead, so these powerful technologies bolster rather than undermine our shared security,” he said.
Putting the public on guard, Sir Ken warned: “We have again entered a new era of national security”.
He called for a “whole-of-society effort” to face threats to national infrastructure, warning that hacks could disable people’s banking services, drones could disrupt flights, and cyber-attacks on hospitals could impact health treatment.
The MI5 director general also said that the suspected terror plot against RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, which prime minister Andy Burnham said was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard, was “not unique in the UK”, with Iranians seeking to expand their hybrid campaign against Britain this year.
In the past twelve months, MI5 investigations have led to more than 50 arrests in Iran-linked operations in the UK, and its state threats caseload has quadrupled in the past decade, he said.
Sir Ken added: “You might be surprised to know that in 2026, MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War.”
He said that there have been dozens of arrests under the National Security Act in the three years since it came into force, with cases linked to Russia, Iran and China.
“Anyone tempted by apparently easy cash from shady overseas taskmasters might want to bear this in mind,” Sir Ken warned.
He said that Russia remains “aggressor number one”, with Russian military and intelligence services “once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare”, citing a cyber-attack on Polish energy infrastructure and an attempt to use a drone to blow up a cargo plane in Germany.
Sir Ken also called out Iranian use of “criminal proxies to try and intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organisations and Israeli sites”.
His warning comes after he revealed Britain faces greater and more complex terror threats now than on 9/11, in an exclusive interview with The Independent last month.
Addressing journalists after his speech on Tuesday, Sir Ken said: “The Iranians in the UK are principally using a modus operandi of hiring criminals to do their biding. Their level of capability is really a function of the sophistication level of those criminals”. But he warned that the UK should be readying itself for more aggressive plots from the Iranian security services.
Speaking about the ongoing threats from terrorism, Sir Ken said that MI5 is still having to respond to attempts from radicalised Islamists to carry out mass casualty attacks in the UK. And an increase in extreme right-wing terrorism, with a growing number of cases where “extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent”.
He cited a case where, a few months ago, MI5 was investigating a radicalised extreme right-wing 13 year old in the UK. This investigation “generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil”, Sir Ken said.
Sir Ken also announced that MI5 has launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre (AITAC) this year, which will produce assessments of the risks posed by the new technology.
Speaking to journalists after his speech, Sir Ken added: “In the case of bioweapons… one concern would be that comparatively low sophistication actors may have a capability uplift in the AI era, if the guard rails don’t operate or do not function as intended."
Sir Ken explained: “It has long been the case that many terrorists would dearly love to have some kind of capability around chemical or biological weaponry, but that hasn’t been easy for them to achieve. One risk, and as I said in my speech this is not yet manifest, but one risk is that AI could enable knowledge to get into the hands of people we would not want to have that knowledge.
“A second additional risk, much discussed… is the possibility that AI could generate novel pathogens not previously seen, so these are among the risks that we are seeking to address.”
When asked about potential Russian interference in the Brexit referendum, Sir Ken said: “There is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed.”
He warned that it is “up to us to decide how far we allow our various adversaries to divide us”, adding: “I am a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, Russian trolls who didn’t appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they’ll be delighted because they are front page news once again.”
Asked whether Britain will be able to get back to a less fractious time, Sir Ken said: “Our planning assumption is not that this is a temporary blip, and we will all be back to normal by next Christmas.
“We are planning on the basis that, in effect, the period of comparative geopolitical stability following the end of the Cold War has sadly ended and we are back in a more contested era now. We are planning on the basis that these risks will endure."
Later on Tuesday, the defence secretary Wes Streeting told MPs on the Commons defence committee: “Fundamentally, I think this country and our allies in Nato face a threat of a kind we haven't seen since the end of the Cold War.”
"We don't seek conflict with Russia. We don't seek escalation. We don't seek to provoke Russia, but we know that every single day Russia is testing us, testing our allies.”
He also said the term hybrid threats was a “sanitised description of what are acts of sabotage, targeted assassinations, effectively state-backed terrorism. So that's the world in which we're living in today".

Bail to key accused charged with Zubeen Garg's 'murder' may weaken case: Late singer's wife
The high court on Friday granted bail to band member Amritprava Mahanta.
The family of late singer Zubeen Garg has expressed dismay and held a peaceful protest on Monday against the bail granted by Gauhati high court to his bandmate, who is one of the seven accused facing trial for the alleged murder of the 52-year-old.
The high court on Friday granted bail to band member Amritprava Mahanta. The cultural icon died under mysterious circumstances on September 19 last year while swimming in the sea in Singapore.
"We waited for a year with the faith of getting justice and our chief minister had also maintained that Garg was murdered and those responsible will be dealt with adequately," Garg's wife, Garrima Saikia Garg, told journalists at the singer-cum-composer's memorial place on the outskirts of Guwahati.
"We were told that the chargesheet filed in the case after a detailed investigation was leak-proof. Then how come one of the prime accused in the case who has been charged with murder managed to get bail from the high court? This is likely to weaken the case,” she added.
Following the high court order, hundreds of Garg's fans gathered at the memorial place located at Sonapur where Garrima Saikia appealed to all for a peaceful demonstration and to get united for justice.
"If those accused in the case get bail, what does it say about the investigation? Won't such people coming out of jail pose a threat to our lives? If someone of Garg's stature fails to get justice, what more can we expect," she said.
Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said that it won't be proper to comment on a decision taken by the judiciary when the case is sub-judice.

"As a government, we can't comment on the orders passed by the high court or the Supreme Court. But judging by how the trial of the case is progressing in a fast track court on a daily basis for close to a year now, we are hopeful of a good outcome," he said on Monday.
Garg’s death last year had sparked a statewide demand for a thorough probe into the matter. A special investigation team (SIT) constituted later said Garg was murdered as part of a planned conspiracy.
Besides Mahanta, six people – Garg's manager, the organiser of the event in Singapore which the singer had gone to attend, another bandmate, Garg's cousin and two security officers – were arrested in the case. All of them are currently in jail.
Last month, a special court granted bail to the two security officers in a separate disproportionate assets case. They continued to remain in prison for their alleged role in Garg's death.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

- Germany won’t be intimidated into dropping its support for Ukraine, chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Sunday as he announced €1bn ($1.1bn) in military aid during a visit to Kyiv. Merz said Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production. Speaking alongside Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Merz also announced €350m for repairs to the energy sector.
- German officials said company executives who travelled with Merz had signed 14 agreements with Ukraine worth about €6.6bn. They included an agreement with Germany’s Diehl Defence for the supply of IRIS-T air defence missiles, as well as a deal for radar equipment with Hensoldt and for jet drone interceptors with Quantum Systems.
- Air raid sirens and explosions rang out repeatedly across the Ukrainian capital during the German chancellor’s visit. A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Later on Sunday, a Russian airstrike hit Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, killing one person and injured another six, mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram.
- In Kyiv, Merz said Germany’s financial help was not only about protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity. “We do it deeply in our own interest, for it is a matter of Europe’s security,” he said, adding that Russia was carrying out cyber-attacks and disinformation campaigns targeting European democracy. Russia has said accusations of hybrid warfare are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
- Zelenskyy said on Sunday he believed Russia might have shared jet-drone technology with its ally North Korea. Earlier in the war, North Korea supplied Russia with millions of artillery shells, and it has since provided ballistic missiles that Moscow regularly uses to attack Ukrainian cities. Asked if Russia had shared with North Korea the technology behind its latest generation of jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy told journalists: “They [Russia] are sharing with North Korea all the technologies. I don’t know about the ballistic and etc but I think yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles.”
- Meanwhile, Ukraine’s military has again used drones to deliver food and medicine to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine,  foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sunday. Oleshky, a frontline town on the Dnipro River, which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has become “a hell on earth” under Russian occupation since 2022, according to residents. Sybiha, who has previously accused Russia of starving residents, said the latest delivery contained almost four metric tons of food and medicine. Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said last month that Russia had not agreed to Ukrainian proposals to allow civilians to evacuate.
- As Zelenskyy on Sunday said the US wanted to hold a new round of peace talks with Ukraine and Russia by the end of October, India said it was seeking a greater role in brokering an end to the war, the foreign minister said. Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said at a Munich Security Conference in New Delhi on Sunday that India had been advocating for a peace deal “for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy, so we have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard”. He said India was starting with Black Sea safety of shipping but also including discussions about grain and energy exports and “on non-attack possibilities”.
