Karnataka has urged the Centre to extend price-control measures beyond cancer medicines to other high-cost, life-saving drugs used to treat cardiac and kidney diseases, following the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s (NPPA) in-principle approval to cap trade margins on certain non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines at 30% of their maximum retail price (MRP).
Addressing presspersons in Bengaluru, Health Minister U.T. Khader said price rationalisation should translate into direct savings for patients, and urged the Union government to extend similar measures to other essential medicines where high treatment costs place a burden on patients.
At its meeting on October 8, the NPPA gave in-principle approval to rationalise trade margins on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines identified under Paragraph 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013. The measure is subject to finalisation of the list of medicines to be covered.
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has been asked to constitute an expert committee under the Directorate General of Health Services to recommend the anti-cancer medicines to be brought under price control. The committee is expected to submit its report by October 14.
The Centre estimates that the measure could reduce the MRP of several anti-cancer medicines by 20% to 70%, potentially saving patients around ₹2,500 crore. “The financial strain of cancer treatment often pushes families into debt, making it inevitable for them to exhaust their savings and sell assets to meet medical expenses,” Mr. Khader said.
Citing examples, the Minister said a cancer drug/injection costing around ₹3,250 was reportedly priced at ₹23,347. Medicines with a landing cost of about ₹3,000 are being sold at a cost of ₹27,000. Under the 30% trade-margin cap, the maximum price of a medicine would depend on its applicable pricing base and can substantially reduce out-of-pocket expenditure for patients, he explained.
Also Read: Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
Karnataka’s representation to the Centre
In a letter dated September 23 to Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda, the Karnataka government had sought national-level action after inspections in the State found substantial differences between the procurement costs of medicines and the prices charged to patients. The State identified pricing concerns involving 253 medicines and consumables with mark-ups.
Karnataka had sought the inclusion of advanced chemotherapy, targeted therapy and other expensive cancer medicines under the ambit of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, along with a comprehensive cap on trade margins for high-cost and life-saving medicines.
The State had also called for expanding the NPPA’s price-control oversight and strengthening enforcement against excessive charging and profiteering.
Disclosure of medicine costs in hospital bills
The State has also sought greater transparency in the prices charged to patients. A circular issued on October 1 asked healthcare institutions to disclose both the purchase or landing cost and the MRP of medicines in patient bills. The instructions are advisory in nature and are proposed to take effect from November 1.
Karnataka’s call follows observations by the Supreme Court questioning why the MRP of essential medicines, including cancer drugs, could not be capped at 16% above the price to retailers, as is applicable to scheduled medicines under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013.
The State said the proposed 30% trade-margin cap on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines should be followed by wider action to cover other essential, high-cost medicines, including those used in cardiac and kidney treatment, so that the benefits of price rationalisation reach patients directly.

India’s leprosy programme is falling short of several projections set for 2025-26. The country reported 91,783 new leprosy cases in 2025-26, 41.2% higher than the projected 65,000. New cases among children were 91.6% above the projection while the rate of Grade 2 Disability (G2D) among new cases was 1.34 per million, against a projected one per million.
India’s national prevalence rate was 0.56 cases per 10,000 population at the end of March 2026, below the elimination target of a prevalence rate below one case per 10,000.
But the burden remains concentrated geographically. Chhattisgarh had the highest prevalence among States/UTs at 1.66 cases per 10,000 population, followed by Jharkhand (1.51), Chandigarh (1.49), Odisha (1.25) and Maharashtra (1.14).
At the district level, 14.8% of districts had a prevalence rate above one case per 10,000 in 2025-26, down from 18.6% in 2013-14 but 114 districts still remained above the programme’s elimination target. Moreover, only 148 districts have provisionally achieved interruption of transmission, against a projected 300.
G2D was also concentrated in a few States/UTs. Chandigarh, Delhi, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Odisha together accounted for 42.5% of the 1,945 G2D cases reported in 2025-26. Chandigarh recorded the highest rate at 13.54 per million, followed by Delhi (11.53) and Chhattisgarh (7.87).
Single-Dose Rifampicin Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (SDR PEP), a preventive dose given to people who have been in contact with a leprosy patient, was administered to 91.2% of the 16.94 lakh eligible contacts in 2025-26, up from 71.4% of the 6.48 lakh in 2019-20.
Source: National Leprosy Eradication Programme (2025-26) and National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy 2023-2027

Welcome to Kernel Panic!, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
Even as AI supercharges digital scamming and cybercrime, it’s also being recruited in the fight to protect potential victims. Governments around the world have consistently struggled to address the global crisis of online crime, grappling with the limitations of attempting to crack down on criminals beyond their borders. This has inspired alternative efforts, like using automation to attempt to go after scammers en masse—perhaps by spamming the spammers to squander their resources. Now, AI platforms are turning these types of experiments into real tools in the fight against cybercrime.
For the last two years, the Australian company Apate, named after the Greek goddess of deception, has been building a system that diverts phone scammers onto calls with AI bots that are trained to keep conversations going as long as possible without, of course, ever actually falling for the scam. The goal is to give scammers enough hope that they stay on the phone, while also collecting intelligence about the scams they’re running.
“What we really like to think is that we’re building the perfect victims for scammers,” Dali Kaafar, the founder and CEO of Apate, tells us. “A minute that a scammer is talking to a bot or an agent is a minute where you’re probably saving hundreds, if not thousands of possible people being reached out to by that exact same scammer,” he says, referencing the ability for scammers to use automated dialing tools.
Kaafar says Apate’s platform, which is used by banks and supported by telecom companies, has around 350,000 bots. They not only pick up calls, but also infiltrate scam chat groups online and respond to text messages with similar goals of frustrating scammers while collecting intelligence from them. He says the company has collected more than 250,000 pieces of information about fraudsters in real-time, from scam URLs to money mule accounts and bank details.
The bots have different personalities, language skills, and profiles, Kaafar says, so scammers hopefully don’t detect that they’re conversing with an AI. Like real people, “sometimes [the bots] do have WhatsApp, sometimes they don’t. Sometimes they pick up the phone, sometimes they just actually hang up on the scammer saying, ‘I'll come back to you later,’” he says.
But are they convincing? Kernel Panic tested the tool using a demo version where users play the role of the scammer and talk to one of Apate’s AI “victims.” The personas are designed to express a healthy amount of skepticism but leave enough openings for scammers to continue to try to win them over, a dynamic that we could immediately feel and found intensely frustrating.
Scammers are likely familiar with this type of skeptical interaction, and Kaafar says that Apate calls regularly go on for more than two hours. In our testing, the Apate system was engaged and responsive, and the timing of the conversation felt natural, even with both of us tag-teaming the AI as a friend, “Lucy,” and her financial adviser “Mickey.” We did not succeed at getting the Apate AI system to invest in our cryptocurrency opportunity even after six minutes of diligent effort. (The returns are truly incredible, though, we swear.)
For now, even with Apate’s massive swarm of bots on the case, it’s only a matter of time before you get your next scam call or text. Cybercriminals initiate billions of messages and calls each year, with the most sophisticated operations running physical, industrial scale scamming sites. And while professional scambaiters and initiatives to infiltrate scam operations have done critical deterrent work for years, law enforcement and research efforts haven’t been able to stop the expansion of digital scamming overall.
But AI could create a new era for anti-scam efforts, not just scammers themselves. Better intelligence sharing between cops, social media companies, banks, and other industries is desperately needed and could potentially be aided by AI-driven monitoring and data analysis. Increasingly, too, innovative efforts have been looking to disrupt cybercriminals by exploiting their “psychological vulnerabilities.” In some cases, these psyops have included directly trolling those behind ransomware attacks. As the focus on disrupting scammers and cybercriminals expands, the use of generative AI as a way to keep them preoccupied, wasting resources, and not launching other attacks appears to be increasingly effective.
Take honeypots, for instance. For years, companies and security researchers have deployed false virtual machines to attract hackers, waste their time, gather information, and understand their secret hacking techniques. Mark Vero, a doctoral researcher at the department of computer science at ETH Zurich, says open source honeypot providers have increasingly been incorporating LLMs into their systems to make them appear more realistic.
In recent research, Vero and colleagues found an LLM-powered honey pot would keep AI agents attacking their system “significantly longer” than a honey pot with more predictable behavior. “The agentic attackers are much more convinced by the LLM simulated honeypots and they also mark them as actual honeypots at a much lower rate,” he says. “If these systems are built well enough, then I think it’s quite advantageous for defenders.”

Newly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as an attorney.
The conservative commentator is now facing scrutiny about her legal qualifications after she was pressed to explain them following her first White House briefing with the media.
As President Donald Trump spoke to reporters after the briefing on Tuesday, one asked him where Zacharia had passed the bar exam.
"What state did she pass the bar exam in? You said she is an attorney. Where did she pass the bar exam? Which state?" the reporter asked.
Trump then turned to Zacharia, standing behind him, and asked, "Which state?"
"When I moved to China," Zacharia answered.
Her response added to the confusion over where she may be licensed to practice law in the United States. State bar exams are generally administered in person within the jurisdiction.
In a statement, Zacharia said she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials." She did not say if she'd passed the bar in any state.
"Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team," Steven Cheung, White House communications director, said. "She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary."
Zacharia does not appear to be listed in the State Bar of California's attorney database, despite living and working in the state. She also does not appear to be listed in the D.C. Bar's member directory.
The Substack publication, Popular Information, reported earlier on Tuesday that it searched records in all 50 states and Washington, DC, and turned up no evidence that Zacharia is licensed to practice law.
Zacharia graduated from California's Pepperdine University in 2007 with a bachelor's degree in political science and government. She then received a law degree from the university's Caruso School of Law in 2011, according to the college.
The White House said that after she graduated, Zacharia moved to China with her husband for his job at an American private equity firm. She worked on international transaction law, according to the White House.
Her LinkedIn page says she served as general counsel for the California-based nonprofit Fix California from January 2024 to March 2025. More than a decade earlier, according to her LinkedIn, Zacharia worked as an associate at the Beijing-headquartered Zhong Lun Law Firm.
Trump announced Zacharia's appointment to the White House in a Truth Social post last week, saying she has an "unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning." He also referred to her as an attorney in the post.
In her own post that followed, Zacharia called serving Trump and the American people the "honor of a lifetime."
"I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work for him for a very long time," Zacharia said during Tuesday's White House press briefing.

Beneficiaries of the Public Distribution System (PDS) across Karnataka can use the ‘Anna Seve’ mobile application to complete their e-KYC process from October 14, allowing them to verify their identity without visiting fair price shops or government offices.
The app, which enables beneficiaries of schemes such as Anna Bhagya to complete e-KYC, was launched by Food, Civil Supplies and Consumer Affairs Minister Rizwan Arshad on October 1. It has so far been available on a pilot basis in eight districts.
Completed so far
According to the department, 1,60,267 beneficiaries in these districts completed e-KYC through the app between October 1 and 12. The app will now be available in the remaining districts as well.
Developed in collaboration with the National Informatics Centre and the Department of e-Governance, the app can be downloaded from the GooglePlay Store.
The facility is expected to help beneficiaries who migrate to cities and towns for work. Many had to travel to their native villages or visit government offices to complete the verification process. Others had to wait in long queues at fair price shops.
Repeat process
Of the 2,67,64,276 beneficiaries in Karnataka required to complete e-KYC, 2,06,76,278 had completed the process as on October 12. Beneficiaries who completed e-KYC more than a year ago must also repeat the process, according to a release from the department.
With October 20 set as the deadline, Mr. Arshad has urged those yet to complete the verification to use the app and finish the process at the earliest.

Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal
A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to rescind his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine."
Last week, Trump announced via social media he had struck a deal with Putin, whereby Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter."
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump wrote.
His announcement stunned lawmakers, who passed legislation this summer directing the president to impose significant tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil.
Those sanctions are aimed at targeting Russian officials, companies and financial institutions helping fuel Russia's war in Ukraine. The legislation was named in memory of the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, who helped negotiate Trump's support for the package.
"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded," wrote six Republican and six Democratic senators in a letter Tuesday to the president.
"The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," it read.
Senators said they recognized the need to lower energy costs for Americans — but maintained that allowing Russian diesel into global markets will offer "limited to no relief to Americans."
They added the deal "only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."
When asked about the letter, the White House referred back to comments President Trump made to reporters on Tuesday about concerns that Russia will use proceeds from the diesel agreement to purchase weapons.
"Nobody's telling me anything," Trump said. "That's a diesel deal. Not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices."
The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse. They were joined by Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.

William Shatner wasn’t sure if the audience would approve of his new documentary or not.
When the 95-year-old star took the stage at the Regal Times Square theater for the New York premiere of The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World he said “maybe you’ll like it, maybe you won’t.” But, the Captain Kirk actor declared, “you’re going to see a lovely film made by people who cared.”
Focusing on the original Star Trek series, which ran from 1966 to 1969, The Sixty-Year Mission is written and directed by Mark A. Altman, creator of the Inglorious Treksperts podcast. The documentary, which screened during New York Comic Con and hit select theaters this weekend, explores the show’s cultural impact and legacy, and also demonstrates how much it was a product of the political climate of the era in which it was made.
“I think audiences are pleasantly surprised that Sixty-Year Mission shows how the ‘60s shaped Star Trek,” Altman explains. For the film, Altman interviewed dozens of prominent fans and stars, from Shatner and Simon Pegg to Star Trek: The Next Generation stars Jonathan Frakes and Brent Spiner. The president’s niece—and Trek fan—Mary L. Trump praises the show’s pioneering representation, specifically Nichelle Nichols’ Lieutenant Uhura. George Takei, who played Sulu, gives a harrowing account of his time in an internment camp for Japanese Americans during World War II. Others discuss how characters like Spock became heroes for queer fans.
As has been well-documented, these considerations were important for Gene Roddenberry, the show’s creator, who died in 1991. He was a WWII veteran with a progressive bent despite years spent in traditionally conservative spaces like the US Army and the Los Angeles Police Department. Altman insists that “Captain Kirk was ‘JFK: Space Captain,’” and that President Kennedy’s idea of a New Frontier was the final frontier that Trek sought to explore.
Shatner, however, didn’t initially see the show that way at all. “I didn't think in those terms when they offered me the role,” says Shatner, who served as executive producer on Sixty-Year Mission. “I thought, ‘I got a regular paid job.’ Only later did the magic of Star Trek happen.”
Part of that magic, Shatner adds, is how “Star Trek had an effect on people’s lives.” Those people come from many backgrounds, and the show remained accessible because of the very special tension that existed within its politics, Altman explains. “Roddenberry was liberal on social issues but hard-nosed on defense, and that is absolutely what Star Trek is,” he says. “We need our phasers to defeat the Klingons, but we believe in a diverse crew.”
Karim Diané, who plays Jay-Den Kraag on Star Trek: Starfleet Academy, notes that as the person playing the first openly gay Klingon character in the franchise, he’s playing someone who means a lot to viewers. “I wish I could release the DMs because the love I've gotten is overwhelming,” Diané says.
Trek even had a point of view on AI that feels incredibly relevant in 2026 as Trump and Silicon Valley leaders talk about a new era of “superintelligence.” The franchise’s most recognizable AI—the android Data from Next Generation—was an ideal version of the technology. In that series Data consistently struggled to be understood, as both smarter than humans and incapable of emotional intelligence. One episode, “The Measure of a Man,” even addressed whether Data was his own being or merely property.
For Spiner, who played Data, AI’s modern incarnation is far from the thoughtful machine he portrayed. “If only AI could be what Data was: responsible, truly concerned about humanity, considering what serves humans best as opposed to what serves profit best,” he says.

For at least several decades, people have attributed the following quote as something physicist Albert Einstein once said: "Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow."
On social media, users' posts pairing the quote with Einstein's name have appeared, for example, on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived) and X (archived).
(@ramblingsloa via X)
However, no evidence supported the claim that Einstein ever said the words. Research into historical records found that other people expressed the exact same thought without Einstein's name as early as the 1970s. Other persons from decades prior shared the same general idea, albeit in different words, about learning from the past (yesterday), that you can only live in the now (today) and have aspirations for the future (tomorrow).
No records from the years during or immediately following Einstein's 1955 death featured the quote with his name. The authoritative compendium "The Ultimate Quotable Einstein" also did not include the quote — or similar thoughts — in its text, not even in its list of misattributions.
If Einstein had truly spoken or penned the thought, credible historical documents, such as books or newspapers, would contain that information. It would not only appear in social media posts and on quote-collecting websites — two types of sources that can lack credibility.
Some posts, for example on Facebook (archived) and Reddit (archived), featured the incorrectly attributed quote with the added line, "The important thing is not to stop questioning." Einstein truly once said that sentence while talking about pursuing curiosity in life. Life magazine printed the "not to stop questioning" quote without the "Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow" part in 1955.
Researching the quote
As a small part of beginning our research, we noted that searching Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo failed to locate any credible historical records documenting that Einstein said, "Learn from yesterday, live for today, hope for tomorrow."
To perform deeper and more meaningful research, we then looked to archives of literature via Google Books, as well as newspapers on Newspapers.com, where we found several interesting results — though none indicated Einstein ever said the words.
For example, in 1965, a Kentucky newspaper credited a teacher named Donna Jean Roberts as saying, "Learn from yesterday and hope for tomorrow, but live today for today."
A 1971 Indiana newspaper article reported, "HERE'S A slogan which makes sense to Mack McGinnis: 'Live for Today—Dream for Tomorrow — Learn from Yesterday."
In 1972, a newspaper in Illinois printed the earliest record we found of the exact quote that users later wrongly attributed to Einstein. The paper credited the thought as the class motto for Gardner High School in Gardner, Illinois. Some books published in the 1970s also featured the exact quote without any direct attribution.
A 2000 classified advertisement for a California mobile glass company featured possibly the earliest newspaper record of the quote containing the attribution to Einstein. According to Google Books, the 1998 edition of "The Michiganensian," the University of Michigan's annual yearbook, also showed the quote with Einstein's name.
In 2011, an author wrote a book with the quote as the title, saying in the text that he was inspired to publish the work thanks to Einstein supposedly penning the thought.
1930 article about meaning of 'Today'
In all of our searches, one California newspaper article from 1930 featured the Chicago Journal of Commerce opining in a unique way about the meaning of "Today":
We live only today. Yesterday we lived, and through all the multitude of yesterdays, each of which had its influence in making us what we are today. What we do and are today will have its effect on what we shall do and be tomorrow.
We all live in the present—not in the past, which is gone forever, nor in the future which we cannot know until time makes it the present for us. We all have aspirations as to what we shall be and do in the future, but we have only our todays in which to put in action the principles and forces by which we may make our tomorrows what we would have them be.
We may, and must, learn from our yesterdays in order to make today count in our ambitions. Our mistakes in the past are warnings. Our achievements alone can encourage us by promises for the future. We all have our settled purposes as well as our past experiences, to guide us. Thus memories have power to help us to the future we desire. The purpose is a powerful incentive, strengthened by the knowledge if what has been accomplished in the past through definite purpose.
We learn from the past that all good things come slowly, that we must earn every advance we make. That is what makes today so prodigiously important to thinking men. It is the introduction to our tomorrow. When we go to bed after having done our level best, we have the finest assurance that we can do better tomorrow.

Pope admitted to hospital for surgery to remove lump on his lung
- Published
Pope Leo XIV has been admitted to Rome's Gemelli Hospital for surgery to remove a lump on his lung, detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks".
It said the operation would take place on Tuesday afternoon.
The 71-year-old pontiff was met at the hospital by a large crowd, some of whom had been waiting outside for several hours to catch a glimpse of him.
They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, waving and smiling back through the lowered back window of his car.
He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured.
It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing.
He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed.
The Vatican said the Pope would be operated on by the Gemelli's thoracic surgery team and promised an update on his condition on Tuesday evening.
His schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous. But doctors say when a lump is removed it will usually be tested to check for any sign of the disease.
The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.
Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo wrote on social media that he'd had an audience with Pope Leo on Monday, and said the pontiff felt "nothing wrong" physically.
He said the Pope had decided to check in for surgery as soon as possible because he was due to travel to Latin America in early November, and was keen to stick to that plan.
The trip is particularly significant because it includes a visit to Peru, where the pontiff was a missionary and then a Bishop for many years.
Despite all the reassurances, the news has shaken Catholics all over the world.
"Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn't expecting anything like this," Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Parolin told journalists on Tuesday.
He agreed that the news was like a "bolt from the blue", but said the cardinals had been struck by the Pope's "serenity" and were confident in his recovery.
Outside Gemelli Hospital, which has treated several popes and is home to a large statue of John Paul II, a few Catholics lingered after the pontiff was admitted.
Carla had come specially, wanting to be close.
"He seems calm, so we are calm too - even though illness is always unpleasant," she told the BBC. "We will wait here and pray."
"I was in St Peter's Square when he made the announcement, and I felt really awful," said Elsa, who was also present. "I was really taken aback," she said, explaining that when Pope Leo was elected she had thought he was a younger, healthier pontiff.
"It turns out he's vulnerable too. I really hope it's something superficial, that can be contained, like he told us."

Afcon final to play out in court - when will Morocco or Senegal be crowned champions?
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes but, in its own way, the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) has been playing out for nearly nine months.
Now, finally, one team or the other - either Morocco or Senegal - willl grab the winner. Only that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.
On Thursday, Sport's highest legal authority - the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) - will hear Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they had won back in January against the hosts in Rabat.
But those hungry for a resolution have already been warned it will not arrive on the same day.
So how did we get here? And what happens next?
What happened in the Afcon final?
In front of 66,000 home fans creating an electric atmosphere inside Rabat's Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco appeared set for a date with destiny as they chased their first Afcon title since 1976.
Instead, the final descended into chaos deep into stoppage time.
With the match still goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had already blown for a Moroccan free-kick.
The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a VAR review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.
Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.
Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Real Madrid's Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the grateful arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.
Or so they thought.
- 'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Senegal's triumph 
  - Published19 January
- Senegal decries imprisonment of fans after Afcon clashes 
  - Published24 February
Why was the Afcon final result overturned?
Unsurprisingly the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing Senegal had breached competition regulations.
Article 82, contained within a chapter titled "Withdrawals", states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team… leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" they shall be "considered the loser and shall be eliminated from the current competition".
In March, a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.
While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, others, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.
The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.
- Afcon final 'deficiencies' dealt with - Motsepe 
  - Published13 May
- Denounce 'abject' Afcon decision - senior Caf member 
  - Published19 March
What is the Court of Arbitration for Sport?
Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.
For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.
More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.
The appeal will be heard by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.
In this instance, the panel will be led by 76-year-old Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
If the panel fails to come to a consensus, its president will make the final decision.
- How does Cas work and why can't Man City appeal to it? 
  - Published28 September
When will we get a verdict?
While the hearing, which will be heard in private at the request of the parties involved, is expected to end on Thursday afternoon, Cas have already warned that this is merely the starting point of the panel's deliberation.
In a statement, the court warned it "cannot state when a final decision will be rendered but it will not be on the day of the hearing".
Having already waited nearly nine months to get to this stage, the bad news is that the Cas code states that appeal verdicts should be delivered a maximum of four months after a hearing, though guidelines also say panels should aim for less than three months.
The good news is that it can be quicker.
In 2020, Manchester City appealed to Cas over Uefa's decision to ban them from European club competitions for breaching financial fair play regulations.
The hearing took place on 8 June with the verdict landing in City's favour on 13 July.
What could the long-term fallout be?
Even though Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has already been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe said back in March that they will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.
The Teranga Lions' walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at a referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, back in April.
"This new rule will also apply to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Thiaw has already been given his marching orders by Senegal, having lost his job following the team's last-32 World Cup exit, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Moroccan dugout back in January, was dismissed in March.
Both men will no doubt still view success with Cas as a moral victory.
Whatever the outcome, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.
The FMRF's senior hierarchy were furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.
The FSF and the Senegalese government have, meanwhile, leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.
Other incidents also irked them, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which eventually led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.
With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.
But while the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

Thundering to a crowd of thousands of far-right supporters in São Paulo on 7 September, Brazil’s Independence Day, the senator Flávio Bolsonaro focused less on his opponent in the presidential election, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, than on someone who is not running at all.
“Whoever votes for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes,” Bolsonaro shouted, referring to the shaven-headed supreme court justice once described as “Voldemort” by Elon Musk.
Although Lula did not appoint Moraes to the court, Bolsonaro’s supporters have linked the two men ever since the judge oversaw the case in which the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup.
Now, just days before the election runoff on 25 October, Moraes is once again at the centre of a presidential scandal – one that Lula believes may have helped Flávio Bolsonaro overtake him to emerge as the frontrunner. The justice once hailed as democracy’s “saviour” for containing Jair Bolsonaro may now have helped pave the way for the family’s return to power.
The scandal began with a police investigation, which found that Moraes’s wife’s law firm had a contract worth about £20m with Daniel Vorcaro, the banker accused of orchestrating Brazil’s largest banking fraud. Text messages also emerged suggesting a close relationship between Moraes and Vorcaro, though the judge denies the messages are authentic.
Investigations subsequently revealed that at least four other justices had links to the disgraced banker, meaning half of the court’s 10 current justices have been drawn into the scandal.
The crisis peaked last month with a ferocious exchange of insults between Moraes and another justice during a televised court session. A series of rulings followed in which the pair – as well as other judges aligned with each side – overruled one another, dominating public debate for weeks.
Lula, the day after losing the first round, blamed his poor result in part on having to “carry on his back … the promiscuity” of the supreme court, in what many political observers saw as an attempt by the president to distance himself from the crisis. His campaign coordinator, Edinho Silva, said that, “in the eyes of society … [Lula] paid the price for that institutional damage”.
Although analysts point to a range of reasons for the far right’s lead, from household debt to a simple preference for Flávio Bolsonaro, many agree that the supreme court crisis played a decisive role, particularly among indecisive voters who, with the electorate generally divided between two similarly sized left and right blocs, are the ones who ultimately decide the election.
“These are people who thought that, just as they see congress, the country’s highest court had become corrupt, too. That deepened apathy among some who might otherwise have voted for Lula and fuelled the anti-system sentiment that feeds the far right,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right and has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters.
“We asked people about the court crisis, and they would say: ‘Everything is very confusing, but one thing we do know is that the big villain is Alexandre de Moraes,’” she said. “Precisely the judge who jailed Jair Bolsonaro now emerges, for these people, as the big corrupt figure and the main villain.”
Conrado Hübner Mendes, a professor of constitutional law at the University of São Paulo and a leading scholar of the supreme court, said Moraes put himself in that position by “embracing the role of heroic protagonist”.
The judge blocked some of Jair Bolsonaro’s moves during his government and drew the ire of far-right figures such as Musk and Donald Trump. The US went as far as to impose sanctions on him, in a move widely seen as an attempt to interfere in Jair’s trial.
On Monday, Moraes authorised Flávio Bolsonaro to resume visiting his father after a 90-day ban imposed in July, when the senator read out a letter from his father that Moraes considered a breach of Jair Bolsonaro’s ban on using social media.
Legal scholars and some on the Brazilian left, while acknowledging Moraes’s decisive role in the coup trial, have also criticised several of his other rulings as authoritarian.
“He took on a huge responsibility, and now he has thrown that away in the most mediocre way possible, with this alleged corruption case,” said Mendes.
While acknowledging the contract between the law firm run by his wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes, and the disgraced banker – who is worth an extraordinarily large sum by Brazilian law firm standards – Moraes denied any wrongdoing. He said he had never ruled on any case involving Vorcaro and that there was therefore no conflict of interest.
Vorcaro has been behind bars since he was arrested in November as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta. He is accused of leading a scheme through his Banco Master involving aggressive fundraising, unrealistic returns and falsified balance sheets that left an estimated £9bn hole, much of it involving public money and pensioners’ savings.
Text messages extracted from Vorcaro’s phone show that, two days before his arrest, the banker asked someone whom police later identified as Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?” Moraes denies being the recipient and accuses a fellow justice, André Mendonça, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, of using the police against him for electoral reasons, allegedly to benefit Flávio’s campaign.
Mendonça is one of the four other justices suspected of having links to Vorcaro. An institute he created is said to have taken out an £800,000 loan from one of the banker’s associates, though he says it has already been repaid. In the other justices’ cases, investigators uncovered links ranging from a £64m contract to an alleged stake in a fund that received £5.2m from Vorcaro. All deny wrongdoing.
No reports had linked Lula to the scandal until Friday, when Veja magazine reported that Vorcaro allegedly said he had paid £4.5m to finance a 2024 Oliver Stone documentary about the president. The federal police and the public prosecutor’s office, however, said the banker had neither made the allegation nor provided evidence to support it in his testimony. Lula denied receiving money from the banker.
Flávio Bolsonaro is being investigated over what happened to the £20m he was caught on tape asking Vorcaro to provide for a biopic about his father. One suspicion is that the money helped cover living and travel expenses for his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, during his self-imposed exile in the US, where he lobbied the Trump administration against Lula. The senator said all the money went towards sponsoring the film, which still has no release date.
Besides Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead, the far right’s sweeping victory ensured an even more conservative congress in 2027, including the senate majority needed to impeach supreme court justices – a demand among his father’s supporters since the former president was convicted.
“With the scandal, the justices handed Bolsonarismo something it still didn’t have: an impeachable offence that could justify their removal,” said Mendes. “A court that ignores conflicts of interest and immerses itself in relationships with political and economic power is a court that has already become corrupted.”
Even if no justice is impeached, should Bolsonaro win, he could be entitled to fill four seats as justices retire during his term, leaving the court with at least six of its 11 members appointed by either him or his father.
“We can expect a court completely servile to the government,” Mendes said, adding that the separation of powers would be at risk and that the justices themselves bear part of the responsibility.
“The court ended up doing to itself the work an autocratic project needs – and brought itself down”.

A former Ukrainian army officer is going on trial in Germany this week over undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany four years ago in one of the biggest acts of sabotage in Europe since the Second World War.
The suspect faces charges of causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public service and being an “accomplice to war crimes” by attacking civilian infrastructure, according to prosecutors.
The attack laid bare Europe's dependence on Russian energy but also raised sensitive questions about Ukraine and its Western allies.
While international observers initially blamed Moscow, there are now increasing suggestions that Ukrainian state security agencies may have been involved — even though Ukraine counts Germany as one of its closest allies.
According to German privacy rules, the suspect will be identified in court only as Serhii K., although he was publicly named as Serhii Kuznietsov in extradition proceedings in Italy.
Here's what we know about the alleged ringleader of the attack and one of the most politically charged court cases of wartime sabotage that will be heard at the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg starting this Wednesday.
Prosecutors say Nord Stream plot aimed to cut Russian gas revenues for war
The explosions on Sept. 26, 2022, damaged pipelines that were built to carry Russian natural gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea.
At the time, European countries were moving to wean themselves off Russian energy sources, following the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Prosecutors say the aim of the plot was to permanently disrupt gas deliveries and prevent Russia from using the revenues to finance its military operations.
The defendant and others allegedly used a yacht that set off from the German port of Rostock. It had been hired from a German company using forged IDs and with the help of intermediaries.
The explosions ruptured the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which was Russia’s main natural gas supply route to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which never entered service because Germany suspended its certification process shortly before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
The suspect allegedly organized and carried out the detonation of at least four bombs between 14 and 27 kilograms (around 31 to 62 pounds) at a depth of 70 to 80 meters (230 feet to 263 feet) near the Danish island of Bornholm.
He was detained in August in an Italian village, where officers raided a bungalow where he was staying with his family. Police said he surrendered without resistance. He was extradited to Germany in November.
A second suspect was arrested on a European warrant in the northern Croatian town of Pula in August. He has applied for asylum in Croatia to fight his extradition to Germany.
Russia has accused the US of staging the explosions, a charge Washington has denied
The pipelines were long a target of criticism by the U.S. and some of its allies, which warned that they increased dependence on Russian gas.
Russian officials, however, have claimed that U.S. and British intelligence agencies were involved in staging the explosions, which Moscow declared “an act of international terrorism,” and have launched their own investigation.
Russia has also accused NATO of involvement in the attack, while several Western countries initially blamed Russia.
More recently, the Kremlin has expressed hope that those who orchestrated the explosions will be held accountable.
Asked what Moscow expects from the trial, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Monday that “we expect objectivity.”
“We expect … that both the perpetrators and those who ordered it will be named. That would be very important. I think no one doubts who it really is,” Peskov said.
Ukraine has denied allegations it was involved in the attack
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts.
He also told reporters in August that Ukraine’s prosecutors and Foreign Ministry were already cooperating with partners and that Kyiv was “absolutely open to joint steps on the investigation,” stressing the importance of keeping Europe’s trust.
Nonetheless, “all the evidence points very clearly to the fact that Ukraine blew up the Nord Stream pipelines, not the Russians, whom they initially tried to pin the blame on,” says Joachim Weber, a security expert at the Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies at the University of Bonn.
“This is, of course, highly explosive politically, because, as is well known, Germany is one of Ukraine’s closest allies, supporting the country on a massive scale with huge sums of money and also by taking on considerable political risks,” Weber said.
However, the German government has so far refrained from comment on the upcoming trial, pointing out that no verdict has yet been reached and the case is in the hands of the independent judiciary.
Even a conviction would likely have little impact on German-Ukrainian relations
Even if it were proven in the course of the trial that Ukrainian government agencies were somehow involved in the sabotage act, that would likely have few consequences for Germany’s relationship with Ukraine, “because we naturally want Ukraine to survive,” not least as a buffer against Russia, said Weber.
“In that respect — even if it sounds cynical to some — Ukraine also serves a purpose for us, and it is in our interest to preserve it,” he said.
The outcome of the trial is unlikely to have major repercussions on German-Ukrainian relations, he argued.
“In short, I don’t see us going through some kind of list of punishments against Ukraine right now,” Weber said. “But we should take this as a warning, so to speak, to view things realistically.”
___
Niemann reported from Bonn, Germany. AP writers Hanna Arhirova in Kyiv, Ukraine and Jovana Gec in Belgrade, Serbia contributed reporting.

Priya (name changed), 32, from Kerala, had been struggling with recurring episodes of depression that affected her ability to carry out everyday activities. Despite taking medication for several weeks, she continued to experience symptoms. With her symptoms persisting, she sought further medical advice and is now undergoing repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). This non-invasive procedure uses magnetic pulses to stimulate specific areas of the brain.
Priya’s experience reveals a challenge in managing depression, say experts. While antidepressants help many people, some continue to experience symptoms despite treatment, requiring doctors to reassess the diagnosis and consider other interventions.

A large randomised controlled trial among heart failure patients in India led by the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST) in Kerala, has found that hospitalisation episodes and all-cause mortality among heart failure patients can be significantly reduced if patients are systematically followed-up by a nurse, with the help of a mobile health application.
The two-year Telemonitoring and Integrated Multidisciplinary care for Heart Failure (TIME-HF) trial found that heart failure patients with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) who received nurse-led collaborative care had a 22% lower risk of death than those receiving usual care. They were also more likely to remain alive without hospitalisation during the two-year follow-up.
The trial results were published in the American Heart Association’s Journal, Circulation, on August 30, 2026.
What makes the trial relevant is that it addresses critical gaps in heart failure care: in Keralam, heart failure registries have reported high mortality post-discharge — 82.7% mortality over 10 years, alongside the fact fact that only 25.4% of the patients with heart failure receive guideline-based therapies. It also holds lessons for the rest of the country: with nearly 27% of all deaths in India being due to heart disease, and 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease occurring between the ages of 40 and 69 years, there is an urgent need for quality, post-discharge care.
What the trial did
The TIME-HF trial involved 1,507 adults at 22 government and private hospitals in Keralam and neighbouring States, with 755 patients assigned to the intervention and 752 to usual care. The mean age was 61.9 years; 77.6% were men, 57.3% lived in rural areas and 70% had relatively low educational attainment. Ischaemic heart disease was the predominant cause of heart failure, accounting for 77.4% of cases.
Results indicated that nurse-led intervention substantially improved prescription of the four major components of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure — renin-angiotensin system inhibition/ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors.
“Our heart failure patients receive sub-optimal care, as most of them do not adhere to therapies or follow up with the doctor on time. There is also the issue of physician inertia. HF Registry evidence indicates that the median survival after diagnosis of heart failure is just 3.7 years. This collaborative care model is proof that survival and quality of life of these patients can be improved if we systematically address the gaps in care so that proven therapies for heart failure become part of routine care,” said lead researcher and additional professor at SCTIMST P. Jeemon.
Centring nursing care
The model put a trained nurse at the centre of the care pathway, who would closely monitor heart failure patients after discharge, educate the patient and family about heart-failure self-care, lifestyle modification and encourage medication adherence.
Nurses reviewed the patients’ medication regimen at discharge to ensure that there was no deviation from the guideline-mediated therapies. This was again reviewed at every follow-up visit with the help of a mobile-health app. The m-health app helped the nurses monitor all physical parameters of the patient real time and to identify warning signs of worsening disease, communicate and connect with patients and physicians so that timely hospitalisation was possible.
All participants underwent scheduled follow-up visits every three months for two years. Adherence to all four guideline-directed medical therapies was only 22.1% in the usual-care group, while it was 37.3% in the intervention group at two years.
“The health system engaging with the patient regularly was the key here. The m-health app gave the patient updates in real time to the nurse. Oxygen saturation levels, weight gain, weight loss, drop in blood pressure or respiratory rate comes as alerts, and then were escalated to the physician,” Dr. Jeemon points out.
The TIME-HF trial thus helped address one of the health system’s persistent weaknesses: that of proper follow-up care of patients with chronic diseases. The model is suited for strengthening chronic disease management and reducing the burden of hospitalisation and mortality in resource-limited settings across the country, experts said.

The Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) legal head, Ratna Singh, alleged that Delhi Police arrested CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde on Wednesday (October 14, 2026).
In a post on X, Ms. Singh said, “Delhi Police arrests Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka, and Ajinkya Shinde at Parliament Street Police Station in today’s Jantar Mantar case.”
She added that the charges included “trespass, bond violation, obstruction of public official’s duty, etc.”
In another post, Ms. Singh said she had been informed that the three leaders were likely to be produced before the Sub-Divisional Executive Magistrate (SEM) at Mandir Marg Police Station within an hour.
On Tuesday (October 13), Delhi Police filed an FIR against Mr. Das, Mr. Ranka and other CJP members for allegedly trespassing into the Jantar Mantar area without authorisation.
The action came hours after the activists entered the heavily barricaded protest site and raised slogans demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Jantar Mantar was recently denotified as a designated protest site.
Mr. Das, Mr. Ranka and several other CJP members were detained early on Tuesday after allegedly entering the area in violation of prohibitory orders.

If you’re a PC gamer waiting to experience Grand Theft Auto 6, there is one question that has been on your mind: when will GTA 6 be on PC? Well, the game is still listed for only PS5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles. But reports suggest a PC port may arrive earlier than expected. With that in mind, we have compiled all GTA 6 PC release date statements, rumors, and leaks. This will give you a realistic outlook on when you can expect to play GTA 6 on your computer.
Will GTA 6 Be on PC at Launch?
Here’s your answer: GTA 6 is not coming to PC at launch.
Currently, Rockstar’s official website lists GTA 6 only for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles, with a release date of November 19, 2026.
Rockstar has not officially announced the PC version yet. However, a GTA 6 PC release is widely expected soon after the console rollout.
In fact, the company’s game release history makes a PC version highly likely. So, until Rockstar announces the PC port for GTA 6 officially, any dates circulating online for the same should be treated as pure speculation.
What Is the Speculated GTA 6 Release Date for PC?
There is currently no official GTA 6 PC release date.
But according to a new GamesBeat report, which cites four credible sources familiar with Rockstar’s plans for GTA 6 coming to PC, we have a new PC release window.
Rockstar Games may target a Q1 2027 release window, meaning the GTA 6 PC release date will be sometime between January and March 2027.
Other recent rumors complement this report and suggest the GTA 6 PC version could release sooner due to the rapid rise in console prices. VGC editor-in-chief Andy Robinson said in September 2026 that there was a “bit of noise” suggesting Rockstar could push the PC version up and it might arrive earlier than expected.
Could GTA 6 Come to PC in 2026?
At this point, a GTA 6 PC release in 2026 looks unlikely. Rockstar is just two months away from the confirmed launch, and its website lists just the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S consoles as the official GTA 6 supported platforms.
Realistically speaking, a surprise announcement seems nearly impossible, and PC players might have to wait until 2027 or later.
History of PC Ports for Previous Rockstar Games
If we’ve learned anything from Rockstar’s past grand escapades, it’s that patience is a virtue, especially for PC players. Think back to the launch of Grand Theft Auto 5. Consoles started the party in September 2013, but we PC fans had to wait until April 2015—a good year and a half!
Below, you can find how long it took for GTA 5, Red Dead Redemption 2, and GTA IV to come out on PC.
| Game | Initial Release Date | PC Release Date | 
|---|---|---|
| GTA 3 | October 22, 2001 | – | 
| Max Payne 2 | October 14, 2003 | – | 
| GTA Vice City | October 29, 2002 | May 1, 2003 | 
| GTA San Andreas | October 26, 2004 | – | 
| GTA 4 | April 29, 2008 | December 3, 2008 | 
| Red Dead Redemption | May 18, 2010 | October 29, 2024 | 
| Max Payne 3 | May 15, 2012 | May 29, 2012 | 
| GTA 5 | September 17, 2013 | April 14, 2015 | 
| Red Dead Redemption 2 | October 26, 2018 | November 5, 2019 | 
Personally, I don’t think Rockstar will take too long to make GTA 6 for PC. Going by previous data, we can see that PC gamers had to wait a maximum of 9 months for the GTA 4 release on PC.
Speaking of GTA 5, the game was first made for PS3 and Xbox 360. Then, it was made for PS4, and then the PC version came almost two years later.
The latest example, Red Dead Redemption 2, is a suitable one for reference, as its PC version came after 13 months. Although the above timelines for Rockstar’s PC ports may seem long, the company will definitely not keep a huge chunk of their community waiting.
That said, we should assume that we might be able to drive through the streets of Leonida on the GTA 6 map on our PCs in early 2027.
Can You Play GTA 6 on PC Through Xbox?
This could have been one of the biggest GTA 6 PC stories and a big win for Xbox, but ultimately, it was one of the messiest reports.
A report from The Verge claimed that Microsoft had secured the streaming rights that could allow you to play GTA 6 through Xbox Cloud Gaming when it launches on November 19, 2026.
For PC players, this sounded like a potential loophole because there is no PC port at the moment, but they still got a way to play the game on a computer. But then Xbox CSO Matthew Ball had to post an official response on X, confirming that was not the case. The Verge’s reporting was, well, incorrect, and Ball stated that the game would not be streaming exclusively to PC.
Understand that with cloud gaming, the game runs on remote hardware and is streamed to your device. A native GTA 6 PC version would actually need to be installed and run on your PC. So, it is not confirmed to be on your computer at launch.
Will GTA 6 Release on PC in 2027?
Given the significant presence of PC gaming in the market as of 2026, GTA 6 developer Rockstar Games cannot ignore the considerable demand within the industry (and community).
However, early 2027 seems to be the most reasonable year to discuss a potential GTA 6 PC release, but it is not confirmed yet.
While this might be speculation, the game will ultimately come to PC, although not when it is initially released worldwide. Even Take-Two’s CEO is considering an updated PC strategy due to the consoles becoming commercially unviable over time.
So, will GTA 6 reach our PCs in 2027? Only Rockstar’s official announcement can confirm it. For now, the historical release pattern, logical development considerations, and even some intriguing industry chatter all point toward a first quarter of 2027 arrival.
The wait might feel like navigating Los Santos traffic during rush hour, but the potential payoff is huge: enhanced graphics, unlocked frame rates, and the glorious world of PC mods (maybe a GTA 6 metaverse). The wait will undoubtedly be worth it. Keep those rigs ready; Vice City in GTA 6 might be hitting our PC screens sooner than you think!
What do you think of the GTA 6 PC release window of 2027? Are you getting a console, or have you already started checking the GTA 6 requirements to upgrade your build? Tell us in the comments.

Nice compact size for smaller hands or reading on the go. Aluminum back makes the e-reader heavier, but not so heavy it's uncomfortable. Colors are beautiful. Double the storage of the plastic version. Compatible with new Kindle Click remote. Aluminum is ad-free (plastic version can be ad-free if you pay extra).
TIRED
Expensive for the least amount of features in a Kindle. No warm light, and no auto-adjusting light like you'll get on the aluminum version of other Kindles. Not compatible with Kindle Page Turn Cover.
The Kindle Aluminum has no right to be this beautiful.
Amazon announced a new Kindle lineup at the start of the month, with new versions of the Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft. The base Kindle is the first one available, with both a plastic version and an aluminum version. It's simply named the Kindle Aluminum, while the aluminum versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft are now the new Signature Editions with extra features (like wireless charging, an auto-adjusting front light, and a couple AI features).
The Kindle Aluminum only offers the AI features compared to the Signature Editions, while also including a different body, 32 GB of storage, and no lock screen ads. It's not really enough to validate the price change, yet still I find myself loving it.
Notably, it comes in two colors, Seaglass Green and Alpine Sky. The latter is currently sitting just a few inches away from me as I write this, glinting in the sunlight. It's the shade of blue I had hoped the MacBooks would be when Apple released its Sky Blue color in 2025, and every single reader friend I've shown it to has said they want it for the color alone. Even my editor, who strongly prefers physical books (which is hilarious given that she edits my ever-growing list of e-reader reviews, including this one), said just looking at my photos made her want one.
It's a smart move on Amazon's part. There's little reason to upgrade your Kindle if you already have one, but most generations only came in black. The last generation just had one color for the Kindle and one for the Paperwhite. Now, with the base Kindle, you have two colors of the plastic version (the classic black and Ube purple) and the aforementioned green or blue aluminum—these options could have plenty of existing Kindle owners champing at the bit to upgrade.
But it's hard to say it's worth it just for the color, since you could always buy a case instead. It's not a bad device, and there are some improvements—just not enough to justify the price tag.
New Body, Same System
The 12th-generation Kindle still has the same 6-inch screen, but the device's overall form factor has changed. The screen is flush with the rest of the body now, rather than sitting indented, and the new Kindle body is actually a quarter of an inch shorter than the 2024 Kindle's. That sounds like a small increment (and it is!), but having both devices side-by-side, it was easy to spot. The new Kindle also felt like it fit better in my palm, perhaps due to the smoother aluminum backing.
It's also heavier, thanks to the backing. Amazon says the Kindle Aluminum is 5.7 ounces, while the plastic 2026 Kindle is 4.9 ounces. (The 2024 plastic Kindle is 5.56 ounces.) Despite the tiny difference in weight between the 2024 Kindle and the new aluminum version, the aluminum felt palpably heavier to me—almost as if felt like my hand was putting more effort into holding it up. I double-checked on my kitchen scale, and it really is only a 0.2-ounce difference. I had my husband try both models, and he agreed that the aluminum felt heavier and was surprised at how small the difference really was. I think the smaller frame makes the weight sit a little differently.
Opening the 2026 Kindle Aluminum sends you to the same interface as any other Kindle. You'll have a homepage and your library page, and the same set of menus by tapping the right-hand corner dots or swiping down from the top of the page. I did find that while the page-turn speed seemed nearly identical, the new Kindle opened up books much faster than the 2024 Kindle. On the latter, I always had to wait a handful of seconds for my latest Kindle Unlimited read to open (I'll own up to it currently being Verity, my first and very likely last Colleen Hoover book), but the 2026 Kindle near-instantly opened it each time.
The other difference turned out to be the front lights. While neither model has a warm-color front light, the Kindle Aluminum's light tone seemed a touch warmer than the bright-blue tinge of the 2024 Kindle. It was still too blue to comfortably read in dark mode before bed, but side by side, I could see an improvement. It's hard to tell in my photo below, but I know I'm not hallucinating after seeing multiple similar photos already uploaded to the Kindle's Amazon reviews.
Colorful Cost
Ultimately, you don't need this Kindle if you already have one, and $190 is a steep price to pay for a model that doesn't even have a warm option for the front light. The real draw here remains the color body, and Amazon has done a good job with this. My TikTok feed is full of e-reader fans talking about the Ube shade, while the shine of the Alpine Sky is one I would've been eyeing had I not ended up reviewing it. I also like that the aluminum body really does feel like an upgrade when I hold it in my hands.
Amazon might be trying to take a page from Apple's playbook for the iPhone, encouraging you to upgrade your Kindle every two years for the new colors, the way superfans update their smartphones. While Kindle has a much lower cost of entry, that's because a smartphone comes with many more features and upgrades. The Kindle will always have one use: as an e-reader that shows you books. Unlike the second- to third-gen Kindle Scribe update, Kindle isn't providing a new homepage experience, though you will get two of the AI-powered features the Scribes have (Story So Far, to recap where you left off in a story, and Ask This Book—coming soon, to ask about a story). You aren't even getting the auto-adjusting light that aluminum versions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft will have.
It's a good gift for Christmas for someone who already has everything, or an excuse to finally upgrade your own Kindle if it's starting to lag. But you might also want to wait and see if the Paperwhite or Colorsoft Signature Editions are the way to go instead, especially since only those two models will be compatible with the new Kindle Page Turn Cover ($80) that will give you on-device page-turn buttons. Neither the 2026 Kindle Aluminum nor the plastic version will be compatible with this accessory, making it even harder to justify upgrading, but they will at least work with the Kindle Click remote ($35).
Again, this isn't a bad Kindle. The faster book openings and slightly warmer (though still not actually warm) front light, and double the storage make it a legitimate upgrade to the 2024 model. If you don't already have a Kindle, it's not a bad choice if you want to get one of the prettiest models available. It's up to you if that's worth spending almost $200 on.
You'll likely be just as happy with the plastic Ube version and spend between $20 and $40 less, depending on whether you want ads or not (though it does have half the storage of the aluminum model, at 16 GB). Still, this is a much higher price than these basic Kindles used to be available for. Hopefully we will see these Kindles on sale for Black Friday, but I wouldn't hold my breath for any good sales this year.

Srinagar, Oct 13: In an initiative aimed at recognising the contribution of golf caddies, encouraging youth participation in sports and promoting golf tourism in Kashmir, prominent hotelier and entrepreneur Akib Chaya, under the banner of Hilltop Hotels, organised the Swing in Autumn Caddy Golf Tournament at the Kashmir Golf Course (KGC), Srinagar.
The tournament, as per a statement, brought together caddies, senior golfers, prominent personalities from the hospitality and tourism sectors, and distinguished guests in a celebration of sportsmanship, opportunity and community participation.
Salman Sagar and Ehsan Pardesi graced the occasion as Guests of Honour, extending their encouragement and support to the participating caddies and the initiative.
The event was also attended by several respected senior golfers, including Ashraf Bakshi, Javed Bakshi, Sohail Kirmani, Ghulam Rasool Guroo, Usman Fazil, Manzoor Abbas and Sameer Bhat, whose presence added significance to the occasion.
Prominent dignitaries from various organisations included Mushtaq Chaya, President, Hoteliers Club; Tariq Ghani, President, Chamber of Commerce and Industry; Sheikh Feroz, President, J&K Hajj and Umrah Services; Sameer Baktoo, President, Eco Tourism; Nasir Hamid Khan, Honorary Secretary, Amar Singh Club; and Murad Kapra, Joint Secretary, Hoteliers Club.
Speaking about the initiative, Akib Chaya emphasised that the tournament was not merely about competitive golf but about recognising the invaluable role played by caddies in sustaining and developing the sport.
“Golf has given me tremendous joy, and having learnt the game at Kashmir Golf Course myself, I feel a personal connection with this place and the people associated with it. Our caddies are an integral part of the golfing community, and they deserve recognition, encouragement and opportunities to grow.”
Chaya further highlighted the potential of golf as a meaningful avenue of employment for Kashmir’s youth.
