The ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 is a practical, performance-driven business laptop featuring a powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, an exceptional keyboard, excellent port selection, and easy RAM/storage upgradability. However, its main drawbacks are mediocre battery life, a dim display limited to 45% NTSC, and an underwhelming webcam.
ASUS offers the ExpertBook series in many configurations. If you want the best business laptop Asus offers, consider the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra. If you are a business owner who wants a premium design without compromising essential business features, the ASUS ExpertBook B Series is worth considering. Finally, the ASUS ExpertBook P Series is for those looking for an affordable business laptop without paying a premium.
In that regard, the ASUS ExpertBook P3 is a sweet spot for people looking for an affordable business laptop. It doesn’t try to compete with the flashy, ultra-thin consumer aesthetics of the Apple MacBook Air or Dell XPS line; instead, it positions itself as an aggressive challenger to the Lenovo ThinkPad and HP EliteBook ecosystems, as well as other business laptop ranges.
I have been using the ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 version (2026) for the past several days. Overall, it has been a solid business laptop. The model I am testing comes with a powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 255H and delivers excellent performance, a reliable port selection, the best keyboard in its class, and plenty of business-focused features.
ASUS has also expanded the ASUS ExpertBook P3 G2 series, now offering more choices than before with both Intel and AMD configurations across different sizes, while also addressing some of the shortcomings we noticed with the earlier ExpertBook P series.
In this full, detailed review, I will share my experience with the ASUS P3 G1, compare it to the original P3 launched in 2025, and see how it stacks up against the recently announced ASUS P3 G2 series. By the end, you should have a better idea of whether the Asus P3 G1 still makes sense or is worth going for the latest generations instead.
Table of Contents
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review
Design and Build: Practical Over Premium
Asus ExpertBook laptops are easy to spot from miles away. Most models across the lineup look the same and follow a very similar design language, with an understated gray finish and a clean, minimal look.
Asus ExpertBook P3 G1 also follows the same design. It may not impress you with flashy looks or an ultra-slim profile, which is something the ExpertBook P3 isn’t trying to do anyway. This is a practical, business-first laptop.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 comes in two chassis variants. The 1A variant has a plastic chassis, and the 2A variant has a metal chassis for those who want an even sturdier, more premium build.
My unit comes with a plastic body, but it doesn’t feel cheap by any means. In fact, it is a step up from some of the older ExpertBook laptops I have reviewed in the past.
Although the chassis is plastic, the matte, grainy finish hides it and gives it a much more premium feel. I love minimal laptop designs, and the ASUS ExpertBook takes that approach even further with nothing but the ASUS logo on the lid. The matte, grainy finish is also fingerprint-resistant; as a result, smudges don’t show up, and it stays clean.
The same treatment continues when you open the lid. The hinge is now slightly stronger. The display is stiffer than ideal to position, but it still wobbles a bit when you type and change its angle.
The lid opens up to 180 degrees, allowing the display to lie completely flat on the surface. It can come in handy if you want to share your screen with someone across the table. One limitation, though: since this variant doesn’t have a touchscreen, you cannot really use the display while it is lying flat.
Build quality is stronger than last generation, but it still has noticeable flex, especially in the center of the keyboard and between the touchpad and the keyboard. Thankfully, I didn’t notice it while typing. The deck doesn’t bend much under normal use unless you press harder.
The rounded corners also make the laptop more comfortable to hold during longer carrying periods.
One thing Asus continues to get right is port selection. In a world where fewer ports have become the norm for a premium experience, Asus ExpertBook P3 supports all major ports, including one Thunderbolt 4 USB-C, one USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C, two USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A ports, a full-size RJ45 Gigabit Ethernet port, HDMI 2.1 TMDS, a 3.5mm audio jack, and a Kensington Nano lock. You get pretty much every port you expect from a business laptop. That also means you can connect most everyday accessories directly to the laptop without carrying a separate dongle.
The chassis is also MIL-STD 810H tested across 24 procedures. The laptop should handle everyday wear and tear. Note that the laptop is not water-resistant.
The keyboard supports backlighting. This makes it easy to see and type in low-light conditions. The backlight also doesn’t leak when you’re looking straight at the laptop. It also has durable keys, and ASUS claims the keyboard is tested for up to 10 million keystrokes to withstand wear and tear over time.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 is available in both 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. My review unit is the 14-inch variant with a WUXGA 16:10 display. The side bezels are fairly noticeable, and there is a rather large chin at the bottom that also houses the Asus ExpertBook logo. Above the display is a physical privacy shutter, which I truly appreciate for business-centric users who want better privacy.
Display: Good for Work, Not for Creative Use
The 14-inch display is a sweet spot if you want something compact without giving up too much screen space.
ASUS ExpertBook doesn’t get the kind of high-end OLED displays Asus offers on some of its high-end laptops or even more affordable VivoBook models. It is a 14-inch IPS-level display with WUXGA 1920 × 1200 resolution, a 16:10 aspect ratio, a 60Hz refresh rate, up to 300 nits of brightness, and 45% NTSC color coverage.
The display quality is decent and gets the job done, especially if you’re buying the ExpertBook primarily for office work. It is perfectly fine for browsing and using office apps like spreadsheets and documents, but if you work on photos or video editing, you will probably want something with better color coverage.
The display also has an anti-glare coating, which does a good job of cutting down reflections and makes it easier to use in bright environments. However, the trade-off is that a matte finish coating removes some of the visual punch you get from glossy panels. Colors aren’t as vibrant, although the text remains sharp.
Watching videos and content on this WUXGA IPS-level panel isn’t a pleasant experience, but as I said, for everyday tasks such as browsing, spreadsheets, and other office applications, it feels comfortable to use, and the text looks sharp enough to read clearly.
Performance: More Power Than Most Office Users Need
Performance is easily one of the ExpertBook P3’s strongest aspects. Asus offers it with either a Core Ultra 5 225H or Core Ultra 7 255H. My unit came with an Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, paired with 16GB DDR5 RAM and a 512GB M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD.
At the heart of the configuration is the Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, a high-performance processor with 16 cores, 16 threads, a maximum clock speed of 5.1GHz, and integrated Intel Graphics. In everyday use, this combination handles almost any task without breaking a sweat. Whether you’re using multiple graphics-heavy applications, running dozens of browser tabs, or switching between office apps all day.
Another advantage is upgradability. Asus ExpertBook P3 comes with two DDR5 SO-DIMM slots, and the existing RAM isn’t soldered to the motherboard, so you can upgrade later if you want to, and it won’t cost you a bomb upfront, which is the case with most modern laptops.
It also has two storage slots: one M.2 2280 PCIe 4.0 slot and one M.2 2230 PCIe 4.0 slot, giving you more room to expand the storage later.
One thing I did notice is that the laptop gets quite warm at the bottom even during something as basic as browsing the web. You can definitely feel the heat when using it in your lap. It is not entirely surprising, though, considering the Core Ultra 7 255H is an H-series processor designed for higher performance.
Keyboard and Trackpad: The Keyboard Is the Star
The keyboard is easily one of my favorite things about the Asus ExpertBook P3. It offers one of the best typing experiences I have had on a laptop after Mac. A lot of that comes down to the 1.5mm key travel, which delivers a great typing experience. The keys are also large and well spaced, giving your fingers plenty of room to move around. It didn’t take me long to get comfortable with this keyboard.
The trackpad is also large enough for daily use. The large surface area makes it easy to move the cursor and also use gestures.
I have no issues with the keyboard and trackpad, though some users may find the fingerprint sensor placement inconvenient because it is integrated into the power button. To prevent accidental presses, ASUS made the power button slightly firmer.
Battery Life: The Biggest Compromise
This kind of performance is always welcome, especially if you regularly handle high-demand tasks. The trade-off, though, is battery life. My configuration comes with a 50Wh, 3-cell battery, and the ExpertBook P3 takes a noticeable hit here.
Even for basic use, I was getting only about 8-9 hours. On medium to heavy gaming, the battery life dropped to 4 to 5 hours, which isn’t the performance you want if you plan to use it on battery power all day.
ASUS bundles a 65W USB-C charger in the box, and it can take your laptop from 0 to 100 in less than 2 hours. That’s fairly quick, but I really wish Windows laptop makers offered more travel-friendly options instead of big, bulky charging bricks and three-pin plugs.
Sound: Decent, but Nothing Special
The speakers are decently loud, but they don’t get particularly loud. ASUS uses two built-in speakers with Dirac audio support. Thankfully, Asus includes a built-in 3.5mm headphone jack, so you can plug in wired headphones or earphones directly without relying on the built-in speakers.
Windows 11 Home: Still Too Cluttered
I have never been a fan of Windows’ cluttered experience. If you’ve used Windows for years, you probably won’t mind much, but if you are coming from a Mac or Linux, you’ll have to deal with Windows’ cluttered experience first.
It took me more than three hours to set up the device, including the unwanted Windows updates I had to install during setup. Plus, the Windows update prompts never stop. Even Microsoft has promised to improve the Windows laptop experience by eliminating these unwanted distractions.
Since this is an ExpertBook, ASUS includes business-centric features, including AI ExpertMeet for meetings. However, this configuration lacks some useful Copilot+ AI features for those who care about privacy and want to run AI features locally on the device. The Core Ultra 7 255H delivers up to 13 TOPS of NPU performance, well short of the 40+ TOPS required for a Copilot+ PC. You may need to rely on cloud processing for more demanding AI features.
Camera: Still Needs Work
ASUS has been pretty good at improving the little things in everyday use, but the camera is still one area that needs work. My configuration comes with a 1080p FHD IR camera with Windows Hello support and a physical privacy shutter. Even on the maxed-out ExpertBook Ultra, the camera quality is rather underwhelming, especially on business laptops like this, where it matters a lot.
Even in good lighting, the camera adds plenty of noise, and in low light, it gets worse. However, you can always connect an external camera if camera quality matters to you. But this is something Asus needs to improve.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review Verdict: Powerful and Practical, but Battery Holds It Back
Overall, if performance is high on your priority list, then the ASUS ExpertBook P3 might be a better choice. Everyday tasks feel quick and responsive, plus it also has plenty of power for more demanding tasks. The excellent keyboard, with 1.5mm key travel, makes typing sessions comfortable, and the full selection of ports lets you connect any peripherals without constantly reaching for or using a dongle. The biggest advantage of the Asus ExpertBook P3 is plenty of room to upgrade later. It offers dual SO-DIMM slots for memory and dual M.2 slots for additional PCIe storage.
Among the pros are also some compromises. Battery life takes a noticeable hit when you push the processor harder, and while the laptop can handle some AI workloads locally, it cannot run the full set of Copilot+ PC features.

As Stelco rejects demand to halt layoffs, NDP leaders call on Carney to nationalize steelmaker
Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis, Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles call for Stelco to be nationalized
Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis and Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles are calling on the federal government to nationalize Hamilton-based steelmaker Stelco, amid layoffs Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says violate the company's agreement under the Investment Canada Act.
In a release Tuesday, Lewis said the federal government should take "immediate action" after Stelco's American owner Cleveland-Cliffs broke its commitment to maintain the same number of unionized workers and similar numbers of non-union workers for five years when it bought the company in 2024.
Joly has vowed to take Cleveland-Cliffs to court, saying Saturday in a post on X that "all options are on the table" as government lawyers consider next steps. But Lewis said Tuesday that going through the courts will take too long to save those whose jobs are in the crosshairs.
"Canada cannot afford to lose its steel industry," he said. "If we’re serious about saving these jobs and the Canadian steel industry, we need immediate action."
An industrial worker walks near the Stelco Hamilton Works on Oct. 9. The American steelmaker announced 300 to 350 layoffs at the plant amid the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
Lewis noted that the United Kingdom nationalized British Steel in July, saying the move protected "thousands of jobs." In September, the U.K. government announced plans for the public takeover of another steelmaker, Specialty Steel.
Lewis also jabbed at Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves, who has expressed support for the U.S. tariffs on foreign steel that led to these layoffs, saying they "are designed to deindustrialize our economy and destroy our manufacturing base."
Goncalves maintains the company is within the law to conduct layoffs because they are temporary, until Canada and the United States reach a trade deal.
"There is no provision in the contract that I have to keep employment at a certain level every single day of the five years," Goncalves told CBC's Rosemary Barton Live on Sunday.
"If that was an imposition of the Canadian government, I would not have accepted."
Ontario NDP says Ford should offer steel industry relief
Speaking at Queen's Park on Tuesday, Stiles pushed for Ontario Premier Doug Ford to "work with the federal government to push Cleveland-Cliffs to give up their ownership interest in Stelco and establish public ownership and Canadian management."
“The cost of not doing this is thousands of jobs. It’s spinoffs. It’s the whole community of Hamilton that is impacted," she said. “The industry will lose out if we let Stelco go under.”
In a release issued the same day, Stiles and her Ontario NDP colleagues from Hamilton — MPPs Sandy Shaw and Robin Lennox — also said Ford should "get back to work and deliver a tariff relief package for the steel industry," as well as a "Buy Ontario First" procurement strategy. The Ontario government remains on a 21-week summer break that ends Oct. 27.
CBC Hamilton asked Ford's office for a response to the calls for nationalization but did not hear back by the time of publication.
When asked last week whether his government would consider such an action, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he would wait to hear Cleveland-Cliffs' response to Joly's letter demanding the jobs be reinstated, and then he would "take appropriate action."
The company has since declined to reverse the layoffs.
Time now to consider public ownership, prof says
Nicolas Lamp, associate professor at the faculty of law and school of policy studies at Queen's University, told CBC Hamilton last week he thinks the government should step in and take public ownership before Canada's steel expertise is lost.
“At the moment when Canada is trying to build a lot of infrastructure, major plants, major projects, it's really a question of whether Canada should just let all that expertise kind of die," he said.
Lamp pointed to the purchase of the Trans Mountain pipeline from Kinder Morgan in 2018 as an example of the federal government taking on major infrastructure from a private company.
Mike Watt, whose career at Stelco spans 20 years, standing outside the Stelco Hamilton Works on Oct. 9 after receiving a layoff notice. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)
“I'm not saying we should definitely nationalize it,” he said.
“I would say that the Canadian government really has to look very closely at what the reasons for these layoffs are and whether a company that was more sympathetic — that had the Canadian workers and also the Canadian national interest in mind — would act similarly.”
Last week, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he supports the government taking legal action against Stelco. He reiterated that Tuesday, but said the best way to fix this problem would be getting a deal to remove the tariffs.
"Our message to the prime minister is get back to the table and get a tariff-free deal," he said in Windsor on Tuesday.
"The workers at Stelco, Stellantis, Ford and every other trade-dependent company in this country are relying on the PM to keep his word and get a deal."
With files from Kevin Maimann, Coleman Molnar, Racy Rafique, CBC Windsor and The Canadian Press

Pressure on Norway in play-off final - Wilkinson
- Published
Rhian Wilkinson says the pressure will be on Gemma Grainger's Norway in their Women's World Cup play-off final against Wales in December.
Wales moved a step closer to reaching the Women's World Cup for the first time as a 3-0 win over Albania in Llanelli secured a 4-0 aggregate success in their play-off semi-final.
Wales now face a step up in a class as they take on a Norway side ranked 14th in the world, but Wilkinson insists Wales can "absolutely" cause an upset as they are reunited with former boss Grainger.
"The pressure is always on the big nations and that's something I think we thrive on," said the Wales head coach.
"We're a small nation, we fight for each other. You see some of the play tonight [against Albania] any you'd be proud of [that] from any team in world.
"[There were some] fantastic levels of play and that's with probably one of the younger teams that's playing in this competition right now, so I think it's an exciting time and why not be excited about the possibility."
The play-off final first leg will be played at the Cardiff City Stadium on Tuesday, 1 December before the return leg in Norway four days later.
Norway, the 1995 world champions, have reached every Women's World Cup since the tournament began in 1991.
They will begin as firm favourites against Wales, who are ranked 17 places below them by Fifa and who have never beaten a top-20 ranked side in a competitive fixture.
But Wilkinson insists Wales, whose only previous major championship appearance was at Euro 2025, can cause Norway problems.
"They're a team that's performing well, that's doing well, as are we and we've got some fantastic players that can absolutely go toe-to-toe with them," she added.
"I've just talked to the staff I think everyone needs a few days off to rest and recover.
"Then we're going to go again, do the best we can to deliver a team that's going to fight for their country."
The complex nature of the qualifying process means that even if they were to upset Norway, Wales may not be guaranteed a place at next year's World Cup.
Depending on which other sides come through the eight European play-off finals, Wales may have to negotiate an inter-confederation play-off next February to secure their spot in Brazil.
"The World Cup is off in the distance - I'll keep saying that because we don't even know if and when we beat Norway if that's the final hurdle," Wilkinson said.
"So it is the next game in front of us - we don't get too far ahead. It's the next job and we've got a lot of work to do as a staff."
Mayzee Davies, Elise Hughes and Hannah Cain found the target as Wales eased to victory over Albania having limped over the line in the first leg last Friday.
"I think we know that the performance away wasn't one that we were particularly pleased with," Wilkinson said.
"I thought we lacked intensity, lacked teeth in our defending, we weren't connecting our passes in a way I know we can.
"Tonight was the absolute reversal of that. I thought from the first minute Angharad [James] led her team in an intense, strong performance where the team really showed what they're capable of. It was fun to watch."

A landmark survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has revealed the once endangered species is thriving.
A population of Aldabra giant tortoise lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.
The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island.
This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.
The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022.
It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.
Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.
Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve.
“This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”
The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.
In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island.
But a recovery programme meant the island became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.
Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it.
“Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.
“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”
Despite the good news, the study’s authors warn that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.
The study authors say invasive mammals remain a key threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings.
The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.
“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.
“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.
“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”

Bihar man dies in custody hours after arrest, 6 cops suspended amid murder charge
Six police personnel in Bihar's West Champaran district have been suspended after 25-year-old Dilshad Ansari died of a head injury hours after his arrest in a narcotics case. While police claimed he was injured trying to escape from a moving vehicle, his family alleged murder. Former MP Ali Anwar sought NHRC intervention.
Six police personnel have been placed under suspension in Bihar's West Champaran district in connection with the custodial death of a 25-year-old man two days ago, police said.
According to a statement issued by the district police, Dilshad Ansari had been arrested on Sunday in connection with a narcotics smuggling case, and he succumbed to a serious head injury at a hospital hours later.
The police party accompanying Ansari had claimed that he got wounded while trying to escape from custody by jumping off a speeding vehicle, though bereaved family members alleged that he had been "murdered."
Accordingly, Superintendent of Police Kumar Gautam ordered suspension of six officials, including Ravi Shankar Kumar, the SHO of Sahodara police station and sub-inspector Arun Kumar, besides four constables.
Meanwhile, former Rajya Sabha MP Ali Anwar, who heads All India Pasmanda Muslim Mahaz, issued a statement deploring the incident and urging Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary to book the police personnel for alleged kidnapping and murder.
Anwar claimed that according to social activists based in West Champaran, "there were no injury marks on the arms and legs of Ansari, which could not have been possible had he jumped from the running police vehicle".
He also urged the National Human Rights Commission to step in and direct authorities concerned that payment of ex gratia be made to dependants of Ansari, who "hailed from a very poor family and had a six-month-old daughter."

With the Vivo V70 series, Vivo took a premium turn. You can check out our detailed Vivo V70 review. Previously, Vivo V series phones had flashy designs, tall displays, and curved screens, designed to attract people who like flashy looks. But the Vivo V70 changed that rather significantly. Vivo has gone for a more compact form factor and a sturdier build that appeals to anyone looking for flagship-level build quality in a Vivo V series phone.
Now the Vivo V80 continues the tradition. It keeps the same compact form factor and solid build, which feels more like a proper flagship than a typical Vivo design. Now has a bigger 7200 mAh battery, ships with OriginOS 7 out of the box, and is the first non-flagship phone with an excellent 144 AMOLED display and a Zeiss camera setup.
However, it also gets a huge price hike. The base variant now comes with 8GB + 128GB priced at Rs 62,999, 8GB + 256GB at Rs 69,999, and finally 8GB + 512GB at Rs 79,999. Vivo V80 sits next to flagship phones where the competition becomes much harder to ignore.
The Vivo V70 found a speed sweet spot for buyers who cared more about cameras than outright performance. So, with the Vivo V80, has Vivo found that sweet spot again, or has it pushed the Vivo V series a little too far this time? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Vivo V80 Review: Great Cameras, Premium Looks and a Price To Match
Compact Build, Flagship-Like Feel
The Vivo V80 looks strikingly similar to the V70 from the front. It keeps the same compact body design with rounded corners on all four sides. In fact, they have almost the same dimensions except the Vivo V80 is now slightly thicker: 157.52 × 74.33 × 7.69 mm (Vivo V70: 157.52 × 74.33 × 7.59 mm), and also slightly heavier at 203g compared to 194g on the Vivo V70 because of the larger battery.
The button placement is also very similar to the V70, with the power and volume buttons on the right being easy to access with one hand. They are clicky and tactile. On the left, it is clean, while on the bottom you will find the SIM ejector, speaker, and Type-C charging port.
You will notice the real difference when you turn the phone around. The camera module now stretches almost across the width of the phone, following the design trend we have been seeing in the phones lately.
Vivo also changed the camera placement to use that extra space better than on the V70, tucking it in with ZEISS branding neatly as well. It comes with a glass back, and the camera module blends neatly into the glass. It also doubles as a natural resting position for your finger while holding the phone. Design-wise, I would rate it 10/10 for its compact form factor and solid in-hand feel.
The device is also IP68 + IP69 rated, so it can protect against dust and water, and it comes in three color options this time. The Stellar Black for those who prefer black phones, Horizon Blue, the one I got, which honestly looks more like olive than blue, and the new Sunrise Anthem color that has a subtle orange, not a contrast look that we found on the iPhone 17 Pro. Here is how all colors look in person.
Sharp 144Hz AMOLED, but Performance Holds It Back
On the front, you get a 6.59-inch 1.5K Amoled edge-to-edge display with minimal bezels on all four sides. Vivo has gone with a flat AMOLED panel once again. The resolution remains the same. But Vivo has bumped the refresh rate to 144Hz from 120Hz.
The processor technically supports it, but pushing both resolution and refresh rate to the highest settings makes the phone noticeably choppier to use. By default, the screen resolution is set to HD, but you can set it to Ultra HD for a sharper display.
OriginOS also lets you choose different screen colors. By default, it is set to natural, but if you want a punchy, vibrant-looking display, you can switch to bright to make on-screen colors pop.
The display is very bright. You get almost all of the advantages of a good AMOLED panel. With its resolution and 459 pixels per inch, the display looks sharp, and the AMOLED panel ensures deep blacks and rich colors. It also has 5000 nits of local peak brightness for HDR content. The display can get very bright, so you can use it comfortably in direct sunlight without visibility issues.
My biggest issue is the same as what I have with the Vivo V70. The phone supports high resolution and the highest refresh rate, but the processor, because of its limitations, struggles to keep the experience smooth. The phone is also Widevine L1 certified, so you can watch Netflix, Amazon, or HD content on other streaming platforms.
Strong ZEISS Cameras, but the Ultrawide Needs an Upgrade
Cameras have long been Vivo phones’ biggest strength. Vivo V80 continues that tradition. Vivo has largely stuck with the same hardware on the V80 as on the V70. That is both a good and a bad thing.
The good thing is these cameras are capable and well-tuned for photography; the bad is Vivo still uses a lower-resolution ultra-wide-angle camera, which definitely needs an upgrade if it wants to compete with flagship phones at this price, especially when it still relies on the camera as its biggest strength.
For starters, it comes with a 50-megapixel ZEISS OIS Main Camera with OIS. It also has a 50-megapixel ZEISS Night Telephoto Camera and a 50MP 3x periscope telephoto zoom. The ultra-wide is the same 8MP ZEISS sensor, with an f/2.2 aperture and a 115-degree field of view.
Vivo V80 vs Vivo X200T: Which Has the Better Camera?
In the past, I compared Vivo V70 cameras with the Vivo X200T, but I also called it an unfair comparison because of the Rs 14,000 price difference between them. But fast-forward to now, after the price increase, the Vivo V70 now sells for the same price as the Vivo X200T, and the latest Vivo V80 is Rs 3,000 more expensive than the Vivo X200T.
I still have the Vivo X200T with me. Now it’s safe to compare both smartphones and decide which one to pick up if you care only about the camera.
Main camera in daylight
First, in daylight, Vivo X200T photos look closer to real life, while Vivo V80 photos look brighter and punchier. The Vivo X200T also handles shadows better than the Vivo V80.
As you can see in the first image, the Vivo V80 loses detail in the bushes, whereas the X200T handles shadows better. The Vivo V80 also has more detail.
Both photos look detailed normally; however, when you zoom in on the Vivo V80, the edges look rough, and the textures look crunchy because of the oversharpening. Both cameras do exceptionally well, but the Vivo V80 might appeal to most users because its contrasty photos work better on social media.
2x Zoom: Vivo X200T Pulls Ahead
Next, both smartphones have a telephoto lens. Side by side, Vivo V80 clearly falls behind in detail. As the images above show, when you zoom in, the Vivo X200T retains more detail than the Vivo V80. As you can see in the image above, the ground behind the cow on the Vivo V80 lacks detail, but on the X200T you can clearly see the grainy structure and other details.
3x Telephoto: Vivo V80 Comes Close
The Vivo V80 comes close to the Vivo X200T in the 3x telephoto shots. When you zoom out, both shots look really good to the eye; the Vivo V80 looks more contrasty and the colors pop, while the Vivo X200T keeps the colors closer to natural.
But again, the Vivo X200T has finer texture. For example, in the second image, when you zoom in, the bird feathers and stone details look better on the Vivo X200T than on the Vivo V80. But the Vivo V80 is also preferable here and retains plenty of detail, though it looks softer when compared side by side with the Vivo X200T. But still, most users prefer Vivo V80 photos simply because of their more vivid and punchy look.
Ultrawide: Vivo V80 Falls Behind
When it comes to the ultra-wide camera, even the specs show that the Vivo V80 falls far behind the Vivo X200T. Vivo still uses the lower 8-megapixel sensor, and it clearly struggles to capture the details. As you can see from the images below, the Vivo X200T shows clear leaves in the bark, whereas the Vivo V80 looks soft. Once again, Vivo oversharpens the image, making it look more contrasty than it does in real life. You can clearly see the difference in the image sample below.
Indoor Shots: The Gap Gets Smaller
Next, in the indoor and close-up shots, once again, Vivo X200T produces natural colors and also natural background blur with crisp and real details, whereas Vivo V80 also does a really good job, and when you look at both samples, the difference is quite small indoors.
Selfies: Both Are Good, X200T Is Slightly Better
Both the Vivo X200T and Vivo V80 produce sharp, detailed-looking selfies. The selfies on the Vivo V80 look cooler than the warmer tones on the Vivo X200T, as you can see in the images below. Both smartphones capture plenty of detail, with the Vivo X200T being slightly better, but not by much.
Shooting Into the Sun: Vivo V80 Struggles More
When shooting directly into the sun, both phones show lens flare. The Vivo V80 struggles more here with the white balance shifting, whereas the Vivo X200T keeps the colors natural and contrasty but still shows a visible ring of light across the frame.
Overall, in comparison, if camera quality is the top priority, and if you want natural-looking colors, a better all-rounder, and also a much better ultra-wide camera, the Vivo X200T takes the lead, while the Vivo V80 is still very capable and comes quite close in many situations. People may also prefer the more punchy look of the Vivo V80 that is ready to post on social media.
The same goes for low-light photos as well. The Vivo V80 is slightly behind the Vivo X200T in terms of retaining details, and some pictures look grainy in comparison.
You can also shoot portraits using the telephoto lens. The portraits look sharp, with strong blur and strong subject separation. You can also use the portrait mode with the telephoto lens to capture close-up portrait shots. Portrait mode also supports several Zeiss portrait styles, which are one of the highlight features of the Vivo V series phones.
And since the Vivo V80 is a camera-focused phone with a ZEISS partnership, you also get camera-focused features that are nice to play around with. It comes with various filters; Zeiss Natural mode is my favorite for getting more natural-looking photos. But still, the Vivo V80 tends to produce slightly punchier colors than expected.
In terms of video quality, the videos shot on the Vivo V80 are decent, bright, and colorful, same as the photos. Whereas the X200T leans toward more natural colors, the Vivo tends to make the overall quality brighter and the colors punchier, which, again, many people might like because of the contrasty colors that are good for social media posting.
Vivo V80 can record up to 4K 60fps from both the front and rear cameras. It also supports several video styles and modes. My favorite is 4K Cinematic Camera mode. Using it, you can produce cinematic-style, color-graded videos.
Fine for Everyday Use, Not for Performance Seekers
Vivo V80 comes with the same Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 used on the Vivo V70. It also comes with downgraded storage, UFS 3.1 compared to UFS 4.1 on the Vivo V70, and LPDDR4X compared to LPDDR5X. Also, the base variant now comes with 128GB instead of 256GB offered on the Vivo V70.
On paper, these are significant downgrades, especially when the Vivo V80 is priced close to flagship territory, where most phones are powered by Snapdragon 8 Elite-class processors.
I understand that most smartphones have recently gone through a price hike, and many smartphones are launching with even 4GB RAM in the budget segment, but those compromises are acceptable in the budget segment; for a phone with this experience, it is harder ot justiy, but considering the rise in memory and component costs, we do not have many choices.
In everyday use, I didn’t notice any big performance drop. Everyday tasks are decently faster. I didn’t have many expectations for the Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, but in gaming and when bumping up the refresh rate, I clearly noticed choppy performance. If performance is your highest priority, this phone clearly isn’t meant for that
Vivo V80 Benchmarks
Easy Two-Day Battery Life With Light Use
Battery life is not really a concern on the Vivo V80. Most smartphones today already come with fairly large batteries and support ultra-fast charging. Vivo also packed a dense 7200 mAh battery in the Vivo V80, and it also supports 90W super-fast charging. It can fully charge the device in under 1.5 hours.
Also, because of the less power-hungry Snapdragon 7 Gen 4, the battery can easily last up to two days with light usage and a full day with heavier use, which includes gaming and everyday tasks like browsing, watching videos, taking calls, and more.
Loud Stereo Speakers With Good Separation
Vivo V80 comes with stereo speakers. Both speakers are equally loud and offer very good stereo separation. There is no 3.5 mm headphone jack, which is pretty much the norm on most phones right now.
OriginOS 7 Is Good, but the V80 Misses Some Features
Vivo V80 is the first phone in India to ship with Origin OS 7 out of the box. OriginOS 7 has plenty of new customization features, including new themes, better lock screen customization options, a new liquid glass design, and a new workbench feature that lets you run five apps at once and switch between them easily. It also comes with useful AI features. Unfortunately, not all of those made it into the Vivo V80.
Vivo V80 lacks both the liquid glass design and the workbench feature because of RAM limitations (Workbench features require devices with 12GB RAM or more). OriginOS 7 still offers plenty of customization features on the Vivo V80. I already covered some of my favorite features in a different post. Adding custom stickers and the new pet pal wallpapers are a few of my favorites.
Vivo Origin OS 7 also brings plenty of AI features to the Vivo V80. After a very long time, I found very few of them useful beyond the AI image editing tools that we initially saw in many phones.
One of the favorite features is Snapshot. You can point the camera at a whiteboard, documents, or any text, and it can extract all the text. In the Notes app, it can arrange the text into tables, lists, and more.
The AI recorder is also useful. It allows you to create transcripts of your recordings, generate summaries, and pull useful insights. There are also plenty of AI camera features as well, letting you generate various AI-generated styles and effects.
Another feature I particularly liked is the Redirect Audio. It lets you play multiple audio tracks through different outputs without interfering with each other. For instance, if your phone is connected to Bluetooth and playing music, you can still watch a YouTube video at the same time using your phone’s speakers without affecting the music playing on your Bluetooth speaker.
Vivo also promised to roll out 4 years of major OS updates and six years of security updates for the Vivo V80, which is a very good software commitment
Vivo V80 Review Verdict: Great Cameras, but Vivo Has Pushed the V80 Too Far
For the asking price of Rs 62,999/-, Vivo has pushed the Vivo V80 a little too far this time. It now sits in the flagship territory, where you start getting phones with much stronger hardware.
It also competes with its own peers like the Vivo X200T, which at least for now feels like an overall better deal if value for your money is your highest priority. However, we are not sure whether the Vivo X200T will continue to exist as a competitor.
Vivo V80 is still a compelling device, especially for the cameras and also the new design. But if you’re open to other options or care about performance, Vivo V80 is harder to recommend. Of course,we all know that smartphone prices have gone up significantly over the past few months, and Vivo V80 is clearly another victim trying to justify its higher price.

Man Utd defender Lisandro Martinez extraordinarily calls out club's hierarchy after Atletico Madrid loss in Champions League
Man Utd's Lisandro Martinez astonishingly attacks club's hierarchy after Champions League loss at Atletico Madrid; Martinez told Amazon Prime: "We expect more from the top, from upstairs, to bring in more players to compete"; he added: "I expect more from our technical director"
Wednesday 14 October 2026 00:06, UK
Manchester United's Lisandro Martinez launched an extraordinary attack on the club’s hierarchy after their 2-0 Champions League loss at Atletico Madrid.
In an astonishing post-match interview, the Argentina international criticised the lack of summer investment in the squad.
The defender said he had expected more from "upstairs", singling out technical director Jason Wilcox, in the most recent transfer window in which they failed to improve their options at left-back and up front.
Man Utd spent £155m on just four major summer signings after a third-place Premier League finish last season, which earned a return to the Champions League for the first time in three years.

"I have to control myself a lot, but sometimes it's a reflection of how our club is at the moment," Martinez told Amazon Prime.
"We had a fantastic season last season, and now we expect more from the top, from upstairs, to bring in more players to compete because many teams have brought in many players as well."
Asked whether he had expected more investment in the squad in summer, Martinez said: "Yes, 100 per cent.
"I expect more from our technical director. I have to be honest. And also, as a player, we have to do more.
"It's also important to build a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night."
Tuesday's loss in Madrid extended Man Utd's winless run to five games, piling pressure on boss Michael Carrick.
"He does his best," he said of Carrick. "But every season is different. You can't stay with what you did last season.
"The teams know how you play, they know every detail. If you don't change, next season is a big problem."
Asked about Carrick's future, Martinez replied: "You start changing, changing, changing managers. But what about [moves his eyes upwards] other areas?"
Martinez looked up and then shrugged, saying, "I can't say more" before deciding to add a final dig.
"Because also tonight it is easy to say the coach, it is easy to say the players, but also we have to see other areas," he said, pointing up and nodding.
Carrick and Tielemans asked about Martinez comments
It was a jaw-dropping interview that Youri Tielemans, one of three outfield summer signings, refused to comment on, while Martinez's outburst dominated the post-match press conference with Carrick.
Asked if he agreed with Martinez's view, he said: "Well, I haven't seen the interview. I've half heard about it in the other interviews I've done.
"I think it's a little bit on the emotions of the game as well, coming here and being disappointed not to get something from the game.
"Straight after a game for me is not the time to talk about that interview because I haven't seen it, so I can't really comment on that.
"But I think it's important for us to move forward quickly, really. I think there's a big game on Sunday, and it's really important that we move forward and we stay focused on that.
"There's disappointment within the group. I'm bitterly disappointed in certain things, and the boys are as well as a group."
Rooney heavily criticises Martinez outburst
Manchester United's all-time leading scorer Wayne Rooney speaking to Amazon Prime:
"It's a difficult one because I always used to think I was outspoken as a player and you want to have your opinion.
"I think he has maybe gone a bit too far. That's for the manager, and that should really stay internal.
"The fans want to hear the players speak; they want to hear the players care, so you can clearly see he cares and he wants the team to invest more money, and more players, and to do that he is probably one of the players who is out the door through his performances. His performances haven't been good enough.
"But I think in some ways he is right in terms of the club needs to invest more, at the top end of the pitch and in defence as well.
"But it looks like that was a bit of an agenda; he's wanted to say that, because that doesn't mirror the performance. I thought the performance was better.
"It's a bit disrespectful to his team-mates as well. He is disrespecting his team-mates because he's saying the team isn't good enough.
"Bruno (Fernandes) is the only one who has any right to come out and say anything like that as captain. And even then it should be behind closed doors if there are issues, which does happen.
"Players have conversations with the manager, the manager has conversations with the board, but that interview is not going to help the situation the club are in at the minute.
"That's going to bring a greater noise around it; the players are not happy, they're not settled, they don't trust in their team-mates. That's not going to help at all."
Carra: It's awful from Martinez
Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher speaking to CBS Sports:
"Doesn't do anybody any good at all, and they will be the story now for the next few days, all about this.
"Now, as supporters, every set of supporters don't like the suits or the guys upstairs, so United fans will lap this up and think it's great. I think it's awful that he's come out and said that right now. I do.
"And when he's saying 'we had a fantastic season last season', they didn't. A manager got sacked last season. They finished third because they had no cup games. They weren't in Europe. They got knocked out of the cup competitions very early.
"The reason they finished third is that Liverpool and Chelsea were that bad as well. Now we're seeing the real Manchester United this season."
Analysis: Martinez unlikley to last long at Man Utd
Sky Sports' Zinny Boswell:
Everyone has heard a Manchester United fan voicing the criticisms made by Lisandro Martinez in Madrid. It is another thing entirely to see a player doing it.
Many of those fans will see Martinez's comments as a necessary intervention to address an issue which long pre-dates INEOS' involvement at Old Trafford but has certainly not been helped by Sir Jim Ratcliffe's minority investment.
Others, like Wayne Rooney, will question the player's motives. Martinez has entered the final year of his contract and cannot claim to have done enough to have earned another. Perhaps he has been told as much. Players who speak out publicly like this do not tend to last long.
Cristiano Ronaldo called out the Glazers in 2022 in his famous Piers Morgan interview and left United within a week. Martinez's compatriot Cristian Romero criticised Spurs' hierarchy in January in an Instagram post and was gone by the summer.
Irrespective of Martinez's motivation, it is hard to argue with his point. United set Carrick up for a fall by failing to sign a left-back or a striker over the summer. The midfield rebuild that was hyped up for many months before the summer has not lived up to expectation either.
It is hard to understand quite what the plan is at United looking back at the last few years. United have had three managers in that window of time. Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick. All with different approaches that bear little resemblance to the other.
Martinez's comments will not help Carrick. But given the sense of hopelessness that has engulfed the fanbase, you can understand why some will welcome his comments. Martinez is right in saying United's issues stretch far beyond the manager.
Your views on Martinez's interview...
Steve: Martinez is 100 per cent right. The board are an absolute disgrace; the biggest club in the world and yet they persist with the same defenders we've had for five years. Teams know our weaknesses; the board have once again let the manager down badly.
Jonesy: I don't agree with Martinez. They had money, but spent it on players like Andrey Santos who can't get in the Chelsea team - what makes him good enough for Utd? I saw professional players unable to execute simple passes, and lapses of concentration in defence, again. Not good enough!
Date D: You can change the manager as much as you want, but when the hierarchy stays the same, you get the same results. Well done, Martinez!
Ciara: For once, a Man Utd player coming out to call out hierarchy. What a legend.
Dantoken: I stand with him. Nothing changes until changes are made at the top of the club.
Garbs: Agree with Martinez, squad should be bigger and more quality. The main issues are with those above off the pitch.

Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of espionage, Moscow said on Tuesday.
Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.
Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, saying Imai was accredited with the ministry but was accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
Japan’s embassy in Moscow told news agency Kyodo that the government was trying to ascertain the journalist’s reported detention.
Russia’s FSB security agency said a Japanese national, who it did not name, was arrested on Sakhalin and alleged he had worked for Japanese intelligence to collect information about Russia’s defences.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Moscow and Tokyo have been locked in a territorial dispute for decades over the status of a string of islands in the Pacific Ocean, off the north-east coast of Japan and to the south-west of Russia’s Sakhalin region.
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.
“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.
The Kuril islands – which Japan calls the Northern Territories – have been under Russia’s control since the end of the second world war, when they were seized by the Soviet Union.
Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an uproar in Japan. Tokyo has said it would continue implementing sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

A video of late actor Nana Patekar is going viral on social media (here, here, and here) amid the Cockroach Janata Party’s protest at Jantar Mantar. In the video, Patekar apologises to a man named Abhijeet before speaking in Marathi. The video is being shared with claims that Patekar was apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending an event and was supposed to accompany him to the protest at Jantar Mantar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke for not attending the protest at Jantar Mantar.
Fact: The video shows late actor Nana Patekar apologising to Marathi film producer Abhijeet Gholap for missing the NAFA Marathi Film Festival. Gholap, who produced the 2011 Marathi film Deool, shared the video on his Instagram account on 8 October 2026, stating that Patekar was unable to attend the festival. The video is unrelated to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke or the protest at Jantar Mantar. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
After reviewing the video with Google’s NotebookLM tool, we found that Nana Patekar speaks in Marathi, apologises to Abhijeet, and regrets not attending an event. Addressing Abhijeet, he says, “It was great working with you in the film Deool.”
Deool is a 2011 Marathi film in which Nana Patekar acted, and Abhijeet Gholap produced it. This suggests that Patekar was referring to Abhijeet Gholap in the video, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke. Patekar also praises Sonali Kulkarni, who acted in the film.
Further search revealed that Abhijeet Gholap had posted the video of Nana Patekar on his Instagram account (archived) on 08 October 2026. In the caption, he wrote, “Nana was unable to attend the NAFA Marathi Film Festival, and he promised he would definitely come this year. We will miss you very much.” In a Facebook post, he wrote, “Nana, you missed your visit. Now we will just keep waiting.”
Abhijeet Gholap is the founder of the North American Film Association (NAFA), which was established to promote Marathi films in North America. According to the organisation’s website, Gholap founded NAFA to bring together actors, directors, choreographers, singers, cinematographers and editors to create Marathi films, web series and documentaries based on local stories and subjects in North America.
To sum up, this viral video shows Nana Patekar apologising to film producer Abhijeet Gholap, not CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke.

10 dead, at least 20 missing after boat capsizes in Bihar’s Raghopur
Around 25 to 30 people were reportedly aboard the medium-sized boat, most of them travelling to attend a feast organised as part of Hindu funeral rituals.
At least 10 people have died and 20 others are missing after a boat capsized in the Ganga river near Rampur Shyamchand village in Bihar’s Vaishali district on Tuesday evening.
Around 25 to 30 people were reportedly aboard the medium-sized boat, most of them travelling to attend a feast organised as part of Hindu funeral rituals.
The boat was ferrying passengers between hamlets along the river when it overturned in the Raghopur police station area. Officials said an imbalance caused the vessel to capsize, though the exact circumstances of the accident remain unclear.
Some passengers managed to swim to safety, while others drowned. Locals rushed to help and alerted the administration after witnessing the incident.
Rescue teams, including personnel from the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), are searching the river for missing passengers. Darkness and deep water have hampered rescue efforts.
Raghopur Block Development Officer Seema Kumari confirmed the incident. A senior police official said the boat had been carrying passengers from one riverbank settlement to another.
Boat capsized in Bihar’s Samastipur
Earlier this year, at least three people died and four went missing after a boat carrying 14 passengers capsized in the Ganga near Sultanpur Diara in Bihar’s Samastipur district in May. Seven passengers were rescued safely, officials said.
The passengers, all residents of Bind Toli in Masoomganj under Patna district’s Barh police station area, had travelled to Sultanpur Diara for agricultural work. They were returning to Umanath Ghat with vegetables harvested from parwal fields when the boat overturned.
Mohiuddin Nagar circle officer Brijesh Kumar Dwivedi confirmed three deaths, saying the deceased included two men and one woman. Officials have established the identities of all three victims.
The Patna district administration said the boat departed from Bind Toli around 5.45 am with 14 people on board. The passengers regularly crossed the river to work in agricultural fields. An initial update from the administration said seven people had been rescued, two bodies recovered and five passengers were missing.
Officials cited strong winds as a possible cause of the accident, while Barh sub-divisional officer Garima Lohiya said the boat’s engine failed midstream. Rescue teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), along with the Patna and Samastipur district administrations, took part in the operation.
As news of the accident spread, local residents and relatives gathered at Umanath Ghat. Authorities continued the search for the missing passengers and carried out procedures related to the recovered bodies.

Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.
Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.
One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.
“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.
In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.
Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.
Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Journalists’ Syndicate, whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.
Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.
The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.
For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.
“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

The story so far: The Serum Institute of India’s indigenously developed quadrivalent human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, CERVAVAC, has received prequalification from the World Health Organization (WHO), allowing the vaccine to be procured by United Nations agencies and potentially supplied to countries running HPV immunisation programmes. The WHO lists its prequalification as effective from September 25, 2026.
The development is significant for India as well as the global effort to prevent cervical cancer. CERVAVAC is India’s first indigenously developed gender-neutral quadrivalent HPV vaccine and targets HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18. It is licensed in India for girls and boys aged 9 to 26 years.
CERVAVAC is the first Indian-made quadrivalent HPV vaccine to receive WHO prequalification. This prequalification means the vaccine has met WHO standards for quality, safety and efficacy, following evaluation of data, samples and manufacturing sites.
Globally, cervical cancer caused an estimated 604,000 new cases and 342,000 deaths in 2020. In India, where cervical cancer remains a public-health burden, the national HPV vaccination programme was launched on February 28, 2026, targeting about 1.2 crore 14-year-old girls with a free single dose; more than 80 lakh doses had been administered by September this year, according to the Union Health Ministry. India’s national HPV vaccination programme uses Merck’s Gardasil-4, a quadrivalent vaccine protecting against HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18.
India also has an indigenous quadrivalent vaccine, CERVAVAC (now WHO-prequalified) and access to other HPV vaccines, including Gardasil 9 and Cervarix, through the private market.
What exactly is WHO prequalification?
WHO prequalification’s biggest significance is access. A vaccine that has already been licensed in India can now potentially enter international procurement channels used to supply national immunisation programmes, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.
WHO prequalification is not a marketing authorisation or regulatory approval. For the prequalification, the vaccine undergoes assessment of its quality, safety and efficacy, including evaluation of data, testing of samples and inspection of manufacturing facilities. A vaccine that meets WHO standards is placed on the WHO List of Prequalified Vaccines, making it eligible for procurement by United Nations agencies and giving countries an internationally recognised assurance about the product and manufacturing standards.
What is HPV and why is this important for prevention?
HPV is an extremely common sexually transmitted infection. Most infections clear naturally, but persistent infection with high-risk HPV types can lead to cervical cancer. WHO estimates that persistent infection with high-risk HPV types causes more than 95% of cervical cancers. HPV can also cause anal, vulval, vaginal and some other cancers, as well as genital warts.
The vaccine is a cancer-prevention vaccine and not just a vaccine against an infection.
WHO’s priority target is girls aged 9–14 years, before exposure to HPV. The organisation recommends either a one- or two-dose schedule for this age group, depending on the vaccine and national programme.
The four HPV types targeted by CERVAVAC are important for different reasons. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk types responsible for a large proportion of cervical cancers. Types 6 and 11 are responsible for most anogenital warts. The quadrivalent vaccine therefore provides protection against both cancer-associated HPV types and genital warts.
Its indication for both sexes also matters. Although cervical cancer is the largest component of the HPV disease burden, HPV can cause disease in men, including anal cancer and genital warts.
What could the WHO listing mean for India?
CERVAVAC’s WHO prequalification does not automatically mean that it will now be substituted into the Indian government programme. Vaccine selection for a national programme involves considerations including regulatory status, evidence, price, supply capacity, presentations, logistics and programme requirements.
But the new status gives India another WHO-prequalified HPV vaccine from a domestic manufacturer. It could also potentially strengthen competition and supply security if CERVAVAC is considered for future procurement.
How many other Indian vaccines have WHO prequalification?
India already has a substantial presence on the WHO prequalified-vaccine list.
Serum Institute is among the largest Indian participants. The company has WHO-prequalified vaccines covering a wide range of diseases, including BCG, diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis combinations, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, measles, measles-rubella, measles-mumps-rubella, meningococcal disease, pneumococcal disease, polio, rabies, rotavirus, rubella and malaria, among others.
Other Indian manufacturers with WHO-prequalified vaccines include Bharat Biotech, Biological E, Zydus Lifesciences, GreenSignal Bio Pharma, Haffkine and Panacea Biotec, among others.
Bharat Biotech’s Typbar-TCV, for example, was the first typhoid conjugate vaccine to receive WHO prequalification; Zydus’s ZyVac TCV received WHO prequalification in September 2026.
What is different about CERVAVAC?
The HPV milestone is distinctive because, until now, WHO’s prequalified HPV portfolio consisted of vaccines manufactured outside India. WHO’s HPV product-choice document lists bivalent vaccines such as Cecolin, Cervarix and Walrinvax, quadrivalent Gardasil, and nonavalent Gardasil-9. CERVAVAC was previously nationally licensed but was not WHO-prequalified.
Its inclusion therefore adds an Indian-made HPV vaccine to the global WHO-prequalified pool.
For India, the larger significance is that a vaccine developed and manufactured domestically can now potentially contribute not only to India’s cervical-cancer prevention programme but also to HPV vaccination programmes elsewhere.
The WHO’s global target is to have 90% of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15, alongside screening and treatment targets for women. By the end of 2025, HPV vaccination had been introduced in 165 countries, but global first-dose coverage among girls was only about 33%, well below the 90% target.
