What ice cream has to do with this year's Nobel Prize in economics
This article first appeared in the Planet Money newsletter. You can sign up here.
On Monday morning, the world's econ nerds tuned in to an announcement from Sweden to learn who won this year's Nobel Prize in economics. And we got a lesson involving … ice cream.
The winners were Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University. The prize committee honored them "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."
To explain what the heck that means — as we will try to do in this newsletter — Timo Boppart, an economist at Stockholm University and member of the prize committee, stood up and walked around like he was giving a TED Talk. At one point, he brought up an image on the screen behind him: an ice cream menu.
Boppart used the ice cream menu to serve up a sweet lesson in economics.
"How do firms actually set prices?" Boppart asked. " This is illustrated here with this ice cream menu. Prices do not adjust [on] a continuous basis. Firms instead set the price of this ice cream for a whole season."
Ice cream was a poetic example. Because prices, like ice cream, can get sticky. In fact, economists use the term "sticky prices" to describe how prices can stubbornly stay put even as economic conditions change.
That seemingly minor detail can have huge consequences for the entire economy. Sticky prices are a cornerstone of what's known as "New Keynesian economics" — a framework that has helped reshape macroeconomic theory and how policymakers think about fighting recessions and controlling inflation.
This year's prize honored work that helped lay the foundations for New Keynesian economics. In the process, Hall, Woodford, and other scholars helped breathe new life into the ideas of economics giant John Maynard Keynes, whose intellectual legacy, for a time, seemed in danger of melting away.
To understand why, we need to go back to the 1970s, when the economy experienced something that, for some, seemed to invalidate Keynesian economics.
Keynesianism gets a brain freeze
John Maynard Keynes is basically the father of macroeconomics, the study of how the entire economy works, including what the government can do to fight recessions, boost employment, and control inflation.
Keynes' breakthrough came in the depths of the Great Depression, when he published The General Theory of Employment, Interest, and Money. He articulated an idea that may seem obvious today but challenged the economic orthodoxy of his time: an economy can get stuck in a prolonged slump, and the free market won't necessarily get everyone back to work on its own. Instead, Keynes wrote, we needed the government to help boost spending, put people back to work, and return the economy to health.
If you've ever taken an Econ 101 class, you've probably heard about the "invisible hand" of the free market. It's the idea that people and businesses pursuing their own interests in competitive markets can help the economy reach its full potential without the government having to step in. Keynes basically argued we couldn't count on the invisible hand to pull the economy out of a slump. We needed the visible hand of the government.
Keynes influenced an entire generation of economists and policymakers. Even Milton Friedman, a strong advocate for the free market, was quoted in 1965 as saying, "We are all Keynesians now." (He later said the quote was taken out of context.)
In the 1970s, however, the dominant Keynesian models — and the policies they helped guide — ran into trouble. Inflation and unemployment rose together — a painful combination known as "stagflation." The existing Keynesian models struggled to explain it.
"For a long time, the recipes of Keynes seemed to work, but they then failed during the oil crisis in the 1970s when high unemployment and high inflation took over simultaneously," said John Hassler, the chair of the Nobel committee, when they announced the prize.
When the old-school models faltered, some economists wanted to reject Keynes wholesale. Economists like Robert Lucas and Edward Prescott — who each won Nobel Prizes — challenged Keynesian economics and its confidence that government policy could effectively smooth out the economy's ups and downs. Call it the revenge of the invisible hand.
A central criticism: The Keynesian models relied too heavily on patterns found in past economic data without adequately explaining the individual decisions behind them. Addressing that criticism meant giving models "microfoundations": starting with the decisions of individual people and businesses to explain how the whole economy works. The economy is made of people, and people think ahead. They anticipate what policymakers will do, and those expectations shape how they spend, save, and invest. If policymakers change direction, people's behavior might too — making old patterns an unreliable guide to whether a new policy will work.
One influential alternative to Keynesianism, developed by Prescott and other economists, became known as "real business cycle" theory. These models assumed that prices and wages were completely flexible, adjusting freely as economic conditions changed. If demand for workers fell, wages could fall too, making workers cheaper to hire and allowing the labor market to balance supply and demand. That left little room for a familiar feature of recessions: people who want to work but can't find jobs.
Gregory Mankiw, now an economist at Harvard University, entered graduate school at MIT alongside Michael Woodford in 1980. They were learning macroeconomics just as economists were fighting over how to rebuild it.
"Lucas and Prescott were ascendant, but a lot of us were skeptical of their conclusions," Mankiw tells Planet Money. " And that's when people like Woodford and Hall sort of entered the stage. The sense was that the people who were rejecting the Keynesian model were throwing out the baby with the bathwater. And so rather than throwing it out, they wanted to sort of fix the problems."
A fresh scoop of Keynes
Hall and Woodford helped rebuild macroeconomics around the decisions of individual people and businesses. Hall broke new ground in understanding how people's expectations about the future shape their spending today. Woodford built on that work, developing a framework that combined forward-looking spending decisions with sticky prices.
To see why sticky prices matter, let's return to the ice cream example. Say there's a recession and demand for ice cream plummets. Shops might not quickly reduce ice cream prices to entice customers back. Maybe changing menus and signs costs time and money. Or maybe shops aren't yet sure whether the drop in demand is temporary or here to stay. Instead, they keep prices frozen, sell fewer scoops, and ultimately may end up having to cut worker hours or lay people off. When prices don't adjust, jobs and businesses take a hit.
The same story goes for wages, which we guess are a bigger factor in the economy than ice cream prices.
" When economists talk about sticky prices, they're also including sticky wages — the price of labor," Mankiw says. "Most people don't get their wages adjusted every month."
Across the economy, that stickiness or "price rigidity" can have big consequences. When spending drops, prices and wages don't quickly and flexibly adjust to keep people buying and businesses hiring. Instead of prices falling to bring supply and demand together, in these models, price stickiness causes production and employment to fall. It helps explain why, during recessions, people who want to work can remain out of a job for long stretches.
" Bringing in those price rigidities into the framework was absolutely key because this is the reason why the invisible hand cannot do its magic and there is room for policy intervention," said Boppart at the Nobel Prize announcement.
In other words, even when people and businesses think ahead and act in their own interests, sticky prices can keep the economy stuck in a slump. Call it Keynes' comeback. In these models, governments and central banks still have a role to play in getting the economy back on track.
This was the promise of New Keynesian economics: take the criticisms of the old models seriously, rebuild models around individual decisions, and preserve Keynes' central insight that the free market won't always bounce back on its own.
"One thing that clearly differentiates Keynesian models from Real Business Cycle models was the flexibility or stickiness of prices," Mankiw says. "Most economists today — not all — but I think most economists today buy into the sticky price assumption."
These New Keynesian models became integral to how governments and central banks think about fighting recessions and controlling inflation.
Woodford's work, for example, helped lay the theoretical groundwork for "forward guidance," a strategy the Federal Reserve used during the Great Recession. The Fed slashed its benchmark interest rate to near zero, but the economy still needed stimulus. So under then-chair Ben Bernanke, the Fed signaled that it expected to keep interest rates low for an extended period. By shaping expectations about future rates, the Fed tried to help lower longer-term borrowing costs and encourage spending today.
Keynes' ideas survived with new foundations. And Mankiw offers an update to Milton Friedman's famous line: "We're all New Keynesians now," he says.
P.S. Throughout this piece, we've called this award the "Nobel Prize in economics." But calling it that is surprisingly controversial. Technically, it has a much clunkier name. Economics wasn't one of the prizes Alfred Nobel created. So how did it join the club? Ricky and I tell that story in the latest episode of The Indicator from Planet Money. Check it out when it's released Tuesday.

On 10 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) organised a major protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which protesters claim led to arbitrary voter deletions. In response to the demonstrations, authorities imposed a security crackdown, shutting down dozens of metro stations, cancelling trains, and enforcing prohibitory orders across the capital. Police have detained thousands of individuals, including political figures like Arvind Kejriwal, Pinarayi Vijayan and Mamata Banerjee, as well as CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who were later released.
In this context, a video (here & here) showing large groups of people rallying on the road is being shared with claims that it depicts protesters marching toward Jantar Mantar. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing protesters marching towards Delhi’s Jantar Mantar during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protest on 10 October 2026.
Fact: The video is unrelated to the October 10 CJP protests. The visuals date to January 2021 and depict the farmers’ protests. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to an Instagram post (archive) from January 2021 linking the footage to the farmers’ protest in Delhi. The same video has since been misattributed to several other events (here, here & here).
Further research revealed that visuals identical to those seen in the viral video were published by media outlets like the Associated Press and Firstpost, as well as on stock image websites like Alamy, in January 2021. According to these sources, the visuals are from the 2021 farmers’ protest. This proves that the viral video predates the October 10 CJP protest and is entirely unrelated to it
To sum it up, an old video from the 2021 farmers’ protest is being falsely linked to the October 10 Jantar Mantar CJP protest.

A skin problem can begin with something familiar. An itch that persists. A rash that returns. A patch that looks different from the rest of the skin. What happens next often depends on where a person lives and whether appropriate care is within reach.
The Global Access to Skin Health Observatory is a landmark global study led by Esther Freeman in collaboration with the International League of Dermatological Societies (ILDS) and L’Oréal Dermatological Beauty. Published in JAMA Dermatology, it brings together data from 158 countries representing 97% of the world’s population.
For India, the findings raise questions about where specialists practise, how patients reach them and what happens when treatment is delayed.
What the numbers miss
The study proposes a benchmark of 5.63 per lakh, derived from countries reporting adequate access to dermatological care. This, however, is a reference point, rather than a universal staffing prescription. Dr. Freeman, who is associate professor of dermatology at Harvard Medical School and director of global health dermatology at Massachusetts General Hospital, places India’s dermatologist density well below the benchmark at around 0.5 to 1 per lakh people.
Ramesh Bhat, the Indian co-author of the study and professor at Father Muller Medical College and head of research at Father Muller Research Centre, Mangalore, cautions against directly comparing India with Europe or the Americas, because their health systems differ. What surprises Prof Bhat is that shortages persist despite the number of postgraduate dermatology training seats. He points to the urban-rural divide, with a concentration of specialists in urban areas, and in many cities in southern India, while rural communities face a different reality, where access even to a doctor may be limited.
The study reports that, globally, 79% of dermatologists practise in urban areas. National averages can therefore conceal substantial local gaps. “Dermatologist density gives us an important starting point, but it does not tell us whether a patient can actually receive care,” Dr. Freeman says.
When care is delayed
For Prof Bhat, the consequences are visible in clinical practice. He identifies “delay in diagnosis, wrong treatment, steroid abuse” among the problems arising when appropriate care is unavailable. He singles out leprosy as a condition where delayed diagnosis has implications beyond the individual patient. His concern brings the discussion back to what happens before someone reaches a specialist and whether the treatment they receive along the way is appropriate.
Dr Freeman emphasises the breadth of skin disease, from common infections to chronic inflammatory conditions and neglected tropical diseases. She argues that skin health must be recognised as an essential part of healthcare, with investment directed towards services that already reach communities.
The question is, how to make those services capable of recognising and managing skin disease safely.
Bringing expertise closer
“We need more dermatologists, but we cannot train our way out of this problem with specialists alone,” Dr Freeman says. Primary-care physicians and health officers already manage substantial amounts of skin disease. She advocates practical training, essential medicines and clear referral pathways, allowing common conditions to be treated locally while complex disease and uncertain diagnoses reach specialists.
Prof Bhat also proposes that medical colleges adopt villages, strengthening their links with surrounding communities. He also sees a role for the district residency programme, which takes residents into district settings, and for health camps in reaching rural and tribal populations.
These approaches sit alongside his call for rural specialist clinics and teledermatology. His emphasis is on extending the reach of existing teaching institutions and services, while giving residents the training needed to work effectively beyond major urban centres.
Making remote advice useful
“Teledermatology can be implemented,” Prof Bhat says. But he cautions that training healthcare workers must not result in unqualified practice or drug misuse. Expanding access requires clarity about who can manage a condition and when specialist assessment is necessary.
Dr. Freeman makes a related point. Teledermatology and Artificial Intelligence use need trained frontline providers, available treatment, and reliable referral arrangements. A patient requiring a biopsy, urgent assessment or specialist therapy must still be able to obtain it. “The goal is not to replace dermatologists, but to make their expertise reach much further,” she says.
A remote consultation needs to connect with treatment and follow-up. Advice alone cannot resolve the practical difficulties of obtaining medicines or reaching a referral centre.
What progress should look like
In 2025, the World Health Assembly recognised skin diseases as a global public-health priority. The next step is translating that recognition into national funding and delivery plans.
Prof Bhat’s priorities include an adequate health budget and insurance coverage for dermatological medicines such as biologics and for procedures. He also calls for better training of dermatology residents and dermatology nursing as a separate speciality within nursing education. These proposals bring together workforce development, treatment affordability and rural services, addressing several barriers to appropriate dermatological care.
Measuring progress will require listening more closely to patients. Dr. Freeman acknowledges that the Observatory relied on national leaders and health-system informants, rather than patients directly. Future work should examine waiting times, travel, affordability and diagnostic delays, alongside outcomes and quality of life.
Her planned next phase will examine selected countries more closely to understand where clinicians choose to train and practise, what retains them in underserved areas and which models improve access in different settings. “Five years from now, success should not simply mean there are more dermatologists,” she says. “It should mean that where someone lives is less predictive of whether they can get appropriate care for their skin disease.”
For India, that would mean earlier recognition, appropriate treatment and dependable referral, with fewer patients left to navigate the gaps themselves.
(Dr. Monisha Madhumita is assistant professor, department of dermatology, Saveetha Medical College and Hospitals, Chennai. mail.monisha.m@gmail.com)

The federal government has released new quality ratings for Medicare Advantage insurers for 2027, with Humana emerging as the biggest winner.
But deep uncertainty remains around Medicare Advantage quality measures, which come with tens of billions of dollars in extra revenue for the highest-performing plans. One health insurance company, Alignment Healthcare, has already threatened to sue the government after its star ratings were downgraded — a now-common occurrence for almost any insurer that is unhappy with its grades.
Nearly 71% of Medicare Advantage enrollees are currently in a plan that will have at least four out of five stars for quality, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Getting at least four stars triggers bonuses, which total $13 billion across the industry annually. Ratings for 2027 lead to bonus payouts in 2028.

U.S. President Donald Trump's Ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) after allegations of improper conduct but insisted she'll "vigorously defend" herself.
Mr. Trump's administration said on Tuesday (October 13) it had asked her to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
The announcement, after days of comments and speculation, came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning.
Ms. Zacharia said Ms. Guilfoyle "has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."
Ms Guilfoyle's departure comes after the possibility was previewed to the AP over the weekend, and Mr. Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday (October 12) in response to reports of her alleged conduct.
"Well, we're looking at it,” Mr. Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he was considering firing Ms. Guilfoyle. “We're not happy.”
Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Mr. Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Ms. Guilfoyle's reported conduct and would likely decide on her future this week.
In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Ms. Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Ms Guilfoyle has not directly addressed the reports. But in a statement released late Sunday, her lawyers denied that she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Mr. Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.
The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations."
The allegations began surfacing weeks ago
After defending Ms. Guilfoyle following the first report, Mr. Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Mr. Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared later, Mr. Rubio — speaking Thursday before leaving Athens — berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn't know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things,” Mr. Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Ms. Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
A second U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department's inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
There was no immediate response to Ms. Zacharia's statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members.
Ahead of Tuesday's announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Ms. Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. "This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity,” Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Ms. Guilfoyle had been treated “the same way as every other ambassador” and argued that an official summons had not been necessary.

ROME – Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff.
The pope has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said.
Leo was admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent routine health check.

Atletico Madrid eased to a 2-0 win over Manchester United in the Champions League on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) to pile pressure on Red Devils coach Michael Carrick.
Pablo Barrios pounced inside the first minute for Diego Simeone's side and after Leny Yoro's 74th minute red card set United back further, Ademola Lookman added another for the hosts in Madrid.
Man United have made their worst domestic start in 40 years and this league phase defeat in the Spanish capital was another blow, with the team now winless in five games across all competitions.
Carrick handed Carlos Baleba his first start for the club since arriving from Brighton this summer, as well as pushing captain Bruno Fernandes out to the right side.
Atletico were without their skipper Koke, after the death of his mother, while coach Simeone selected Julian Alvarez from the off for the first time this season at the Metropolitano stadium, after he tried to force a departure this summer.
"Defend what we love," Atletico fans ordered their supporters with a banner display before kick-off and the Rojiblancos were ahead after just 50 seconds.
Alex Baena found a way in behind United's defence and cut the ball across for Barrios, with Ayden Heaven unable to keep the midfielder's shot from crossing the line.
Bryan Mbuemo might have equalised for the visitors, nudging the ball through Cristian Romero's legs but firing just wide.
Alejandro Grimaldo came inches away from extending Atletico's lead with a free-kick which hit the angle between post and crossbar.
The hosts thought they had a second when Johnny Cardoso finished neatly from the edge of the box before half-time but the goal was disallowed after a VAR review showed the ball had struck Marcos Llorente's hand during the build-up.
Alvarez, yet to score this season for Atletico, hit the post early in the second half.
United rallied and Fernandes's lob drifted narrowly wide before the Portuguese playmaker hit the crossbar from the left of the box after a corner routine.
However the three-time European champions suffered a setback when defender Yoro was harshly dismissed after a VAR review for bringing down Canada striker Jonathan David as the last man.
It opened the door for Atletico to grab their second, with David foiled by goalkeeper Senne Lammens but London-born Nigeria international Lookman on hand to tuck home the rebound after 79 minutes.
Carrick withdrew playmaker Fernandes, looking ahead to the weekend visit to face rivals Leeds in the English top flight, where improvement is badly needed.
Atletico goalkeeper Jan Oblak saved from United substitute Matheus Cunha in the final stages but there was no way back for United.
Simeone's side were able to claim their first points after an opening defeat at Liverpool.

The Arc Raiders Frozen Trail update introduced many new gameplay mechanics, including the Weapon Amplification system. If anyone wants to upgrade their weapon beyond the regular level 4 upgrade, it is now possible in the game. However, if you are confused about the Weapon Amplification System and want to learn more about which weapons can be amplified, here is everything you need to know.
What Is Weapon Amplification in Arc Raiders?
Weapon Amplification system is a new mechanic introduced in the Arc Raiders Frozen Trail update. Previously, the maximum level you could upgrade a weapon to was level 4. Now, the new Weapon Amplification system allows players to upgrade their favorite weapons to a fifth quality level.
More importantly, players can now choose the designated upgrade path they want among the branches of nodes for their weapon. Currently, 15 weapons in Arc Raiders, namely Anvil, Aphelion, Bettina, Burletta, Canto, Equalizer, Hairpin, Hullcracker, Il Toro, Jupiter, Kettle, Osprey, Rascal, Rattler, and Renegade.
How to Unlock Weapon Amplification in Arc Raiders?
Since Weapon Amplification is endgame content in Arc Raiders, players must grind in order to unlock the system in-game. Players are tasked with finding various resource materials from Amplification Modules to research items needed to amplify the currently available weapons.
With that in mind, here is how to unlock the Weapon Amplification system in Arc Raiders:
- First, players need to research Topside Living Conditions, complete the Gather Building Materials, and Safeguard the Building Site to unlock the Outposts in Arc Raiders.
- Once you have successfully set up an Outpost, you need to expand the space to level 4 by adding your preferred rooms.
- Doing so will unlock upgrades for the new Research Station and the old Gunsmith workbench.
- Now, you need to gather different materials and upgrade both the Gunsmith and Research Station to level 4 in the game
- After you unlock the Gunsmith level 4 workbench, you can see the ‘Amplify’ option available for selected weapons in the Weapon Upgrades tab.
How to Amplify a Weapon in Arc Raiders
Once you have successfully unlocked the Gunsmith IV workbench in Arc Raiders, you are now eligible to amplify 15 different weapons. So, here is how to amplify one in Arc Raiders:
- Go to the Gunsmith level 4 workbench.
- Then head to the Weapon Upgrades tab.
- Make sure your preferred weapon has already been upgraded to level 4.
- You can then select a weapon of your choice and hit the Amplify button to upgrade it to level 5.
- One important thing to note is that an amplified weapon cannot be reverted, as it is a permanent upgrade.
To amplify your favorite weapon in Arc Raiders, you need to collect the desired Amplification Module. Amplification Modules are a new resource material introduced in the Frozen Trail update and are available in five versions, from Mk. I to Mk. V.
Now, if you are amplifying a common weapon, you need an Amplification Module Mk. I. An uncommon weapon means Amplification Module Mk. II, and so on. Basically, as a weapon’s rarity increases, an apt Amplification Module is required for an upgrade. So, here is a list of amplification weapons and their required Amplification Modules:
- Amplification Module Mk. I: Hairpin, Kettle, Rattler (Common)
- Amplification Module Mk. II: Burletta, Il Toro (Uncommon)
- Amplification Module Mk. III: Anvil, Canto, Osprey, Rascal, Renegade (Rare)
- Amplification Module Mk. IV: Bettina, Hullcracker (Epic)
- Amplification Module Mk. V: Aphelion, Equalizer, Jupiter (Legendary)
If you are wondering where you can find the Amplification Modules in the game, you can get these resource materials from the Fallen Emperor as well as the Frigate in Arc Raiders. Additionally, to unlock specific upgrade nodes in the branch, players must also complete certain objectives and gather resource materials for the Research station.

Now that you have learned about what Weapon Amplifications are and how to amplify one, it’s time to know more about all weapon amplifications available in the game. Achyuta Samanta has been unanimously elected the first President of the Indian UniSport Federation (IUSF) at its inaugural Annual General Meeting on Sunday.
Addressing the members after his election, he called for collective efforts to prepare Indian athletes for the upcoming Commonwealth Games in India.
Recognised by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, the Federation aims to strengthen university sports, promote transparent governance and create greater opportunities for young athletes across the country.
Under his leadership, as the Founder, at KIIT and KISS, the institutions have developed a comprehensive sports ecosystem featuring more than 30 sports facilities, professional coaching, sports science, nutrition, medical care and rehabilitation support.

As many as 24 KIIT and KISS athletes have represented India at the Olympic Games, Asian Games, Commonwealth Games and World University Games. KIIT has also served as India’s nodal university for the World University Games since Napoli 2019.
More recently, 54 students from KIIT and KISS represented India at the 20th Asian Games held in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. At the continental sporting event, athletes from KIIT and KISS won a total of 21 medals, comprising three gold, seven silver and 11 bronze medals.
As IUSF President, Dr Samanta has emphasised fair competition, accountable governance and athlete-centred development.
Samanta has held several positions in national and international sports organisations and received recognition for his contributions. He previously served as President of the Volleyball Federation of India and currently serves as President of the Odisha Volleyball Association.
He is also associated with the International Volleyball Federation (FIVB). Over the years, he has developed strong relationships with leading international sports bodies, including FIFA, FIVB and FIDE. In recognition of his contributions to the promotion of volleyball and chess, he has received the highest honour conferred by the FIVB.

A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.
The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.
The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe through police operations, transnational investigations and ongoing court cases involving brokers, active members, cells or operational networks. It does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias.
The identified groups include Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG); the Clan del Golfo mafia, and the guerrilla organisations ELN and dissident factions of Farc in Colombia; Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command) and Comando Vermelho (CV, or Red Command); Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua; and the US-originated Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs, which are also prevalent in El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, in Mexico.
These organisations have built a more prominent presence in Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, while their activities have also been noted in Germany, Romania, Croatia and Slovakia. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (Gi-Toc) also includes Bulgaria.
Daniel Brombacher, a political scientist and director of the Europe Observatory at Gi-Toc, said: “There is something new happening with a presence of Latin American groups in geographies where there’s no pre-existing infrastructure.
“This phenomenon is no longer limited to the traditional gateway countries,” he says. “Recent police operations have uncovered Mexican-run methamphetamine labs in southern France, north-eastern Poland and Brandenburg, south of Berlin. Latin American groups are also appearing in Romania and Bulgaria along the Balkan route.”
Latin American national authorities and experts suggest the list may be even longer. An unpublished report by the São Paulo public prosecutor’s office, partly based on data from the Brazilian intelligence agency (Abin) – which the Guardian reviewed – shows, for example, that the PCC, now Brazil’s biggest criminal group, operates in 16 European countries, including the UK, Ireland, Iceland, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.
The suspicion that Latin American cartels and factions are seeking to become established in Europe is not new. Since at least the 1980s, Colombian criminal organisations such as the Cali and Medellín cartels had footholds in regions of Spain such as Galicia. In 2013, a Europol report in 2103 warned of their rise. But what authorities are witnessing now is on an another level.
A Europol report this year states that “Latin American MTCNs [most threatening criminal networks] have also settled in the EU, from where they direct operations that affect the EU. This is particularly the case for mobile criminal networks involved in organised property crime.”
Interpol, led by the Brazilian federal police officer Valdecy Urquiza, has been approached, but has not commented.
The problem has become more visible over the past decade. Drug production in Latin America in that time has increased roughly fourfold to reach a record of about 4,100 tonnes in 2024. This comes after growth of up to 35% at the beginning of the decade. More cocaine is now produced in Colombia than during the era of the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar. Nearly all the world’s cocaine and many related substances originate from Latin America, particularly Colombia.
Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, an academic at the Autonomous University of Coahuila in Mexico who is an expert on organised crime, says: “The main ones are the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco cartel [CJNG] in Mexico; the Comando Vermelho and the PCC of Brazil; the Gulf Clan and different factions of the Colombian Farc; the Lobos and the Choneros of Ecuador; and Tren de Aragua of Venezuela.”
He believes that the Latin American presence in Europe is even more widespread than is generally recognised. “Sinaloa cartel and the CJNG have a presence in more than 20 European countries. Obviously, that does not mean they dominate or have large cells,” he says. “Rather, they are business emissaries.”
The UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2026 World Drug Report on illicit crimes states that global cocaine production in 2024 was between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes – more than four times higher than it was in 2014. South America remains the main production hub, with coca cultivation covering a record 385,000 hectares over the past decade – three times the 2014 figure.
Europe has emerged as a key market because it offers organisations higher profit margins than the US. Since the beginning of the decade, European police have confiscated more drugs than American forces, and data indicates that Europe now represents about a quarter of global consumption.
Europol recently reported that out of 731 MTCNs operating across Europe, 149 are connected to Latin American organisations. Of these, 67 have Latin American members, and 22 mainly consist of Latin Americans.

When a filmmaker tells a story based on real events, especially ones that are inspiring or heroic, there’s always a risk of hagiography. “Clean Hands” is a movie where the storytellers either take a lot of license with an actual person’s life to add drama, or don’t seem aware just how unflattering their subject’s behavior actually is. Written, produced and directed by Jake Allyn (“Ride”), the film chronicles the relationship between real-life Hagerstown, MD narcotics officer Kevin Simmers (Zach Braff) and his efforts to rescue his daughter Brooke (Esther McGregor) from the grip of drug abuse. But while the “happening right under his nose” details lend a heartbreaking edge to a sadly familiar story, the script’s argument against criminalizing addiction reconciles uneasily with its portrayal of Simmers’ determination to save Brooke by any means necessary.
Simmers is a hero cop, looked up to by his colleagues and liked better than one might expect by the local townspeople, given his by-the-book approach. Though he maintains a close relationship with 19-year-old Brooke, he’s blindsided when he learns that she’s addicted to Percocet and has been consorting with abusive dealer Brick (Kraig Dane). After unsuccessfully trying to enroll her in a private rehab facility, Simmers learns that she’s moved on to heroin; he takes a tough-love approach to let her get arrested, hoping to scare her straight. But when even that fails, he becomes determined to cut off her supply at the source, pursuing local addicts in the hopes of apprehending anyone who might deal her drugs.
Popular on Variety
Despite the support of his religious wife Dana (Abigail Spencer) and colleagues on the police force, including an ambitious deputy (Lucas Till) eager to succeed him as the precinct’s role model, Simmers’ efforts to help get Brooke clean fail over and over again. As he faces the prospect of losing her to addiction, he begins to conceive an alternative path for struggling drug abusers, even while witnessing members of the Hagerstown community — including some of his fellow officers — exploiting addicts instead of helping them.
Given the infomercial pasted at the top of the closing credits for Brooke’s House, the rehab facility Simmers created in response to his daughter’s addiction, it feels safe to assume that the former police officer fully endorsed this portrait of him and his family’s struggles. Yet the typical disclaimer absolving the filmmakers of responsibility for dramatizing these real people’s lives is oddly posted at the beginning of the closing credits rather than at the very end, suggesting that some of the narrative leaps taken here by the filmmakers are bigger than usual. To that end, one can understand why Allyn wouldn’t want to risk misrepresenting Hagerstown law enforcement. But should audiences accept at face value every action taken by Simmers in his crusade to save his daughter?
By all accounts, he was a dedicated cop with honed instincts as an investigator, and a loving father to Brooke — so much so that, in the film, Dana accuses the two of them of being addicted to each other. But the character’s compassion towards perpetrators and his cool detachment under pressure seem only to apply when he doesn’t have an active stake in a crime. When he does, he seems willing to abuse his power and take any measures that he thinks will result in whatever he’s already decided the outcome should be — whether that’s lying to a healthcare provider to get his daughter treatment, or arresting an individual he deems complicit in Brooke’s condition.
As the film tells it, Simmers eventually learns that waging war against dealers and community enablers makes less of an impact on people who are addicted than providing them consistent, patient, loving support. But the character is so relentless for so long with his methods that it’s hard not to pin a portion of the blame for Brooke’s addiction on him.
Again, that seems distantly like the point (or at least one point) of “Clean Hands.” But Allyn is entirely too interested in Simmers’ police work, meaning high-pitched chases and strong-arm interrogations, to strike the right balance between his day job and his earnest efforts to help his daughter. As a viewer, it’s possible to forgive a character who’s so determined to protect his daughter that he takes overbearing or inappropriate measures, but when the film wants the crime stuff to be tense and exciting — amplified with music by instrumental rock act Those Who Ride With Giants — it undercuts the humanity of what that character is facing.
Simmers marks a departure from the kinds of roles for which Braff is best known, and the actor commits to the character’s tenacity and determination in a way that suggests he’s either prioritizing authenticity regardless of how the character is perceived, or he misunderstands how sympathetic Allyn’s version of Simmers can be. The problem is the contrast between his well-meaning actions and their impact on others: Brooke faces beatings in jail because her father antagonizes the guards and other inmates, God-fearing Dana flinches every time he drops an f-bomb or angrily dresses down a rehab administrator, and until the very last scene in the film, he ignores or dismisses the addiction, poverty or desperation of anyone he encounters who’s struggling.
McGregor offers a welcome counterbalance as Brooke, whose general disposition emanates from her relationship with her father, even as it’s hobbled by troubles the script pinpoints with delicacy. Though the film doesn’t quite know what to do with Dana as Simmers bulldozes his way to a cure for Brooke, Spencer similarly offers grace — or at least a less rigid form of support — that hints at how his initial way of helping may not be the most effective one.
To whatever extent this story is told accurately, Simmers was of course doing the best that he could to reckon with a challenge he’d dealt with in the line of duty, but never with a person so close to him — and years of repetition reinforced a one-size-fits-all reaction to an affliction that must be addressed individually. But the film builds to the founding of Brooke’s House and its immediate, overwhelming success, indicating that all Simmers needed to do was change his tactics, instead of the more meaningful, moving change in his perception of addiction as something to be mechanically repaired. A handful of appealing performances aside, “Clean Hands” ignores too many messy realities in favor of quick solutions; the stuff that gives a true story like this power is the hard work and struggle that happens between an epiphany about oneself and the reality of implementing its lessons in the world.

Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates, resident tells BBC
A resident of Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region, says that the atmosphere is calm but people are very stressed after fighting broke out between government troops and the party that controls the region on Wednesday, raising fears of a return to full-scale civil war.
He says that many banks have been running low on cash for months, leaving people to rely on mobile banking, with fears that could now be blocked.
An adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister accused the Tigray People's Liberation Front of launching an all-out offensive, including in the two neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara. The Tigrayans say they are engaged in defensive combat.

The State informed the Kerala High Court that in-principle approval had not been granted to Keralam for establishing an All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS).
The Division Bench of Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice V.M. Syam Kumar enquired into the reason why Keralam was not prioritised for building an AIIMS, even though the matter had been pending for almost 10 years. The Bench was considering a petition seeking establishment of an AIIMS under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY).
The court observed that the matter was presently at the stage of inter-ministerial consultation and any decision for setting up an AIIMS could be taken only after the continuation of the PMSSY scheme for the next five financial years, FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, was approved.
In a previous order, the court noted that the idea of having an AIIMS in Keralam was raised in June 2016 and four locations were identified for this purpose. The court opined that Keralam should be considered on a priority basis considering the density of population, and asked the Union government to take a conscious decision concerning the proposal for the institute.
Prioritising other States
The Deputy Solicitor General of India, O.M. Shalina, informed the court that since Keralam had better health-care conditions than other States, the Union government was prioritising those States with a weaker health sector. How can we stop astronauts from building up dangerous static electricity on the Moon? To find a solution, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) launched a crowdsourced initiative seeking innovative engineering ideas to address the problem. NASA calls it the "Lunar Grounding Challenge." The space agency is offering up to $150,000 in prizes to whoever wins the 'Lunar Grounding Challenge.' The US and NASA hope to land an American astronaut at the lunar South Pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions. They fear risks involving "tribocharging" from walking on the lunar surface and "plasma charging" from the ambient plasma generating electric charge on the spacesuit. "This problem is severely compounded when entering lunar shadows and Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs). In these dark zones, the spacesuit can buildup a substantial negative potential due to a lack of ambient ion flux and the absence of photoelectron emission to balance ambient electron collection," NASA explains. It added that the risk occurs when an astronaut returns to the spacecraft. "Because the lunar surface lacks a natural environmental mechanism to bleed the charge accumulated on spacesuit away, the astronaut may become a walking, high-voltage capacitor," the US space agency says. It further explained that in the sunlit region, the stationary lander will hold slightly positive electrical potential. When a highly negatively-charged astronaut approaches the vehicle, the extreme voltage differential can trigger electrostatic discharge (an instantaneous electrical arc, or a spark) during physical contact. "A rapid discharge from the astronaut to the lander risks degrading vital suit layers, damaging sensitive suit electronics, threatening the oxygen-rich environment inside the suit, and delivering dangerous electrical shocks to the crew," NASA says. To find a solution to this problem, NASA is seeking innovative designs as part of the Lunar Grounding Challenge. NASA has asked industry partners for ideas that can help an astronaut avoid "becoming a walking, high voltage capacitor", including issues such as an electrical arc that could damage spacesuits, spark fires in the oxygen atmosphere of a spacecraft, or create electrical shocks. This challenge seeks innovative concepts for an Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) mitigation solution to neutralise the astronaut in a safe and timely manner under this extreme charge differential before astronauts directly interact with the lander. Registrations for the challenge opened on October 5, and the submission deadline is January 15, 2027. Find link to submit your application here: https://work.crowdplat.com/challenge/lunar-grounding-challenge NASA says the proposed solution must minimise mass, volume, and power impacts and be operable in the harsh lunar environment’s surface conditions. The solution must be less than 20-kg and dimensional and power constraints will be defined during challenge design. The solution must support up to four Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) over 10 days being exposed to the lunar environment. Moreover, the suspended lunar dust and heavy dust buildup on a suit in these environments significantly increase arcing lengths, allowing sparks to jump across larger gaps than they would in a clean vacuum. "Therefore, the solution must aim to avoid a sudden arc that may come into contact with the outer pressure garment (suit) or the lander," the agency explained. This Challenge has two phases: 1) Concept Design Submission and 2) Concept Refinement. NASA did not release a target date in its press release for when the tech would be available for astronauts, but the agency is planning on a long-term moon base for astronaut missions that would be largely ready to go in the 2030s if schedules hold. 'State of the Game': Independent Football Regulator's report finds most English clubs living on financial brink
The Independent Football Regulator published its draft ‘State of the Game’ report on Tuesday, which found that while English football generated £9bn in revenue last season, 94 per cent of clubs in the top five divisions were loss-making
Tuesday 13 October 2026 17:15, UK
The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has produced a 'State of the Game' report, which has taken a forensic look at English football over the past 18 months, concluding that the game's finances are dangerously exposed, with the majority of clubs living on the edge of financial disaster.
The IFR added that interest and investment from around the world continues to grow within English football, but the underlying foundations of the pyramid are under intense strain and require urgent reform.
Despite over £9bn generated in revenue, 94 per cent of clubs are loss-making, with long-term security being put at risk through excessive short-term spending to keep up with rivals. This, the IFR says, has led to a "dangerous cocktail of rising debt and an over-reliance on owner funding, leaving clubs and their fans at risk".

The report acknowledges that the success of the Premier League has driven economic success, making English football the "richest, best and most deeply competitive in the world".
However, it points to "financial cliff-edges between and within leagues", with the average Premier League club making more than eight times the revenues of an average Championship club, and the system of parachute payments paid by the Premier League to Championship clubs relegated contributing to significant overspend by clubs in the Championship.
Indeed, the report highlights player wage inflation leading clubs to take big risks chasing a place in the Premier League.
The State of the Game report found that lower down the pyramid the pressure from operating costs was also on the rise, with 17 EFL and National League clubs incurring costs exceeding revenues. These clubs would be loss-making even if they did not pay their players.
It uncovered too that more than 60 per cent of EFL and National League clubs are technically insolvent, with their liabilities exceeding the book value of their assets.
And it found that more than a quarter of clubs would be unable to survive for more than one month if owner funding was withdrawn, with the majority lacking a basic contingency plan to mitigate their risk.
'We're trying to take an interventionist approach'
Chair of the IFR David Kogan told Sky: "I think what we see in English football is two completely different positions.
"The first is £9bn comes in every year, yet we have 94 per cent of the clubs of the 160 we regulate are trading unprofitably.
"We have 32 clubs that have got less than 30 days' cash cover in their accounts. So if the owner walks away or drops dead, they're insolvent and go bust.

"So what we see in football is rising debt. It's a problem of cash cover and liquidity within clubs, and it's a lack of management, and what financial management? And now we're in a position to help those clubs achieve a more stable future."
Kogan added: "What we're implying is today there's enough money going through into the Premier League and the EFL and into their individual clubs for the sun to shine. This is exactly the moment when we need to address structural issues because once that sun stops shining, those clubs will be in real trouble.
"So what we are trying to do is get ahead of the problem and take an interventionist approach with individual clubs that need it to help them get to the point of being stable and secure because too many clubs get close to the edge and depend on one thing and one thing only, which is a new owner coming down the track.
"That supply of owners may dry up, and supply of media money may dry out so we have to now get ahead of the game and give them levels of security and stability that allow them to go into the future."
The IFR's six-point plan...
The IFR report offered solutions, issuing a six-point plan to address some of the issues it has identified.
The plan includes measures for clubs to improve how they manage financial risk, including holding more cash and putting robust contingency plans in place in case owner funding is withdrawn; it also outlines how revenue distribution should be reformed to ease cliff-edges throughout the pyramid, urges action on rising losses and calls on clubs to show how they take fans' views into account, and the steps they are taking to improve diversity and governance in the boardroom.
It also highlighted yet again that the current distribution arrangements in English football create risk and should be reformed.
For several years the Premier League and EFL have been discussing and negotiating a new financial distribution model, but no agreement has yet been finalised. The IFR has consistently said, and has said once again in this report, that it is preferable that the Premier League and EFL come to an agreement themselves, but again mentioned that the IFR could apply a "back-stop" power to intervene if the Premier League and EFL do not come to an agreement.
The IFR said its goals on reform of the current distribution model were to:
- Maintain the Premier League as the leading football league in the world and the Championship as the leading second-tier competition.
- Maintain vital funding for the wider game.
- Mitigate the financial impact of relegation from the Premier League.
- Reduce the distortive impact that parachute payments have on financial incentives within the Championship.
- Protect clubs by giving clubs the opportunity to rebuild their balance sheets and reduce risk.
- Consider short-term support to clubs that face severe financial distress.
Kogan said: "There are three moves that are taking place that we think will help on this.
"First is that the Premier League and the EFL are currently discussing a new distribution deal with the game, which will radically change the amount of money going from the Premier League down to the lower leagues. And that will have associated with it controls on how that money is spent, which actually will go to the stability of those lower leagues, but we're going to see more money flowing down, assuming the deal is done, and we're going to see cost controls involved in that.
"The second is that from November onwards we're going to be licensing clubs, and by licensing those clubs we're going to intervene directly in individual clubs where we think they've got exposures that we can help them resolve and that includes things like having a business plan that involves having cash cover more than 30 days; it involves having genuine provision for the debts that they've raised.
"And the third thing we're doing is working with leagues to actually look at cost controls over a longer-term basis to actually build in financial stability as we go forward."

Death toll rises to 6 as Hurricane Simon and Rachel remnants unleash floods in Mexico
Hurricane Simon and the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel have led to six deaths along Mexico’s Pacific coast
ENSENADA, Mexico -- The death toll from Hurricane Simon and the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel rose to six Tuesday after heavy rains triggered flooding and landslides along Mexico’s Pacific coast, authorities said.
Hurricane Simon continued moving slowly off Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 1 storm, bringing heavy rain to Nayarit and Sinaloa states, where authorities remained on alert for rising rivers and flooding. Over the weekend, the hurricane brought heavy rain to the southern state of Guerrero, killing one person.
But the worst damage was reported farther north, in the coastal city of Ensenada, Baja California, where flooding caused by Rachel’s remnants killed at least five people.
The victims included a 13-year-old girl whose body was found Sunday, two women ages 30 and 35 and a 4-year-old boy whose bodies were recovered Monday, and an unidentified person found near a stream Tuesday, the state prosecutor’s office told The Associated Press.
Five others remained missing in Baja California, including three in Ensenada and a father and son who went fishing Saturday in San Felipe, on the Gulf of California, and never returned.
About 300 military personnel, police and rescue workers searched along Ensenada’s El Pipila stream Tuesday, while the Mexican Navy continued looking for the missing fishermen, state civil protection authorities said.
Floodwaters swept away vehicles, damaged homes and cut off access to some communities.
Johana Nuriulu, a resident of Ensenada’s Buena Vista community, said the flooding began overnight, shortly after heavy rain knocked out electricity.
“We heard a loud noise that sounded like ocean waves, but very intense,” she said. When she stepped outside, she discovered a nearby stream had overflowed.
“The water was sweeping everything away; it took a cabin ... animals, everything.”
Elsewhere near Ensenada, Mexican soldiers used helicopters to rescue 32 people, including 13 minors, from Rancho Genesis, a camp for orphans staffed by missionaries.
The army said 22 of those rescued were foreign nationals. Baja California Security Secretary Gen. Laureano Carrillo said they included Americans and Germans.
Simon was moving parallel to Mexico’s Pacific coast Tuesday, threatening more rainfall in Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa.
The hurricane was centered about 180 kilometers (110 miles) west of Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco, with maximum sustained winds of 150 kph (90 mph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami. It was moving west at 4 kph (2 mph).
In southern Guerrero state, Simon’s heavy rains toppled trees and utility poles, blocked roads and flooded homes in coastal communities, including the resort city of Acapulco, Gov. Evelyn Salgado said.
A 71-year-old person died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo, the state capital, she said.
Authorities also took preventive measures in the port city of Mazatlan, Sinaloa, ahead of the storm, national Civil Protection Coordinator Laura Velázquez said Monday.
Meanwhile, conditions were improving in the tourist destination of Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco, where residents began resuming normal activities as the rain subsided.
State authorities ordered schools to reopen Tuesday, while operations at Puerto Vallarta’s airport gradually resumed.

Police in New Delhi detained scores of protesters on Saturday as thousands of officers and paramilitaries patrolled India’s capital, metro stations were shut and mobile internet suspended to guard against a youth protest demanding India’s chief election officer quit.
The protest, called by the “Cockroach” youth movement, hopes to draw thousands of demonstrators who want the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to quit over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party.
Television images showed police in the city’s central business district chasing down a few dozen young protesters, before they were loaded into vehicles and taken away.
About 200 protesters were detained in the area, a police source told Reuters. Those detained outside Delhi included protest supporter Dhruv Rathee, a popular figure on YouTube, a police spokesperson said.
Touted by organisers as a protest to “save democracy”, it aims to be the biggest of the demonstrations that were launched last week after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s deputies had questioned and disagreed with him over the revision process that saw about 130 million voter names removed.
Opposition parties have long alleged the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage.
Kumar has not commented. The election commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.
The BJP says Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth are some of the reasons for its electoral dominance and that opposition parties are misleading the country because they are unable to win elections.
Near daily protests by opposition groups pose a new political challenge to Modi, just months after similar demonstrations forced his education minister to quit over exam paper leaks.
It also comes months before a series of important state elections starting in early 2027, including in the BJP-ruled most populous state of Uttar Pradesh.
The protesters, led by the self-named Cockroach Janta party, that began as an online satire, said they would gather at Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning – a site designated for protests by authorities in the heart of New Delhi.
Delhi police said on Friday they had not given permission for the protest because the request did not come on time, adding that CJP had violated undertakings given during previous protests, and that authorities had to enforce the law and maintain peace.
Police said protesters would face the force of the law if they violated the ban.
Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders rejected the police decision and said they would go ahead with the protest.
Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi. However, the supreme court on Friday said some trains must still run and there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.
“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” the CJP chief, Abhijeet Dipke, said on X.
“Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.”
Mobile internet services in a radius of 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area were ordered suspended from Friday night to Saturday night, ANI news agency reported citing a government order.
The CJP has said “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.
Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions.

Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
- Published
What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?
That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.
The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.
The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.
The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.
Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.
With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.
"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.
The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".
Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.
"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.
Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".
Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.
"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.
"But I did wrong."
It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).
Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.
"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.
"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.
"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."
The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.
In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head".
"To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".
In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.
That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.
Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece.
"You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says.
"And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."
The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.
When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.
But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships.
"I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."
As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US.
"Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim.
"In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat.
"Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."
The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.
In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.
At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.
Kim says that began to change as they filmed.
"I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."
Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.
She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.
On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career.
"Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview.
"And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."
Kim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule.
"But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.
The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted.
"It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim.
"I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."
In the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised.
"Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says.
"She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power.
"That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'.
"So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."

Union Minister of State L. Murugan resigned from the Union Council of Ministers and the Rajya Sabha on Tuesday, saying he wanted to return to grassroots politics and focus on strengthening the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in Tamil Nadu ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.
In his resignation letter to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Murugan said he wished to dedicate himself full-time to the party’s expansion in the state and take the prime minister’s message of “Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas” to people across Tamil Nadu.
In a statement posted on X, Murugan described his tenure under Modi’s leadership as a great honour and said he now wanted to work alongside party workers at the grassroots.
“It has been the greatest honour of my life to serve Bharat Mata and Tamil Nadu under the leadership of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri @narendramodi Ji,” he wrote.
Murugan also reflected on his political journey, which began during his college years when he joined the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh-affiliated student organisation. He said he was inspired by the nationalist ideals of Mahakavi Bharati, Sardar Patel and Syama Prasad Mookerjee.
He said the principle guiding his nearly three decades in the ABVP and the BJP had been “Nation First, Party Next, Self Last”.
Murugan emphasized that PM Modi’s recognition of grassroots workers had strengthened his belief that dedication and service could create opportunities regardless of a person’s family background.
Murugan is a former president of the BJP’s Tamil Nadu unit and was elected to the Rajya Sabha from Madhya Pradesh.
His term in the Upper House was due to end in 2030, but he sought to step down before its completion.
He took over as the BJP’s Tamil Nadu chief in 2020 and joined Modi’s Union Cabinet in July 2021 during a Cabinet reshuffle. K. Annamalai succeeded him as the party’s state chief.
Murugan comes from Tamil Nadu’s Namakkal district and belongs to the Arunthathiyar community.
Before taking on organizational responsibilities in the BJP, he was active in student politics through the ABVP.
His resignation comes as he seeks to return to party organization and grassroots mobilization in Tamil Nadu, with the BJP looking to strengthen its position in the state ahead of the 2029 general election.

How Google's new laptops compare to traditional Chromebooks.
