Neon Don is really pissed at his ex-wife’s lawyer. He’ll tell you any chance he gets while he shotguns lines of pixelated bad guys. He’s also not real—his likeness has only existed for a few minutes in a top-down cyberpunk-style shooter game, generated in the Google Labs service Playground.
“Keep shooting!” Neon Don says as he mows enemies down. “Brenda took everything else away!”
Playground, which Google launched this week, is part of Google Labs, the company’s landing page for its various AI experiments that haven’t made it into an app or official service quite yet. (Google has done this before with things like music production). It works similarly to Horizon Create, the game generation service Meta announced in September.
Playground is essentially vibe coding for video games, letting people describe in plain language what kind of game they want to make in a chatbot-like interface. Playground then builds a working in-browser version of a game. You can add further instructions to tweak the design from there. If you have assets you want to use as a reference, you can upload photos, videos, or models. Otherwise, the visuals and designs are all AI-generated.
The process of making a game is very straightforward, conversational, and responsive. That means it is perfect for dummies like me with little to no video game development chops or even decent coding skills. By simply throwing out some ideas, I built three playable, stable, and not even remotely good games in one day.
Pork Drop
My first work was Pork Drop, a result generated from the prompt “Tetris but with cute pigs instead of blocks.” I typed that in, hit Build. The AI chugged, then spit out a farm-themed version of Tetris with little pig faces drawn on every block.
I had to iterate a bit to realize my vision, telling the AI not just to stick pig faces on the blocks but to have the blocks shaped like distorted pigs. “Each block is a pig,” I wrote, “contorted into the shape of the Tetris blocks. Make ’em look a little squished but still cute!” This resulted in a clean, playable version of Tetris, though the occasional block looked like a T-posed pig with its legs spread-eagle. The AI suggested the title Piggy Stacker, but I thought mine was better. (I’m right.)
Dinner Darling
The next game idea came courtesy of my colleague Jay Dayrit, who, when asked what kind of game I should make, immediately requested, “Gay dinner party.” I typed that in.
With no follow-up requests, the result was a 2D flash-style game called Dinner Darling. The art looks like everyone is a Bitmoji. You’re placed in the shoes of a very stressed-out-looking host, Julian, who is tasked with hosting a fancy dinner party with fussy guests who can’t seem to sit in their chairs at the table. As timers count down, you have to prepare various artisanal bruschettas and espresso martinis for your increasingly angry guests.
After it generates, I give the game a shot and fail miserably, unable to figure out the controls in time to bring my guests a timely pastry or cocktail. (Sasha, one of the guests, required numerous espresso cocktails in a row.) “PARTY CATASTROPHE,” the game-over screen read.
There is no mention of anybody’s sexuality in the game at all, but when I lost, Dayrit called from across the office, “See? You're bad at the game because you're straight!” Well played, Playground.
My colleague Reece Rogers was less impressed when he looked at the game. “This is very unrealistic, because there’s not a vegan or dairy-free option,” he said.
Neon Don
The game that took the most work is the one that has since been played the most by random people on Playground. (Anyone can sign in with their Google account and play these user-generated games.) I’m up to seven unique players as of publication, which apparently means this game is my masterpiece.
I asked the AI to make a “cyberpunk-style rhythm game” where you play as a “very divorced” grizzled ex-cop who battles waves of rogue agents and corrupt politicians. It started as a Beat Saber–type title, but I asked the AI to make it more like the top-down shooter Hotline Miami. The result was Neon Don (title mine), a top-down, arcade-like shooter with pulsing synth wave background music.
Neon Don is also the game I tried to push the content bounds on, to see what Playground would let me get away with.
I described the enemies, and Playground AI added its own details on top, including “bulky, wide builds with prominent beer bellies straining against their tight tactical shirts and cargo pants” and “custom tough-guy swagger animations.” OK, Playground, go off.
The game had several small issues at first. I countered them and added features a little bit at a time. I dictated systems for level scaling, boss generation, and better enemy variety. I flagged mobility issues, like the player getting stuck, and it fixed them. (And occasionally introduced other problems.) I asked it to develop a text-based snark system that made the main character respond to combat with witty in-character quips like “Keep shooting! Brenda took everything else away!” or “I’ve taken worse hits from my ex-wife’s lawyer!”
I imagine that a real game developer would know what to actually say to sharpen features and make the game more fun or playable. Some of the top games people have created on the platform are much better than mine, since I tended to lean on more vibe-based iterative changes like, “Make Don taller” or “more divorced.”
Game Plan
After a certain point, Google throttles your usage of its Playground service. Every new game and iteration therein uses up more of your allowance. (Note for all my new loyal fans: Updates on my titles will be coming on October 14 when my usage allowance refreshes.)
That means my games still have many issues. I wanted to add a “Backflip” button to Neon Don, but the AI called it “Doge flip,” which I think sucks but cannot change until my usage credits recharge. I want to change the difficulty and add more weapon options. I want to do a lot of things, but I ain’t paying for more usage credits.
Playground does make me interested in the actual art of making video games. It’s fun and somewhat intuitive, and there are tangible results you can play with in real time. People are probably going to make some interesting stuff with it. But the limitations keep it from being truly useful.
Also, when you scroll through the Playground games, an unmistakable sameness permeates everything. Different game genres wind up with almost identical menus and music. You start to see the same types of combat options and style choices.
Playground is fun for a bit. But soon it becomes pretty clear it’s AI slop all the way down. Tell that to your ex-wife’s lawyer.

In October 2026, a rumor spread that U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico, a Texas Democrat, had received treatment at a mental health care facility in Ohio.
The claim erupted after Talarico, a state representative, disappeared from the campaign trail for nearly 10 days. On Oct. 11, the candidate told Dallas NBC affiliate KXAS's Phil Prazan in a video interview he'd been lying low at home due to a bout of influenza (archived).
Still, social media posts claiming he had actually been hospitalized at a mental health facility the whole time multiplied on Facebook and X, where one post said, for example, "the flu thing was a BIG FAT LIE" (archived):
Many Snopes readers emailed, asking us to verify whether the rumor was true.
As we outline below, we found no credible evidence to support the claim Talarico had received treatment at a mental health facility. Both the facility named in these rumors and Talarico himself denied the claim on social media. In addition, the timing of his alleged discharge didn't match Talarico's schedule. Snopes obtained visual evidence, which we reviewed but aren't publishing due to privacy concerns, that Talarico was at his home in Austin every day for the entirety of his bout of flu.
For these reasons, we rate the claim false.
Two conservative influencers, Nick Sortor and Rhein Amacher, started the rumor, offering as evidence the recording of an alleged employee of the Lindner Center of Hope in Ohio appearing to say Talarico had just been discharged.
Both Talarico and the Lindner Center of Hope denied he had ever been treated there.
We reached out to Sorter and Amacher, as well as to Talarico and the Lindner Center of Hope, for clarity and we will update this report should we receive a response.
The rumor originated on X
The rumor spread less than a month before the election, at a time when almost all polls in Texas showed Talarico narrowly ahead of his Republican opponent in the race, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
On Oct. 11, Sortor and Amacher posted a short audio recording on X of a phone conversation between a male voice asking for "James Talarico" and a female voice, allegedly that of someone who worked at Lindner Center for Hope, appearing to say he was discharged earlier that evening.
Sortor (archived) and Amacher (archived) posted within minutes of each other, just after 1 p.m. Eastern time. Both claimed Amacher had had the exchange with the purported employee. In his post, Amacher wrote that a person who he understood to be an employee of the center said Talarico had been discharged "within the previous 24-48 hours":
I personally contacted @LindnerCtrHope in Mason, Ohio, to determine whether Talarico was or had previously been a patient.
During my recorded call, an individual identifying themselves as a female facility employee reportedly stated that Talarico was no longer a patient and had been discharged within the previous 24–48 hours.
In the recording, however, the person tells Amacher the patient was "just discharged this evening." The recorded exchange went as follows:
ALLEGED EMPLOYEE: I do not find anyone with that name for the last four days that's been discharged, and they're not here in the building.
AMACHER: OK, so nothing for James Talarico?
ALLEGED EMPLOYEE: Um… let's see, looks… well… this is what it's today… Looks like he was just discharged this evening. That's why I don't have it.
Amacher's post included a purported screenshot of a call log showing he had attempted to contact the facility three times that day: at 8:53 p.m., 8:56 p.m. and 8:59 p.m.
A subsequent X post by Amacher on Oct. 11 indicated the exchange took place "yesterday" — Oct. 10. We reached out to him for more details.
Talarico's whereabouts on Oct. 9 and 10
On Oct. 9 — the day before Amacher's alleged call — Talarico made an appearance at the Austin City Limits festival, as photographs on the reputable image bank Getty Images show.
The evening of Oct. 10, Talarico attended Kacey Musgraves' concert in Dallas, according to a post by Talarico's campaign at 2:30 a.m. Oct. 11, indicating the video had been shot in the hours before (archived):
(An earlier post by another X account confirmed Talarico was at the concert.)
Musgraves played in Dallas Oct. 10 and 11, according to the website of the venue, the American Airlines Center.
In a seeming attempt to justify the discrepancy between the time the alleged employee told him the patient was discharged and Talarico's appearance in Austin the day before, Amacher posted again on X saying that the time of a patient's discharge could be registered some time after the person has left the facility (archived):
Mental health facility denies Talarico was a patient
On Oct. 11, in response to the rumors, the Lindner Center of Hope posted on X to say Talarico had never been a patient (archived):
Talarico shared the post, adding that he has never been to Ohio (archived):
Further, Talarico spokesperson JT Ennis posted on X that the claim was a "lie" to "promote a pathetic conspiracy theory" (archived):
Lastly, Snopes obtained visual evidence of Talarico being at home every day from Oct. 1 to 8, the day before he went to the music festival in Austin.
Talarico has long been open about having Type 1 diabetes, a condition that increases the risk of complications when the person comes down with the flu, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
For further reading, Snopes has covered several rumors about Talarico, including the claim that he is vegan.

Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
- Published
At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said.
The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.
IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere.
Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says.
The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered.
"This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."
Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.
Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.
Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.
IOM said it was providing assistance to 64 of the survivors at its response centre in Obock, including healthcare and support to "restore contact with their families".
The UN agency was working in "close collaboration" with local authorities to help migrants and "prevent deaths at sea and on land", it added.
More than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, during an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey, according to IOM statistics.
In March 2026, nine people were killed and 45 went missing following a similar incident as Thursday's.
The conflict in Yemen has also displaced more than 130,000 people across the country, the UN refugee agency said last month.
Thousands of Yemenis have fled to Djibouti to escape the civil war between Houthi fighters and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
Djibouti is a tiny former French colony that sits just across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen.

Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.
This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.
Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP won state elections in West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.
Mass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. The Cockroach movement was born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.
This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakes impossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.
There is still reason for hope in India. The Indian Express newspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011, corruption scandals became evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.

The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has attached assets worth ₹140 crore belonging to Earth Infrastructure Ltd, its subsidiaries, promoters, their family members and associated entities as part of a money laundering investigation into alleged fraud involving ₹2,004 crore.
The ED's Delhi Zonal Office-II has attached immovable properties linked to the company and its promoters, including Avdhesh Kumar Goel, Rajnish Mittal, Atul Gupta and Vikas Gupta, among others.
According to the ED, Earth Infrastructure Ltd and its associated entities allegedly collected ₹2,004 crore from more than 19,425 homebuyers and investors by promising timely delivery of residential and commercial units, along with assured returns.
However, the agency alleged that despite receiving substantial sums, several projects were left incomplete and possession of the promised units was not handed over to buyers. This allegedly caused financial losses to homebuyers and investors.
The ED's investigation has also indicated that a substantial portion of the funds was allegedly diverted and siphoned off through various group companies, associated entities and individuals.
The money laundering investigation was initiated following five FIRs registered by the Economic Offences Wing (EOW) of the Delhi Police against Earth Infrastructure Ltd, its directors and related entities under various provisions of the Indian Penal Code.
Separately, the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) filed a criminal complaint against the Earth Group's promoters and directors under Section 447 of the Companies Act.
The ED said its investigation found that proceeds allegedly generated through the scheduled offences were used, in part, to acquire movable and immovable assets in the names of entities and individuals linked to the group's promoters and directors.
In a statement, the agency said, "Investigation has further revealed that a part of the proceeds of crime generated from the scheduled offences was utilised for the acquisition of movable and immovable assets in the names of various entities and individuals connected with the promoters/directors of the group,"
In April 2026, the ED conducted searches at several premises linked to the Earth Group across Delhi-NCR under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA).
During the searches, the agency seized cash worth ₹6.30 crore and jewellery valued at ₹8.78 crore. It also recovered documents relating to more than 100 immovable properties estimated to be worth over ₹100 crore.
The ED subsequently arrested Avdhesh Kumar Goel, Rajnish Mittal, Atul Gupta and Vikas Gupta on June 1 under Section 19 of the PMLA, 2002.
"Investigation has established the central role of Avdhesh Kumar Goel, Rajneesh Mittal, Atul Gupta and Vikas Gupta in the planning and execution of the fund diversion through a complex web of transactions. They were arrested on June 1, under Section 19 of the PMLA, 2002, after following due legal procedure," said the ED in a statement.
The agency filed a prosecution complaint against the accused on July 29, seeking their conviction and the confiscation of properties worth more than ₹212 crore.
With the latest attachment of assets worth ₹140 crore, the ED said the total value of attachments and seizures in the case has reached ₹352 crore, including seizures made under Section 17 of the PMLA.
The investigation remains focused on tracing the alleged proceeds of crime, the movement of funds through entities associated with the Earth Group and the acquisition of properties allegedly linked to the money laundering offence.
(With inputs from news agency ANI)

Which smart TV brands offer the longest software support?
Not all smart TVs will receive updates for long, and some don't have any specific policy.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
No matter the price of a TV you buy, you likely consider it as a long-term investment. You thus expect it to receive support from the manufacturer for as long as possible.
In olden times, when you bought a TV, the only worry you had was it eventually breaking. But with smart TVs, there's also software to consider. Most modern TVs come with their own operating systems and apps, and need to be updated semi-regularly for the best performance and to patch security issues.
Unfortunately, there's no universal standard for how long you can expect a TV to get support for. It varies significantly by manufacturer, and the relevant information isn't always easy to find. But you're in luck, as we've done the tedious work of finding out.
Samsung offers long-term software support, but not every brand matches that commitment
If you have a Samsung TV from 2024 or later, Samsung will provide seven years of software updates for its Linux-based Tizen OS. This commitment, made in 2024, also applies to select models from 2023. That means if you have a Samsung TV from 2024, you can expect apps to work smoothly and firmware updates to roll out until at least 2031. Older models won't get major new versions of Tizen. They'll likely receive occasional maintenance or security firmware updates, though.
In early 2024, LG introduced the webOS Re:New program, which guarantees four years of webOS updates for TV models from 2022 onwards. These come with a one-year delay compared to the latest webOS release on the newest TV models. For example, webOS 26 debuted with 2026's TVs, and will come to a 2025 TV one year later.
Sony doesn't offer a fixed period of support for its TVs. Rather, it differs depending on which model you own. For example, for 2025's Sony Bravia K-65XR80M2 OLED, Sony's support page has April 2029 as the end-of-life date. Meanwhile, the Sony Bravia 2 II K-65S25VM2, which was also part of the 2025 lineup, will apparently receive security updates until June 2030.
Unlike LG and Samsung, Sony doesn't have use a proprietary TV operating system. Models released after 2021 use the Google TV platform; prior to that it was Android TV.
Like Sony, TCL doesn't guarantee a fixed period of support. All we really have to go on is the company's Software Security page, where it claims to "typically" provide security updates for at least two years after "the first shipment of a certain device model." This page doesn't explicitly mention TVs, though. Depending on the model, TCL sets primarily run on Google TV (or Android TV for older models) or Roku TV.
Software support also varies by region
In Europe, the majority of Hisense TVs run on the company's proprietary VIDAA OS. Since 2025, it has pledged support for "up to" a whopping eight years on these models. Unfortunately for those in the US, you're less likely to pick up a Hisense TV that uses VIDAA, with many models instead running Android TV, Fire TV, Google TV or Roku TV. Therefore, long-term support is in the hands of the company whose OS your TV ships with.
For a long time, Roku was known for its streaming devices and operating system that it licenses to TV brands like those listed above. But what if you buy one of Roku's own Pro, Plus or Select Series TVs? Roku doesn't specify a fixed period of support for these, and the first came out in 2023, so it's still too early to establish a pattern. But given that software is the company's focus and it frequently pushes out updates, you can reasonably expect a healthy lifespan for its TVs. Roku doesn't publish end-of-life dates for its streaming boxes either, though some people claim to have used one unit for as long as 10 years.
What about the ultra-affordable TV brands like Vizio and Insignia? The former runs its own Vizio OS, which functions in much the same way as its better-known rivals and includes more than 300 apps. Vizio pushes out automatic firmware updates regularly, but doesn't guarantee a fixed period of support for any of its models.
Insignia TVs employ Amazon's Fire OS, so you can assume you'll get software and security updates for as long as Amazon commits to with its own devices. The Amazon Fire TV Software Security Updates page says that commitment is at least four years.
Don't fret once your model is out of support. Buying a streaming box is an inexpensive way to extend your smart TV's life and maintain access to updated versions of your favorite apps.

US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, court filings show.
The former student, Jerome Richardson, who has since graduated from Temple University, is among 39 people charged with conspiring to violate worshippers’ civil rights and interfering with religious worship at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota, in January. Protesters said they targeted the church’s January 18 service because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, also led ICE’s St. Paul field office. Those charged include journalists Georgia Fort and Lemon, a former CNN host, who say they were there to cover the demonstration.
Twelve days after the protest, judges in two states began signing warrants authorizing agents to use so-called cell-site simulators, commonly known as Stingrays or IMSI catchers, to target Richardson’s phone: one in Minnesota on January 30 and another in Pennsylvania the next day. The purpose, his lawyers wrote in a motion seeking to exclude the tracking evidence, was “locating and arresting him.”
Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants targeting the phones of Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate. They separately sought pen register orders, which can log the numbers a phone contacts, for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon. It's unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications.
The records reviewed by WIRED do not establish whether investigators actually deployed a cell-site simulator to locate Richardson or whether judges approved the applications targeting Fort and Lundy. In a July letter filed in court, Fort’s lawyers said prosecutors “did not know” whether the surveillance applications had been authorized or had yielded evidence.
Cell-site simulators impersonate cell phone towers to locate a target’s phone. In doing so, they can also collect identifying information from any nearby cellular device, including those belonging to people who aren’t suspected of a crime. That indiscriminate collection has made the devices controversial among privacy advocates, who describe them as dragnet surveillance tools.
The use of cell-site simulators has long been shrouded in secrecy. FBI records released in 2023 showed that police borrowing its simulators had to agree to keep details of their use secret, even in court. Privacy advocates have long warned that the devices could be turned against protesters and journalists.
“Using an advanced surveillance capability such as a cell-site simulator against members of the free press for reporting stories that are unfavorable to the president is an appalling attack on the First Amendment,” says Cooper Quintin, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a tech-focused civil liberties nonprofit. Quintin has spent years researching the devices and developing tools to help people detect them. Using EFF’s detection software, WIRED found evidence suggesting a cell-site simulator was deployed near the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, though who operated it and for what purpose remain unknown.
Attorneys for Lemon, Lundy, and Fort did not respond to requests for comment. Richardson’s attorneys declined to comment on the record.
The previously unreported warrants are a product of a campaign of contentious investigative tactics waged by federal agents in pursuit of people connected to the protest at Cities Church. According to court records, the Department of Homeland Security demanded journalists’ telephone and YouTube records under a customs authority that requires no prior judicial approval. Agents also sought records identifying everyone who had purchased a particular beanie at REI in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area over a period of more than two years. Defense attorneys have identified 92 customs summonses and are challenging the government’s authority to issue them.
The cell-site simulator warrants raise serious questions about both the accuracy of the information investigators presented to judges in their effort to obtain authorization for surveillance tool’s use, as well as why they sought such intrusive tracking to find Richardson in the first place.
The affidavits supporting the applications to track Richardson claimed video showed Fort, Lemon, Richardson, and others “chanting with agitators.” Prosecutors have since conceded that Lemon and Fort did not chant. According to her lawyers, the government acknowledged that the false claim appeared in at least 15 warrant affidavits.
DHS policy says cell-site simulators are deployed only “in the fraction of cases in which the capability is best suited to achieve specific public safety objectives,” but it’s unclear what specific public safety reason justified its use in this case. Investigators obtained a second simulator warrant to locate Richardson, then a senior at Temple University, two days before he walked up to a federal courthouse in Philadelphia and voluntarily surrendered. He was released on bond that afternoon.
The Justice Department responded to WIRED’s request for comment by writing in an email that the department “speaks through its court filings.” DHS declined to discuss ongoing investigations or investigative methods and referred questions to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Minnesota, which did not respond to a request for comment.
The warrant was signed January 31, the same day Richardson posted a YouTube video saying he expected to enter federal custody “in the coming days,” suggesting he had no intention of fleeing. It is unclear whether the warrant preceded the video, leaving questions about why investigators sought such an intrusive tool to find someone who was publicly anticipating his arrest and whom prosecutors agreed to release the day he surrendered.
While Richardson’s suppression motion asks to suppress evidence obtained from the phone tracking, it does not specify whether agents used a simulator or obtained evidence through either.
A former federal prosecutor who spent a decade working on counterterrorism cases says using a simulator to locate someone is not necessarily unusual. But based on the court records they reviewed about Richardson’s case, they called the government's tactics aggressive: “I don’t understand why it would be at all necessary.” They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record
Richardson, a St. Paul native, had led an NAACP chapter at 16 and served as executive director of Minnesota Teen Activists, according to his fundraiser’s organizer. He described his work for Lemon as handling logistics and connecting him with local contacts. He drove the journalist to Cities Church, where Lemon livestreamed the demonstration and interviewed protesters and churchgoers. Prosecutors allege Richardson joined chants and obstructed congregants.
In his video, Richardson defended his role. “I was proud to support his work,” he said of Lemon. “This is the price of being unapologetic about humanity and love of Christ.”
The government’s initial effort to obtain arrest warrants met resistance from judges. A magistrate judge refused five of eight warrants, and after an appeals court rejected the Justice Department's bid to override that decision, the department withdrew its request. In a filing with the appeals court, the chief judge wrote that two of the five “were not protestors at all; instead, they were a journalist and his producer” and that there was “no evidence that those two engaged in any criminal behavior.” Prosecutors later secured a grand jury indictment on January 29.
The way the government chose to arrest some defendants has also drawn objections from defense lawyers. Lemon’s attorneys say in court filings that prosecutors rejected their offer to arrange his surrender; agents instead arrested him shortly before midnight at a Beverly Hills hotel while he was covering the Grammy Awards. Fort’s lawyers say agents arrested her at home rather than allowing her to turn herself in.

The Goa Police on Tuesday defended before the Goa Bench of the Bombay High Court the detention of seven Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) members during a protest at Azad Maidan in Panaji, citing the outfit’s history of protests without permission. The court, which had ordered their release on Sunday, adjourned the hearing till October 19.
On Sunday evening, a Bench of Justice Valmiki Menezes and Justice Amit Jamsandekar heard a plea moved by advocate Malisa Simoes challenging the detention of Afreen Shaikh, Jack Sukhija, Bupesh Bind, Aditya Parulekar, Listan Noronha, Shamino Fernandes and Milind Rane. The court noted an allegation that no order had been passed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) prohibiting any gathering at Azad Maidan or any part of it, and said the detention may not have been authorised. It noted that Executive Magistrate Dattaprasad Toraskar, who was at the site, had instructed the police to detain the seven for entering Azad Maidan.
The Bench directed the Panaji Police Station to release them, on the condition that they would not protest that night. The advocate for the detainees gave an undertaking to that effect, without prejudice to the detainees’ rights and contentions. The Bench also directed the State to file an affidavit.
In the affidavit filed on Tuesday through Panaji Police Station Inspector Vijaykumar Chodankar, the police justified the detention. They cited three instances in which CJP members organised protests without permission and alleged that the outfit patronised Umar Khalid.
The affidavit cited a protest on July 25 over the NEET exams, during which Mohammed Zanskar Danish (30) was found at a dharna at Azad Maidan with a placard reading “Umar Khalid” and “Sharjeel Imam” and a bag reading “Palestine will be free”. The police took Danish to the police station for inquiry. A number of protesters gathered outside, and the police asked them not to cause a nuisance or block the road. They also asked them to show permission from an authority to hold the dharna in front of Police Headquarters, Panaji.
On Sunday, the affidavit said, several CJP members and others, mostly from outside Goa, gathered at the entrance of Azad Maidan and shouted slogans against the Union Government, the State Government and Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. The police said protests were not allowed inside Azad Maidan under an October 9, 2026 order of the District Magistrate, North Goa. They added that CJP protesters had earlier violated conditions imposed by authorities. The police made arrangements as per a scheme issued by superiors. When the protesters entered Azad Maidan, one sustained injuries after a fall. The police detained all seven at 4:30 p.m. under Section 172(2) of the BNSS, 2023, saying they did not have permission to protest.
The police denied the allegations of use of force. They said the protesters were not arrested, so there was no question of communicating grounds of arrest, and that force was used only to prevent the protesters from taking the law into their own hands. They also stated that no injuries were caused to any detainee and denied dragging the protesters into a vehicle. Taking the affidavits on record, the Bench adjourned the hearing.

Trinamool Congress (TMC) MP Dola Sen on Tuesday filed a police complaint under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) over an alleged security breach and an attempted knife attack on former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee in West Bengal.
According to the complaint filed by the party, the incident took place after an allegedly intoxicated intruder breached the perimeter gates of a high-security zone.
The complaint identified the woman as Tannishtha Saha, who was reportedly a civic volunteer and a drug addict. It alleged that she approached Banerjee in a violent manner and attempted to attack her with a knife.
The TMC further claimed that the woman used abusive language and, while allegedly intoxicated, tried to approach Banerjee aggressively.
In her complaint, Sen detailed how the woman allegedly bypassed the initial security checks and caused a disturbance in the area.
Meanwhile, TMC national spokesperson Nilanjan Das questioned the BJP government over the law and order situation in the state.
In a post on X, Das wrote, "Disturbing incident. At 6 PM, one Tannishtha Saha, reportedly a Civic Volunteer, attempted to murder our former Chief Minister, @MamataOfficial a Z category protectee with a knife. Speaks volumes about the state of Law and Order under the @SuvenduWB administration."
Expressing concern following the incident, the TMC said it was alarming that someone could approach the residence of a Z-plus category security protectee, raising questions about a possible larger conspiracy.
"In view of the above, you are requested to record this as information under Section 173 BNSS and take cognisance of the photos and videos enclosed herewith as reference," the complaint mentioned.
Earlier today, members of the Mamata Banerjee-led faction of the TMC protested in Kolkata's Rajabazar, seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
The demonstration took place after Banerjee returned from Delhi, where she had met the Gandhis and other INDIA bloc leaders amid the ongoing controversy over the voter revision process.
The party's student and youth wings had proposed a march from Rajabazar to Park Circus. However, the police halted the procession, saying the organisers had not obtained the necessary permission. The protesters subsequently gathered in Rajabazar and raised slogans against the BJP and the Chief Election Commissioner.
The Mamata Banerjee-led faction maintained that it had notified the police about the demonstration through email. Kolkata Police, however, said it had received no official communication and insisted that written permission was mandatory for organising such a rally.

The tenders for Bengaluru Smart Infrastructure Limited’s (B-SMILE) eight elevated corridors, which have now been cancelled, were based on a common template that combined provisions from two standard contract documents while also introducing additional conditions found in neither, according to the Urban Development Department’s (UDD) tender-cancellation order. The report noted that no government approval had been obtained for this hybrid or composite document.
According to the report, the tender documents combined provisions from the K/W-4 contract and the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways’ (MoRTH) Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) documents, while also adding more than 10 conditions that were not part of either standard.
Fair competition?
The report flagged key eligibility criteria that deviated from MoRTH norms, raising questions about bidding conditions and fair competition. It also highlighted inconsistencies in contractual provisions, eligibility criteria and financial requirements.
The report identified 13 conditions common to all eight tenders that deviated from both standards. These included the absence of a time limit for milestone payments and interest on delayed payments, as well as the deletion of the clause governing the valuation of variations in the scope of work, leaving no provision for changes in scope. The tenders also limited delay damages to 10% of individual milestone payments rather than the total contract price.
Further, while maintenance was stated to be included in the estimated annual payment, it was also specified as separately payable at 0.25% or 0.50% of the contract price annually. For the Sirsi Circle project, this amounted to around ₹20.19 crore against an estimated maintenance cost of ₹4.01 crore, the report noted.
Other concerns included making contractors liable for delays caused by utility agencies, the absence of a contractual right for contractors to terminate the agreement even in the event of the authority’s default, and the removal of arbitration provisions without providing an alternative dispute-resolution mechanism.
The B-SMILE tenders did not permit joint ventures, whereas MoRTH allows them for projects valued above ₹100 crore. The report also flagged the use of a five-year period to assess technical capacity, instead of the 10-year period prescribed in a MoRTH letter dated November 2, 2020, for stand-alone specialised projects. It noted that the flyover-length criterion was used in the Minerva Circle tender to reject a bidder.
Financial model
To qualify for bidding, five tenders required contractors to have turnover equivalent to 200% of the estimated annual payment in two of the preceding five years and liquid assets of 33.33%, without a net-worth test. The remaining three adopted MoRTH’s requirements of 15% average turnover and 5% net worth.
Thus, the requirement ran opposite to the size of the work, the report said. It cited the Pipeline Road corridor, valued at ₹327.46 crore, as requiring a turnover of ₹654.92 crore, while Sirsi Circle, valued at ₹538.28 crore, required a turnover of ₹80.74 crore. It noted that no source or recorded rationale had been provided for adopting the 200% turnover model for five projects and a different financial model for the remaining three.
With these tender conditions flagged, the UDD directed the SPV to cancel the tenders, although B-SMILE was on the verge of issuing work orders after Cabinet approval.
‘Will refloat tenders’
A B-SMILE source told The Hindu that they had “hybridised” standards to secure better contract conditions, but approval had not been obtained. “We will get government approval and then refloat the tenders soon,” the source said.

Barring a catastrophic midterm polling miss, Democrats are on track to win a majority in the House of Representatives next month. Come the new Congress in January, that will mean a new House speaker — and if all goes to plan, that will be current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.
The man who will likely be the next House speaker, explained
How House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries ended up on the verge of the speakership.
If elected, Jeffries, from New York, will be the first Black speaker of the House. Though Jeffries has been in Congress for nearly 14 years now — and many of those years have been spent in Democratic leadership — he also remains something of an enigma.
The New Yorker’s Jason Zengerle profiled Jeffries back in May. He spoke with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about who Jeffries really is, his path to what would be a historic speakership, and what he really stands for.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
In your profile of potential future Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries, you start with a story that people might find surprising. And I was wondering if you could tell us said story.
[Jeffries] was in Florida, raising money, which is one of his central responsibilities as a minority leader. And he was being driven to a Democratic donor’s house in Palm Beach. And while he was being driven there, he got an alert on his phone letting him know that Donald Trump had posted a message to Truth Social in which he rehashed a bunch of the 2020 election conspiracies. More significantly, [Trump] had included a depiction of Barack Obama and Michelle Obama as apes.
Jeffries has this reputation for being a very calm, deliberate, not angry person, oftentimes to his detriment. I think a lot of Democratic partisans wish he would be more angry. But the way he told me the story, he was legitimately pissed off. And he realized that he needed to respond in some way. And he didn’t think that a tweet would be sufficient.
He wanted to do an Instagram post, and he looked into his aide’s iPhone, and he said, “Fuck Donald Trump.” And as soon as he was done recording the video, I think he started to have second thoughts. And they sent the video up to Washington for a social media team to edit, and he told them, “Let’s bleep out the word fuck.” And for him, it was a smashing social media success.
I was in his office in the Capitol six days later, and he was telling me this story and basking in some of the reflected glory and talking about all the social media love and talking about the real-world love. But then he kind of paused, and he said something like, “You know, but I still haven’t heard from my mom, and I’m a little worried about that.” Which I thought captured him pretty well.
“I don’t think you’re going to see a new Hakeem Jeffries if he’s speaker. I think he’s going to, especially rhetorically, perform the same way he has before.”
Why did you want to start your profile of him with that story? What does it tell us about who this individual is?
I thought it captured the dilemma he faces in some ways, just in the sense that he is this very deliberate, calculated political figure, very conventional. And he is operating in a political space these days that doesn’t really reward or appreciate that approach.
Oftentimes that approach is not successful. I think he’s trying to adapt to the new rules of the road, and he’s kind of doing it in fits and starts, and sometimes he’s more successful than others. But I still think, even when he is successful, he has some qualms about it.
How long has Hakeem Jeffries wanted to be speaker of the House?
When he got to Congress, in 2012, he definitely wanted to become a player. He wanted to be in leadership, chair a committee, whatever. He was someone who had his eye on that.
But at the same time, the Congressional Black Caucus had started to think a little bit differently about what they could achieve in Congress. For a long time, they wanted their members to get chairmanships and things like that, or maybe be majority whip. But by the time Jeffries got there, they started to think that we could actually get a speaker. And his arrival kind of coincided with this realization on the part of the CBC. And I think a lot of CBC members viewed Jeffries as a potential future speaker, and they started to groom him for that.
Pretty soon after that, Nancy Pelosi started to think of him as someone who would be a good member of her leadership team. And I think by 2018, that’s when it really became apparent that he was going to be someone who could potentially be speaker.
What does he actually stand for as the most powerful Democrat in the House?
I think, quite intentionally, he doesn’t stand for anything. I think that in some ways has been key to his success. He has managed for the most part to avoid being kind of pigeonholed or put anywhere on the ideological spectrum. He is very critical of the far left of the party, especially the DSA. He views the DSA as college-educated young white people who are coming to Brooklyn and displacing older Black working-class people.
I was talking to this former Democratic congressional aide and basically asking this person the question you’re asking me: What does he stand for? And this person was trying to explain it and finally just was sort of exasperated, and he said he’s intentionally trying not to stand for anything. He’s sort of like hotel art. He just is, and it’s satisfactory.
We don’t have a lot of case studies for how he manages his caucus because they haven’t been in power. But I think maybe one of the most telling examples was the shutdown, because Democrats were, in a way, the power brokers there. Tell us how Hakeem Jeffries managed that.
That was probably his greatest success as minority leader. When Trump took office for the second time, especially for those first few months, I think all of the congressional Democrats, and Jeffries especially, were really on their heels. They could not figure out how to deal with this guy and what they were going to do to stop him. Jeffries was even complaining that he didn’t have any leverage. But then he eventually realized that a shutdown would be at least a little bit of leverage.
The real question was, what was the shutdown going to be about? And there were a lot of Democratic members of Congress who wanted it to be about authoritarianism or corruption. They wanted it to be at all these different issues. And Jeffries was really insistent that we need to make this about one issue, and we need to make it about healthcare.
The Democrats were the ones who caused the shutdown. And normally, the way shutdowns have worked in the past, it’s the party that causes the shutdown that gets the heat from the public. But this time around, I think because Democrats were so consistent in saying that this is about healthcare, and Republicans were so scattered in their own messaging and their own explanations of what was going on, Democrats’ polling numbers went up, Trump’s and Republicans’ went down, and that was a real victory for Jeffries.
Did that whole incident put Jeffries on the president’s radar in a way that he wasn’t?
It comes, and it goes. For a long time, he wouldn’t mention Jeffries at all.
I guess the way to tell if Trump is thinking about you is if he posts about you on Truth Social, and he started to post about Jeffries a lot — all the usual kind of insults he lobs, especially at Black politicians, that Jeffries was low IQ and a thug. But yeah, he does seem to be paying a little bit more to Jeffries now than he was before.
And do we think Jeffries is ready to go toe to toe with the president of the United States if that’s what voters decide he’s to do this November?
In his mind, he’s ready. And I think in his own stilted, rehearsed, steady fashion, he will go toe to toe with Donald Trump. He will talk about affordability, and he’ll talk about corruption, and he’ll talk about the “so-called president.”
I don’t think it will necessarily be satisfying for a lot of Democratic voters out there and Democratic partisans, but I don’t think you’re going to see a new Hakeem Jeffries if he’s speaker. I think he’s going to, especially rhetorically, perform the same way he has before. But I think it’s going to take him a little while to figure out how to do the job.

Orangutans released back into Borneo forest after devastating fires
- Published
Eight orangutans have been released back into the wild in Borneo after they were taken into captivity when their habitat was threatened by wildfires over the summer.
Three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males were freed in a reserve in the west of the island on Friday, International Animal Rescue Indonesia (Yiari) and the forestry ministry said.
Indonesian authorities rescued 46 orangutans from fires in August and September. Wildfires in the region are usual for the country's dry season but intensified this year.
The apes are critically endangered. Around 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, according to conservation group WWF.
While Indonesia is among many countries to grapple with wildfires each summer, this year's were more intense due to the El Niño ocean warming phenomenon, which makes weather patterns more volatile and intense.
Yiari CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said relocating the eight orangutans to the reserve was a "necessary step" when their habitats became unsafe.
Among them was Mama Nopi and her offspring Nopi, Naufal and Nopan, who had been surviving in a coconut and rubber plantation before their rescue in early September, Yiari said.
Fires had incinerated the surrounding forestry, restricting their access to food and bringing them closer to humans.
Mama Lifa and her child Lifa were found in a patch of acacia trees entirely surrounded by oil palm plantations.
The degradation of their habitat by wildfires as well as a lack of food sources prompted their rescue in mid-September.
Mama Man and her baby, Man, had been monitored by animal rescuers since June, when they were found living in a plantation area adjacent to a small patch of forest.
Fires that spread near to the site restricted their roaming area further, leaving them without a safe route to other forestry. The threat of exposure to the blazes led to them being evacuated in early September, Yiara said.
The reserve these orangutans were released into was chosen because it there is food and water available and it is connected to other forested areas.
Yiari's Argitoe Ranting said: "We want to ensure that rescued orangutans are not simply moved from one place to another, but actually have a chance to survive in their natural habitat."
Last month, the International Union for Conservation of Nature warned that wildfires were burning in habitats containing 52% of Borneo's orangutan population.
It says a large portion of the ape's habitat will become inhospitable to them if climate change continues at its current pace.
This year's El Niño has become the strongest on record and is expected to have a knock-on effect on the climate into next year.
Experts have also pointed to land-clearing practices used to make room for plantations as another factor facilitating the spread of wildfires in Indonesia, with naturally fire-resistant forests replaced by less dense and shaded vegetation.
That the orangutan's original habitats had been burned and fragmented to the point they could no longer sustain the primates was the main driving factor behind relocating them, Yiara said.

In the 54th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu, Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, discuss the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, experimental approaches to studying human brain development, and incidents from Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya that highlight barriers to healthcare access.
The episode begins with the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. The discussion explains how optogenetics uses light-sensitive proteins to control the electrical activity of selected nerve cells. By activating or inhibiting specific neurons, researchers can investigate how neural circuits influence movement, memory, emotions and behaviour. The technique has become an important tool in neuroscience research, including studies of neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, it remains largely a research tool and is not a routine treatment for brain disorders.
The next segment examines an experimental approach described as ‘xenocortication’, in which human brain tissue is transplanted into the brains of mice. Researchers have been exploring this approach to study aspects of human brain development that are difficult to reproduce in laboratory-grown cells or animal models alone. The discussion looks at how the transplanted tissue may receive a blood supply, develop connections and interact with its surroundings within a living brain. The approach could help researchers investigate human neuronal development and mechanisms involved in neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders. However, it remains experimental, and findings from such models cannot be assumed to reflect human brain development fully. The work also raises ethical questions about the use of human neural tissue in animal research.
The episode then turns to barriers to healthcare access, examining how social discrimination and inadequate infrastructure can prevent people from receiving medical care. In Uttar Pradesh, a Dalit woman was allegedly denied admission to a government hospital while in labour and was forced to deliver outside the facility. Her family alleged that untouchability was involved. The incident highlights how discrimination can obstruct access to care even when a health facility is physically available.
Another incident in Meghalaya’s West Khasi Hills district, an ill child died in his mother’s arms while his parents were making a three-hour trek to reach the nearest hospital. According to the village headman, the family had tried to arrange a vehicle after the child’s condition deteriorated, but no driver was willing to travel to the village because of the poor road conditions. The incident draws attention to the difficulties faced by people in remote areas, where distance, road connectivity and the availability of transport can delay access to emergency medical care.
The episode ends with a fun-fact segment on why mice are widely used in laboratory experiments. The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, a rumor circulated that U.S. President Trump said he would be "the last Republican president."
People on X and Reddit shared the alleged quote, with some including a video clip. In the clip, Trump appeared to make the comment during a political rally. 
The quote was correctly attributed to Trump.
However, some posts sharing the quote and accompanying video clip omitted context clarifying Trump's meaning. He was referring to a hypothetical scenario where Democrats control both houses of Congress and the White House, suggesting their policies would result in him being "the last Republican president." 
The president made the comment during a speech at a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on Oct. 12. At the rally, Trump endorsed incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted and the Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, who are on the ballot for Ohio's midterm elections.
Trump's full speech can be viewed on C-SPAN. At the 1:02:00 mark, prior to the statement in question, Trump says, "We achieved more in two years than any other presidency in the history of our country, but now the radical-left Dumocrats want to burn it all down" — using a term he favors for the Democratic Party. 
The president continued to criticize his opponents' alleged voting record, saying, "Every single Dumocrat in Congress voted against our record tax cuts. They voted against no tax on tips. They voted against no tax on overtime, and they voted against no tax on Social Security for our great seniors."
These comments, and others he made later, make it clear that Trump was theorizing he'd be the "last Republican president" if Democrats won key races in the midterm elections and subsequently took control of the White House.
The rest of his statement from the moment in question is as follows (emphasis ours):
They voted against voter ID, and they voted against proof of citizenship when you vote, so why did they do that? Because they want to cheat, OK? I saw a guy interviewed a week ago, a congressman, a Democrat. They said, why don't you want to have somebody show their voter identification or proof of citizenship? "Uh, well, uh. Uh, it's racist. That's right. That's right. It's racist." They come up with more s***, I mean it's …
[applause]
"It's racist. It's racist." They're crazy. They voted against securing our border, and they want to have the border open. You know, if they get in, they're going to open the border, and you're going to have two more states: Washington, D.C., where Republicans get 3% of the vote, and Puerto Rico, where Republicans get 4%. So we'll have four more senators. They want to have 23 people on the Supreme Court. They want to end the Senate, so you guys will be out of a job. What are you doing running? You'll be out of a job based on them. They want to end the Senate.
They want to basically destroy our country and that's what they want to do and if they get in, they will do that. They'll be able to do that. You know, if they get in and you have a bad presidential election in the next because we have some very good people, but if you had a bad presidential or one of these lunatics got in, you will— Look at me right now. And you will say he's going to be the last Republican president in the history of our country. I will be. I will be. I will be the last Republican president because they will add about 12 more electoral votes. They'll add four more senators. They'll add 10 more congresspeople, approximately. They're going to rig the Supreme Court through … just a lot of people.
The GOP YouTube channel posted a livestream of the entire rally, including the other speakers. In that version, Trump's statement begins at the 2:53:55 mark and matches the content of the C-SPAN clip.

A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.
At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.
Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”
Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”
Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.
An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.
Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.
“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.
Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.
The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.
The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.
The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.
In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.
Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.
According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.
The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.
“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.
Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.
Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.
The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.
Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.
This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”
When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.
Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

For over a decade now, the only “official” way to play Hideo Kojima’s cult classic, P.T.—the long-discontinued “playable trailer” for Kojima’s canceled “Silent Hills” project—has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files.
Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the “P.T. for PC” project “because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed.” The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create “every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene,” according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version.
The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. And while PS4 emulators recently reached a point where they could run P.T. completely, this native port also sports extra features, like upscaling and frame-generation, a camera mode, experimental third-person and VR support, and a “museum” section where you can look at and listen to in-game assets (including “unused content”).

At the United Nations High Level Meeting (UN HLM), in New York in September 2026, India made official remarks on the Political Declaration on Pandemic Prevention Preparedness and Response (PPPR). The Declaration is part of the emerging global legal regime on pandemics led by the WHO-Pandemic agreement (PA).
Shaping the framework
The PA was adopted by 124 member-states in 2025, including India. No country voted against it, while 11 abstained, reflecting alignment across high-, middle- and low-income countries (HICs/LICs/LMICs). The negotiations hinged on how to balance national sovereignty with international cooperation and solidarity, exposing the fault lines between the Global North and the Global South. Key issues included whether a global treaty can set binding targets for measures such as ‘One Health’ without securing funding for countries with fragile health systems. Or whether national pandemic regulations can be harmonised through global frameworks. And whether private manufacturers can be required to share vaccines in real time at affordable prices.
The PA is not yet open for ratification because negotiations are still ongoing for an annex concerning the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system. PABS could help ensure that, during a pandemic, LICs and LMICs receive a fair share of vaccines, medicines and other therapeutics.
Even without ratification, the PA has created a first-of-its-kind global legal regime for the PPPR. Operationalisation requires countries such as India to balance interests of the HICs, LICs and LMICs. This will determine whether the PA will further entrench the inequities of the COVID-19 pandemic or make global health governance truly inclusive.
Editorial | Landmark agreement: On the draft WHO Pandemic Agreement
At the UN HLM, India succeeded in enshrining the multilateral components of the PA within the principle of national sovereignty. India reiterated its commitment to strengthen global pandemic preparedness but stressed that effective pandemic management requires that international coordination is demonstrated. The first is equitable access to drugs, vaccines and therapeutics and the creation of global public goods, such as digital infrastructure (which admittedly align with its own national priorities).
The second is a respect for national sovereignty and the primacy of member-states in shaping global policy interventions according to national circumstance. As a contrast, the United States rejected the Declaration, calling the PABS and WHO’s role in declaring pandemics as a challenge to its national interests.
India’s line
In its remarks, India has acknowledged the concerns of the Global North and the South. Both sides have upheld national sovereignty as paramount in several provisions. The African countries did not give consent to commitments to monitor the human-animal-environment interface, a key source of pandemic outbreaks, without significant funding, which was not guaranteed by the Global North. Similarly, countries in the Global North did not want binding targets with regard to technology transfer (and other similar provisions).
But as India said at the UN HLM, ‘Global Solidarity must be demonstrated through action’; India must be an active player in the finalisation of the global PPPR regime. India is already actively engaged in the PABS negotiations and must lead the Global South in the post-PABS context. India can consider three options. First, developing partnerships on technical areas of the PA (One Health, surveillance, health workforce strengthening) to build trust with other countries in the Global South, and a ‘store’ of operational solutions to tricky national sovereignty problems.
Second, leveraging its leadership role within existing global political groupings. For example, the H20 summit (a health and development G-7 and G-20 partnership) will take place under the United Kingdom’s G-20 leadership at the end of 2027; pandemic preparedness is one of the core health agendas. During India’s G-20 presidency in 2023, India launched the Global Initiative for Digital Health and holds considerable influence within the platform’s health initiatives. Another is ‘Partners for Multilateralism’, which was launched in 2026 by the European Union (co-sponsors are Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, India and Kenya).
Third, strengthening and aligning domestic policy and regulatory architecture around its own priorities for the PA. Global leadership always rests on domestic strengths. India must ensure that its national policies on PPPR such as regulation of access to biological material and distribution of the benefits uphold the highest standards of equity which India can then demand at the global level.
A South-South health role
An equitable global regime on PPPR is in India’s interests as much as a responsibility towards the Global South. India is the pharmacy of the world, manufacturing one of the largest shares of vaccines in the world in terms of volume. Yet, it needs an equitable global vaccine distribution regime. The patents for the vaccines that India manufactures are held by global pharmaceuticals. India is also import-dependent for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs).
India needs access to the latest technology from the Global North to strengthen the manufacturing of high-grade personal protective equipment and medical devices. At the same time, India needs to lead South-South Cooperation and share its technological strength with other countries in the Global South.
India’s health system has a continental scale, and as India’s Health Secretary stated at the UN HLM, its interventions in digital health infrastructure, laboratories networks and One Health are valuable as global public goods. An effective PA needs an engaged India, and a strong PA will strengthen India’s own pandemic management.
Priyadarshini Singh is a Research Fellow at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP). This article is based on a forthcoming CSEP working paper on the Pandemic Agreement.
