Trump commercials paid for by the US government continued airing on TV the day after a judge blocked the ads because they likely violate a US law against government-funded publicity or propaganda.
In the most widely aired commercial, Trump railed against his perceived enemies and said he would “liberate America from these villains once and for all.” The campaign also included a commercial praising Trump’s record as president, another in which Trump calls the US the “most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history,” and commercials related to the Iran war and the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
US District Judge Jennifer Rochon issued a temporary restraining order (TRO) blocking the ads on Sunday, October 11, which took effect at 6:45 pm that night. The order said the government must cancel the ads, “including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026.”
The Trump administration had told the court on October 10 that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) advertising purchases were set to expire on October 11 and would not be renewed. Despite that, the ads continued airing the night of October 11 and on part of October 12. This was also a week after Trump’s October 5 statement that he would start paying for the ads “myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”
A US attorney yesterday filed a status report saying that the government is now complying with the order and issued an apology. “As Your Honor is aware, the Court emailed the TRO to the parties yesterday at 6:46 p.m.,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald wrote in a filing. “Counsel for the Government emailed the TRO to agency counsel at 7:58 p.m. Agency counsel did not become aware of Government counsel’s email until this morning. The undersigned apologizes to the Court and the plaintiffs.”
The ads aired as part of a $20 million purchase order that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) made on September 20 with LMD Agency, an ad firm. The DHS told the court that the ad placements through October 11 cost $19 million.

In October 2026, a claim (archived) circulated that the conservative commentator Charlie Kirk, who was fatally shot on Sept. 10, 2025, once said children could watch public executions "at a certain age" as an "initiation."
Claims about his alleged quote circulated as U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said the U.S. military was planning to livestream the Army firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the Fort Hood shooter.
One Facebook user wrote that "Charlie Kirk once argued that children watching public executions 'at a certain age' would be 'an initiation.'"
Snopes readers contacted us asking about the truth of this and other Facebook posts (archived, archived) with similar claims about what Kirk said.
Snopes previously investigated what Kirk said about children watching public executions in September 2025 and found that Kirk did say that he thought children could watch public executions "at a certain age" and that this could serve as an "initiation."
The commentator spoke about children watching executions during an episode of "Thoughtcrime," his panel discussion show, on Feb. 15, 2024. During that show, Kirk said about the death penalty that (at 49:35), "It should be public, it should be quick, it should be televised."
Later in the show, Kirk and his panelists discussed whether children should watch public executions and Kirk said (at 50:17), "I think at a certain age it's an initiation," though the panel did not agree on what that age was. Kirk did acknowledge during the podcast that public executions and the death penalty were (at 51:17) "heavy" topics but supported public access as a way to deter crime.
Given the above, we find social media users correctly attributed the quote about children of "a certain age" viewing public executions as an "initiation" to Kirk.
What Kirk said
Kirk and his co-presenters Jack Posobiec, Tyler Bowyer and Blake Neff were discussing capital punishment in the context of whether they believed convicted pedophiles should receive the death penalty.
About 40 minutes into the show, the discussion about capital punishment moved on to whether it should be public and, if so, who should watch. Kirk said (at 49:35), "It should be public, it should be quick, it should be televised."
He added (at 49:53), "You could have like 'Brought to you by Coca Cola' and no, I'm not kidding. By the way, I would totally tune in to see some pedo get their head chopped off. Convicted by a jury of their peers. I'm talking about a real thing."
The discussion moved on to whether children should watch publicly broadcast executions. Kirk said (at 50:17, emphasis ours):
I think at a certain age it's an initiation. No, but hold on, you see, if all of a sudden, you look at some of these savages like in Indiana, there was this guy that went in and killed a pregnant woman and her three kids. And, you know what, I want to watch that execution, that'll make my day better. I want to see him on a public block and get him be publicly executed, and I think that would be justice. You think children should have … you should see … what is the age? At what age should you start to see public executions?
Bowyer and Neff each suggested 16- and 12-year-olds, respectively, as appropriate viewing ages. Kirk said (at 51:13), "But it should also be taken in a holy way. Now, I don't mean holy in a bad way, I mean that, like, this is heavy."
Kirk did not say that executions should be mandatory viewing for children or give an opinion on what age he thought was appropriate to start. He did, however, express a belief that making executions public would deter future crimes. The hosts said (at 51:42):
KIRK: I want you to imagine everyday, all of a sudden they said: "And today, remember that awful five, you know, the guy that went and shot up a school?" Because, you know, left hates school shooters, and so do we and, but they focus on the gun, I think they're evil. So, you know, you take one of these school shooters and they say, "Today we're going to publicly execute this person." And they read off—
POSOBIEC: How about the Super Bowl?
KIRK: Yeah, or the shooters at the Super Bowl thing, and you read off what they did and you don't celebrate it, you know, you just say, "Look, this is what they did and if you do this, this will be your fate," ready, set, go. Boom, end of life. And say— As a question— Here's a question for anybody that might be, you know, not persuaded. Would crime go up or down?
BOWYER: It would go way down
KIRK: Down. So then why is this even a question?
Six states — Texas, Florida, Alabama, Tennessee, Oklahoma and Arizona — have carried out a total of 30 executions so far in 2026, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit group that provides data and analysis on issues concerning capital punishment.
According to a DPIC report from 2018, of the 17 states that carried out executions by lethal injection between January 2011 and August 2018, 14 "prevented witnesses from seeing at least some part of the execution" and 15 "prevented witnesses from hearing what was happening inside the execution chamber."
For further reading, Snopes has fact-checked a number of quotes attributed to Kirk, including whether he called Martin Luther King Jr. "awful" or said some gun deaths were "worth it" in order to have Second Amendment. We have also investigated whether the U.S. military could legally livestream Hasan's planned Dec. 3 execution.

Easy-to-follow workouts based on my DNA and readiness score. Variety of chill yoga or breathwork sessions plus more intense strength, dance, and cardio workouts. The app tracks nutrition and sleep and analyzes meals.
TIRED
Workouts are short—ranging from five to 40 minutes. DNA results are interesting, but there’s no quick fix to fitness. Premium price.
When I was asked to review AlterMe’s fitness system that claims to use DNA and biometric data to create a personalized fitness, nutrition, and recovery program, I was intrigued. I’ve used some of the best fitness trackers before, but have never tried a system that combines DNA testing, personalized workouts, nutrition insight, and its own smart wearable all within a single ecosystem.
I’m someone who needs constant fitness motivation to stay on track. Rather than push myself through strenuous weights and cardio, I prefer feel-good Pilates and an ice bath at my local David Lloyd gym. But in an effort to step out of my comfort zone and try something a little more challenging, I decided to give AlterMe a go.
I’ve used numerous fitness apps over the years, such as Bala and Freeletics, but not one that suggests specific fitness workouts based on my DNA testing results. AlterMe combines guidance across exercise, nutrition, sleep, and recovery, going beyond simply reporting on your DNA and biometric data to suggest small, manageable actions to drive behavioral change over time.
There’s no denying that it comes at a premium price, but having workouts and nutrition guidance in one place helped me build better habits—even if the DNA insights weren’t particularly revelatory.
Getting Set Up
Photograph: Emily Peck
AlterMe’s all-in-one health and fitness program is built around a DNA test and a smart ring that measures data and provides insights and workouts in the app. It’s convenient, but this is an expensive offering. The entry-level AlterMe Essential plan is $1,299, and the AlterMe Advanced plan is $1,899. Both offer biometric tracking, nutrition insights, and fitness workouts accessible from the app, but the Advanced plan gives you a more in-depth DNA analysis and lifetime membership as opposed to the Essential’s three-year membership.
Upon signing up and answering questions on my weight-loss goals, height, weight, and general fitness levels, I was sent both a DNA cheek-swab kit and a ring sizing kit. I emailed AlterMe to confirm my ring size and sent the DNA swab back in the mail. Within two weeks, I received my AlterMe smart ring and had booked in a date to talk over my Fitness and Wellness Genetic report with an AlterMe representative. I’ve been diving in and out of the app and following the fitness workouts for over six months now.
A Tailored Fitness and Wellness Genetic Report
AlterMe app via Emily Peck
Research into genetic influence on athletic performance is still developing, and AlterMe acknowledges that its genetic findings reported through DNA testing have not been clinically validated. However, the company conducts its own research to produce a personalized Fitness and Wellness Genetic Report. It says it uses “a rigorous genetic interpretation process that adheres to strict scientific standards” with “scientific integrity” and “robust research.” AlterMe also states that saliva samples are processed in the US in a CLIA- and CAP-certified lab that meets local regulations.
With this in mind, I approached the DNA test report with equal measures of skepticism and intrigue, as should anyone curious to get more insight into their health and well-being.
The report claimed to use my DNA to reveal how my body responds to different types of exercise, nutrition, recovery, and stress. It suggested types of exercise to suit me and how I could approach training and recovery. Strength training, for example, was identified as the best fit for my genetic profile, while my genetic response to carbohydrates was rated as “lower than average.”
Perhaps not surprisingly, the report told me that I’m “externally motivated to exercise,” suggesting I may not naturally enjoy physical activity just for the sake of it. That certainly felt familiar.
Representatives at AlterMe explained how these assessments are determined: “Our assessment looks at markers associated with several traits, including how body composition changed during exercise interventions. For cardio-related body composition response, the markers in our scientific review are ADRB2 rs1042713 and LPL rs328. For resistance training, the model draws on a set of obesity and body composition markers, including variants near FTO, GNPDA2, NEGR1, and SLC39A8.”
So far, everything was sounding on point. But despite the personalized insights, I hadn’t discovered anything particularly groundbreaking.
Smart Ring Bling
Photograph: Emily Peck
AlterMe has its own smart ring wearable, designed to provide health insights and work alongside the app. The ring uses PPG sensors to monitor metrics such as heart rate and blood oxygen, alongside a temperature sensor and an accelerometer to track activity. It then uses data including my HRV, resting heart rate, sleep, and recent activity load to turn the raw measurements into a “Readiness score” from 0 to 100, before suggesting a workout tailored to my current state and my DNA insight.
This type of health tracking is similar to what you get with Oura's Ring 5 offering. The key difference is that AlterMe is a more closed ecosystem, combining its wearable data with its own genetic insights to generate an AI-powered workout plan every day based on my biometrics.
Oura, meanwhile, provides detailed sleep, activity, readiness, and broader health insights as well as guided fitness content within its app and integration with services such as Apple Health. Its primary focus, however, remains tracking and interpreting your health and activity data, whereas AlterMe puts more emphasis on the personalized workouts it prescribes.
The ring has a titanium outer frame and comes in either a gold finish, silver, or Stealth black. My gold finish has picked up some scuff marks over the couple of months I’ve been wearing it. While the gold finish looks good, I found the ring quite bulky—and thicker than the sleek Oura Ring 5—which means it sometimes gets in the way when I’m lifting weights.
Tailored Workouts Depending on ‘Readiness’ Score
Within the stats section of the app, I was able to view my daily calorie burn, step count, distance covered, sleep duration, and readiness score—all data the ring was providing. The app then provides a daily workout to follow. The workouts can be as low-key or as challenging as I want, depending on how I am feeling. I could choose from stretch, strength, cardio, yoga, or combat-style sessions, so there’s no excuse to skip a workout. As AlterMe representatives told me, the biometric data collected can help make a recommendation, but it can’t capture every detail about how I feel—soreness, illness, stress, injury, or demands of the day may change what feels right, for example—which is why you get the option to choose your level.
“Giving you a choice is also an intentional part of the AlterMe experience,” say AlterMe representatives. “Without choice, it’s hard for you to stay consistent. We want to offer useful guidance while leaving you in control of your effort. Your choice adds context and makes the plan easier to fit into real life.”
On the days I had poor sleep the night before, the app recommended a lighter workout or recovery session—the 15-minute breathwork session has become a particular favorite. On the days I’d slept well, I was tasked with a more strenuous session depending on my current level, from beginner to level 6.
While the workouts are easy to access and follow, I found them short—20 minutes was the average workout time, with 40 minutes being the longest session I tried. But it is possible to stack the workouts if you want to push yourself further. There’s also a way to track activities such as a run or group workout outside the guided library of workouts.
I trust that the app was recommending workouts to suit my health stats and genetic traits, and I mostly felt good when following them. But there were some days when I was feeling terrible due to poor sleep, and the app was telling me that my readiness score was high, which left me feeling a little confused. But I dutifully obliged with the suggested workout—even if I did opt for a shorter 20-minute session. On the days I had forgotten to wear my ring to bed the night before, the app would ask me to self-score from 1 to 10 on how I was feeling before a workout was suggested.
AI Nutrition Coach and Body Scanning
Exercise is just one piece of the fitness puzzle, and one of the pros of the AlterMe app is that it has a nutrition tracker. Rather than having it provide a single diet plan, I like the way the app can generate meal and snack ideas by referencing my DNA to keep me hitting my macro targets. You can generate a recipe and then log it if you decide to make it. Simply by clicking “generate recipe” I could get breakfast, lunch, dinner, and snack ideas in under 20 seconds. The recipes are pretty enticing too—Zesty Lemon Herb Grilled Chicken Qith Roasted Green Beans and Quinoa was one I tried. But I found the snack ideas most helpful, as I’m always thinking about snacks—Roasted Edamame With Smoked Paprika and Sea Salt is a particular favorite.
In the Nutrition tab of the app, I could access personalized calorie and nutrition guidance based on my DNA results, weight, BMI, activity level, and weight-loss goals. My DNA report suggested I have an average response to protein and a low response to carbs and fats. I like how easy it is to log food in the Nutrition tab in the app and instantly see whether I’d hit my protein, fat, and carb macro goals. I often forgot to track everything I ate, but on the days I remembered to do so, I found it easy to track my calorie intake and meals.
AlterMe app via Emily Peck
The app also has a 3D/body composition scanning feature to analyze body shape and provide stats on things like BMI, estimated body-fat percentage, and lean mass.
You do need to put in your height and weight when you sign up, but this feature adds more. As AlterMe told me, BMI is calculated from height and weight, but the scan provides a much fuller view by creating a standardized 3D model and estimating body-fat percentage, lean mass, body shape, and body part circumferences. Repeated scans help show whether and where the body is changing, giving members a clearer way to compare their progress with their goals. You need to use your phone camera to capture a picture of your body shape, but turning as it takes photos. I found this feature a little intrusive, as I didn’t really want to take photos of myself to put on the app. But if this doesn’t bother you, I think this is a compelling extra.
Is the AlterMe App Worth It?
There are numerous workout apps and wearables that can track your health data, but this personalized program that combines DNA testing, a smart ring wearable, and on-demand workouts in one ecosystem is a unique offering. It’s convenient, but pricey, and it's important to note that while the DNA testing can be insightful, it hasn’t been clinically validated. There are also understandable privacy concerns around handing over DNA data, although AlterMe notes on its site that it destroys samples after testing and extracted DNA is retained for just 45 days for quality assurance.
My journey with AlterMe has generally been positive, but it hasn’t altered me. It has made me more aware of what I eat and made me feel physically stronger due to the regularity of my training sessions. I like wearing the ring and having an app that suggests an optimum workout based on my biometrics. Having a tailored workout to follow has made me feel good—particularly on the days that I haven’t felt like training. When I feel stuck in the gym and not sure which exercises to do, I take out the app and simply follow a workout. It makes me feel like I have a personal trainer in my pocket, ready to bark orders at me whenever I need a little push. I think if you’re willing to follow the workouts and track your nutrition, AlterMe can be a helpful tool for building positive habits and improving fitness. You could, alternatively, use the money and invest in a good personal trainer—whatever you decide, it’s always nice to have options.

(Bloomberg) -- Saudi Aramco’s executive headquarters in eastern Saudi Arabia was hit during a missile attack by Yemen’s Houthi militants on Tuesday, causing a fire in a part of the complex, the kingdom’s energy ministry said.
The strike on an office complex in Dhahran caused a limited fire and no injuries, according to the ministry. The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said Houthi missiles had targeted several cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, including the capital Riyadh.
Shrapnel from an interception fell in part of a residential area in Dhahran, the coalition said. Aramco didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Quick answers to key questions
A Houthi missile attack hit Aramco’s executive office complex in Dhahran, causing a limited fire. Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said there were no injuries.
No injuries were reported from the strike on the office complex. The Saudi-led coalition said shrapnel from an intercepted missile fell in part of a residential area in Dhahran.
Dhahran is at the heart of Saudi Arabia’s oil economy and is home to Aramco’s headquarters. The kingdom’s largest oil fields are in the Eastern Province and the Persian Gulf.
The warning came after the Saudi-led coalition told civilians to evacuate an oil facility in Houthi-controlled Sanaa. The Houthis also urged oil workers to stay away from Saudi sites that could become targets.
A refinery in Jazan had been shut after an earlier attack, and a key oil export port on the Red Sea coast had also been targeted. A cross-country pipeline used by Aramco to transport oil to world markets was temporarily shut after an attack launched from Iraq.
The missiles launches are part of a wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent days that has also targeted airports around the country, which left at least 18 people dead and hundreds injured.
The latest Houthi attacks come after the Saudi coalition had warned people in the vicinity of an oil site in Houthi-held capital Sanaa in Yemen to leave the area “for their safety.”
Oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia has also been targeted during the escalating hostilities with the Houthis.
A refinery at Jazan in the kingdom’s west has been shut since an earlier attack, while a key oil export port on the Red Sea coast has also been targeted. A cross-country pipeline that’s been the main means for Aramco to get its oil to world markets was temporarily shut last month following an attack launched from Iraq.
Dhahran, located along Saudi Arabia’s Persian Gulf coast, is at the heart of the kingdom’s oil economy. In addition to Aramco, the region is home to a university specializing in petroleum engineering and a major air base. Saudi Arabia’s biggest oil fields are located in the deserts of the Eastern Province and in the Persian Gulf.

Anthropic seeks rehearing of case over Pentagon's security risk branding
Oct 13 : Anthropic asked a US appeals court on Tuesday to reconsider a ruling that upheld the Pentagon's decision to label the AI company as a national security supply chain risk over a dispute about safety guardrails on its technology.
• A federal appeals court in September upheld the designation in a 2-1 decision, agreeing with the Pentagon that the firm's safety restrictions could compromise military operations. The Pentagon's blacklisting of the company has cost it billions of dollars in lost business, Anthropic has said.
• The court's majority said the Pentagon acted reasonably after Anthropic refused to allow its AI to be used in autonomous weapons or mass surveillance, and the court rejected the firm's claim that it faced retaliation by the Defense Department over its views on AI safety.
• In its petition on Tuesday to the US Court of Appeals in Washington, DC, for a rehearing, Anthropic argued that the panel majority misinterpreted and transformed a federal law "aimed at hostile foreign actors into one that presumptively reaches every government contractor."
• The court let the Pentagon take action against Anthropic "without any pre-designation process and despite straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety," the company said.
• In a separate lawsuit in August, a federal judge in California struck down a parallel designation under a different law.
• Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for regulation covering all US frontier AI companies, while the Trump administration has favored a pro-growth approach.

Perhaps the days when auto shows debuted new models aren’t entirely over. The big trade shows for cars were a gateway drug for many, expos where you could see the newest models of today and the concepts of tomorrow. But automakers increasingly got tired of sharing the spotlight with each other. New reveals moved offsite to events the night or even the week before the show itself. One by one, brands pulled out of auto show after auto show until there was little left to see. And then the pandemic hit.
But the news out of Paris, where its auto show held media day yesterday, seems like we stepped back into a time when automakers would debut new cars aplenty. That retro vibe extends to the cars themselves, with plenty of familiar nameplates reimagined.
France’s Renault has a long and glorious history of delightful concept cars, and more on what it brought to Paris later. But the star of the show was arguably Stellantis, with strong work from Citroen, Peugeot, and Fiat, to name but three. But this article is meant to irritate you, because I’m pretty sure none of the stuff you’re seeing here will come to the United States. And it’s doubly irritating considering what Stellantis’ brands do offer us over here, doubling down on the same malign trends I saw back in 2020: did you know they’re about to relaunch a V8 Hellcat-powered Charger?
EVs can be small and cheap, apparently
The European concepts show us that, as those Kneecap chaps have it, there’s a better way to live. A sense of utopia was responsible for the original Citroen 2 CV; it had to be cheap enough for a farmer to buy it and rugged enough to get produce to market without breaking it. I’m not sure whether the 2 CV Concept also has to be able to transport eggs across a rutted field without breaking any (although the glove box is a clue), but Citroen says that affordability, lightness, practicality, and versatility were top of mind during the design process. The press release probably didn’t need to also say the company imbued it with distinctive character or charm; that’s quite obvious from the design.

South Africa's deputy police chief resigns after being charged with sexual offences
- Published
South Africa's deputy police chief has resigned three weeks after he was charged with sexual offences.
A lawyer representing Lt Gen Shadrack Sibiya submitted his resignation letter at his disciplinary hearing on Monday, a police spokesperson said.
The charges relate to allegations that he sexually groomed a 16-year-old girl and raped an 18-year-old woman. He is also facing a charge of trafficking.
Sibiya has denied all the charges. He says he did have sex with the 18 year-old but says it was consensual.
He has been in custody since he was arrested three weeks ago after his bail application was denied.
Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said in a post on X that his departure from the police force was regarded as a dishonourable discharge, external.
The case comes as the police service is in the spotlight at a major public inquiry over allegations of corruption and collusion with criminals.
The inquiry, known as the Madlanga Commission, began in September 2025 and has heard accusations that Sibiya received a gift of 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract.
He denied the allegation.

It’s a big year for Apple firsts. The company launched the first MacBook Neo, unveiled its first folding iPhone in September, and installed a new CEO for the first time in 15 years. Now comes the Apple HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.
Rivals like Google and Amazon have made countless screen-enabled smart speakers since voice assistants invaded the home a decade ago. But Apple stuck with a smaller smart home ecosystem centered on its HomePod speakers, even removing the iPad as a hub device a few years ago, which forced users to buy an Apple TV or HomePod to get started. Maybe that’s why it hasn’t found much success in the home.
Announced Tuesday at an event in New York City, the 7-inch smart display arrives alongside several other new smart home devices as part of Apple’s bid to revitalize its lagging ecosystem. The HomeView costs $299 and comes in two versions—a speaker base and a wall-mounted display—both priced the same. Preorders are live, with sales kicking off on November 13.
A Big Apple Watch
The first thing I thought of after seeing the Apple HomeView in action is that it looks like a blown-up Apple Watch. The 7-inch square screen has multiple “faces” you can swipe through, exactly like the smartwatch. You can even customize the face’s colors and add different complications for more glanceable information.
The faces can range from a clock, your favorite photos of friends, family, or pets (you can even use shared albums) to weather updates and, yes, Snoopy animations. Swipe up for the home screen, which is more like an iPhone or iPad, with apps neatly arranged alongside widgets. Except the HomeView doesn’t run iOS or iPadOS—it runs the generically named HomeView software.
It doesn’t have an App Store. Instead, Apple has a curated selection of apps, including FaceTime, Messages, and Safari. A handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps. If your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup. (There are no video streaming apps like YouTube, Netflix, or Disney+, but if those companies choose to make their apps available on the CarPlay framework, they will show up on the HomeView; for now, you'll have to consume videos by using the Safari browser.)
To get the most out of the HomeView, you need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (an iPhone 15 Pro or newer)—you can’t set it up with an iPad.
The aluminum hardware, powered by Apple’s A18 chip, comes in four colors: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray (Apple color-matches the woven cable, too). The standard HomeView has a speaker base with a screen that tilts manually up or down for angled viewing, but you can also buy a wall-mountable version. The latter offers three mounts to choose from, one of which is DIY-friendly and has a visible power cord that needs to run to an outlet. The other two are designed for professional installers, either hardwired or connected via Power over Ethernet (PoE).
Technically, the primary speakers—two full-range drivers—are built into the screen. But the standard HomeView has a base that houses a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators for stronger bass. It sounds pretty good based on a very limited listening experience, and can fill a large room quite well. The wall-mounted variant won’t have that extra oomph but Apple claims it tunes the audio for wall placement.
The 7-inch Liquid Retina display has familiar elements, like True Tone, which adjusts the screen’s color temperature to match the room’s lighting. The ambient light sensor can also reduce display brightness from 500 nits to 0.3 nits, which is the lowest brightness Apple has ever engineered on a screen. That’ll be helpful if you place the HomeView on the nightstand.
That is, if you're comfortable placing a camera-equipped display in the bedroom. A 12-megapixel Center Stage camera and four-microphone array sit on the front, but they aren’t just for FaceTime calls. The camera handles facial recognition, allowing the software to adapt to whoever is looking at the screen. Apple says all of this data stays on device.
“Trust is becoming increasingly important with rising consumer expectations around privacy and security,” writes Anshika Jain, principal analyst at Counterpoint, in an email to WIRED. “In fact, Apple could actually benefit from its privacy-first approach.”
You can add up to six iCloud accounts, and the user interface will adapt to each person, like Google’s Pixel Tablet. That means your wife can tint every app icon green and have no widgets on her home screen, but if you stand in front of the HomeView, it’ll switch to your setup. You won’t be able to view other household members’ sensitive messages and personal information. For this personal content to show up, you don’t just have to stand in front of the HomeView—your iPhone needs to be on the same Wi-Fi network and must have been recently unlocked.
The HomeView can also recognize voices, which helps if Dad asks Siri AI to “Play music.” It will play from Dad’s music library and his preferred music app, rather than another iCloud user’s music. If you have multiple HomePods or HomeViews, you can manage your speaker groups in the HomeView’s interface.
The HomeView also supports Apple’s Handoff tech, so you can bring your iPhone close to send a Safari recipe to the smart display, or have it continue the podcast you were listening to on your commute. In the middle of a FaceTime or phone call? Put your iPhone near the HomeView, and it’ll transfer it over.
Betting on Siri AI
Like any smart display or smart speaker, Siri AI powers the HomeView. It is, after all, the main way to interact with the device (though yes, there’s a keyboard you can pull up to type). Apple spent a great deal of time revamping Siri this year, finally launching a more capable assistant in iOS 27.
Siri AI on the HomeView understands your personal context from your iPhone, so if you ask it to play a song your friend Eric recommended, it’ll know right away what you mean by looking at your Messages history. You can ask when your brother Jeff will likely arrive at your home from the airport on Thursday, then set a schedule for Siri to turn on the coffee maker 15 minutes before his estimated arrival. All of this can be done with natural language, meaning you don’t have to say specific commands for Siri AI to understand you.
One neat trick is the HomeView’s ability to convert recipe pages from Safari into digestible content. Load a recipe, and it will let you view the ingredients or “Start Cooking,” no need to read three paragraphs of the author’s relationship to the stew. It automatically converts the recipe into step-by-step instructions, even auto-populating timers for relevant steps so you can start individual timers as you progress.
Naturally, the HomeView is also designed to control all of your smart home devices, too. You can create a widget for any device you have added in the Home app to quickly control it on the HomeView. And if you swipe to the left from the home screen, you’ll see the “Camera” face, which shows a live stream of connected security cameras (you can view nine feeds at once).
Much like the upcoming iPhone Duo folding phone, Apple is late to market. The company is betting on tight iPhone integration, glanceable Watch-like software, and a more context-aware Siri to make the HomeView feel more like a screen you’ll actually want on your counter. Everything hinges on whether Siri can hold up its end of the bargain—and the voice assistant doesn’t exactly have the best track record.
“The greater challenge is to make AI useful for everyday interactions,” Jain says. “Apple must provide a more capable Siri experience and ensure seamless control across its entire product range in order to stand out from the competition.”

South Africa have slipped to third place in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) 2025-27 standings following their 214-run defeat to Australia in the first Test at Durban. The result has strengthened Australia's position at the top of the table, while New Zealand have moved into second place.
The defending champions entered the series in second place but dropped to third after suffering their second defeat in five matches in the current WTC cycle. South Africa now have a points percentage (PCT) of 60.00, while New Zealand sit second with 72.22 per cent.
Australia, meanwhile, consolidated their position at the summit with nine wins from 11 matches, taking their points percentage to 81.82. Bangladesh and India occupy fourth and fifth places, respectively, with points percentages of 55.56 and 51.52.

Hazlewood, Renshaw power Australia to dominant Durban victory
Australia secured the 214-run win at Kingsmead after Josh Hazlewood produced a career-best performance of 6/49 on the fifth day. South Africa, chasing a target of 421, were bowled out for 206 despite Aiden Markram's fighting 75 off 237 deliveries and Marco Jansen's 35.
Hazlewood broke the hosts' resistance by dismissing Wiaan Mulder for 29 before removing Jansen and Simon Harmer in the same over. 
Mitchell Starc then ended Markram's determined innings, while Hazlewood claimed the final wicket by dismissing Anrich Nortje.
The foundation for Australia's victory was laid by Matt Renshaw, who scored a magnificent 190 in the first innings and followed it up with 82 in the second. Australia posted 390 before declaring their second innings at 314/6, setting South Africa a challenging target.
South Africa had managed 284 in their first innings but struggled to sustain their chase on the final day. The defeat also marked Temba Bavuma's first loss as South Africa's Test captain.
Renshaw was named Player of the Match for his outstanding contributions with the bat and ball. Australia now lead the three-match Test series 1-0.

Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India’s election chief on Sunday, as a court ordered the release of the “cockroach” movement founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and two other senior leaders.
Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday, as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi.
Indian authorities on Saturday deployed a sweeping crackdown across Delhi and detained thousands of protesters as the youth “cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fuelled anger at the prime minister, Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Reuters reported police detained more than 2,000 people to thwart Saturday’s protest. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.
Most detained on the first day of protests were released on Saturday night, police said.
Opposition parties and critics of Modi’s government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters.
The UN human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said: “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled.” He urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
India’s foreign ministry said the UN’s approach was “selective” and its statement constituted “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
The protests are calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years.
Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party.
Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
The BJP and the commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The “cockroach” movement, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi’s education minister.
The CJP has called its protests against Kumar “Season 2” on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India’s election system was reformed.

Andy Burnham will welcome Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday in a demonstration of support following US president Donald Trump’s diesel arrangement with Russia.
The Prime Minister is expected to utilise the bilateral visit to announce accelerated military assistance for Kyiv, alongside promises of extra sanctions targeting Moscow.
As part of the increased aid, the UK will speed up deliveries of lightweight multirole missiles, which have proven effective at countering Russian jet-powered drones.
On Monday, Britain will also prompt its international partners to step up pressure on Moscow, as Chancellor John Healey uses IMF talks in Bangkok to advocate for a ban on Russian liquified natural gas (LNG).
Ahead of the talks with Mr Zelensky, the Prime Minister stated that British support for Ukraine remained "rock solid" and was "vital for keeping us safe here in the UK".
He stated: "My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer: we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe."
The Downing Street meeting follows what Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband characterised as a "very difficult few days" in transatlantic relations after Mr Trump moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel ahead of US mid-term elections dominated by high fuel prices.
In response to the deal, the UK committed to "maintain pressure on Russia", while Mr Burnham spoke directly to Mr Zelensky on Saturday to convey his "complete solidarity" with Kyiv.
The move comes after the US president suggested in recent days that Ukraine requires a new leader, whilst claiming that Vladimir Putin is more eager for a peace deal than officials in Kyiv.
On Tuesday, the Ukrainian president revealed his government was given no prior warning by partners regarding a Russian ballistic missile attack the previous night, sparking fears that the US had ended intelligence sharing with Kyiv.
However, Mr Trump responded to this by insisting that Washington continues to share intelligence with Ukraine as he departed the White House for a campaign event in Alaska later that day.

Here's what to know if you're unsure about your measles immunity status
Measles is the most contagious disease known. It can rip through a population without immunity like wildfire. Just look at what's happening in Pennsylvania, says Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a public health effort led by the National Infectious Diseases Foundation.
"In January in Pennsylvania, they had 12 cases. Now we're seeing 100 plus cases per week and over 1,000 cases in Pennsylvania," she says. "If Pennsylvania can see it spread that fast, that can happen in any state that has low immunization rates."
As vaccination rates have fallen across the country, many communities have become vulnerable. Nationwide, more than 4,000 measles cases have been reported this year alone — the highest number in 35 years. Pennsylvania has reported five deaths. New York state declared a measles emergency.
Stinchfield says the recent measles surge has got many people wondering if they're at risk.
"It's a very common question for people to ask, 'am I immune? Am I OK? What do I need to do?' And that is exactly the right question everyone should be asking themselves right now," Stinchfield says.
The best defense is vaccination. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is 97% effective — meaning 97% of people will have an immune response.
"The measles vaccine is safe. It's highly effective, and it confers lifelong immunity," says Dr. Adam Ratner, a pediatric infectious disease physician in New York City and author of Booster Shots, a history of measles.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
But what if you don't know your immunization history, or you only got one dose of the measles shot? Should you get another dose? Infectious disease experts say that depends on several factors.
If you were born before 1957
People born before 1957 are presumed to be immune because back then, measles was so common, just about everyone got it in childhood, says Dr. Larry Kociolek, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago and an associate professor of pediatrics at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
"It was thought that pretty much everyone in the U.S. was infected with measles as sort of a rite of passage in childhood," Kocielek says. He says anyone who's ever had measles can be confident they're protected.
That is of course, if you survived. Before vaccines, measles used to kill 400 to 500 people each year in the U.S.
If you were vaccinated before 1968
People who were born after 1957 and vaccinated before 1968 may need an additional dose. That's because a small group of people who were immunized during that time received an early, less effective version of the vaccine that used inactivated or killed virus.
If you're not sure which vaccine you got, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends talking to your doctor about getting one or two doses of the MMR vaccine.
If you only got one dose of the MMR vaccine
At first, children in the U.S. received just one dose of the MMR vaccine. But that changed in 1989, after public health officials determined that a single dose wasn't enough to prevent outbreaks. That year, the official recommendation switched to two doses of MMR vaccine for children, which is still in effect today.
Kids need the higher protection "because they tend to be at higher risk of exposure, since they're oftentimes in group settings like schools and daycares," Kociolek says.
If you're in a higher-risk group
One dose of MMR vaccine is 93% effective, and traditionally, Kociolek says, that was considered enough protection for most adults, unless they were at higher risk of being exposed to measles. Health care workers, people in a college setting and those travelling abroad are all in this group. If you live with or are in close contact with someone who is immunocompromised, you also need two doses of vaccine to protect them.
But given the recent, dramatic rise of measles across the country these days, "if you are living in areas with high measles activity, it does make a whole lot of sense for adults to go ahead and get that second dose," Kociolek says.
Ratner says it's definitely worth asking your doctor if you should get a second dose.
While measles is often considered to be a childhood disease, a large proportion of people sickened this year have been unvaccinated adults — and people over 20 who lack immunity are at higher risk of serious complications.
No matter your age, "measles is a serious disease," Stinchfield says.
She notes that getting two doses of the vaccine can also help others at higher risk who can't get the MMR shot, including people who are pregnant, severely immunocompromised and infants under 6 months of age.
If you really don't know your immunization history
If you're just not sure if you're protected against measles and you can't find records of immunization, you could get a test to check your blood antibody levels. But those tests aren't perfect, says Dr. William Moss, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
"It's possible that a person could actually be protected and test negative on one of those," Moss says.
Depending on your circumstances, your insurance might not cover the blood test. But most private insurance plans and Medicaid must cover another MMR vaccine at no cost.
Moss says if you can't confirm how many doses of MMR vaccine you've had, "I would say it is easier and less expensive to just get another MMR vaccine, and there is no harm in getting a second MMR vaccine or even a third, additional MMR dose."
After all, it's much better to be protected than infected.

2026 అక్టోబర్ 2న, ఓటర్ల జాబితాలో అక్రమాలు జరిగాయనే ఆరోపణలపై ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేశ్ కుమార్ రాజీనామా చేయాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ, అక్టోబర్ 10న ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద భారీ నిరసన చేపట్టనున్నట్లు కాక్రొచ్ జనతా పార్టీ (CJP) ప్రకటించింది. ప్రత్యేక సమగ్ర ఓటర్ల జాబితా సవరణ (SIR) ప్రక్రియను వెంటనే నిలిపివేయాలని, 2025 జూన్ 25 నుంచి ఓటర్ల జాబితా నుంచి తొలగించిన పేర్లన్నింటినీ తిరిగి చేర్చాలని కూడా CJP డిమాండ్ చేస్తోంది. లెఫ్ట్ వింగ్ విద్యార్థి సంఘాలు కూడా ఈ నిరసనలో పెద్ద సంఖ్యలో పాల్గొంటామని ప్రకటన విడుదల చేశాయి.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, బజరంగ్ దళ్ వంటి హిందూ సంస్థలకు చెందిన కార్యకర్తలు నిరసనను వ్యతిరేకించేందుకు జంతర్ మంతర్ వైపు వస్తున్నారంటూ పలు వీడియోలను (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. ఈ వాదనల్లో నిజమెంతో ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 10 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఢిల్లీలోని జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద జరిగే CJP నిరసనను వ్యతిరేకించేందుకు బజరంగ్ దళ్తో సహా హిందూ సంస్థల కార్యకర్తలు సిద్ధమవుతున్నట్లు వైరల్ పోస్టులు పేర్కొంటున్నాయి.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోలన్నీ నిరసన ప్రకటనకు ముందే ఆన్లైన్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నాయి. వీటిలో పశ్చిమ బెంగాల్లో జరిగిన రామనవమి బైక్ ర్యాలీ, UGCకి సంబంధించిన ర్యాలీ, ఛత్రపతి శివాజీ పట్టాభిషేక వార్షికోత్సవ వేడుకలు వంటి వేర్వేరు సంఘటనలకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు ఉన్నాయి. జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద తమ కార్యకర్తలను సమీకరించే ప్రణాళిక లేదని బజరంగ్ దళ్ కూడా స్పష్టం చేసింది. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టుల్లో చేసిన వాదనలు తప్పు.
వీడియో 1:
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేమ్లను ఉపయోగించి రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఈ వీడియో నవంబర్ 2022 నుంచి ఆన్లైన్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం (ఆర్కైవ్). అయితే, ఈ వీడియో మొదట ఏ సందర్భంలో చిత్రీకరించారో స్పష్టంగా తెలియలేదు. కానీ, గత కొన్ని సంవత్సరాలుగా ఇదే వీడియోను వివిధ అంశాలకు సంబంధించి పలుమార్లు ఉపయోగించినట్లు గుర్తించాం (ఇక్కడ). దీంతో, 2026 అక్టోబర్ 10న జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద జరిగిన నిరసనకు ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదని స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
వీడియో 2:
కాషాయ జెండాలు పట్టుకుని రోడ్డుపై ప్రజలు ర్యాలీ ఈ వీడియో 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచే ఆన్లైన్లో అందుబాటులో ఉంది (ఆర్కైవ్). అయితే, ఈ వీడియోను మొదట ఏ సందర్భంలో చిత్రీకరించారో దృవీకరించలేకపోయినప్పటికీ, జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద నిరసన గురించి ప్రకటించడానికి మూడు వారాల కంటే ముందే ఈ వీడియోను ఆన్లైన్లో అప్లోడ్ చేశారు.
వీడియో 3:
భారీ సంఖ్యలో ప్రజలు కనిపిస్తున్న ఈ వీడియో 2026 జూన్ నుంచే ఆన్లైన్లో అందుబాటులో ఉంది. (ఆర్కైవ్). 6 జూన్ 2026న రాయగఢ్ కోటలో ఛత్రపతి శివాజీ పట్టాభిషేక వార్షికోత్సవం సందర్భంగా జరిగిన వేడుక దృశ్యాలను ఈ వీడియో చూపిస్తోంది.
వీడియో 4: 
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేమ్లను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఈ వీడియోను షేర్ చేసిన ఒక ఎక్స్ (X) పోస్ట్ (ఆర్కైవ్) కనిపించింది. ఆ పోస్ట్లో “బజరంగ్ దళ్, ఆర్ఎస్ఎస్ ఇప్పుడు వీధుల్లోకి వస్తే ఎలా ఉంటుందో ఊహించండి” అనే క్యాప్షన్తో ఈ వీడియోను షేర్ చేశారు. అయితే, ఆ వీడియోకు సంబంధించి ఎలాంటి అదనపు వివరాలను అందులో పేర్కొనలేదు. కానీ ఇది 22 జూలై 2026 నుండే, అంటే జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద నిరసన గురించి ప్రకటించడానికి ముందే సోషల్ మీడియాలో షేర్ చయ్యబడుతోంది.
వీడియో 5:
ఈ వీడియో గురించి ఫ్యాక్ట్లీ ఇంతకముందే ప్రచురించింది. UGC 2026 ఈక్విటీ నిబంధనలను ఉపసంహరించుకోవాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ, కర్ణి సేన జైపూర్లో చేసిన ధర్నాను ఈ వీడియో చూపిస్తుంది.
వీడియో 6:
ఈ వీడియో యొక్క కీ ఫ్రేములను ఉపయోగిస్తూ రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చైయగా ఈ వీడియో 2026 జూలైలో జరిగిన ఒక ర్యాలీకి సంబంధించినదని మేము గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోకు 2026 అక్టోబర్ 10న జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద జరిగిన నిరసనకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు.
అదేవిధంగా, జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద జరుగుతున్న నిరసనను వ్యతిరేకించేందుకు బజరంగ్ దళ్ కార్యకర్తలు అక్కడికి వస్తున్నారంటూ కొన్ని ధృవీకరించని వీడియోలను (ఇక్కడ) షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. అయితే, బజరంగ్ దళ్ ఈ వార్తలను ఖండించింది. అక్టోబర్ 10న జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్ద తమ కార్యకర్తలు సమావేశమయ్యే లేదా అక్కడికి వచ్చే ప్రణాళిక ఏదీ లేదని, కొందరు వ్యక్తులు తప్పుడు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారని X ద్వారా తెలిపింది (ఆర్కైవ్).
చివరిగా, CJP నిరసనను వ్యతిరేకించేందుకు హిందూ కార్యకర్తలు జంతర్ మంతర్ వద్దకు వస్తున్నారంటూ సంబంధం లేని పాత వీడియోలను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has denied being rolled by Anthony Albanese after the prime minister personally intervened to stop a tax office ban on credit card payments a day before stopgap funding was announced.
After sustained criticism of the government’s handling of the ban on tax bills being paid by credit card, Chalmers last week announced new funding for the ATO to ensure card payments could continue until the end of the financial year.
Albanese has since revealed he acted after discussions with Andrew McKellar, the boss of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI), earlier than previously known, prompting suggestions Albanese had undermined Chalmers.
But, when asked if he had been rolled, Chalmers denied the prime minister went over his head to intervene on the ATO’s decision to ban credit card payments.
“If you just let me set it out for you, [the] prime minister and I were in discussions on Wednesday of last week,” he said on Wednesday morning.
“He had a view and I agree with it, that we needed to step in to provide this longer transition period to allow the ATO the time to get it right. We had the same view.”
Albanese said at Parliament House on Tuesday night that he acted when concerns were raised with him.
“Andrew [McKellar] did text me last Thursday morning and by Friday morning we had an announcement,” he said.
“That was an example of a relationship that takes time to develop. That trust, where you can have a discussion and say ‘it is in hand, I agree with what you are saying and I will get it done’.”
The tax commissioner, Rob Heferen, announced earlier this month that the ATO would stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills from 1 December. The move followed a ban on surcharges announced by the Reserve Bank.
Heferen said continuing to accept card payments would cost the ATO almost $200m a year, as those costs could not legally be passed on to card users.
But some business owners, particularly smaller operators, use credit card payments as a cashflow tool, managing their liabilities by using credit when required. Estimates suggest about 5% of small businesses use credit card payments for tax bills.
The ATO is an independent authority and the government cannot direct the tax commissioner’s decisions.
Chalmers told ABC radio on Wednesday he was involved in the conversations with ACCI as well, describing the intervention as a joint decision with the prime minister.
“I have an open door. I’ve met with ACCI in recent weeks, in fact, and we were engaging on these issues as well,” he said.
He said he had discussions with Albanese last Wednesday, before he and the assistant treasurer, Daniel Mulino, took a proposal to ministerial colleagues.
The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, told News24 the intervention was more evidence of Albanese overriding Chalmers.
“The prime minister has a kink for punishing small businesses and a fetish for humiliating his treasurer,” he said.
“So I say this is a consistent pattern of behaviour where the prime minister constantly goes in, overrides his treasurer, humiliates him in public. I suspect it’s going to sour the relationship somewhat.”

Academy Award-nominated actor Josh Brolin has opened up about his emotional reaction to reading the script of Whalefall, the upcoming survival thriller from 20th Century Studios and Imagine Entertainment. Based on Daniel Kraus’s bestselling novel, the film stars Austin Abrams, Brolin, Elisabeth Shue, John Ortiz, Jane Levy and Emily Rudd. The film is set to arrive exclusively in Indian cinemas on Friday, October 16.
Josh Brolin recalls sobbing after reading Whalefall script; says “I didn’t just cry; i sobbed”
The story follows Jay Gardiner, played by Abrams, who ventures into the waters off California’s Central Coast to search for his deceased father’s remains. His underwater expedition takes a dangerous turn when he is swallowed by a massive sperm whale. With only an hour of oxygen remaining, Jay must find a way to survive, drawing on the lessons his father taught him.
Reflecting on his first experience reading the screenplay, Brolin spoke about how deeply the story affected him. “I slowed down when I was reading it because I didn’t want it to end,” says Brolin. “I finished it, I put it on my chest, I wrapped my arms around my chest, and I sobbed. I didn’t just cry; I sobbed, because it resonated with me so deeply, and it was poetic and visceral, and emotional.”
Brolin plays Mitt Gardiner, Jay’s father, whose influence remains central to the narrative. Producer Allan Mandelbaum explained the character’s importance to the story, saying, “Our story actually starts with Mitt,” explains producer Allan Mandelbaum. “He is the catalyst for Jay’s adventure.” Mitt is portrayed as a local diving legend, a member of the Monterey Dive Club, and a man with a deep passion for the sea.
Discussing his approach to the role, Brolin said, “Mitt is pretty tough as a father,” says Brolin. “I think of him as this seafaring, nautical-obsessed, Steinbeck-obsessed character, and I don’t know if I’ve ever been so willing and happy to dive into something. He is such a great character, and what I love about him is that he has a presence throughout the entire film, and he’s really driving the narrative.”
Mandelbaum also spoke about why Brolin was suited to the part. “Josh is the perfect guy to bring the essence of the character to life,” he said. “Josh is someone who rides motorcycles; he goes out on boats. He feels like an everyman in a way that really felt like the perfect fit for Mitt.”
Producer Brian Grazer highlighted the actor’s screen presence and confidence, adding, “Josh has a force, a presence, and a tremendous sense of confidence to be able to deal with stuff like that, and to be able to rise to that occasion, as he does in this film.”
Directed by Brian Duffield, Whalefall features a screenplay by Duffield and Daniel Kraus. The film is produced by Brian Grazer, Brian Duffield, Jeb Brody and Allan Mandelbaum, with Doug Merrifield, Richard Abate and Will Rowbotham serving as executive producers.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Bhopal Municipal Corporation (BMC)'s Mayor-in-Council (MiC) has approved handing over the Adampur landfill site to a Saurashtra-based company for the next five years.
The company will scientifically process the 800 metric tonnes of fresh waste arriving daily from the city. The same company is already engaged in clearing the 6.5 lakh metric tonnes of legacy waste accumulated at the site.
While the previous tender was valued at Rs 52 crore, the new tender is worth Rs 48 crore. Approval for this was granted on Tuesday by the Mayor-in-Council, presided over by Mayor Malti Rai.
In a meeting on Tuesday, MiC approved floating green municipal bonds worth Rs 200 crore to fund its financial contribution to the AMRUT 2.0 (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation) scheme.
It also approved a 6-7 times hike in allocation for shifting the GI water pipeline in the Kolar six-lane project. Initially, Rs 8.02 crore was allocated, but the expenditure increased by Rs 53.3 lakh, prompting approval of the additional amount.
MiC has approved the empanelment of consultant Hiten Rathi for the detailed project report (DPR) under PMAY-HFA-2.0.
MiC has also approved a third extension for M/s SRS Infra Project Limited till Dec 31, 2026, for completion of Ganga Nagar and Shyam Nagar projects under PMAY-HFA (Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana).
In the case of the Kalkheda PMAY-HFA project, approval has been granted for an extension till Mar 31, 2027, for M/s ISKON Infratech Private Limited to complete the project.
Velji Ratna Sorathia Infra Private Limited has been given time till Dec 31, 2026, for completion of the remaining work under the PMAY-HFA project at 12-number Bus Stop, while Sai Construction has been given a fourth extension till Oct 31, 2026, for completion of work under PMAY-HFA at the same site.
The council has also approved the Dipadi PMAY-HFA-2 project in public-private partnership (PPP) mode.
MiC has cancelled the previously approved project. It has also approved a minimum tender value of Rs 12 crore for M/s SRS Infra Project Limited for construction of 768 houses under PMAY-HFA-2 at Rajendra Nagar.
Administrative approval has also been granted for Rs 64.5 crore for construction of 528 houses under the same scheme at Kashturba Nagar. Similarly, administrative approval has also been given for Rs 27.5 crore for construction of 256 houses at Nayapura.

James McAvoy recalls his first day on the set of Band of Brothers and says a co-star bullied him.
During a visit to Bravo‘s Watch What Happens Live while playing “Spill the IMDb-tea,” McAvoy made the revelation while keeping mum about the names.
After being shown a photo of the HBO series, McAvoy took a closer look at the image and said, “Hold on, let me just see, is he in there? No, I don’t think he is in there. Ah, yeah, he is.”
“All right, so, I’m not going to tell you who it was,” he added. “[But] … one of the guys in that picture decided to bully me, on my first day as a professional actor out of acting school! So he got him and his buddies to just stand and point at me and laugh at me, for like three minutes.”
McAvoy explained that the scene he was shooting involved “a ton of actors,” adding, “It was one of those scenes with everybody in it, and we’re in a bar. And I had a scene, and all these guys were, like, in it for nine, 10 months, and you get one line in one episode and one line 10 episodes later. They were all pissed. And I come in for one episode, and I’ve got an arc and scenes. I’ve got tons of lines.”

Over the weekend, the World Health Organization released a disease outbreak report on the events surrounding the death of a Russian infectious disease researcher earlier this month, highlighting that Russia has yet to report a confirmed cause of death. With that “key uncertainty,” the United Nations health agency said it remains impossible to assess the risk of the event or whether the public health measures Russia took were adequate to prevent spread of the unknown disease.
The WHO reported that, so far, it has seen no evidence of ongoing transmission of the mystery disease. “However, confidence in the assessment remains limited by the absence of a confirmed etiological diagnosis, and the remaining uncertainty regarding the source and mode of exposure,” the agency wrote in its report.
The agency laid out the order of events as information trickled out from Russian authorities, noting that it only became aware of the death via media reports on October 2. The WHO subsequently made contact with Russian authorities and requested information on October 3, 6, 7, and 8.
Limited information released
Early media reports indicated that the lab worker had become ill on September 29, possibly following an incident at the lab, the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East. Some early reports suggested that the researcher—who was identified by media as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova—died of the plague after breaking a test tube.
On October 2, the Irkutsk branch of Russian health agency Rospotrebnadzor (RPN) said in a statement that a “special sanitary-epidemiological expert commission” had already met over a suspected case of a high-threat pathogen. Sanitary and epidemic control measures were put in place, including identifying, monitoring, and testing all contacts. At the time, RPN said that all contacts had tested negative for high-threat pathogens.
On October 6, Russia’s National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations (NFP) first responded to the WHO’s information requests, saying that no case of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk Oblast. The NFP confirmed that an APRI lab worker had died from a severe case of pneumonia after developing symptoms compatible with an acute respiratory viral infection. The worker was tested for a number of high-threat pathogens, but all the tests had come back negative. Doctors categorized the cause of death as being from pneumonia of undetermined etiology.

Not since Zhang Yimou’s 2002 wuxia spectacle “Hero” has China landed an Oscar nomination for Best International Feature — and this dry spell surely won’t be broken with this year’s bombastic submission “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” Like most of the country’s entries over the past decade, this blockbuster epic — a summer box office hit at home — makes for an extravagant display of the strength of the nation’s commercial film industry. Strength, in the sense that no modest operation could conceivably pull off the technical wizardry and large-scale worldbuilding showcased here, where an entire city is at one point turned into an inferno of crumbling buildings, and a massive military base is, in a later scene, ambushed in a rain of blazing pyrotechnics.
The film is also, as expected from this state-backed production, blatantly propagandistic — but in a way that is particularly baffling, and shockingly tasteless. If those sound like the elements for a good time, in the B-movie sense, then you are also correct. Against the odds, “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is also, both regrettably and miraculously, extremely watchable. The Jekyll part of your brain will tell you to leave but the Hyde-side will keep you seated in morbid, twitchy-eyed fascination over the film’s two-and-a-half hour runtime.
Popular on Variety
To cut straight to the point, this is a film in which China symbolically emerges from the rubble of the Iraq War as a pacifistic patriarch and guardian of all the world’s children. Director Wen Muyue delivers this subtext through the story of Xu Fu (Shen Teng), a debt-ridden chef who agrees to temporarily take over a Chinese restaurant in the fictional Gulf-region city of Bahata, intending to return to his daughter and mother in China in two years time.
Flash-forwards to an elder Xu Fu with liver spots and a conspicuous scar on his cheek tell us that he will indeed make it back to his family, but it’ll take much longer than a few years — the frankly absurd reasons for his delay a consequence of his, let’s say, geopolitical misfortunes. He’s a man in the wrong place at the wrong time, though, cleverly, the film makes the point that a good Chinese meal is never unwelcome. In fact it’s globally in demand — a lifeline that ensures Xu Fu’s survival through the film’s whirlwind of events.
Before we get to the grisly images of dead children covered in ash, the film starts out as a feel-good dramedy in which Xu Fu adapts to his new surroundings. Frazzled softie Ma Junsheng (Jiang Qiming), the restaurant manager, is our hero’s bridge between China and his new home, translating for Xu Fu between Arabic and Chinese during tense but diplomatic discussions with the restaurant owner Zaid (Sherif Sabby). Glossy, mouthwatering closeups of grilled meats and bubbling stone-pot stews testify to the success of Xu Fu’s kitchen takeover. Nurturing local talent is also on the agenda when he takes on a mentee, Seif (Omar Sharif — no, not that one), an angsty orphan who learns to sublimate his rage into the art of Chinese cooking. Though as the film goes on, this anger grows into a furious, war-hardened desire for retribution. Does a delicious roasted duck stand a chance? It does, in this film’s mind, with the help of the preternaturally compassionate Xu Fu.
“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is something of a both-sides film in that both the Americans and the not-so-thinly-veiled Iraqis are gross caricatures of themselves, and there’s particular ire reserved for that most treacherous of abominations: Chinese-American … food. In epic-handshake-meme solidarity, Xu Fu and Zaid agree that their restaurant will never serve U.S.-style Chinese dishes like General Tso’s chicken; and when the US troops bomb Bahata to smithereens and occupy the city, a crass Chinese-American private (Aarif Lee Zhi-ting) bullies his way into free meals at Xu Fu’s restaurant. Not a pushover but a practical-minded realist, the chef takes the punches, striking up a booze-smuggling deal with the Americans to keep the orphans living in his restaurant safe.
The maddening implausibility that sustains the film’s relentless, weirdly hypnotizing forward momentum means we’re never in one place — or one mood — for too long. Zaid’s home is bombed in one intensely melodramatic sequence that culminates in a slow zoom over Zaid cradling his dead wife and child. Next thing we know, he’s radicalized and joins a terrorist group. Xu Fu, Ma Junsheng and Seif — the cooking trio — are promptly captured by the U.S. Army and forced to preside over the kitchen on base. This allows for more sumptuous shots of delicious food while Xu Fu is, for whatever reason, targeted by an aggro, block-jawed American soldier. Xu Fu and Ma Junsheng also play surrogate dads to Seif, whose increasingly violent eruptions threaten to change the course of his life more than once.
For all its dewy-eyed sentimentality, the film is also startlingly brutal and bloody, making for a deranged whiplash effect that’s felt most powerfully in the film’s final act, which is set in a terrorist stronghold where pipsqueaks are brainwashed into becoming suicide bombers. Cozy, brotherly scenes (as when Ma Junsheng slips Seif a smuggled can of soda) are directly followed by executions and montages of plush-bear-wielding kiddies invoking jihad. There’s a slickness to the carnage that rubs uncomfortably against the film’s humanist ethos, rendering artificial (for all Shen Teng’s trembling and mouth-contorting labors) the horrific tragedies that befall its characters. It’s a vision of wartime brutality that’s both blithely matter-of-fact and desperate to pull at our heartstrings; utterly delusional, in other words, and hard to look away from.

NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Tuesday said that if China wants a normal relationship with New Delhi, the border between the two countries has to be stable.During a conversation at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, Jaishankar said that India and China do not have an agreed border and that the issue has persisted for decades."We don't have an agreed border between India and China. This is not a new issue; it's been going on for multiple decades... From 1975 till 2020, a good 45 years, no blood was shed on that border. The last time there were fatalities was in 1975. In this period, India-China relations did grow," he said."Then in 2020, when we were in the midst of the Covid lockdown, we had a series of border issues, and it culminated in a clash in which a number of soldiers were killed on either side," Jaishankar added.Jaishankar said that if peace and tranquillity in the border areas are disturbed, then the relationship will have consequences."For us, what it represented was a very profound departure from the situation that was prevailing since 1975. If the peace and tranquillity in the border areas are disturbed, then the relationship will have consequences. Those consequences were very visible for the next five years until we were able to restore the peace and tranquillity.
It took four years of negotiations," he added."The point we make to the Chinese is: 'If you want a normal relationship, if the rest of the relationship is to move, it's common sense. It's a no-brainer that the boundary has to be stable, that we need peace and tranquillity in the border areas.' As the border areas are settling down, they have settled down to a great extent since 2024; the relationship is commensurately moving towards normalcy," he further said.This comes after the ministry of external affairs reiterated that the Union territory of Ladakh is an integral and inalienable part of India after the Chinese foreign ministry opposed the naming of certain strategic locations in Ladakh.
