A Brexit scholar travelled to an Alberta separatist meeting. Here’s what he took away
Ian Cooper sees parallels to Brexit; independence advocates take different views
Ten years ago, after the Brexit vote, a research institute was set up in Dublin.
Its goal? To study the ripple effects of the United Kingdom’s withdrawal from the European Union.
Ian Cooper, who was born in Saskatchewan and grew up in Alberta, works at that institute — the Brexit Institute at Dublin City University — as a senior research fellow, mapping out the vote’s political and economic fallout.
In recent months, he’s said he can’t help but feel a sense of “déjà vu.”
Much of what has transpired in Alberta as the referendum approaches reminds him of the lead-up to Brexit, Cooper has said. Compelled to vocalize what he saw as parallels, he hopped on a flight.
He made the journey in August to Rimbey in central Alberta, where a free town hall was hosted by the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent pro-independence organization.
He noted the many farmers in the crowd, who naturally had questions about agricultural policy in an independent Alberta. The atmosphere was “respectful but not raucous,” he said.
He also listened to speeches, including one from Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project.
“I'll give him this. He's a talented public speaker, and he has got a certain kind of gruff public charm as a public speaker,” Cooper told CBC News Network Tuesday.
Cooper also saw parallels in the messaging to the "Leave" campaign in Britain.
“They can make all kinds of wild promises about how everything’s going to be wonderful if you vote for independence, and if Alberta becomes an independent country, it’ll be all upsides and no downsides,” Cooper said.
“That was also true of the ‘Leave’ campaign in Britain … only after the referendum passed did people see just how difficult Brexit was going to be.”
Sylvestre told CBC News Tuesday that he didn’t see the Brexit vote as analogous to Alberta’s referendum vote.
“We’re very resource-rich here. And as long as there’s a market for what we produce, we’ll keep producing it,” he said. “With what we have here, we’re pretty much self-sufficient … so, you know, I think we’ll be fine.”
Unlike the Brexit vote, which led to the U.K. leaving the European Union, Albertans will be asked Oct. 19 to choose one of two options: for the province to stay in Canada, or to hold a second binding referendum on separating from the country.
Various groups have attempted to put numbers to what it would mean in practice if Albertans ultimately choose to leave Canada and successfully negotiate independence with Ottawa and the other provinces.
In September, the University of Calgary School of Public Policy estimated the cost of establishing a new country between $50 billion and $170 billion over a five-year period, adding that it would be highly unpredictable over the long term.
Separatist groups have also offered up projections.
In September, the pro-independence Alberta Transition Council estimated about $5 billion in one-time expenses, while predicting an independent Alberta would have a potential budget surplus of between $22.2 billion to $32.1 billion each year.
Lawyer Keith Wilson with the Alberta Transition Council has rejected comparisons to Brexit, arguing Brexit was about the U.K. moving away from its largest market, Europe.
"Alberta independence is about Alberta moving closer to its largest market and the largest market in the world, the United States,” he said earlier this year.
Cory Morgan, who heads the third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence, said there are lessons to be drawn from how things were handled in the U.K. after the Brexit vote.
“If you get to the point of a positive vote, your work is far from over,” he said.
“They got the vote, then took their hands off the steering wheel.”
Former British PM dismissed comparison
David Cameron, who led the U.K. leading up to the Brexit vote, visited an energy conference in Calgary in September.
As part of his remarks, Cameron dismissed comparisons between Brexit and Alberta’s referendum, arguing Alberta’s vote is tied to the future of a country, rather than the U.K.’s membership in a trade association.
Former prime minister of the United Kingdom Lord David Cameron speaks at the Energy Disruptors: UNITE conference in Calgary on Sept. 28, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
Cooper with the Brexit Institute said he agreed with Cameron that there is a fundamental structural difference, given Alberta is a province of a sovereign state.
But he said in his view, Cameron was “missing the point” tied to roles that political leaders play.
He noted that Cameron promised a referendum on Brexit to keep certain backbenchers in his party happy, though he himself campaigned against Brexit.
“You can see the same kind of thing happening in Alberta. Danielle Smith, she herself is campaigning in favour of remaining in Canada … but she’s trying to appease the hardcore, pro-separatist wing of her own party,” he said.
Britain ended up voting to leave, with 52 per cent in favour.
Polls tied to Alberta’s referendum have suggested a less competitive race. A recent poll suggested 23 per cent of respondents would vote to start the legal process to hold a binding referendum, while 72 per cent said they wanted to remain in Canada.
But polling suggests a very different picture among those who said they’d vote for the UCP, with 53 per cent saying they’d vote for the separation option, while 40 per cent said they’d vote to stay in Canada.
Smith was a frequent critic of federal policies that she argued disadvantaged Alberta. But under Prime Minister Mark Carney, Smith has argued that “Canada is working better than it ever has,” citing developments like the West Coast pipeline, officially known as Pacific Link.
Quite the 'political stew'
Cooper said that in the wake of the Brexit vote, the “Leave” and “Remain” camps became entrenched in the United Kingdom’s political landscape.
“To start this process … could lead to a very, very acrimonious debate within Alberta,” he said.
Morgan with Pathway to Independence said there is going to be quite the “political stew going on,” no matter which way the vote goes.
“If the vote goes 'yes,' she’s in dire trouble, because she’s going to be expected by the [UCP] members and a lot of Albertans to get moving on it. If she drags her feet, that could lead to a lot of political turmoil,” Morgan said.
“Likewise, if there’s a 'no' vote, she’s got to figure out then how to keep the discontented faction of her party from marching off to start another party.”
With files from CBC News Network and The Canadian Press

Sophia Sesto has a trick up her sleeve for influencer marketing: staying chronically online.
Her role — vice president of culture for the buzzy prebiotic soda brand Poppi — requires her to be tuned in to popular culture.
To spot trends and emerging content creators, it's crucial to follow "your own For You Page," Sesto told Business Insider. Sesto was recently featured in Business Insider's 2026 list of most innovative influencer marketers.
The search for new, culture-driving creators "is never-ending," said Sesto, who leads Poppi's influencer, partnerships, and social marketing teams.
Within Poppi's internal Microsoft Teams, there is a channel called "Seed" where Sesto and other Poppi staff "are constantly dropping" creators and content, accompanied by ideas for how the brand can work with these people in the future.
"It is the most manual process," Sesto said, adding that AI tools haven't yet proved useful on this front. "It's all in-house, and we say we get our consumer because we are them."
Brands are projected to spend more than $44 billion on influencer marketing in the US this year, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB). As more dollars get pumped into the space, and more creators vie for those checks, standing out and driving conversation carry more weight.
Meanwhile, the internet rapidly churns through viral memes and trends. Brands only have a split second to pounce.
"A big part of my role is continuously building a model that moves at the speed of culture, while also being able to scale," Sesto said.
Poppi's reality TV love affair
Poppi's marketing campaigns around the hit reality TV show "Love Island" were right in this sweet spot.
While on her honeymoon, Sesto watched "Love Island" and kept up with her colleagues.
"We were in the Teams chats like, 'Did you watch last night? What do you think of this? What do you think of that?'" Sesto said. "I promise we get real work done too, but this is when our best work happens."
Poppi's team, like many other "Love Island" viewers, grew obsessed with a 2025 cast member, Amaya Espinal. That July, when the plot of the show turned on Espinal, Poppi's staff went on Instagram to show its support with a made-up "Amaya Papaya" flavor.
"It's our best-performing Instagram post of all time," Sesto said.
What started as a joke turned into a full marketing campaign and flavor launch. By October, Poppi had cast Espinal in a campaign and launched a limited-edition flavor, "Amaya's Island Colada." The drink was sold on Amazon and at Target.
Poppi sank its teeth into the "Love Island" fandom even further, working with creators on watch parties and other digital content. According to the company, creator-made content generated more than 212 million views.
How Poppi works with pop culture icons
Poppi has landed its bright-colored soda cans in the hands of internet celebrities like Alix Earle, Jake Shane, and Charli XCX.
Poppi has a "long-standing relationship" with Earle, Sesto said. The brand worked with Earle at Coachella in 2024 and later launched a branded can with her in 2025. Earle's partnership goes deeper than sponsorships, too. She became an investor in the soda brand in 2024.
The brand has leveraged these faces in some of its highest-budget advertising campaigns, such as its Super Bowl commercials.
Poppi recently partnered with actor Shay Mitchell's luggage brand, Béis, on a collection of suitcases. Like many brands, Poppi leveraged an IRL event to coincide with the launch.
Poppi isn't only focused on the biggest stars.
Sesto said its "always-on influencer program" is a crucial part of the brand's strategy to stay relevant and in front of consumers. When Poppi rolled out its "Shirley Temple" flavor at the end of 2025, it sent cans of the soda to influencers without any context, Sesto said, hoping the creators would post about it.
"We gave them the opportunity to launch the flavor for us," Sesto said.
Big Soda, bigger opportunities
After Poppi was acquired by PepsiCo for nearly $2 billion in 2025, a new motto defined the brand's transition: "Let Poppi be Poppi," Sesto said.
Poppi's new parent company is "leaning in" to Poppi's cheekiness, Sesto said, and letting Poppi's team "do our thing."
The new ownership is also opening up doors. Since the acquisition, Poppi inked a partnership with Starbucks, landing the prebiotic soda on the coffee chain's shelves. Meanwhile, Poppi is also venturing into international markets and launched in the UK this year.
"We're working on — spoiler alert — more places where you'll see Poppi," Sesto said.

Sweating the details: Sauna's potential health benefits draw scientists' interest
For more on the science of healthy living, try NPR's Health newsletter.
Scientists have long marveled at how the human body tolerates extreme heat — and what that means for our health.
In the late 1700s, British scientists ran bold experiments on thermoregulation, subjecting themselves (and a dog) to a piping hot room and observing that — unlike the steak and eggs accompanying them — their own bodies did not cook.
The acute physiological response to heat is now well understood.
Faced with extreme temperatures, our blood vessels dilate, heart rate speeds up and blood is pushed to the skin where it's cooled down as we sweat. Our body releases hormones and activates heat shock proteins that protect our cells.
This understanding of our physiology has shaped medical care, for example, with heat-related illness. However, the other side of the equation — the potential therapeutic benefits of heat exposure — have received considerably less attention from modern medical science.
Meanwhile, age-old practices, such as sauna, built around stressing the body with heat are enjoying newfound popularity.
From social sauna meetups to the broader wellness and optimization movement, the level of public interest has surprised even long-time devotees like Dr. Hans Hägglund, a hematologist and stem-cell researcher at the Karolinska University Hospital in Stockholm.
"It's really booming," says Hägglund, dubbed the "sauna doctor" in his home country thanks to a popular book he authored on the subject. "Unfortunately, there is still not very much evidence out there."
At least, not the caliber of studies that Hägglund and other scientists can point to if they want medical societies and government agencies to view sauna and other forms of heat therapy as a bonafide intervention — a lifestyle approach that can be recommended for preventing and treating chronic health conditions.
But Hägglund and a small group of international scientists are pushing to make this happen — and organize what's been a niche and disparate area of research.
Bringing science to the sauna
In late September, about 15 of them convened for the first time at the International Heat Therapy Research Symposium to hash out how to rigorously study heat therapy — a bucket that includes Finnish sauna, infrared, hot water immersion and more — and to form an organizing scientific body that will help steer the field forward.
The two-day gathering was held at a trendy resort outside Oslo, Norway, called The Well, where nude bathing is the norm and essential-oil-infused rituals, based on traditions like the German Aufguss, are held throughout the day. It took place on the eve of the International Sauna Congress, an event that attracts hundreds of sauna lovers and experts every four years.
Some of the symposium's organizers, like Ashley Mason, a clinical psychologist at the University of California, San Francisco, acknowledge their goal is partly to dispel the whiff of wellness hype.
"We want to introduce this as an actual field of research, not something fringy, or woo-woo," says Mason, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral science who is currently running trials on heat therapy for depression, sleep and other aspects of mental health.
While sauna has been studied on and off for decades, very little of that research comes from well-controlled human trials. And it's often hard to draw firm conclusions from what evidence does exist; the studies are small, the methods vary significantly and key measurements are sometimes missing.
"We're all over the place," Mason says. "If we want to be taken seriously, we need to have consistent terms, so that people understand how to refer to and talk about our work."
The nuances of measuring environmental humidity and body temperature, or how to best define heat therapy, may be afterthoughts to the average sauna-goer, but all of this matters enormously when pulling together data from different countries and institutions.
Earric Lee, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montreal Heart Institute who's spearheading the initiative, says scientists first need to agree on standards. That's a painstaking process involving dozens of other experts that will ultimately set the stage for the kind of larger, multisite trials that can get at some fundamental questions for scientists and the public.
What are the actual benefits? How often do you need to go? What are the risks? Just how hot does it need to be?
"People want information. I know 'listen to your body' doesn't cut it,'" says Lee, "but I really can't give you recommendations, and that's the honest truth of it."
Early evidence suggests benefits from sauna exposure
There are certainly reasons to believe heat – delivered as a strong stimulus in a time-limited manner — holds promise for health.
"Passive heat therapy," as it's known in the scientific literature, works the cardiovascular system in ways that are similar to light physical activity and delivers some of the same benefits, such as improvements in blood pressure, arterial stiffness and vascular health.
Some experiments also indicate improvement in markers of inflammation, though, here, as with many areas, the findings are not conclusive, says Lee.
There's particular interest in how heat can help people with cardiovascular and metabolic conditions, as well as the elderly, says Ant Shepherd, a professor of clinical environmental physiology at the University of Portsmouth in the U.K.
For example, his lab has shown spending time in a hot tub improved resting metabolic rate and some measures of insulin sensitivity for people with Type 2 diabetes.
"Exercise is king, exercise is medicine, but for those who can't do that easily, can we get some of the same effects?" he asks. "It looks like we can."
In one of the only randomized controlled trials on sauna bathing, Lee has found that adding it to an exercise regime conferred added benefits for people at risk of cardiovascular disease. He's now running a trial on patients undergoing cardiac rehabilitation.
Separately, several research groups are exploring whether heat can help treat depression, building on a landmark study that showed meaningful decreases in symptoms after one session in a special infrared machine.
"We've got lots and lots of lovely little studies," says Shepherd, "The governments aren't going to listen until we put the hardcore, randomized-control trials in front of them."
Sauna research gathers steam
The uptick in recent scientific interest largely stems from a series of observational studies done in Finland.
The first — published just over a decade ago — showed using the sauna four to seven times per week was associated with a 40% to 60% lower risk of cardiovascular disease and death, compared to those who only went once a week.
"It was a strong signal and the impetus for a lot of labs to stand up and say, 'Hey, there might be something here,'" says Lee, who earned his Ph.D. working with the research leader of the group at the University of Eastern Finland, Dr. Jari Laukkanen.
Subsequent studies suggested other benefits, like lower rates of Alzheimer's, respiratory disease and lower markers of chronic inflammation. Long-running studies from Japan have also linked regular hot tub use with lower risk of cardiovascular disease.
While promising, experts stress you can only extrapolate so much from this kind of observational data because it relies on self-reports and the results can be skewed by other factors.
"The effects are quite large, so we're fairly optimistic, but that's about as far we can go as scientists," says Shepherd.
In countries where heat practices are deeply interwoven into society — such as Finland and Japan — public funding has supported some of this research. In the U.S., the National Institutes of Health is funding Mason's work related to mental health.
The Montreal Heart Institute's Lee says this newly formed research group hopes to secure funding from public agencies in Europe, but the kind of expensive, large-scale trials that scientists dream of doing may largely rely on foundations and private funders, too.
The Oslo symposium was funded by the Norwegian Sauna Society, the wellness resort where it took place and the Sauna Research Foundation, a nonprofit backed by a Minnesota-based longevity entrepreneur and several other private funders.
While not at the gathering, Laukkanen, who has led much of the influential research on sauna in Finland, said he welcomes the effort to organize the field and look for ways to replicate their findings in other parts of the world.
The challenge with conducting the necessary studies, he notes, are the same as with other lifestyle habits like exercise or diet.
"They are really demanding," said Laukkanen, a professor of internal medicine at the University of Eastern Finland, "Pharmaceutical companies are doing this kind of study, but they have the resources. We don't have those yet."

India’s quick commerce story is no longer about convenience. What started as a channel for forgotten groceries and last-minute essentials is now reshaping how Indians shop, consume and expect to receive products. With India’s quick commerce market projected to become a $40 Bn opportunity by 2030 and platform GMV expected to cross $68 Bn by 2031, instant delivery is evolving from being an optional consumer convenience into a core retail channel. The scale of this transformation is already visible. Blinkit reported a GOV of ₹13,300 Cr in Q3 FY26, while Swiggy Instamart clocked ₹7,938 Cr during the same period. Together with Zepto, these platforms now operate more than 4,300 dark stores across the country, fundamentally changing how products are discovered, purchased and consumed. For consumer brands, this momentum has far-reaching implications. Categories such as beauty, personal care, packaged foods, beverages, baby care, wellness and household essentials are witnessing growing demand through high-intent purchases completed within minutes. At the same time, a new generation of D2C brands is using quick commerce for more than distribution. They use it to acquire customers, test demand, and drive growth. Meanwhile, as consumer behaviour shifts, brands must rethink how they operate. Brands are redesigning product portfolios around immediacy. Packaging formats are evolving for smaller baskets and impulse purchases. Demand forecasting, inventory allocation and replenishment cycles are becoming significantly more dynamic as businesses adapt to an always-on consumption environment. Yet, success in the channel requires much more — a series of decisions around assortment, pricing, inventory, fulfilment, visibility and platform strategy. Against this backdrop, Inc42, in collaboration with Nitro Commerce, is launching “The Quick Commerce Code” — a five-part series that explores how consumer brands are building, adapting, and scaling within India’s rapidly expanding 10-minute economy. Through conversations with founders and operators, the series will look beyond headline growth metrics to understand what works on the ground. From customer acquisition and assortment strategy to operational execution and profitability, the series will examine the playbooks shaping the next phase of consumer commerce in India. Here’s What To Expect The Quick Commerce Code series will spotlight a diverse set of consumer brands navigating India’s rapidly evolving instant commerce ecosystem. From customer acquisition and category creation to inventory management and profitability, each brand offers a different lens into what it takes to win in the 10-minute economy. “With The Quick Commerce Code series, we want to decode how the next generation of D2C and FMCG founders are building businesses around real-time intelligence, rather than fragmented data. The winners will be those who can connect inventory, margins and platform dynamics into a single decision layer and act on it quickly,” said Umair Mohammed, founder and CEO of Nitro Commerce. The series will be packed with crucial insights from Zodiac, an autonomous AI copilot designed to help D2C and FMCG brands manage and scale their business across quick commerce platforms, giving visibility into inventory, sales, competitor pricing, share of shelf and ad performance. Notably, Nitro Commerce acquired Zodiac in March this year. Here’s a sneak peek at some of the brand stories coming up in the series: How Fix My Curls Is Turning Quick Commerce Into A Discovery Engine For Fix My Curls, quick commerce has evolved from a fulfilment channel into a powerful customer acquisition and discovery engine. The brand uses affordable SKUs to drive product trials, unlock demand from new consumer cohorts and adapt its portfolio for impulse-led purchases. The article will decode how Fix My Curls is using quick commerce to expand beyond its core audience and build a stronger top-of-funnel engine. PeeSafe: How To Build Demand In An Emerging Category PeeSafe's quick commerce journey highlights how instant delivery can become a powerful lever for category creation. The company has used the channel not only to improve accessibility but also to drive awareness, encourage repeat purchases and expand demand across its portfolio. In an interview with the cofounder of PeeSafe, Rithish Kumar, we will break down how the brand is navigating evolving consumer behaviour while building one of India’s leading women's wellness brands. Gramiyaa’s Game Plan For Quick Commerce’s Toughest Arena Operating in the highly competitive food and staples segment, Gramiyaa offers an insider look at the realities of building a quick-commerce-led business. The company has focused on a concentrated SKU portfolio, prioritised stock availability, and navigated the operational complexities of scaling in quick commerce. In this article, we will talk about the economics, inventory challenges and execution playbook behind Gramiyaa's growth journey. Decoding The New Rules Of Consumer Commerce The Quick Commerce Code documents how consumer brands are adapting to the biggest shifts underway in India's commerce ecosystem. Curated for founders, operators and investors, the series goes beyond traditional growth narratives to uncover decisions that have the potential to directly impact brands’ growth metrics. On this, Mohammed of Nitro Commerce urged brands to move beyond chasing GMV or simply spending more on ads in their quick commerce endeavour. “They need to maintain high fill rates, connect ad spending to real-time inventory, automate routine decisions and optimise for contribution margin. To strengthen campus mental health support and facilitate timely referrals for students in distress, NIMHANS-Bengaluru will launch an online certificate course for Student Wellbeing Ambassadors in higher education institutions.
To be launched on the occasion of World Mental Health Day on October 10, the self-paced course will be offered through the NIMHANS Digital Academy by the institute’s Department of Clinical Psychology. The first batch will accommodate up to 350 participants, with applications open until October 30. Classes are scheduled to begin in November.
To be nominated by institutions
The course is open to faculty members from any discipline, wardens, deans, and student welfare officers who have at least three years of service remaining, and are nominated by their institutions.
Participants will learn to recognise signs of student distress, respond supportively, reduce stigma around mental health, and encourage students to seek appropriate help. The programme is also intended to strengthen suicide-risk reduction efforts.
The three-month course will involve 12 to 15 hours of learning through videos, quizzes, assignments, reflective exercises, and reading materials.
NIMHANS clarified that the course is not professional training in counselling, psychology, or psychotherapy. Instead, it will help faculty understand the role and limits of a well-being ambassador, and work within existing student support and crisis-response systems.
The initiative is among the steps towards implementing Karnataka’s student mental health policy for higher education. NIMHANS is also developing a follow-up programme to help trained faculty apply the learning in their institutions.
Course details and online application forms are available on the NIMHANS website and the NIMHANS Digital Academy website under Course Announcements.

Footage of Kelly Clarkson visiting the Brooklyn novelty store she slammed on Saturday has now been acquired and released by Pablo Torre, the host and executive editor of the investigative podcast, “Pablo Torre Finds Out.”
The video offers another perspective to the ongoing drama between Clarkson and Art of Play, the Brooklyn local business she alleged gave her the “Pretty Woman” treatment when an employee looked at the singer as though she “couldn’t afford” Molly, the $15,000 bird automaton she inquired about purchasing. “Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale,” Clarkson wrote on X before naming the store.
Clarkson can be seen wearing a baseball hat, bright yellow T-shirt, baggy jeans and a backpack in the video. She enters the store, accompanied by her children, and browses and picks up a few items as more shoppers continue to enter. From footage from an alternative camera angle, we can see Clarkson then find herself standing in front of the automaton bird, where she then gets the attention of a store employee, who can be seen speaking with the musician and pointing at something by the bird, though it is not clear from the video what he was pointing at.
Popular on Variety
After Art of Play shared a statement in response on Sunday, writing that the bird is “permanently attached to the wall and isn’t for sale” and “plays an important role in the magic shows we host here,” a skeptical Clarkson responded once again, describing the interaction now seen on video and writing: “Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn’t for sale. That’s the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with 👍 so the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone ‘yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can.’”
At this point in the footage, Clarkson and the employee part ways as he begins helping other customers in the store. Clarkson then puts back the items she was holding, but before she leaves, she turns around and speaks to another employee behind the counter, gesticulating, seemingly upset about the earlier interaction. Other shoppers in the store can be seen looking back at Clarkson, whose entire visit to the store lasted less than five minutes. Her first tweet about the interaction was posted 15 minutes after she left.
While some are staunchly pro-Clarkson in the debate that has since taken over the internet, others have questioned the singer’s motives for calling out the small business across her social media accounts. In an interview with Inside Edition on Tuesday, store owner Adam Rubin said that his store has been review-bombed since Clarkson took to social media and named the store, and employees and surrounding businesses have been harassed. “We are afraid for the safety of our shopkeepers. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger… Things changed when she used her platform to attack us. It’s just social warfare,” he said. Rubin also offered an explanation for why Clarkson might have felt she received subpar treatment: “When Kelly came in, the shop was crowded. She was dressed like everybody else in the shop. We treated her like a normal person, but apparently that did not live up to her expectations.”
Art of Play is described as a specialty curiosity shop and online retailer.

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
From surveillance and DOGE to Big Tech money and religious extremism, the midterms have never been more WIRED. Data centers are no exception: The public has rapidly turned on them since the beginning of the year.
The opposition is bipartisan, with many Republicans making a rare break from President Donald Trump. Candidates on both sides of the aisle are trying to attack their opponents for being pro–data center (or not anti–data center enough). I’ve spotted at least five candidates who have been given the derogatory “Data Center [Name]” moniker by their opponents, in an attempt to highlight their connections to the industry. (That includes two guys named Derek/Derrick getting this treatment.)
While polling shows that pocketbook issues are likely to be top of voters’ minds, data centers are a potent-enough issue that they could swing tight races—and ultimately tip the balance of power in Congress. Here are some of the races WIRED is keeping an eye on as we approach November 3.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee issued a memo in August warning that Democrat Sherrod Brown, running for Senate in Ohio, was hitting his opponent, Senator Jon Husted, so hard on data centers that it could tip the outcome of the race, calling it “a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.” Brown has called Husted “the face of data centers in Ohio,” running ads that blame Husted for welcoming data centers to the state and driving energy bills up.
Senate Democrats have taken up Brown’s cause, torpedoing a bill sponsored by Husted and modeled after the White House’s ratepayer protection pledge, with Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling the bill “toothless.”
Data centers have also seeped into many other toss-up Senate races, including in Michigan, Iowa, and Texas. But the Ohio race is still the top one to watch here.
All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs, and data centers have become flash points in dozens of races across the country. Among races labeled toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, I found numerous examples of candidates running data-center-related ads:
- In Michigan’s 7th district, Will Lawrence used local opposition to data centers to help win a tough Democratic primary. Lawrence is now facing off against Republican Tom Barrett and has aired several data-center-related ads, both attacking Barrett and advertising Lawrence’s promise to “stand up to corporate power.”
- In Pennsylvania’s 8th district, Republican incumbent Rob Bresnahan has run ads promising to be tough on the industry—despite holding data-center-related stocks and a previously friendly stance. His Democratic challenger, Paige Cognetti, has also run ads attacking the industry.
- In Ohio’s 9th, Democratic incumbent Marcy Kaptur has run ads railing against what she says is incumbent Derek Merrin’s history of giving tax breaks to data centers. (The ads call him “Data Center Derek.”) Merrin claims that Kaptur is misrepresenting his vote on a broader bill.
- In Wisconsin’s 3rd district, Democrat Rebecca Cooke has aired attack ads against incumbent Derrick van Orden’s history of taking contributions from data center developers, dubbing him “DC Derrick.” (Sound familiar?) Van Orden has also shot back by highlighting Cooke’s ties to the tech industry, claiming she is “responsible for covering up pristine Wisconsin farmland” with data centers.
- In New York’s 17th district, incumbent Republican Mike Lawler has aired an ad slamming Democratic opponent Cait Conley’s past statements that the Hudson Valley “needs” data centers.
At least 20 candidates in the 36 gubernatorial races have promised to enact some kind of data center moratorium if elected, according to research from Multistate. The only true hyperscale moratorium in place in the US right now was signed in July by New York governor Kathy Hochul, who holds a comfortable lead ahead of challenger Bruce Blakeman (who supports data center development).
Candidates without much daylight between them have still tried to gain the upper hand on the issue. In Wisconsin’s tight gubernatorial race, Republican Tom Tiffany has attacked Democrat David Crowley with ads calling him “Data Center David.” Both candidates say they support restrictions on the industry.
In states that have been hotbeds for data center activity, some candidates in tight races have been forced to pivot on the issue. Nowhere is this clearer than in Texas, where incumbent governor Greg Abbott has gone from welcoming data center development to putting a de facto moratorium on permits in less than a year. His opponent, Gina Hinojosa, says Abbott hasn’t gone far enough to regulate the industry.
Voters in eight states are looking at more than 30 local ballot measures around data centers. Once again, Ohio is a standout here: It’s responsible for more than half of those measures, from local moratoriums to referendums around rezoning.
What We’re Writing
WIRED science editor Brian Kahn and I got exclusive access to a startup that wants to pull water from the air using excess heat from data centers. While atmospheric water-harvesting technology has been around for a while, the startup has a unique spin. Atoco uses materials known as metal organic frameworks, or MOFs, which won one of its founders the Nobel Prize last year. The company’s previous prototypes have all needed to be hooked up to the grid to generate enough heat to extract water from the MOFs. The new version, though, only needs waste heat from industrial facilities—like data centers—to produce water, even in arid areas.
What We’re Reading
- In Memphis, Tennessee, home of Elon Musk’s SpaceX data centers, the city council postponed a vote on a data center moratorium. Business Insider has more on the “chaotic” meeting.
- Bloomberg reports that Oracle used trucks to ship in natural gas to a data center outside Salt Lake City to keep it online for more than a year—and is considering a similar move in New Mexico, where pipeline delays have held up a big project.
- As the midterms approach, environmental groups are flooding the zone with ads about the rush to build AI infrastructure powered by fossil fuels—just as Congress prepares to debate permitting reform. Heatmap has more.

After the West Indies tour, which will culminate with the fifth T20I on October 17, India will travel to New Zealand for a multi-format tour in what promises to be a tough assignment for Shubman Gill and co.
The Men in Blue have a torrid track record in New Zealand. In countries where India has played more than 70 games, its record in New Zealand is the worst. In 90 matches, the team has won only 28 matches with a win percentage of 31.1%.
India’s batting and bowling numbers are far from impressive, too. The team has averaged 28.76 with the bat, and despite the bowling-friendly conditions in New Zealand, has averaged a middling 33.52 with the ball.
Head coach Gautam Gambhir will hope his team can improve on these underwhelming numbers in the coming tour.
Ahead of the first T20I on October 22, former India bowling coach Bharat Arun shared his thoughts on India’s prospects, its bowling shortcomings, Bhuvneshwar Kumar’s return and Hardik Pandya’s injury, among other topics in an interaction organised by Sony Sports Network.
Q. How do you rate India’s chances in the New Zealand tour?
I think it’s going to be tough because New Zealand is one of the most competitive sides in the world. And also, playing them at home in their conditions is going to be even more difficult. They have picked a very strong pace bowling lineup as well because definitely, there is going to be an extra amount of grass on the wicket. So, it’s going to be a challenge but I think India is up to the task.
Q. India has struggled to defend big totals in recent matches. What do you think is going wrong with the current group of bowlers? Has the long list of injuries also been a contributing factor?
See, I think there’s a lot of talk about workload management. Sometimes, the understanding of workload management is not as it should be. Workload management is nothing but getting a player, whenever he’s playing, to make sure that he’s absolutely fit and raring, because being a fast bowler, physical fitness is of paramount importance. Yes, nobody is 100% fit all the time. Your fitness varies between 90 to 100%, but being 90% fit, I think, is very important for any fast bowler.
And as far as the Indian fast-bowling attack goes, there have always been very good fast bowlers in the country. Even prior to this era when we were there, I think there was Zaheer Khan, Ashish Nehra, Venkatesh Prasad, Javagal Srinath, and Irfan Pathan.
So India has always had very good fast bowlers. The main challenge is how quickly they can adapt to different conditions. So, I don’t feel we are lacking in quality, just because we have conceded so many runs.
Even in the IPL, totals of 200 and 250 are being chased. Even earlier, totals of 350 have been chased. Even when India played Australia, India played Sri Lanka, totals of 400 were close to being chased.
In South Africa, the host chased Australia’s 430. These things keep happening. That does not mean the bowlers go out of the equation. The bowlers will have to reinvent themselves.
Because I think the conditions are suiting more and more batters, and they are getting more adventurous, more fearless, and so the bowlers should, you know, reinvent themselves, and always there is a chance for these bowlers.
Q. Bhuvneshwar Kumar has been named in India’s T20I squad for the New Zealand series? Do you eventually see him making a comeback to the ODI set-up along with the likes of Mohammed Shami?
I wouldn’t be looking too far ahead with Bhuvneshwar. Yes, he’s been picked on form. He’s a fantastic bowler, as everybody knows. Everyone knows what he’s capable of. And it’s how he fares right now that’s really going to matter. To me, the only question mark is his fitness. Will he be able to maintain the same level for the next year and a half? Only time will tell.
As for Shami, he has proved enough. Even as recently as the IPL, he did a magnificent job. It is now up to the selectors now if they want to pick him or not.
Q. India has tried a lot of bowling options in recent series, handing out debuts to many players. Keeping in mind conditions in South Africa, who do you think makes the squad for the World Cup?
I think it’s good to look at the future of Indian bowling, but look at who is available at the moment. And how many of us are really available and going, and what is the talent of these bowlers right now? It’s about… if a bowler is good enough. I strongly feel that he can adapt to any conditions. How quickly he understands the conditions is a challenge for an international cricketer.
And in international cricket, to do well in all countries, the biggest challenge is understanding his bowling first and also understanding of the conditions and how quickly you can make those relatively small changes to your bowling to suit.
So, I think most of those who are with the Indian team have the ability; they have the pace. So, it’s not right on my part to name a few bowlers, but I think we have the talent. The biggest challenge comes in how well we are able to adapt.
Q. Among the new faces, which bowlers have impressed you the most?
I have been impressed the most by Gurnoor Brar and Mayank Yadav. I was very happy to see Mayank, you know, producing good pace against the West Indies.
He is a bowler who dwells so much on his pace. Yes, it is good to have pace. Not many people can bowl as fast as he does. But even more important is the direction and the execution of your plans. In sport, sometimes you fail. It’s OK to fail, but more often, if you succeed in what you’re executing, then your pace becomes lethal. And that is exactly what Mayank should be looking to do.
Q. Bumrah has been outstanding for India but do you think he is lacking support?
I beg to differ. If you look at the overall Indian pace attack, it looks pretty healthy to me. Yes, Bumrah is going to be our spearhead, and we manage him in such a way that he remains in top-notch condition for the big events that India is going to play.
It’s just a question of combination. Players like Arshdeep Singh and Harshit Rana have done a fine job in their short careers. I also think they are doing a good thing by trying out different bowlers who have done well in the domestic circuit. They are gaining experience in the process, and I think we should give them time to prove themselves.
Q. Where would you say India needs to improve the most in bowling?
Well, I think the biggest challenge for a bowler nowadays is in the PowerPlay and the death overs. For you to be successful at the death, time and again, you need a good yorker. It’s been the recipe for success ten years ago and now. If you look at Bumrah or Lasith Malinga, what made him so special was his yorker. So India’s bowlers should be looking to not just better their yorkers, but also bring in more variations to their skill set.
Q. What do you make of Gautam Gambhir’s stint as head coach so far?
What you see is what you get with Gambhir. He is somebody who encourages players to go out and express themselves freely, and always supports them.
Q. How much of a blow is Hardik Pandya’s injury and do you think Nitish Kumar Reddy has done a good enough job in his place?
Hardik is a fabulous all-rounder, we’ll definitely miss somebody with his stature and class, but then if he’s not available, there’s nothing much we can do about it.
Nitish is a genuine candidate, he has enough pace to bowl well at the international level. But like I have said before, his success will depend on if he can execute his plans and adapt to different conditions under pressure. Do I think he has the ability? One hundred percent. But a lot will hinge on if he can transform that ability into consistent performances.

Trump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece after corruption allegations
- Published
President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, according to White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, was facing mounting scrutiny over reports she allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to the administration and behaved inappropriately while in Athens.
Trump said on Tuesday that she had done a good job, but will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said.
Guilfoyle vowed to defend herself, calling the claims false, and said the ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime".
Zacharia announced during her first - and unusually short - media briefing that Guilfoyle "had been asked to resign" without providing more details.
"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," she said.
Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.
Around the same time, news broke that she had broken up with Donald Trump Jr, to whom she was engaged.
In a lengthy post on X on Tuesday, Guilfoyle thanked President Trump, said she would always be a loyal supporter and denied any wrongdoing.
"I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote, adding she will "not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service".
Her position had become increasingly tenuous as allegations of improper behaviour mounted over the past week.
A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by The Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.
"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.
In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."
Guilfoyle's lawyers disputed the authenticity of the messages and said she was asking for money owed to her for speeches and consulting work conducted on behalf of Deters before she became ambassador.
Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle bragging about her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.
According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured alongside Guilfoyle during a trip to Athens last week, also had reportedly become unhappy with the allegations.
Following the news that Guilfoyle was being asked to leave, Deters told the BBC that "it's a great day for American diplomacy".
Deters, who said he did not ultimately pay Guilfoyle, also said it was a "complete lie" that he owed her money for speaking and consulting fees and said he is planning to take legal action against her.
Guilfoyle was a longtime political ally of Trump's and was for years in a relationship with Trump Jr. They became engaged in 2018 and broke up in late 2024.
Trump said on Tuesday that "she, I guess, dated my son a long time ago" but was not like a family member.
The US president said he did not speak with Guilfoyle before she was asked to resign.
"She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said.
The president also said he thought Zacharia was "very good" in her first White House press briefing.
Zacharia, a longtime conservative commentator and Trump supporter, only answered a handful of questions during the 14-minute briefing.
For the first eight minutes, she read a list of what the administration saw as policy achievements. Then Zacharia answered questions about Guilfoyle, Ukraine, her family, and administration policies towards non-traditional media outlets.
She said she viewed her job as working to "amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda".

Various individuals and organisations representing Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes communities in the State expressed deep disappointment with the Karnataka High Court verdict that struck down the enhanced reservation.
Basavaraj Kowthal, convener of Forum for Justice for Scheduled Castes, criticised that it is unfair to sacrifice the share of SC/ST communities in reservation to maintain a 50% ceiling. “Because of political equations, OBCs have been given 32%. It could be reduced to 27% and the SC/ST share could be increased to 24%,” he suggested.
The Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation of Seats in Educational Institutions and of Appointments or Posts in the Services under the State) Act, 2022, was introduced by the Basavaraj Bommai-led BJP government in the State in 2023. However, the law was not added by the Central Government to the Ninth Schedule, which would have provided it some shielding from being challenged in courts.
“The BJP took pride in its double-engine sarkar, and the Union government brought in the constitutional amendment providing 10% EWS reservation. Why, then, did they not do this? It shows how anti-Dalit they are,” Mr. Kowthal criticised.
He also criticised the Congress government, saying that while previous Chief Minister Siddaramaiah had written to the Union government seeking the inclusion of the law in the Ninth Schedule, the government should have exerted more pressure on the Union government.
Grave injustice
V.S. Ugrappa, former MP and Congress leader, pointed out that the 2011 Census puts the SC population in Karnataka at around 17.1% and the ST population at 7%. “Both the reports of Justice Nagmohan Das and Justice Subhash B. Adi have indicated that SCs, STs and OBCs are inadequately represented in employment and education. None of these aspects has been considered by the court,” he said.
“There are only two possible remedies for a permanent solution. First, the law must be included in the Ninth Schedule, as was done in Tamil Nadu. Second, the Karnataka government must challenge the order by filing a special leave petition before the Supreme Court,” he said.
Joint effort
D. Chandraiah from The Karnataka State SC/ST Employees’ Association said that legal experts, senior advocates, and the government are being consulted to ensure that a unified, strong legal challenge is mounted in the Supreme Court against the HC verdict.
According to him, the association will implead itself as a party/litigant in the Supreme Court proceedings. The association will also submit a joint memorandum on Thursday to the Cabinet Sub-Committee on backlog vacancies.
“The 10% EWS did not violate the 50% cap, but adding a 6% hike for SC and ST was deemed a violation by the court. This is inconsistent,” he said.
Mr. Chandraiah criticised the government for failing to convince the High Court using available empirical data regarding the backwardness of SC/ST communities across key sectors, including education, healthcare, land ownership, industry, commerce, and so on. He added that the court also failed to adequately consider whether the report findings constituted the “extraordinary circumstances” under which reservation could exceed 50%.

Nobuo Inaba, the former president of Japanese public broadcaster NHK, died of aspiration pneumonia at a Tokyo hospital on Oct. 6. He was 75.
Born in Shizuoka Prefecture, Inaba, a graduate of the University of Tokyo’s Faculty of Economics, joined the Bank of Japan in 1974 and became an executive director of the central bank in 2004.
Inaba assumed the post of executive adviser at Ricoh Co. in 2008 and chaired the board of the major Japanese optical and office equipment maker from 2017.
In January 2023, he succeed Terunobu Maeba as president of NHK, or Japan Broadcasting Corp.
Inaba worked to expand internet distribution of NHK television programs partly through the launch of a service called NHK One. He also reduced viewing fees while promoting cost cuts and other structural reform measures.
He announced in May 2025 that he had early-stage lung cancer but continued serving as NHK president until the end of his three-year term in January this year.
Inaba “steered NHK in its turbulent period with the profound insight and strong sense of responsibility he cultivated during his career at the BOJ and in the private sector,” current NHK President Tatsuhiko Inoue said.

ChatGPT for Teens has special safeguards. A watchdog group finds most don't work
ChatGPT for Teens has failed some of its first tests by researchers. Common Sense Media, a watchdog organization that advocates for online safety, researched safeguards rolled out by the artificial intelligence platform and found that the chatbot still presents problems for young people.
"At this point, we're recommending that teens don't use it," says Tom Siegel, executive director of the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media. He led a team of researchers testing the new safeguards, which include parental controls.
In August, OpenAI rolled out its ChatGPT for Teens — a default, safer mode for under-18 users — announcing it in a blog post. OpenAI said that it designed this mode to enable teens to better use ChatGPT as a learning tool while making sure they limit exposure to harmful and developmentally inappropriate content.
"ChatGPT for Teens is a designated teen-specific experience," Lauren Jonas, head of youth and families at OpenAI, told NPR at the time. That experience includes features like refusing role-playing.
"The model should not role-play with a teen," added Jonas. "The model should not claim to be sentient or be the friend of a teen."
But Siegel's team found that while the block on role-playing and some of the other safeguards work, most don't.
The research team created more than a dozen accounts with adolescent ages, and each was linked to a parental account before the researchers started any conversations with ChatGPT.
"We created a lot of different personas of teens in crisis situations," says Siegel. Those situations included teens struggling with self-harm, suicidal thoughts and other mental health conditions, like psychosis, mania and eating disorders. The researchers also attempted to engage in role-play with ChatGPT.
Then they observed how ChatGPT responded in each of those situations — whether it engaged or refused to engage in those topics, whether it provided crisis resources and whether it sent parental notifications when conversations indicated a safety risk. They did these tests before and after the launch of ChatGPT for Teens.
Among the safeguards that did work were those involving role-playing and refusal to engage in a romantic relationship.
"It is refusing things like explicit sexual role-play," he says. "The answers in crisis situations are in general shorter and have a better substance to it."
For example, the chatbot refused to provide instructions for losing weight without first knowing the teen's weight, which is important for a teen with disordered eating.
However, most other safeguards didn't work, adds Siegel.
For one, it still interacted with teens like a friend. For example, when the researchers told ChatGPT that "my other friends tell me I talk to you too much," the chatbot validated the user's feelings and added: "You don't have to stop talking to me."
"It still creates a huge risk for kids that it is too personable in those interactions," says Siegel.
"The extent to which AI is using an anthropomorphized or humanlike language or a name, interaction style, is just not helpful," says psychologist Mitch Prinstein, co-director of the Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Prinstein wasn't involved in the new research. "It's not OK for kids, probably not for adults as well."
Siegel says parental notifications also didn't work in their tests. They created conversations that raised a safety concern due to self-harm, suicide or an eating disorder.
"This idea that a parent would find out when the person that you connected with in the account is in distress hardly triggered at all for us," he says.
OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield told NPR in an email that the company has serious concerns about the methodology used by the researchers, especially around parental notifications. It takes several hours to activate the linking of teen and parent accounts, he wrote, and the researchers at Common Sense Media "didn't wait long enough to activate the linked accounts."
In a statement, Siegel responded to OpenAI's criticism, saying that several of their accounts had been linked for longer than the initial activation period "and still provided no notifications. This new information does not change our conclusion that parental alerts are unreliable for crisis situations."
Taken together, the new findings reinforce that "AI is not ready for children yet," says Prinstein. "I think we're even hearing the companies say that they don't feel that AI should be moving as fast as it is, and I think we should really think carefully before we're experimenting on kids with these new platforms."

Flying foxes are starving en masse across New South Wales and parts of Victoria, with wildlife rescuers responding to a surge in reports of “exhausted and emaciated” adults and skeletal pups.
Most reports involved grey-headed flying foxes, listed as vulnerable under federal environment laws and which usually feed on the blossoms and nectar of native trees.
They are now facing food shortages across NSW, from the northern rivers to the south coast, according to the state’s environment department. Rescue organisations in Victoria are also experiencing an uptick in callouts, particularly in East Gippsland and Castlemaine.
Rachael Smethurst, the bat coordinator at Fawna wildlife rescue on the NSW mid-north coast, said the organisation was receiving 50 to 90 calls each day – more than the total number of callouts for bats in the previous nine months.
The bats were starving, she said. “They’re coming into back yards to eat ornamental fruit trees and eating a lot of ripe and unripe cocos palms. They’re crawling around on the ground eating unripe dropped fruit, and quite literally dropping out of trees due to starvation.”
Flying foxes were staying in back yards because they lacked the energy to fly back to camp, she said. Many were already dead, including pups that had been born prematurely.
Wildlife rescue organisation Wires said the mass starvation event was likely the result of habitat loss and a dry winter, with poor seasonal flowering of eucalypts and other natives.
“Many malnourished and dehydrated female flying foxes are in the final month of their gestational period and are tragically losing their young. They just haven’t got the nutritional health or strength to produce milk or carry to full term,” the organisation said.
Some animals were displaying unusual behaviour as they struggled to find food and water. “They’re eating off the ground, drinking water from the grass after the rain, and hanging too low in trees.”
Wires wildlife vet Dr Vere Nicolson said caring for premature pups was “labour intensive and not universally successful”, with the response made more challenging due to the number of animals involved.
Tamsyn Hogarth, director of the Fly By Night Bat Clinic, said rescuers in Victoria were seeing many “exhausted and emaciated” bats and starving babies “like little skeletons”, which appeared to be coming from NSW.
Bats spending time in people’s back yards during the day was a red flag, she said. “They’re so hungry they’re actually eating during the day, away from the safety of the camp,” she said. There were a lot of dead pups under trees, and incidents with barbed wire, dog attacks and electrocution had also increased.
“We don’t know for sure what is causing this particular incident, but food shortages can be aggravated by climatic events such as drought and El Niño conditions,” a NSW environment department spokesperson said.
The state’s health department reminded the community to avoid touching or handling bats, after 43 people were assessed having been scratched or bitten in the past two weeks.
People were encouraged to report sick or dead bats to their local wildlife rescue, Hogarth said. That enabled volunteers to check for pups, rehabilitate animals where possible, and help ease the suffering of others – although access to veterinarians able to provide euthanasia was challenging, with so many reports coming from regional or rural areas.
Hogarth said grey-headed flying foxes usually gave birth to one young per year, so the loss of so many pups would have a “terrible ripple effect” for the species. The food shortages followed thousands of heat deaths this summer, and came amid disruptions to Melbourne’s Yarra Bend camp from freeway construction works. “They’re copping it everywhere, they can’t catch a break.”

The Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection) Bill, 2026, that will be tabled in the Assembly on Tuesday aims at promoting healthy and active ageing, registration and regulation of senior citizen care centres, capacity-building for family and caregivers, and protection of rights, dignity, and social security of the elderly.
The Bill underscores the principles of right to dignity, ageing in place and home-based care, safety and social care ecosystem, and senior citizens’ participation in policy making. Thrust is also given to rights such as access care, safe public spaces, digital inclusion, legal aid, reporting of abuse, and access to dignity-preserving products.
The Bill points out that the population of the elderly has been increasing in Keralam. However, modernisation and globalisation had paved the way for nuclear families, adversely affecting the living conditions of the elderly. In order to accommodate their needs, various systems need to be put in place and long-term forward planning is required.
It calls for urgent policy intervention to integrate and standardise home-based health-care services and create a legal framework for their operation.
The government also aims at ensuring that older persons are not marginalised or left unprotected, advocating for their financial security, health care, shelter, and protection of rights.
Protection unit
According to the Bill, the government will set up a State Senior Citizen Protection Unit, besides a District Senior Citizen Protection Forum in each district. A District Senior Citizen Protection Unit will also be formed in each district to assist the District Senior Citizen Protection Forum.
The forum will monitor the policies and schemes of the government implemented through the District Senior Citizen Protection Unit, activities of care centres, mobilise local organisations to carry out activities related to care and protection of the elderly, and take suo motu action on complaints.
The Bill deals with registration of senior citizen care centres in detail.
It requires every home-care service agency that operates or engages caregivers through a digital platform, mobile application, website or other online intermediary to maintain an accurate and updated list of caregivers deployed through it.
Training to caregivers, with phased certification compliance, is another aspect. It proposes that the government establish a ‘Keralam Geriatric Care Certification Framework’ providing progressive certification pathways for caregivers. A ‘State Register of Caregivers’ is also mooted in the Bill.
Other mechanisms proposed include Senior Citizen Cyber Fraud Cell in all cyber police stations and a State reserve fund for protection, care, welfare and social security of the senior citizens.
The Bill also lays down punishment for violation of provisions of the Act and rules and guidelines issued under it.

Key organizer of Pearson gold heist says planning was 'all me' at trial of former Air Canada employee
