‘Catastrophic’ brake failure, neglected repairs contributed to deadly Columbia Icefield crash, judge finds
3 people killed in tour bus rollover on Athabasca Glacier in Jasper National Park
A complete failure of the braking system triggered by neglected mechanical repairs contributed to a deadly tour bus rollover in the Columbia Icefield, a fatality inquiry has concluded.
In a report made public late last week, Judge Vaughn Myers of the Alberta Court of Justice details a string of catastrophic oversights that preceded the rollover that killed three passengers and severely injured 14.
It was the afternoon of July 18, 2020, when a heavy-duty vehicle known as an Ice Explorer — carrying 24 tourists across the scenic expanse of the Athabasca Glacier in Jasper National Park — tumbled down a steep embankment, landing on its roof.
Dionne Durocher, 24, of North Battleford, Sask., Kamleshbhai Patel, 58, and Griva Patel, 28, of Edmonton, were ejected from the vehicle and died of their injuries within minutes.
In his findings, Myers calls on the tour company Pursuit — also known as Brewster — to make a series of safety improvements, concluding that warnings about the faltering safety of the vehicle went unheeded in the days and weeks before the crash.
The investigation determined the Ice Explorer had dangerously worn components, inadequate brake power and lacked routine maintenance.
Rapid speed, no braking force
Myers said the fatality inquiry, held in October 2025, sought to examine not only policy measures that could prevent similar tragedies but also “questions that were not clearly answered” by the RCMP and Occupational Health and Safety investigators, most critically any lapses in the maintenance of the vehicle.
Ice Explorers are large, wide-bodied, three-axle, off-road buses, also known as snow coaches, that have been used in the Columbia Icefield since the 1980s.
They’re purpose-built for icy terrain, with specialized brake systems that include a transmission lock-up to assist when the machine is on a descent — but only if the vehicle is in gear.
Court heard that, in the moments before the crash, the Ice Explorer was descending a steep slope known as the Lateral Moraine Road.
The vehicle was in neutral and, lacking engine-retarding force, accelerated to a speed between 41 to 49 km/h, far beyond its maximum powered speed of 14 km/h.
The driver applied the manual brakes, but due to severe mechanical defects, they failed.
The driver lost control and the bus rolled one and a half times down the slope, with passengers ejected into the rocky terrain below.
“There are two primary contributing factors,” Myers wrote. “The first is the driver, for reasons unknown, negotiating the lateral moraine in neutral and without the six-wheel drive engaged,” Myers wrote.
“This configuration, on such a grade, would create a situation in which vehicle speed accumulates rapidly. Unable to use engine power to slow the bus, the driver would have to rely on conventional braking.”
Pursuit’s policy at the time was for drivers to put the Ice Explorers in neutral at the top of the hill and then, at the start of the steepest descent, put them in gear.
In this case, the bus was never put into gear or it popped out of gear almost immediately, the judge found.
“This leads to the second primary contributing factor: effective braking force. During the mechanical inspection, it was determined that this vehicle did not have sufficient braking power to stop the vehicle, even in ideal situations.”
'Worn, improperly inspected'
An inspection after the crash showed that only one of the six wheels had the power to safely brake as required.
Court heard that five days before the crash, a driver formally reported a major braking issue on a daily inspection report. He noted that full pedal depression was required to stop the rig and requested an inspection of the brake slack adjusters.
But the defect wasn’t inspected or repaired, nor was it carried forward on subsequent daily reports as the company required, the judge found.
Furthermore, on-site mechanics were new and inexperienced with Ice Explorers and also lacked proper training, the inquiry found.
“In short, the brakes suffered a catastrophic failure because they were worn, improperly inspected and concerns with respect to the brakes functioning were not attended to,” Myers wrote.
'Inconceivable to the court'
Court also heard the Ice Explorer bus had been serviced two months earlier by Wajax, a company that offers repairs and maintenance for heavy-duty vehicles.
It was sent to Wajax for a scheduled 1,000-hour inspection, returning to service just 12 days before the fatal crash.
However, the judge noted serious issues with the Wajax inspection report, which was undated and did not reference a specific vehicle.
“The inspection report tendered indicated the brakes were satisfactory and passed inspection,” Myers wrote.
“It is inconceivable to the court that the tires were removed to properly inspect the faulty braking. Secondly, the court has serious concerns whether this inspection report actually applied to this vehicle.”
Myers said the lack of seatbelts and the route itself were contributing factors. Parts of Lateral Moraine Road reach an incline of 40 per cent, exceeding the maximum limit of 36 per cent specified by the Ice Explorer manufacturer.
The court determined that though medical response was prompt, no intervention could have saved the victims.
Myers called on Pursuit to improve its inspection protocols.
The company must ensure that external maintenance and inspection reports are dated and detail exactly what work is performed on which vehicle, and that a copy is kept inside for driver review.
The company should also work alongside OHS and the provincial government to immediately implement a training program for all mechanics working on its Ice Explorer fleet, Myers wrote.
The judge encouraged OHS and Alberta Transportation to establish a rigorous, standardized three-year service and inspection procedure for off-road tour vehicles and a new policy for defect reports.
RCMP didn't lay criminal charges in the crash, but Pursuit pleaded guilty in 2023 to two charges under the Alberta Occupational Health and Safety Act and was fined $475,000.
In a statement to CBC News, officials with Pursuit said the operator has since made significant safety changes including enhanced driver training, seatbelts in all Ice Explorers, and updated processes for vehicle inspection, maintenance and defect reports.
“[We] will continue working with the appropriate authorities to ensure our practices meet the standard expected of us.
“Our thoughts remain with the families of Dionne Durocher, Griva Patel and Kamleshbhai Patel and with everyone affected by the July 2020 tragedy at the Columbia Icefield.”

Now that Candle Media‘s glow has dimmed further with the sale of its Hello Sunshine majority stake, fresh questions are being raised about the firm’s future.
The financials around the deal for Reese Witherspoon’s company, which she is buying back from Candle in partnership with France-based Mediawan, have not been disclosed. But one veteran financier familiar with the transaction told Deadline it likely represents a loss of several hundreds of millions of dollars for Candle. The main culprits: a $900 million valuation when the firm took a majority stake in Hello Sunshine in 2021 – a sky-high level given its output and lack of profitability – and dramatic changes in the media landscape of late.
Five years ago, Candle lit up with $2 billion in backing from private equity mainstay Blackstone. At the time, the industry was on a major streaming binge, and the company had two titans at the helm in co-founders Kevin Mayer and Tom Staggs. The two had spent years together in high posts at Disney, helping to pull off major M&A deals like the Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm acquisitions and the thunderbolt merger with Capital Cities-ABC that brought ESPN into the fold.
Watch on Deadline
Today, industry observers wonder if the next logical move for Candle would be to swing a deal for the company’s main remaining asset, kids entertainment powerhouse Moonbug. Private equity firms, after all, view their funding and portfolios in terms of returns within years, not decades.
Moonbug, which produces CoComelon, is in better financial shape than many of its peers. But the nearly $3 billion Candle paid to acquire it has set a high bar. One source familiar with the strategic thinking of Mayer and Staggs says a deal to unload the company is not imminent but has been actively explored. As it has regrouped, Candle has cut staff and restructured from its origins as a buyer of assets to primarily an operator of them.
A Candle rep declined comment when contacted by Deadline. Blackstone did not respond to a request for comment.
Difficulties for private equity-backed players extend far beyond the entertainment sector, and stem largely from higher interest rates. In an article about the increasingly tenuous state of small- and mid-sized private players, published Tuesday in parallel with the Hello Sunshine news, the Wall Street Journal quoted a banker as saying the situation is approaching a “period of reckoning.” As money returns to the sidelines, private equity fundraising is on track for its worst year since 2020.
The rate-driven increase in the cost of borrowing money is squeezing a lot of firms like Candle, given that they have to try to sell assets at even higher levels to account for the difference in rates. For those in the media business, however, demand for streaming programming is also receding as Netflix and other players tighten their belt and the industry braces for the impact of the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. Skydance, their new parent company, is promising at least $6 billion in cost savings related to the deal. Podcast platforms, which once splashed cash around, have also cut their spending.
One of Candle’s early investments, along with Hello Sunshine, was a minority stake in Will Smith’s production company Westbrook. Less than three months after that deal was announced in January 2022, Smith became an industry pariah after slapping Chris Rock onstage at the Oscars, earning a 10-year ban from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. While Smith has returned to starring roles, the episode added another wrinkle to the already difficult task of profiting from film and TV production.
Along with Westbrook, the company invested in Spain-based Exile Content Studio and social media storytelling firm ATTN:.
No one who has done business with Mayer and Staggs or who is familiar with the company’s operations blames them personally for the firm’s struggles. It simply seems to be a case of unfortunate timing.
Given their largely charmed run at Disney, where each served a tour of duty at the company’s strategic planning division before rising to higher positions, both are sought-after and respected executives. Even after Candle’s founding, the pair were retained by former Disney CEO Bob Iger as consultants. David Zaslav brought Mayer in as he was about to close the Warner Bros. Discovery merger in 2021. Drawing on the expertise he developed at Disney overseeing the launch of Disney+ and leading a number of sports initiatives, Mayer also served as chairman of sports streamer DAZN just prior to Candle’s launch.
“We did move aggressively,” Mayer said of Candle during an appearance on a Deadline-moderated panel at last month’s Zurich Summit. “When I thought about what I wanted Candle to be, I wanted it to be a modernly configured media company that had a flywheel around great storytelling told by great storytellers.”
Candle spent some $4 billion on acquisitions, Mayer recalled, musing about how different that outlay is from the massive level of Disney and other giants. “There is a certain minimum scale you probably need to make an impact,” he said.
Moonbug, while it accounts for three-quarters of Candle’s spending, is a property with heft in the YouTube-driven creator economy. At the Zurich conference, Mayer noted that CoComelon‘s Netflix incarnation was the streamer’s most popular title from 2021-2024. (It has fallen off since then, and shifted to Disney+.) The company’s YouTube channel gets 13 billion views a month, he said, more than all of Disney including ESPN and four times the viewing of MrBeast.
“There’s no doubt they’d look to do a deal if they get an offer in the right ballpark,” one investor says. “But in today’s climate, is anybody going to step forward to make that kind of offer? That’s really the question.”
For Mayer and Staggs, despite their sterling reputations, “this is going to take some time for people to get over,” the investor added. “Though this business can have a short memory if the money is right.”

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”, has brought renewed attention to using light to investigate fundamental biological processes. These include memory formation, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders, as well as processes involved in infectious disease.
Editorial | Let there be light: On the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology/Medicine
For Nishith Gupta, professor of Biological Sciences at BITS Pilani, Hyderabad, and founder of the Intracellular Parasite Education and Research Labs (iPEARL), the recognition has a personal significance in his own scientific journey.
Mr. Gupta’s decades-long collaboration with Hegemann at Humboldt University of Berlin, where Hegemanna is Hertie Senior Professor of Neuroscience, helped extend optogenetic approaches beyond neuroscience into his study of Toxoplasma gondii, an intracellular parasite that infects humans, mammals, and birds.
Interactive Guide | Nobel Prize 2026
Optogenetics enables scientists to control selected cells or biological processes using light-sensitive proteins.
The Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine stated: “It all began with Peter Hegemann’s curiosity. He wondered how Chlamydomonas, a single-celled alga, is able to swim towards a light source. In the early 2000s, he and Georg Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, an algal protein with unique properties, found on the surface of the cell. When it is illuminated by blue light, a channel opens through the protein. Charged ions then flow into the cell, creating an electrical impulse. They found that regardless of which cell they put the protein in, those cells became light sensitive.” In 2005, Deisseroth showed that introducing channelrhodopsin into rat neurons allowed blue light to trigger nerve signals. In 2007, he showed light-based control in mice.
In contrast, Mr. Gupta, Mr. Hegemann and others used light-regulated enzyme adenylate cyclase, which converts adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the primary energy of a living cell, to produce cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate (cAMP). This molecule acts as messengers, helping transmit signals within cells.
Put simply, the researchers showed that light controls the enzyme, the enzyme produces cAMP, and cAMP helps regulate what happens inside the parasite (Toxoplasma gondii): how it enters cells, moves, and exits cells. This landmark study was published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry in 2013.
While Mr. Deisseroth, Mr. Hegemann, and Mr. Nagel’s optogenetics “solves one of humanity’s great mysteries, how our incredible brain works”, Mr. Gupta, Mr. Hegemann and others’ found light-regulated signalling to investigate parasite’s lifestyle, and infection.
Mr. Gupta says that working alongside Hegemann in Berlin, with their laboratories in neighbouring departments, was an important part of this scientific journey. Joint funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG) supported their collaboration.
After Mr. Gupta relocated to India, Mr. Hegemann continued to support his research through Mr. Gupta’s Wellcome Trust–DBT Senior Fellowship project at BITS Pilani. Researchers from his team continued to visit Hegemann’s group in Berlin.
For Mr. Gupta, the Nobel Prize awarded to Mr. Hegemann and his fellow laureates underscores the far-reaching consequences of fundamental research. A protein that evolved to help an alga sense light has become a tool for probing the brain, investigating infection and understanding how cells function. He says the broader lesson is that technologies developed to answer one biological question can open entirely new avenues of research.
“Light has become more than a means of observation; it is a way to intervene, test, and uncover cause-and-effect relationships,” Mr. Gupta says.

On September 21, 2026, students of King George’s Medical University (KGMU), Lucknow, protested over the death of Divyanshi Yadav, a 2025-batch B.Sc. Nursing student who died of dengue. A student at the protest site told PTI that though Divyanshi was suffering from the disease, she still had to attend college. “Despite being on the deathbed, she was tense about her attendance. Students are forced to come to the college daily to mark attendance, ignoring their medical conditions. We get messages from teachers telling us to come to the college after taking medicine,” he said.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
In September 2025, Subhangini, 23, another nursing student who was in her first year at Bhopal Memorial Hospital and Research Centre (BMHRC), died due to jaundice. A current student, on condition of anonymity, told The Hindu, “There was poor quality of food and water on campus, and the case was mishandled by BMHRC Hospital; her medical leave was not approved, and she had to perform her duty even in an ailing condition.” However, the university denied the allegations.
In most institutions, medical leave requires medical documentation and is granted for serious illness or when a student is severely injured in an accident. The older University Grants Commission (UGC) 2003 regulations required universities to prescribe a minimum attendance of 75% for students to be eligible for examinations, but the 2025 regulations no longer set a universal 75% threshold. Instead, they leave minimum attendance requirements to individual higher education institutions (HEIs) through their statutory bodies.
In most HEIs, the minimum attendance requirement is 75-80%, with a 10% accommodation for medical emergencies. This minimum attendance criterion is higher in medical and engineering institutes, as per their regulatory bodies. For nursing students like Divyanshi, the Nursing Council of India’s guidelines mandate 80% attendance in theory and 100% attendance in practical areas. This framework leaves medical-leave protection largely to institutional rules, producing significant variation in what happens to students when illness interrupts their education.
Problems for students with chronic illnesses
Alex is a third-year B.A. Visual Communication student at a university in Hyderabad. Having transverse myelitis, he became paralysed from the chest down at the age of 10, and the organs on the right side of his body stopped working. Doctors said he would never walk. Defying this, he has regained his ability to walk, but this is accompanied by chronic pain below the chest, subluxations, partial dysplasias, fatigue, and muscle spasms.
Alex holds a 100% merit-based scholarship, and in order to keep it, he must maintain a CGPA of 8 and above and 75% attendance. After he dislocated his kneecap in college in September 2024, doctors recommended a month of complete rest. However, he said, “I was told by the college authorities to either come to college regularly and maintain the 75% attendance or take a year's break and come back to college next year.” His medical leave was denied, stating, “Medical exemption only applies in case of hospitalisations.”
“However, my scholarship would not hold the following year. So I would have to write my exam again and apply for a scholarship again, which was not something I was able to do because of my financial situation. So I had to continue coming to college without taking the recommended one month’s leave. I took one day off, and I continued going back to college every single day,” Alex added.
Alex had to navigate a campus that had minimal accessibility, a long commute to the university, and he was not given leniency for assignments or for showing up to class a few minutes late. This affected his social life on campus and his health. “If I did take that one month’s rest, there was a chance I would have recovered fully. But since I was not able to do it, I still have not recovered. It’s been three years, and I keep dislocating my knee and wear braces to this day.”
A student of Interior Design with an autoimmune condition at a private university in Noida said, “I provided all medical documents explaining my condition; however, the department head asked me to take amla and attend classes.” The student described the process of applying for a leave as frustrating: “I was made to feel like my condition was not important; it came from my own laziness and was something that could be managed with willpower... I was an out-of-station student and had to navigate my illness alone, which was both mentally and financially demanding.”
Attendance adds to evaluation, and the student saw a marked dip in grades. Support, such as make-up assignments, was also not extended by administration or faculty. The student said, “As practical classes are a day long, missing one day amounts to six to eight hours of class time, dipping the attendance to 70-80 % even if two or three classes are missed.”
Cases of unconventional medical proof
Jay was a B.A. English major at a university in Delhi NCR, and months before he joined the university, he had developed chronic pain due to a genetic condition. He had to maintain 75% attendance in every subject, with an 80% requirement and 5% provision for medical leave.
Jay missed many morning classes due to his pain flaring up. As his teachers were accommodating, he was able to sit for his first-year exams. “I had to drop out as my situation worsened in second year. I didn’t have a proper diagnosis; a lot of reports and tests indicated inconclusive results. This couldn’t be taken as enough evidence at that time, and due to considerably low accessibility on campus as well as inflexible leave criteria, I dropped out.”
Tejasdeep Sehgal, a fourth-year student, has had a hearing impairment since the age of 12 and uses a hearing aid. The office of learning support at his university in Haryana provided him with a shaker alarm clock and transcription services that he says are helpful.
Last year, Tejasdeep’s hearing aid stopped working, and he could not listen properly. He then went to Delhi to have it fixed. “It took me two days to get it fixed, and it was a technician who fixed it; therefore, I didn’t have a prescription for it. I had unexcused absences for the classes I missed. However, it could have escalated into a situation where I would not be able to produce documentary proof of my condition to get medical leave.”
A student of Jawaharlal Nehru University’s Japanese department had a viral fever with body pain and had to take leave for two weeks. The student had informed the professor about it over email. When she rejoined class, she was told she was not sick and was asked to write an application to the centre and produce medical documentation. This dismissal by the professor caused the student severe anxiety and panic attacks. The university administration later asked the professor to write an apology letter to the student.
Another student said, “We are constantly told by our seniors not to fall in the bad books of some professor, as they have access to grant scholarships and fellowships and influence your career outside college.”
Describing a similar incident, a Delhi University student said they were made to stand in class. “I was told I was a good student, but irregular in classes. The philosophy professor quoted a scholar on resilience, which made the experience of my sickness seem like laziness. I left the class crying. I felt my hard work would not amount to anything because I was a sick person.”
A fifth-semester student of Humanities, who had been seeking college counselling sessions, upon needing further assistance, had to seek a psychiatrist outside college. The student later missed an exam due to an anxiety attack and was denied approval of medical leave. “I had all the documentation from a fully accredited clinical psychiatrist, and I was told it would have been easier to vouch for me if I was seeking help from college counsellors, who were not psychiatrists and could not have helped me at that time.” The student was made to do multiple rounds to the college healthcare centre, and their leave was still not approved. They had to take the paper again next semester. “The process was bureaucratic and draining.”
Sensitising institutions
Sayan Chaudhuri, a scholar of critical pedagogy and higher education, says, “Teachers and administration need to be sensitised to how chronic illnesses or other conditions might be playing out. I think without that understanding, you can’t have a meaningful intervention. What administrations really need to think about is the kinds of bureaucratic hurdles that are there. Often, administration stands at a huge distance, and you feel a sense of fear about approaching. So there is a need for a culture where it is established that you can get leave, and it shouldn’t feel like it’s a difficult task or it needs certain kinds of skills to be able to ask for a leave.”
He says the problem also lies in the hurdles students face when seeking medical leave. “A documentation-heavy policy is going to run into a contradiction, because the assumption will be that the document can be provided well in advance to the requisite authorities who can go through it, understand it, and approve it. And we know that’s not how it’s always going to work. There will be many things that will fall out of this system. We have to really think of developing a more local understanding of things where teachers can play a proactive role at times, mediate between the administration and the student, because otherwise that contextual understanding may not be there. Medical resource centres and health centres are often very depleted. Counsellors are not always working in a very empowered way, where they can stage interventions in a collaborative and meaningful manner,” he said.
Debaditya Battacharya, Assistant Professor in the Department of English at Jamia Millia Islamia, a researcher of Indian higher education and university histories, says, “National Education Policy 2020 lumps questions of mental health, ability, and disability together under this socioeconomically disadvantaged groups (SEDG); this rubric is indicative of the myopia of policy. Ability is treated as meritocratic given; it is not at stake anymore; it is either the basic minimum you take for granted or simply reduced to an ability enhancement course. But university life has to account for different capacities for ability and disability”
“There is no objective parameter that can justify any figure, whether it be 75 or 65,” Dr. Battacharya said, because students come to university with radically different circumstances. For some, meeting a particular threshold may be relatively easy; for others, especially students from marginalised backgrounds, it may involve negotiating pressures outside the classroom as well.
He says, “It’s teachers who are expected to come with that space of understanding what a student’s real-life circumstances are, as they deal with students in the flesh”. He suggests student-faculty committees hear cases that merit genuine attention on a case-by-case basis, in a consultative and democratic fashion. He says the system should retain the purpose of attendance, maintaining the integrity and spirit of the teaching-learning process without reducing individual students and their circumstances to a single percentage.
(Zain Younis is a Master’s student at Jamia Millia Islamia)

An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, according to a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who federal prosecutors describe as a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and US permanent resident, allegedly spent several weeks querying an unspecified “productivity agent” and an “AI chatbot” to plan his alleged surveillance operation. He used an internal OpenAI tool to ask about meetings scheduled in the targeted conference room.
He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, according to prosecutors and the court filing.
OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device that had not been installed in Alfozan’s bag at the office.
Alfozan couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. He made an initial appearance in US district court in San Francisco on Tuesday on one charge of “use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison. He joined OpenAI in July 2025 and was fired last Friday to coincide with his arrest.
Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan aimed “to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” but prosecutors nor OpenAI have offered any information so far about a potential motive.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement on X. “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.”
OpenAI discovered the bug—which was allegedly “concealed in toilet paper” and “inserted into a USB port on the back of a television” in the conference room—on September 30 during a countersurveillance sweep.
Alfozan previously worked at a cargo logistics startup and at Meta, according to a purported LinkedIn profile for him. In a recent podcast interview, Alfozan said he was also part of a group of Saudi engineers in Silicon Valley who offered consulting services to Saudi organizations.
The LinkedIn profile lists Alfozan as a part-time “venture partner” at RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm based in Saudi Arabia. Neither RAED Ventures nor Meta immediately responded to WIRED’s request for comment.
Last year, the Trump administration signed a pact with Saudi Arabia granting the kingdom access to advanced chips and AI technologies that might otherwise be restricted over national security concerns. Saudi investment firms remain a major source of capital for US tech companies.
Executives Only
According to the complaint, Alfozan allegedly planted the listening device “no later than on or about September 28, 2026.”
The conference room Alfozan targeted “can be reserved only by executives and executive assistants,” and is typically used “for internal leadership meetings,” “technical and product sessions,” and “external briefings” with business partners and government officials, according to the complaint. It is frequently used for discussions involving “highly confidential” information, including about research, products, business strategy, and government relationships, the complaint stated.
OpenAI’s statement called the recording device “sophisticated.” Authorities allege that the device Alfozan planted was called Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, “a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage.” It currently retails on Seeed’s website for $13.99. OpenAI’s security team tried to export the data stored on the microSD card, but were unable to review it because it was encrypted.
After discovering the device, OpenAI says it notified the FBI and was able to connect it to Alfozan after reviewing chat logs and surveillance footage, and searching a bag he left unattended at the office. The company then gradually disabled his access to company systems as the investigation was ongoing.
According to the complaint, OpenAI security personnel discovered the bag that Alfozan left unattended in a printer room on October 5. The security team went through the bag, which contained a second encrypted Seeed listening device and other personal items connected to Alfozan, including his wallet. Prosecutors say Alfozan later reported the bag as missing to OpenAI and subsequently recovered it from the company’s lost and found.
He followed up with unnamed personnel at OpenAI to say that some of the items that were supposed to be in the bag were still missing—including a credit card, about $500 in cash, and two AirPods—but neglected to mention the second listening device, which had been removed from the bag by OpenAI security.

For Indian enterprises adopting AI, choosing the technology is only part of the challenge. Deciding what to own, how much to spend, and where AI can deliver measurable business value is becoming just as important. A December 2025 government backgrounder, citing Nasscom’s AI Adoption Index, said 87% of enterprises in India were actively using AI solutions. As adoption expands, technology leaders face a more complex choice: buy ready-made solutions, build capabilities in-house, or access models from external providers. Frontier models have made it easier to add AI capabilities to products and workflows. But the decisions around cost, speed, data, and business outcomes are increasingly intertwined. For enterprises and startups, the challenge is to identify which parts of the AI stack can create a lasting advantage and which to source externally as the technology evolves. These questions shaped the second roundtable held on the sidelines of Inc42’s inaugural CTO Summit 2026, where technology leaders discussed how they are building AI-led systems and organisations. Moderated by Abhinav Johri, partner, technology consulting, EY India, the conversation brought together: Govind Soni, cofounder, CoinSwitch & Lemonn Harsh Sahu, cofounder and CTO, Matters.ai Kiran Reddy Singam, VP, product and tech, BigHaat Shanti Kuropati, founder, SeedlingLabs Shiv Buddharaju, VP, engineering, Oxmiq Labs Vikas Roy, director, engineering, Vahan.ai Vinay Rai, executive VP, technology, Netradyne Vivek Manoharan, CEO and CTO, Gravitas Building An Edge With Context And Workflows The conversation began with a question: as AI moves from experimentation into core business processes, does every problem require a new technology layer? Matters.ai’s Sahu argued that the starting point should be a deep understanding of the domain. Knowing where existing solutions fall short can help technology leaders build differentiated products. “I feel that founders and tech leaders need to know their specific domain really well to not only see the existing gaps but also use AI to fill in those gaps in a way that was never done before,” said Sahu. This emphasis on domain knowledge led to a distinction between the intelligence a company can source and the business context it develops itself. SeedlingLabs’ Kuropati argued that while frontier models change rapidly, proprietary data, context, and workflows can offer a more durable advantage. “If it is around data or context, you have to own it, irrespective of which frontier model you are working with, because that eventually becomes the moat for any AI-native founder, while the rest of the technology solutions remain largely the same,” said Kuropati. For CoinSwitch & Lemonn’s Soni, operational context matters most when accuracy directly affects customers’ money. “When you’re dealing with customer money, all operations become very critical, and accuracy can’t be compromised. So whenever you’re building something, that has to be built on top of that 10-year-old context, and not just with some new technology in isolation,” said Soni. What To Own, What To Rent Retaining control of context does not necessarily mean owning every technology layer around it. The discussion moved beyond the traditional build-versus-buy framework to examine what companies need to own, what they can rent, and how those choices change over time. Oxmiq Labs’ Buddharaju said these decisions span multiple dimensions, with one choice often affecting another. In AI, the workload involved in developing a product can also differ substantially from what it takes to serve customers at scale. “Technology choices are not simply about buy versus build. The real question is what you want to own, what you want to rent, and for how long. In AI, that distinction becomes even more important because the workload for building a product can be very different from the workload for serving customers,” said Buddharaju. Netradyne’s Rai made the case for renting intelligence. With frontier models evolving rapidly, he argued that building and maintaining an in-house model could leave companies playing catch-up. “Unless regulation requires us to run our own models, we are better off renting intelligence right now. The leaders keep changing, and an open-source model that is ahead today could leave you behind within weeks. For most companies, speed and flexibility matter more than owning the model itself,” said Rai. Making AI Economics A Product Decision Alongside ownership and flexibility, participants examined another test for AI deployment: its impact on business economics. BigHaat’s Singam said technology decisions must be tied directly to business metrics, with their contribution to margins assessed before deployment scales. “Whenever we deploy anything, we look at which metric it is moving and whether that change is positive or negative for our contribution margin. Whether it is fulfilment, RTOs, users or technology costs, we need to understand the economics before we scale,” said Singam. For Gravitas’ Manoharan, this assessment begins at the product development stage. A model’s ability to perform a task is only one consideration. The cost of running it also determines which features are viable. “Cost economics really matters to us, and it defines the product features we build. When we develop AI, we have to ask whether the economics will be sustainable within one or two years,” said Manoharan. He cited the example of converting US healthcare clinical charts into ICD and CPT codes. While AI models could produce useful outputs, the cost of processing each chart had to be weighed against the existing BPO-led process. This comparison makes unit economics an early filter for deciding which AI features to pursue. At Vahan.ai, Roy said AI expenditure is similarly linked to measurable productivity gains. The objective is to automate processes and increase the number of placements each telecaller could handle. “Clients care about outcomes, while we care about efficiency. For us, AI meant automating processes and asking which human decisions AI could handle. The real test was whether that could help us do more placements per telecaller,” said Roy. Across the roundtable, a common approach emerged: retain control of the context that differentiates the business, stay flexible on the models powering it, and assess the economics before scaling. For technology leaders navigating the next phase of AI adoption, these decisions will shape both the systems they build and the value they deliver.

flydubai probe widens as 2 Maldivian pilots detained in UAE over ‘plot to down aircraft’: Report
The two pilots were taken into custody on October 3, and their families have been formally notified of their detention by the Maldivian Embassy in the UAE.
Two Maldivian pilots working for flydubai have been arrested in the United Arab Emirates in connection with an alleged attempt to hijack and crash a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, media reports said. The case relates to a September 30 incident in which Indian Captain Smit Machchhar was injured while resisting an alleged attack by an Omani co-pilot.
The two pilots were taken into custody on October 3, and their families have been formally notified of their detention by the Maldivian Embassy in the UAE, Maldivian news portal Adhadhu reported.
Authorities in the Maldives have not commented on the arrests. The UAE has also not released official details about the allegations against the two men or clarified whether investigators have established their involvement in the suspected plot.
What is known about the arrested pilots
According to the Male-based newspaper Mihaaru, as quoted by news agency PTI, the two pilots are believed to have interacted with Hammam al-Hammami, the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking Machchhar, at their workplace. They are also reported to have lived in the same building as him.
However, authorities have not disclosed the nature of their alleged links to the incident or the evidence, if any, against them.
News portal edition.mv reported that the two men are among six Maldivian nationals employed as pilots by flydubai. They are also reportedly the airline's most recent recruits from the Maldives.
The arrests came as UAE authorities expanded their investigation into the alleged attempt to seize control of flight FZ1073 and crash the aircraft.
How the alleged mid-air attack unfolded
Flight FZ1073 was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 174 passengers and crew members on board when the alleged attack took place on September 30.
Reportedly, al-Hammami allegedly attacked Machchhar with an axe and stabbed him in an attempt to take control of the aircraft and carry out a "terrorist attack".
Despite being seriously injured, Machchhar resisted the alleged assault and managed to unlock the cockpit door. Crew members and passengers then entered the cockpit, overpowered the co-pilot and helped stabilise the aircraft.
The plane subsequently made an emergency landing at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia.
The UAE identified the accused as 29-year-old al-Hammami and described the incident as an attempted terrorist attack.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

Poland blames Starlink sabotage on Russia
Poland blames Russia for an arson attack on a Starlink satellite station in September and two Turkish citizens have been arrested in connection with the sabotage
WARSAW, Poland -- WARSAW, Poland (AP) — Poland is blaming Russia for an arson attack on a Starlink satellite station in September and two Turkish citizens have been arrested in connection with the suspected act of sabotage, authorities said.
The suspects, whose names were not released in line with Polish privacy rules, were arrested in Germany, Polish officials said Monday. They are accused of deliberately setting fire to Starlink infrastructure on Sept. 23 in Wola Krobowska, Poland, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Warsaw.
“We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland’s minister overseeing intelligence services, said in a news release, noting that Russian intelligence services are increasingly turning to people with ties to the criminal underworld.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, in a post on X, called the incident “another act of hybrid warfare.”
Other details were not immediately available.
The Poland arson in September was one of more than 210 incidents across Europe that Western officials consider sabotage and malign activity linked to Russia tracked by The Associated Press since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
A British court last year found three men guilty of arson in a March 2024 plot that targeted a London warehouse with Starlinks for Ukraine inside. British prosecutors said it was masterminded by Russia’s intelligence services.
Officials say one goal of the attacks is to undermine support for Ukraine, spread fear and discord in European societies and drain investigative resources. Russia often uses proxies for such attacks and some perpetrators say they have no idea they have been hired by Moscow.
Tech titan Elon Musk has allowed the Ukrainians to use his Starlink satellite communications system inside their own territory, including in Russian-occupied regions, but has restricted use of the satellite system inside Russia. Starlink has become deeply embedded in Ukraine’s military operations, with commanders and soldiers relying on satellite connectivity to communicate and coordinate operations.
Russia’s intelligence services are carrying out almost “daily acts of subversion,” Siemoniak said Tuesday at a security conference in Warsaw.
“There is not a week where activities do not happen,” and the same goes for other European countries, he said, adding that the activity is aimed at countries that support Ukraine.
He said Russia’s covert malign activity in Poland started in early 2024 as Russia recruited disposable agents on platforms like Telegram to carry out attacks, including against a shopping center.
“Our enemy — that is Russia’s intelligence services — changes its methods of operation and has unlimited resources,” Siemoniak said.
Fighting against Russia’s intelligence services is not like taking down an organized crime group where the group is convicted and the case is closed, he said. In the case of subversive activity, as soon as you cut one head off, another grows and “you never know what direction they will pursue next,” he said.
“In cases of the subversive activity, it’s like the story of the dragon whose heads keep growing and you never know which direction they pursue next,” Beate Gangås, Norway's director-general of the Police Security Service, told the conference. “We are in the most serious situation since the Second World War.”

Chuck Hoskin Jr. fondly recalls watching a room full of Cherokee immersion students crowd around a screen to watch How to Train Your Dragon. Except Hiccup and Astrid weren't speaking English—the protagonists were speaking Cherokee, dubbed by voices from the local community.
“They're hearing it in our mother tongue—that didn't happen a generation ago,” Hoskin Jr., principal chief of the Cherokee Nation, tells WIRED. “We're a long way, thankfully, from rote classroom instruction and memorization to a world where kids can see the sort of creativity that sparks imagination and helps every kid become more articulate and literate.”
The Cherokee Nation has around 1,500 active speakers left, and most are over 70. Hoskin Jr. says the community is rapidly losing that generation, which is why it has spent time training up second-language learners. It even has a baby immersion program, hoping their first words are Cherokee.
“The foes we’ve had historically are the so-called Age of Discovery, colonization, the displacement of our people economically and geographically, boarding schools,” he says. “But it's nothing compared to the mathematics we’re up against now. Which is why we’re filled with this urgency every day to do all we can to find partners that can help us accelerate what we want to do.”
One of those accelerants is Apple. The Cherokee Nation has long collaborated with the iPhone maker, and Cherokee was the first Native American language included in iOS in 2010. Today, Apple says its iOS keyboard supports more than 200 languages and language variants, with a handful added last year in iOS 26, like Haitian Creole and Nez Perce. In iOS 27, it expanded support for Indigenous languages to include other Native American languages like Blackfoot, Comanche, and Northern East Cree.
The goal is to meet young people where they already spend much of their waking hours: phone screens. Hoskin Jr. says that to revitalize and save a language, it has to become accessible. Apple says the effort isn't as simple as translating words. It’s a multi-year endeavor that requires deep research, and the company leans on community members for their expertise.
But the process doesn’t start in Cupertino. It actually begins with Unicode. You may have heard of the name—it’s the organization that approves and standardizes the new emoji that appear on your smartphone every year. It also handles time zone localization, currency names, imperial versus metric, and so on.
Before you can type or read a character on a smartphone screen, it needs to exist as a recognized character in the Unicode Standard. “Everything does start with Unicode in terms of a language, but it actually starts with characters and scripts,” says Unicode CEO Toral Cowieson. “We now have more than 157,000 characters that are included.”
Cowieson calls Unicode a kind of digital Switzerland—a neutral consortium where rivals like Apple, Microsoft, and Google sit at the same table as linguists and volunteer contributors. (Cowieson told WIRED earlier this year that Unicode had only four full-time employees.) Proposing a language, verifying it, and then encoding the character set can take three to five years.
After a script is encoded, platforms like Apple and Google need to add font support. Without this step, a character could appear as an empty box—often called “tofu.” Next is orthography: a set of rules and systems for writing a language. Often, languages have a well-defined orthography, but when it’s not standardized, communities use ad hoc replacements because historically available keyboards don't support it.
Take the glottal stop—the speech sound made in the throat between the syllables when you say, “uh-oh.” Some languages have distinct characters for glottal stops, but as some keyboards don’t support them, many indigenous cultures use alternatives, like a question mark, to represent the sound. That's when Apple connects with the community to figure out the best way to represent the sounds in digital text.
That brings us to the keyboard layout. When a community already has an established physical keyboard layout—like Osage—Apple adapts it directly to the software keyboard. Some cultures prefer the QWERTY layouts people are already familiar with.
Other languages need more custom approaches. For example, Nez Perce, or Nimipuutímt, does not use capital letters. Rather than having the Shift key toggle traditional uppercase letters, Apple repurposed it to reveal an accented secondary layer, so users don’t have to hold down individual keys to see those characters, which can slow typing. In the Cherokee language, each character mostly represents a consonant combined with a vowel sound, a form known as syllabary. Apple added adaptive vowel keys on the bottom row, so when a user types a consonant, these keys change to show the vowel combinations they can make.
That’s a newer change to the Cherokee keyboard—one Apple approached the community about, meaning building a keyboard for a language isn’t a one-and-done project.
But digitizing an indigenous culture’s language hasn't always been harmless. Genner Llanes-Ortiz, a Maya scholar and researcher at Bishop's University, studies how Indigenous people use digital technologies to reclaim language heritage. He recalls how Māori speakers rejected proposals to sell their language to tech companies.
“There’s a historical memory about the ways of dispossession that Indigenous peoples have experienced in the world,” Llanes-Ortiz says. “Māori working in their own revitalization efforts have been very firm in protecting access and storage of their linguistic materials because they have been exploited. They have experienced extraction of knowledge in the past.”
Language sovereignty and data ownership are top of mind, according to Chirasree Mandal, an Apple software engineer. “We don’t own anything, and we make it very clear that we are not trying to silo any data that we gain from this process,” she says. “It’s about making sure that the best choice for representing someone’s language is being made on our platform so they feel good using it.”
For its part, a Google spokesperson tells WIRED it has a long history of bringing lesser-known and Indigenous languages to its platforms so people can communicate, pointing to collaborations to integrate languages like Manx and Māori. Google also says it’s exploring how generative AI can simplify the coding and research required for new languages, but “successful integrations require direct participation from native speakers” for the keyboard to meet the community’s needs.
Hoskin Jr. says that writing in syllabary is seen as a badge of honor for young Cherokee speakers. People type their names in Cherokee on Facebook—that’s empowering. But he sees that progress as vulnerable to broader political rhetoric in the US that pushes a monolithic, English-speaking America, which he says bypasses several chapters, including Native American history.
“The greatest enemy we have right now for saving the Cherokee language is the passage of time and the fragility of human life,” Hoskin Jr. says. “Time is precious to everyone, but particularly precious to us in this mission.”

Kusal Mendis’ unbeaten 87, ably supported by Kamindu Mendis’s 27-ball 40 helped Sri Lanka chase 169 against Pakistan to register an eight-wicket win in Rawalpindi on Tuesday. The result gave the Lankans a consolation win with Pakistan sealing the series 2-1.
Kusal was adjudged the player the match for his sublime knock which is also his career-best score in the format, while Pakistan’s Sahibzada Farhan was name player of the series.
Sri Lanka won the toss and opted to field. Farhan’s 47-ball 76 was in stark contrast to an underwhelming showing by the rest of the top and middle order. Eshan Malinga’s double strike in the fourth over started the slide with Farhan struggling to find support.
That eventully arrived first from Abdul Samad, whose 10-ball 15 alongside Arafat Minhas’ 20-ball 34 pushed Pakistan’s score to a respectable 168/8 in 20 overs.
Dasun Shanaka finished as the pick of the bowlers for Sri Lanka with figures of 3/21 and a stellar economy of 5.25.
In reponse, Mohammad Imran removed Lahiru Udara off the fifth ball of the chase to put some early pressure on the Lankans. But a two-part resistance both around Kusal, first with Sineth Jayawardene and then with Kamindu, helped Lanka clinch victory with 17 balls to spare.
Kusal also became the top-scorer for Sri Lanka in the format with 2791 runs, going past Pathum Nissanka’s tally of 2784.

The Coimbatore Medical College Hospital (CMCH) administration on Tuesday replaced the brown paper covers used to dispense medicines to patients with fresh ones after instructions printed in Hindi on the former triggered a row, with many criticising it as contradicting the two-language policy of Tamil Nadu.
DMK leader and former Minister for Industries T.R.B. Raja was among those who criticised the inclusion of Hindi instructions on the covers.
“(It) seems like the three-language policy is being implemented in Tamil Nadu hospitals too! First Karur... Now the same situation in Coimbatore as well”, he posted on X, along with a photo of a pharmacy cover purportedly issued by CMCH, with instruction in Tamil, English and Hindi. He had posted earlier that similar covers with instructions in three languages were being used in Karur.
A senior official from CMCH said the covers with instructions in three languages were printed and supplied by Chinthamani Cooperative Society and no one had flagged any issue with the instruction in Hindi.
“We replaced these covers with new ones on Tuesday evening,” said the official, adding that such covers had been in use for a long time.
A source from the pharmacy section of the hospital claimed that similar covers with instructions in three languages had been in use during the previous regime as well. Meanwhile, pharmacists were instructed not to use the covers with instructions in three languages and use the new ones, containing Tamil and English.
According to CMCH authorities, the hospital handles around 3,000 to 4,500 outpatients a day, and a large number of migrant workers working in the city and nearby areas seek treatment at the hospital.
