In theory, getting a donor liver in the United States when you need one should be an extremely equitable process: The sickest patients with the greatest chance to benefit from a donated organ should jump to the front of the line regardless of their gender, race, or other factors.
The liver transplant system tried to fix its sex bias. Did it work?
The algorithm that ranks candidates just got an update and the results are in.
But in practice, things look quite different.
One study from 2020 showed that women were 8.6 percent more likely than men to die waiting for a liver transplant and 14.4 percent less likely to receive a deceased donor liver transplant compared to men. That gap may not seem enormous, but it still represents a significant disparity. As it turns out, it’s rooted in the very system that’s supposed to make the process fairer, a process that unintentionally ranks women lower on the waitlist for livers.
The system in question is known as the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD). The scoring model has been used since 2002 to rank candidates on the waiting list based on how likely they are to survive without a liver transplant in the short term. The higher your score, the reasoning goes, the sicker you are and the more urgently you need a liver transplant.
One of the values used to calculate the score is creatinine — a waste product made by muscles as they break down proteins or other compounds to release energy. In medicine, the creatinine levels in your blood are used to determine how well your kidneys are functioning because they process and remove creatinine.
And this is where the system designed for equity gets a little less than equitable for some patients.
Creatinine levels are affected by muscle mass, and women typically have lower muscle mass than men. A man and woman experiencing the same level of kidney dysfunction will therefore have different levels of creatinine in the body. The MELD model doesn’t take this difference into account — and so lower levels of creatinine in a woman’s blood can make her seem healthier than she is, bumping her farther down the liver waiting list.
In 2023, Dr. Ray Kim, a transplant hepatologist at Mayo Clinic in Arizona who developed the original system, debuted a new model called MELD 3.0. The model not only seeks to address the sex disparity in liver access but also improve the accuracy of scores for all patients. Among other changes, it takes into account the sex of the transplant candidate and uses it to adjust the MELD score by 1.33 points for women. This is meant to address the difference in creatinine levels between men and women and provide a more accurate understanding of how sick a female patient really is.
Simple fix, right? Even though MELD 3.0 took the sex disparity in liver access seriously and developed changes to combat it, early research on its efficacy found that even this new and improved system hasn’t yet brought men and women to parity on the liver waitlist.
And the problem may lie less with what MELD 3.0 did than with what it did not do, prompting the question: Are we focusing on the wrong problem?
Sex matters…but so does size
Before the MELD score, liver transplants were largely conducted on a first-come, first-served basis. Those who were added to the waiting list first, received livers first. If a really sick candidate was added to the waiting list late, say because of delayed diagnosis, they would almost certainly die while waiting for a liver to become available.
The original MELD fixed that problem by creating a measure of urgency that was easy to calculate. The initial model used three main blood test values — bilirubin, creatinine, and a measure of blood clotting time — and later improvements also took into account the sodium level.
Key takeaways
- Women are more likely than men to die waiting for a liver transplant in part because the system used to rank candidates on the liver waiting list underestimates how sick women are.
- In 2023, the liver transplant system adopted a new version of that scoring model, which adds 1.33 points to women’s scores to correct for differences in muscle mass between the sexes. Early research shows that the new model increased transplant rates for women, but the gains were transient.
- Experts say that the score is only part of the problem. A donated liver has to physically fit inside the body receiving it, so smaller candidates end up waiting longer for a liver they can accept.
- The organ allocation system currently has no way to prioritize smaller livers toward smaller patients, who are more often women. Fixing this is likely the key to ensuring equitable liver access for men and women.
Traditionally, the MELD model assigns a score between 6 and 40 to liver transplant candidates. MELD 3.0 adds 1.33 points to women’s scores to account for the differences in creatinine levels between the sexes. The new model also measures albumin, an additional biomarker, and adjusts for interactions between the different variables.
Sommer Gentry, a professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and contributor to the paper on MELD 3.0, said that using sophisticated algorithms with more biomarkers not only helps to better predict risk for women, but using a more accurate model also benefits the whole population. The researchers estimate that this fine-tuned MELD 3.0 model will reduce at least 20 waiting list deaths per year. Last year, around 800 liver transplant candidates died while waiting for a liver.
But creatinine is only one of the two main problems that create a disparity in liver access for women. The second, Gentry says, is body size, an issue that’s not addressed by MELD 3.0. A transplanted liver has to physically fit inside the body of a recipient, and women are typically smaller than men, so a very large liver cannot be offered to a small woman. But the reverse is not necessarily true because receiving a liver that is small for the potential recipient doesn’t typically harm the candidate.
“The smaller you are, the less likely you are to be offered something that’s actually going to work for you,” Gentry said, adding that women end up waiting longer to receive a liver that will actually fit their body.
Part of the conversation on sex disparity in liver access is based around which of the two problems — creatinine or body-size interventions — to fix first, and whether it is possible to create equity by addressing just one of the two, Gentry said. MELD 3.0 was an attempt to remove the former barrier.
“I think that some other papers are coming out that suggest that perhaps the other aspect of size matching is still a concern and still possibly not addressed by the resulting liver transplant system,” Gentry said.
Why is the new model still falling short?
Gentry believes that MELD 3.0 has increased liver transplant rates for female candidates since its adoption in 2023. But early research, however, suggests that the new model falls short of fixing the problem.
Studies done on MELD 3.0’s impact on liver transplant rates for women indicate that the model increased the number of liver transplants for female candidates — but the gains were short-lived.
An analysis published in July of nearly 10 million daily records from over 60,000 candidates on the US liver transplant registry found that rates of completed liver transplants for women increased in the period immediately after MELD 3.0 was implemented, but the increase was temporary. Women’s estimated odds of receiving a transplant drifted back to pre-MELD 3.0 levels by the end of the study period, 15 months after the new model was implemented. Women on the waiting list and women who had received a transplant also had higher scores in the three months right after MELD 3.0 took effect, but their scores later fell back to levels comparable to those of men.
Both the successes and shortfalls of MELD 3.0 demonstrate how rethinking existing policies and standards can help reduce inequities in organ access and healthcare.
The authors think that the early surge in liver transplant rates for women was a onetime catchup. MELD 3.0 pushed a group of women who had been stuck on the list — sicker than their old scores suggested — over the priority threshold all at once, leading them to receive liver transplants.
Notably, the one effect that did persist was that under MELD 3.0, women received more “organ offers” than before. Every time a deceased donor liver becomes available, the system generates a ranked list of the patients suitable to receive that organ. Under MELD 3.0, the number of times an available liver was offered to a female candidate increased, probably because their (more accurate) MELD 3.0 scores better reflected how sick they were. But they’re not necessarily receiving those livers, presumably because of organ size issues.
These findings suggest that revising the MELD criteria alone may not be enough to eliminate the sex disparity, especially if the body-size disadvantage is part of the problem.
The authors say that a patient’s sex is merely a poor proxy for the real issue — we don’t have allocation systems in place to ensure that candidates with smaller body sizes also have the same robust access to livers.
Toward liver donation equity for all
If we could figure out how to better address questions of body size in organ donation, the benefits could be enormous. According to Gentry, body-size disparity affects the organ allocation system in general. Similar issues arise with heart and lung transplants too, where the size of the organ relative to body size has to be taken into consideration during organ allocation.
She says that a size-aware organ allocation system would therefore benefit patients on the waiting list across the board. Whether an available organ is the right fit for the potential recipient should be weighed heavily in allocation algorithms, rather than just a list of ranked waitlisted candidates.
“That should be a larger consideration in sorting the patients who will be offered a certain organ — to ask if this organ is especially suited to one kind of patient over another,” Gentry said.
Under such a system, she said, smaller livers could be offered first to the smallest candidates on a ranked list of those who are also sickest. The assumption is that a smaller candidate will have to wait longer for a viable liver that fits them, even if they have a very high MELD score.
For such a policy to be instituted, the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network – a nonprofit that oversees the distribution of donor organs — would have to approve it. And before such a system could be presented to the regulatory organization, more research is required.
It is often the case in medicine that our definition of what counts as a healthy body is measured against the average white male. This too often lowers access and quality of care for both women and people of other races. For example, the standards for creatinine levels in blood reduced access to kidney transplants for Black transplant candidates for years until recent efforts were made to start correcting it.
In that sense, both the successes and shortfalls of MELD 3.0 demonstrate how rethinking existing policies and standards can help reduce inequities in organ access and healthcare. The conversations and critiques that followed its rollout have exposed a clear gap in organ allocation strategies, one that disadvantages a large group of patients. Closing that gap, not just in liver transplantation but across the board, could bring us a step closer to equity while also making more efficient use of the organs available to save lives.
“There’s no mechanism right now, if a small liver is available, for offering it preferentially to the small women who might not be able to accept lots of other organs that are becoming available,” Gentry said. While fixing the model to rank women more accurately on the liver waiting list is a start, including body-size considerations in the organ allocation system might be the real bottleneck to address.

- Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 4 introduces Brittle Ice, a fragile block found in the Ice Caves that cracks and breaks under players and most mobs.
- Jukebox Playlists let players automatically play and loop music discs stored in chests placed above the Jukeboxes.
- This snapshot tweaks the freezing mechanics, improves ice block visuals, and changes how Drowned transform in powdered snow.
Minecraft players can now enjoy uninterrupted music sessions and explore a new fragile block with the latest snapshot. The Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 4 introduces Brittle Ice and Jukebox Playlists alongside several tweaks to the freezing mechanics and mobs. If you enjoy building massive structures with the in-game music turned on, this snapshot has something exciting to offer.
Minecraft Gets New Brittle Ice Block and Smarter Jukeboxes
Brittle Ice is a new block that generates naturally in the Minecraft Ice Caves as part of the crevasse feature. Unlike the regular ice blocks, Brittle Ice starts cracking when a player or a mob steps on it and eventually breaks, thereby bringing a new risk-reward mechanic for exploring this biome. However, the Frostbite mob in Minecraft can walk across Brittle Ice without destroying it.
The only way to obtain this block is by using a tool with the Silk Touch enchantment in Minecraft. If you’re wondering how it generates, simply allow water to flow into the Blue Ice block horizontally, and the water block will turn into Brittle Ice. The Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 4 has thus given us a way to make a Brittle Ice farm, similar to how you would make an Obsidian block in Minecraft.
Meanwhile, the Jukebox playlists make the in-game music system more convenient. You can place a Chest, Trapped Chest, or any variant of a Copper Chest directly above the Jukebox to create a playlist using the music discs in Minecraft.
The Jukebox plays the discs in slot order, while skipping the empty slots and non-music items. Once all music discs are played at least once, the playlist loops back to the beginning. Once the Minecraft Jukebox finishes a disc, it swaps the one being played with the next available disc in the chest. If the Jukebox finds no available music disc, it plays the current one again.
Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 4 Tweaks Freezing Mechanics and Mobs
Beyond the two major additions, the new snapshot makes several smaller changes to the blocks and entities introduced in the Minecraft 26.4 update.
Frosted Ice now emits a vibration event when it changes state. On the other hand, Ice, Frosted Ice, and Brittle Ice no longer display their internal block faces when placed next to each other.
Zombies, Drowned, and Husks are now immune to the freezing damage. Therefore, using your new Potions of Freezing in Minecraft will not be a great idea to escape from them.
Another change to the Minecraft mobs is that now, the Drowned transforms into a Zombie before converting into a Frostbite when submerged inside Powder Snow.
Currently, all of these experimental features are available to test by downloading the latest Minecraft 26.4 Snapshot 4. So, what are your thoughts on the new dangerous element brought to the Ice Caves in Minecraft? Tell us in the comments below.

Rory McIlroy says LIV Golf was 'half a good idea, executed poorly' but would welcome players back to DP World Tour
Speaking ahead of DP World India Championship, Rory McIlroy speaks about LIV Golf, saying breakaway was 'half a good idea, executed poorly'; Northern Irishman no longer feels LIV Golf is threat following PIF's withdrawal of support; McIlroy says he would welcome LIV players back
Tuesday 13 October 2026 18:42, UK
Rory McIlroy believes LIV Golf was "half a good idea, executed poorly" and the breakaway is no longer a threat to the traditional game as it tries to relaunch after filing for bankruptcy.
Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) ploughed in £3.7bn over four years, luring the likes of Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau away from the PGA Tour, before withdrawing its support this year.
That led to Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the United States with a view to relaunching as LIV 2.0, having received a potential $300m (£227m) backing from BC Partners Capital providing a specified number of players re-sign for the new venture.
Rahm has already announced he will not be continuing and news this week that any player signing up for LIV will be barred from DP World Tour membership and Ryder Cup eligibility has delivered a crippling blow.
"LIV had probably like, half of a good idea that was executed pretty poorly," McIlroy told the Bloomberg New Economy forum in New Delhi, where he is playing this week in the DP World India Championship.
"They had a lot of capital but I think a lot of that capital was wasted in some ways and I think they could have used that money a lot more strategically and could have partnered with some of the governing bodies of the game and certainly could have done better things with it instead of just enriching tour pros who were already making a lot of money.
"BC Partners have come in and seen an opportunity (but) it looks like every day that goes by there's another player that was on LIV who is not going to join LIV 2.0 so I think it is going to be very difficult to get out of this Chapter 11 bankruptcy and go forward.
"But if they do it is certainly not going to be a threat to the traditional order of the game as it once was."
A more pertinent issue now seems to be what happens to those players quitting LIV.
The PGA Tour invokes a one-year suspension, denying them access until August next year, and while the DP World Tour has stiffened its rules its membership remains divided.
"I'm sure some members who stayed loyal would feel hard done by if these guys can just walk straight back in but, on the other side, having these players back on the tour is good for business and it can drive revenues up and everyone can benefit from that," added McIlroy.
"I would vote for them to come back. A rising tide lifts all boats and I think having some of these players back is beneficial for the business of the tours."
It is not a view shared by six-time DP World Tour winner Joost Luiten.
"Four years ago they didn't give a s*** about the DP World Tour," he told Today's Golfer.
"They made a decision to go after the money and now all of a sudden, the money is gone and they want to come back and act like nothing happened. I don't think that's right.

Pope Leo XIV's surgeon confirmed that he has lung cancer, and he had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, the Vatican said Tuesday (October 13, 2026).
The tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.
The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about 3 hours, the statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said.
Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli Hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localised nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.
The Vatican on Monday cancelled all Leo's audiences through Oct 20.
But the decision to have the operation clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.

Their last victory was against Azerbaijan champions Sabah FK on 10 September. Their only other win this season came against newly promoted Ipswich at Old Trafford, when they had to come from behind.
United finished third in the Premier League last term to seal a Champions League return for the first time in three years.

"Atletico have an amazing team and they deserved to win today.
"I expect more [investment]. 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox].
"I have to be honest, as players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.
"Tonight it is easy to [blame] the coach, easy to say the players but also we have to see other areas."
Martinez's view has been echoed by many external observers and has also been mentioned by some inside Old Trafford.
The failure to bring in striking support for Benjamin Sesko and competition at left-back for Luke Shaw have both been highlighted in a summer when United spent £155m on three midfielders to the exclusion of any other position.
Minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe was sat next to United chief executive Omar Berrada in the Metropolitano Stadium on Tuesday.
"You can't keep changing, changing, changing the manager," said Martinez. "What about other areas? I can't say more.
"Last season we did everything, we created the base to create an amazing team."
Martinez's comments have echoes of similar ones made by his Argentina defensive partner Cristian Romero against the Tottenham board last season.

Martinez has one year left on his United contract and has yet to agree an extension.

Carrick was initially asked for his response live on TV before heading to the post-match news conference where he was questioned about Martinez's comments by three different reporters.

"Straight after the game is not the time to talk about that interview and I can't really comment on that. It's important for us to move forward quickly.
"As group, I don't doubt the togetherness and us wanting to win. I know results-wise, it's easy to look and think there's something deeply wrong, but the players have been great in their willing."
Asked if he would speak to Martinez about his comments, Carrick said: "I need to find out a bit more about it before I can say if and what is going to be done."

Passenger train derails in central Pakistan, killing at least 5 and injuring 35
Officials in Pakistan say a passenger train has derailed, killing five people and injuring 35 others
MULTAN, Pakistan -- MULTAN, Pakistan (AP) — A passenger train derailed in central Pakistan early Tuesday, killing five people and injuring 35 others, police and a Pakistan Railways spokesman said.
The train was traveling from the southern port city of Karachi to the northwestern city of Peshawar when it derailed in Sher Shah city in Punjab province, railway spokesman Kaleem Akhtar said.
Rescuers recovered all four bodies and evacuated the injured from the train’s 14 cars, he said. The injured were taken to a hospital for treatment, but one died before he could be transported, rescue officials said. Emergency responders and paramedics were dispatched to the scene, he said.
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed grief in separate statements and urged authorities to provide the best possible medical care to the injured.
Train accidents are relatively common in Pakistan, where the railway system has suffered from decades of underinvestment, outdated tracks and aging signal systems. In 2023, ten cars of a passenger train derailed in southern Pakistan, killing 30 people and injuring more than 90 others.

Light utility helicopter enters final stages of certification: Officials
The LUH is intended for reconnaissance and surveillance, logistics support, troop movement, casualty evacuation, training, disaster relief, and high-altitude operations
The indigenously developed light utility helicopter (LUH), critical to meeting the operational requirement of the Indian Army and Indian Air Force, has entered the final stages of certification and mission equipment integration, officials familiar with the matter said on Tuesday.
Once the Centre for Military Airworthiness and Certification (CEMILAC) clears the helicopter for induction into service, Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) aims to deliver the first 12 limited series production LUHs to the army and IAF in FY 2027-28, officials said.
“Some improvements are underway to boost the helicopter’s performance and operational capability. Flight testing and certification activities for these enhancements are currently in an advanced stage for issuance of a ‘military type certificate’ by CEMILAC for the LUH’s induction into service,” said one of the officials cited above.
Ongoing flight trials are focused on refining the helicopter’s autorotation characteristics and integrating an automatic flight control system (AFCS) to reduce pilot workload and improve lateral stability, among other things, HT has learnt. Autorotation is an emergency manoeuvre that enables a helicopter to land safely following engine power loss.
CEMILAC’s certification framework for the LUH has been shaped by stringent military airworthiness requirements and the operational demands of Army Aviation, the officials said. Military airworthiness certification requires an aircraft to demonstrate safe and reliable performance across an extensive operational envelope. “For the LUH, this includes operations in hot-and-high conditions, mountainous terrain, and sandy and dusty environments typical of Army Aviation missions,” said a second official.
Operational feedback from the LUH flying units of the two services will be incorporated into subsequent production batches. The state-run aircraft maker expects the army and IAF to place combined orders for at least 187 light helicopters. The LUH is intended for reconnaissance and surveillance, logistics support, troop movement, casualty evacuation, training, disaster relief, and high-altitude operations.
HAL has established dedicated LUH production facilities at Tumakuru, with an initial capacity of around 30 helicopters annually, scalable to about 60 based on future requirements.
LUH will replace the ageing Cheetah and Chetak helicopters, whose safety record has been blemished by a string of crashes. The military is looking at a swift replacement of these helicopters that were designed six decades ago.
The army will begin phasing out its Cheetah and Chetak fleets in a year or two and replace them with LUHs over the next eight to 10 years, as part of the Army Aviation Corps’ drive to modernise its capabilities. The planned two-pronged replacement approach involves inducting LUHs and leasing similar choppers as a stopgap to meet critical requirements.
HAL licence-produced 625 Cheetah and Chetak choppers for use across defence services. It no longer builds them but is responsible for their maintenance and repair. In 1970, HAL signed an agreement with French aerospace firm Aerospatiale to produce Cheetahs, eight years after it partnered with another French firm, Sud-Aviation (now Airbus), to manufacture Chetaks.

Two months after the release of an open letter on potential safety issues tied to a rare disease drug sold by Neurocrine Biosciences, patient advocates and some experts are expressing growing alarm over the perceived risks of the therapy.
The drug, approved to treat Prader-Willi syndrome, which can cause an insatiable feeling of hunger, has been linked to the deaths of seven people and the hospitalization of nearly 100 others — all since the treatment, called Vykat XR, was approved 18 months ago.
Case reports on those deaths and hospitalizations that were submitted to regulators, and that were obtained by STAT through the Freedom of Information Act, do not prove causality; many of the Vykat cases involved complex medical issues and multiple medications. But some experts say the evidence is sufficient to conclude Vykat is causing unacceptable harm.

Man who witnessed deadly roller-coaster fall at Six Flags prays it was 'just a freak accident'
Nick Mendenhall had just ridden Goliath with his son before a man fell to his death
When Nick Mendenhall decided to surprise his 14-year-old son with a trip to Six Flags, he had no idea the day would take a tragic turn.
A 42-year-old man fell to his death on Monday while riding the Goliath roller-coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, north of Atlanta. Police say he was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride.
Six Flags has since closed Goliath and nine similar roller-coasters at six of its North American parks — including two at Canada's Wonderland north of Toronto — while investigators work to determine what went wrong. La Ronde in Montreal has also temporarily closed a roller-coaster that was acquired under the park's previous Six Flags ownership.
Mendenhall had just ridden the Goliath with his son about 15 minutes before the fatal fall, and was watching nearby when it happened. He told As It Happens guest host Dave Seglins what he saw. Here is part of their conversation.
Nick, how are you and your son holding up after what happened?
We're good. I'm still processing. There's been a lot of phone calls and messages and texts [from] people that want to talk to me about everything. And so I'm trying to process it while talking through it. I think it's in some ways, it's a healthy thing. In some ways, I think, it's little bit of a challenge. But I'm good. I am good.
And my son is doing fine.... He didn't see what I saw. He was in line for another ride when it happened. So he did not physically see it.
Can you tell us about the ride a little? Have you ridden the Goliath before?
Yes, probably 20 times in the last eight weeks. We have passes and we go often. And it's one of our favourite rides in the park. We actually had gotten off the ride about ... 10 to 15 minutes before the accident happened.
Was there anything in particular that brought you and your son to the park yesterday?
My son had asked me several times if I would take him to the park on Monday because he didn't have class. And I had told him, no, I didn't think so, I was working.
So I kind of surprised him. I started my work day a little bit early, and at about 1:30, I said, "Hey, bud, let's go to the park."
I was on phone calls and working, and he and I were just hanging, but he was fine with me working. And so when everything happened, I was on a call with a co-worker as I saw it all happen, and I said, "Hey, I gotta get off the phone. A man just fell off the roller-coaster."
Can you tell us what you saw from your spot on the ground?
I can, and I want to try to word this in a way that's respectful and respectable.
I'm standing, I don't know, 30 or 40 feet away from the track, probably. I think I was probably 50 to 100 feet from him. I mean, I was close enough that I knew that he was a middle-aged guy. I knew it was not a kid. I knew there was only one person.
The roller-coaster car comes over a little hill that people were referring to as a bunny hop.... It's basically the last one of the ride, right before the ride ends … and I was just watching the car as it came across the track.
I saw the man come up out of his seat, I mean, almost as if you were hovering because he's moving at the same speed as the car. And his hands are kind of out in front of him. And he, almost in a diving motion, went head-first down into another car. And I was just praying, you know, "God, let this man stay in that car." I knew it was the very end of the ride and I'm thinking, "Man, if they can just hold on to him, maybe he's OK."
As the car coasted up the last little hill, it makes a hard left-hand turn into a straightaway where it brakes and then is the end of the ride. And as it made that turn, I saw him come out of the coaster altogether and fall.
At that point, I only had about a few feet of visual reference because there's a fence between where I was standing and where the track was. There's quite a bit of distance and a fence. So I saw him fall. I could not see him land or anything like that and, quite frankly, I'm glad I didn't. And more than anything, I'm glad my son was in line for another ride and didn't physically see it happen.
Just horrific.
Very, very much.
What went through your mind as you're thinking you're just watching the ride and, suddenly, this person flies out?
I think I was trying to process 150 things at one time. I don't really know what I was thinking. You know, obviously there's an instant adrenaline rush. I mean, I was shaking a little bit.
But I turned. There was a woman there that called 911, and so I didn't call 911, because sometimes the worst thing you can do is have 30 people call 911 for the same problem. There was a park employee walking up the hill. I said something to the park employee, like: "Did you see what just happened?" And they had no idea, the employee that was walking uphill. And I said: "Someone just fell out of Goliath."
I called my wife who was on her way to the park with my other three kids and herself.... I didn't want her to come to the park at that point.
I grabbed my son. He's in line. I go up to the entrance of that line and I call his name and I say, "Hey, I need you to come here a minute."
And, you know, [it's] very calm. No one's really panicking on the ground because I don't think very many people saw what happened.… I'm not sure anyone else really saw it the way that I did.
Do you have any sense of what went wrong?
None. And I don't want to speculate. So many people were posting that it was the park employees not doing their job, and they were saying just things that were just, there's no way anyone could know.
We go so often and I've never experienced a feeling of unsafe behaviour from the employees. I've never thought that they weren't doing their job. I mean, most of these are high school kids and young adults that are working their jobs for the summer and … we need to be worried about what they saw and what they experienced from a trauma perspective, not pointing fingers at them.
I hope it comes out what the cause was. And, man, I hope and pray that it was just a freak accident and it was no one's fault.
But even if it was, man, to be pointing fingers and saying things like that, that those kids will probably hop on social media and they'll see, is just, it's so sensationalist. It's so just heartbreaking.

Early voting in the U.S. midterm elections is underway. Voters are deciding which party will control Congress, as well as numerous state legislatures and governors' offices. Snopes' fact-checkers are flagging rumors surrounding the election, debunking false statements by candidates and suspicious voter fraud claims with nonpartisan research and expert sources. Join our effort to keep this election fact-focused by becoming a Snopes member.
Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, some social media users are warning that any election ballot marked by a poll worker could be disqualified, whether it is "a letter, a checkmark, a star, an R or a D any writing of any kind."
The rumor has spread on numerous occasions. Snopes addressed the claim before both the 2020 and 2024 elections. Posts typically feature the same copypasta, shown below (emphasis ours):
A very reliable good friend of mine just finished the pollworker training, and she texted this to me ....."Just finished Poll Manager training! I passed all the classes. I want you all to know something...when you are checking in at the polls and they happen to write anything on your ballot before they give it to you to put in the voting machine...a letter, a checkmark, a letter star, an R or a D any writing of any kind...please request a new ballot. Your ballot will be disqualified if it is written on. Please be on the look out. Make sure poll workers do not write on your ballot. It will cause your ballot to be disqualified."
Please forward this to everyone you know. Make sure poll workers do not write on your ballot. It will cause your ballot to be disqualified.
(Facebook)
The rumor is not true. Many election officials have clarified that a poll worker marking a ballot does not disqualify it. It was not possible to find any evidence of a U.S. state disqualifying ballots containing markings, unless it renders the voter's selections unreadable. Several states (such as North Carolina) actually require poll workers to mark ballots as part of the verification process.
In 2024, Commissioner Ben Hovland, chairman of the U.S. Election Assistance Commission, reportedly told Reuters some marks that poll workers add are acceptable and that rules regarding markings usually have to do with the voter's identity. Snopes contacted the EAC seeking comment. We will update this article if we receive a response.
When addressing the rumor ahead of previous elections, we spoke to several officials who confirmed the rumor is false.
Spokespeople for the Maryland State Board of Elections and Maine's Bureau of Corporations, Elections and Commissions said the claim is misleading. Laws governing elections in Minnesota, Missouri (PDF page 108, Section 2 of "Counting of Votes") and Texas (PDF Page 7) also require poll workers to mark ballots.
Debra O'Malley, communications director for the Office of the Secretary of the Commonwealth in Massachusetts, told Snopes in 2020 (detail in brackets ours):
There is no reason any poll worker [in Massachusetts] would ever mark anything on a ballot, with the very rare exception of a challenged ballot. If a ballot is challenged for legal cause, the voter's name and address, as well as the challenger's, are written on the ballot to be reviewed only in the case of a recount or court order. Again, this is very rare.
She continued: "Ballots are not disqualified at the polling place. If a tabulator cannot read a ballot, the voter is offered a new ballot. If they do not want to spoil their ballot, it is set aside to be counted by hand at the end of the night."
We reached out to O'Malley for an updated comment. We will add her response if she replies.

Canada is front and centre in Nevada's midterm elections amid anger over Trump-induced travel slump
Canadian travel to Las Vegas continues to crater amid U.S. President Donald Trump's attacks on Canada, and the tourism slump in Sin City has become a major midterm election issue.
Nevada Democrats are trying to capitalize on the decline, blaming Trump's trade war and threats toward Canada — the state's largest source of international tourists.
"The Trump Slump is real, and Las Vegas tourism is tanking," the party said in one of its campaign messages ahead of the November vote in this crucial swing state.
"Nevadans are struggling under Trump's tourism crisis," is another line the party has deployed as it puts the fractured relationship with Canada front and centre in this election.
Pedestrians cross an overpass along the Las Vegas Strip, with the Trump International Hotel visible in the background. Nevada Democrats are trying to capitalize on the economic fallout from Trump's trade war with Canada, which they blame for hurting tourism. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)
The party and its ally, the powerful Culinary Workers Union Local 226, which represents about 60,000 casino and hospitality workers in the state, are trying to tie the decline in Canadian tourism to local Trump allies such as incumbent Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, who is in a suddenly close race despite his earlier popularity.
"Donald Trump is directly responsible for this — it's all his fault and it's totally unnecessary," Diana Valles, the president of the union, said in an interview with CBC News.
"God knows why he's doing it, Canadians are our biggest customer. But, at the end the day, Trump's not paying any price. It's the workers and the families that are here," she said, while vowing to ramp up attacks on the GOP as the midterms loom to at least inflict an electoral price.
Visitor numbers, airport arrivals and hotel occupancy rates all fell again in August. Barely half of all rooms in downtown Las Vegas were occupied that month, and casino executives are pointing to the Canadian boycott as one reason for weak demand.
Canadian visits to Las Vegas dropped by 17.4 per cent last year — easily one of the sharpest declines on record. In fact, Canadians staying away contributed to the largest in drop in visitors outside the COVID-19 pandemic since the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority began keeping records in 1970.
Data from Harry Reid International Airport compiled by CBC News shows Canadian airlines are bringing even fewer passengers to Las Vegas than in 2025, suggesting this year could be even worse.
"If you look at a place like Canada, we are off considerably," MGM Resorts CEO Bill Hornbuckle said on the gambling giant's recent earnings call. "Las Vegas is still down on international travel."
In an Oval Office meeting with Trump in September, Hornbuckle said a travel industry plan to draw 100 million international visitors to the U.S. each year depends on the president's actions.
"Travel is difficult," he said. "We need your help, we need your direct involvement, and we know we can make this better."
Trump's one-word response: "Right."
People walk along Fremont Street Experience past an animatronic Donald Trump fortune-telling machine modelled after the classic Zoltar arcade figure in June 2026, in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)
Caesars Resorts CEO Tom Reeg characterized it this way when discussing the company's recent quarterly loss: "There's a unique flavour to what's gone on with Canada."
What's unique is travel from Canada has fallen far more than from any other country tracked by local authorities. Visits from Mexico, which is also caught up in a tariff dispute with the U.S., are actually up slightly year over year.
Martyn Daly of Winnipeg made annual trips to Vegas for years but has avoided the city since Trump began lashing out at Canada, threatening its sovereignty and imposing tariffs.
"We're just so upset with Trump's total lack of respect, the way he's been treating Canada — he's just totally lost it," Daly said in an interview.
"We don't agree with the 51st state stuff," he said. "Not going to Vegas is just our small way of saying, 'We're not going to take it.'"
Daly is happy to see that Trump's treatment of Canada has become an election issue in Nevada.
"I just think the more pressure he's under, the better," he said of the president.
Daly is facing some pressure of his own: he's been bombarded with casino offers for complimentary nights at various hotels, deals he says are noticeably better than before the Canada-U.S. dispute began. Some casinos have even been accepting the Canadian dollar at par.
As Canadians such as Daly stay away, some casino workers say the official numbers don't fully capture the impact on a city that has long relied on visitors from its northern neighbour.
Spencer Ridenour, a bartender at Chandelier inside the Cosmopolitan casino on the Strip, said his workplace is "losing customers left and right."
A Vegas Golden Knights hockey game did not sell out Thursday, the first time that's ever happened in the franchise's nine-year history. The team's opponent? The Toronto Maple Leafs.
"We used to have Canadians coming for hockey games, they used to come out before and after a game. I have not ID'ed a Canadian in months — this is serious stuff, it's not good for our economy," he said.
Patrons exit the Cosmopolitan hotel on Las Vegas Boulevard in Las Vegas in August 2026. Visitor numbers to the city have fallen 7.5 per cent — the largest decline outside the COVID-19 pandemic since the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority began keeping records in 1970. (Frederic J. Brown/AFP/Getty Images)
Nevada's unemployment rate is among the highest in the U.S., and workers in its tourism-dominated economy are reporting more frequent shift cuts and fewer hours.
"Our members are paying the price of this craziness that is going on in the White House," Valles said.
Republicans in the state have highlighted Trump's "no tax on tips" policy, enacted last year, which has benefitted hospitality workers in Las Vegas in particular.
But if the tips dry up, the policy means less.
"We are in a silent recession here in Las Vegas, and it is because of Donald Trump’s trade war," Ridenour said.
A spokesperson for the state's Republican governor did not respond to a request for comment.
People walk along Las Vegas Boulevard in Las Vegas in August 2026. (Frederic J. Brown/AFP/Getty Images)
Canada has also become an election issue in closely fought congressional races.
Democratic Rep. Susie Lee, who faces a tight race in her suburban Las Vegas district, is leaning into an anti-trade war message. In her 30-second campaign ad, Lee twice mentions the trade war and says her Republican opponent, Marty O'Donnell, supports Trump's "expensive" tariffs on Canadian and other goods.
O'Donnell has defended Trump's trade policy as "a form of diplomacy to level the playing field on trade or to protect our national security."
David Damore, a political science professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, said it's unusual for Canada to factor into any U.S. election, let alone become a significant talking point in a key battleground state.
"The Democrats are certainly playing this up quite a bit. And these races probably wouldn't be as close if it weren't for the tariffs and the lack of Canadians coming across the border," Damore said.
People walk through the casino floor at Resorts World Las Vegas. Political observers say locals are well aware of the drop in Canadian visitors — and that it could influence the midterm election results. (Bridget Bennett/AFP/Getty Images)
He said locals are well aware of the absence of Canadian visitors, making the issue easy for Democrats to campaign on.
"So, between the tariffs, the high gas prices, the decline in visitation, it's really combustible for the Republicans out here right now," he said.
But even if the Democrats take control in Nevada or D.C., he's not expecting much to change.
"There's nothing they can do about a president who goes out of his way to insult our neighbour and one of our biggest allies."

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.

Loneliness among parents whose adult children have migrated abroad is associated with higher psychological distress, difficulties in regulating emotions and problematic series watching, an exploratory study by researchers from NIMHANS has found.
The findings assume relevance on World Mental Health Day, observed on October 10, which draws attention to mental health and the need to address psychological well-being. The study highlights the emotional challenges that parents may experience when their children settle abroad and everyday family interactions become less frequent.
64 ‘empty-nest’ parents
Published in BMC Research Notes, the study examined 64 ‘empty-nest’ parents aged between 45 and 65, whose adult children had emigrated and lived away from home for at least two years. The sample comprised 30 fathers and 34 mothers from different families in Karnataka, Haryana and Punjab. Most belonged to middle socioeconomic backgrounds and nuclear families, and more than half had been in the empty-nest phase for over five years.
Rajesh Kumar, associate professor in the department of clinical psychology at NIMHANS and the corresponding author of the study, said the findings highlighted the relationship between loneliness and emotional well-being among parents adjusting to life without their children at home.
“We found a significant association between loneliness and psychological distress. Loneliness was also associated with difficulties in emotion regulation and problematic series watching, which refers to excessive or difficult-to-control viewing that interferes with everyday functioning. This also resulted in the risk of developing non-communicable diseases (NCDs),” he said.
Loneliness significantly predicted psychological distress even after accounting for age and gender. Of the 64 participants, 22 (34.3%) were classified as having higher levels of loneliness, while 42 (65.7%) fell into the lower-loneliness group. Those reporting higher loneliness also reported greater psychological distress, more difficulties in regulating emotions and higher levels of problematic series watching, Mr. Kumar said.
Social changes
Manoj Kumar Sharma, professor in the department of clinical psychology at NIMHANS and head of its SHUT Clinic, said the findings needed to be understood in the context of the emotional and social changes that parents may experience when their children settle abroad.
Dr. Sharma, who is one of the authors, cautioned that the study did not establish that loneliness causes psychological distress or excessive series watching. As it was cross-sectional, it could identify associations but not determine the direction of the relationships, he said.
Mothers reported greater loneliness
Women in the study reported significantly higher levels of loneliness and psychological distress than men.
The researchers said that this was consistent with earlier research suggesting that mothers may experience greater emotional difficulties during the empty-nest phase, potentially reflecting their involvement in caregiving and emotional relationships with their children.
Possible coping mechanism
The researchers said digital media and streaming services could provide an easily accessible form of solitary leisure for parents experiencing less day-to-day interaction with their children.
However, the study did not examine why participants watched series or whether they used viewing deliberately to cope with loneliness or negative emotions. The researchers cautioned against assuming that excessive viewing was necessarily a coping response.
Other factors that could influence media use include social support, physical mobility, retirement, living arrangements, marital relationships, the frequency and quality of communication with adult children, and access to technology.
Social and psychological support
The findings underline the need to pay greater attention to the emotional well-being of parents whose children migrate abroad, as changing family structures and international migration can reduce opportunities for regular face-to-face interaction, Dr. Sharma said.
The authors said interventions to strengthen social connectedness, promote adaptive emotion-regulation strategies and encourage healthier technology use could potentially help parents navigate the empty-nest transition.

- A new report suggests Rockstar plans to release GTA 6 on PC in Q1 2027.
- GamesBeat's latest report cites four sources close to Rockstar and familiar with the studio's plans.
- The sources chose to remain anonymous to “avoid damaging business relationships.”
PC players may not have to wait a year or two for the release of GTA 6, as a new report suggests the PC version will launch within the first three months of 2027. Previous reports claimed GTA 6 PC could release sooner due to rising console costs, and the latest report gives a new release window: Q1 2027, or between January and March next year.
GameBeat’s latest report, published on October 13, 2026, says Rockstar plans to release the highly anticipated GTA 6 PC port a few months after its November 19, 2026, console debut, particularly within the first three months of 2027.
According to the outlet, the report comes from four sources familiar with Rockstar’s plans who have chosen to remain anonymous to “avoid damaging business relationships.”
Of course, this doesn’t guarantee that GTA 6’s PC version is dropping early next year, but over the past few weeks, multiple reports have stated the same. So, the report carries definite weight. This would also mean Rockstar is finally breaking its tradition of bringing its GTA games to PC nearly a year or two after the initial release.
The PC launch could also coincide with the launch of GTA 6 Online multiplayer, which Twitch CEO Dan Clancy says is coming in 2027. It all lines up perfectly, and we might even hear updates on the PC port during Take-Two’s November 9 earnings call, which takes place 10 days before GTA 6’s global launch on consoles.
If the open-world title releases on PC in early 2027, it would likely be the first platform to run the game at 60 fps. Rockstar has already confirmed that GTA 6 is locked at 30 fps at launch on all consoles, including the PS5 Pro.
So a PC version will definitely surpass a console’s performance barrier. Now, all we need is an official update from Rockstar, and PC players can finally start warming up their rigs for Vice City.

Mrunal Thakur has addressed speculation about her possible involvement in Allu Arjun and Atlee’s upcoming film Raaka, but has stopped short of confirming whether she is part of the project. Mrunal Thakur neither confirms nor denies Raaka casting rumours, says film announcements will come on social media

Mrunal Thakur wants to enjoy the process of acting
Beyond the speculation surrounding her next projects, Mrunal spoke about her approach to choosing films and learning from each experience. She said, “I just want to enjoy the process. Apple’s ad introducing its new HomeView smart display is a little unusual. It’s fast-paced and unruly, depicting a family of five as they rush through the morning routine. There’s yelling and mess, misplaced keys and discarded eggshells. Apple’s typical vibe is clean, simple, orderly; this commercial is chaos.
Apple’s HomeView ad is confusing to everyone except parents
The chaos is surprisingly real for an Apple commercial.
But the spot has parents — those with teen children in particular — feeling seen.
I’ll admit that it stressed me out the first time I watched it, too. Mornings getting my five-year-old out the door are a special breed of chaos, and usually culminate in us playing whatever ad-libbed game will get him to put his shoes on. But it’s not quite as intense as this one, which features dad making french toast, mom losing and finding keys in her pocket, a proxy battle over the thermostat, a teenage boy helping himself to whipped cream from a can, and an unexpected video call. There’s also a microdrama about the daughter’s ride to school with a boyfriend nobody knew about that ends with everyone gathered around the HomeView watching the security camera feed of the two of them departing the porch. It’s a lot for just over three minutes of screen time.
If I know anything though, I know to trust my colleague, senior reviewer and parent to two teens, Jen Tuohy on matters of the home. Her take? “The most unrealistic part of the video is that no one is holding an iPhone.”
Other parents of teens shared similar reactions on Threads. When tech analyst Benedict Evans posted about the ad feeling stressful and confusing, CNET editor at large Bridget Carey chimed in to defend it, saying “It was exactly what my morning is like and it was the most real ad I’ve ever seen from Apple.” Others agreed, calling it “accurately captured” and that it “hit home,” no pun intended, at least I think.
Even if Apple didn’t need to do much to heighten the stakes of a family getting out the door, there is of course plenty of sleight-of-hand at work when it comes to making the HomeView appear so essential. The family has seemingly drilled a hole directly into the middle of their kitchen island to accommodate the charging cable, for one. And what sibling is going to check a text message from a secret boyfriend on the communal kitchen screen with their brother sitting at arm’s length? I don’t believe any teenager trusts Apple’s privacy features that far.
The confusion about the commercial is understandable. This is a far cry from the quiet luxury lifestyle everyone seems to enjoy in Apple’s Vision Pro ads. There’s also Evans’ observation that the HomeView doesn’t really solve any of the problems that come up throughout the coarse of the video. In the case of a spontaneous FaceTime call from the grandparents, the screen in the middle of the kitchen seems to make things worse.
But maybe morning chaos isn’t the problem that’s being solved. If the alternative is five people all interacting with their own phones, then the HomeView presents a different picture where everyone gets the essential information they need from one shared screen and stays more present.
A screen that makes you be more present is a lovely idea, but the real test will come when it’s in in real households. Is the HomeView going to be enough to convince families to put their personal devices down? Will everyone just ignore it and keep scrolling on their own iPhones? These are questions worth answering before you start drilling holes in your kitchen island! In any case, an ungovernable morning routine is probably a feature of a busy household, not a bug. Just ask a parent.

Katrina Kaif recently made a rare public appearance following her pregnancy, which led to discussions about her appearance on social media. The actress faced body-shaming and online trolling, with several users comparing her recent pictures with older photographs. Amid the criticism, actor Richa Chadha has spoken out against those targeting women over changes in their bodies after motherhood.
Richa Chadha slams trolls body-shaming Katrina Kaif after pregnancy; says, “They are just losers and they deserve to be ignored”
In a conversation with India Today, Richa, who became a mother in 2024, addressed the issue of body-shaming and questioned the tendency to criticise actresses who balance their personal lives with their professional commitments. She also argued that such behaviour does not necessarily originate within the film industry, pointing instead to social media users who target celebrities.
Richa said, "See, I don't think women should listen to anybody commenting on their body. The industry is very respectful of women who have babies and who have careers. All the fantastic actresses from Madhuri to Juhi Chawla to Rani Mukherjee, Sonali Bendre. I don't think it's the industry. It's the common man of India who is ugly and balding and has a disgusting paunch who thinks that commenting on Katrina Kaif or Aishwarya Rai is somehow making his life better. It's so funny. I find it really useless, and I honestly do think that it deserves much less space even in media discourse."
Richa Chadha Says Online Trolls ‘Are Just Losers’
The actor also pointed to the anonymity offered by social media, which allows people to post critical comments about celebrities without revealing their identities. She said that such users often believe they have the freedom to judge people who have achieved considerable recognition in their respective fields.
Richa added, "Industry is not like this. It's common people who have been emboldened by the anonymity of social media. Who think that they have hit the jackpot by leaving anonymous comments. They are beggars in their lives. But they think that they can talk about people who are like Miss World and Miss Universe. Like we owe them something. That's not how the world works. They are just losers and they deserve to be ignored."
Katrina Kaif Addresses Online Trolling
Meanwhile, Katrina Kaif recently spoke about online criticism during an event in the UK. The actress emphasised the importance of not allowing social media narratives to influence one's self-worth or personal decisions.
She said, "I think we really need to be careful in letting the narrative on social media affect our self-worth. If we start trying to cater to all of them, I think that really hampers your ability to make choices for yourself. Personally, if every time I face critique or comments, I let that dictate my actions, I think I would have been paralysed with fear and unable to move ahead in my life,"
Both actors have addressed the impact of online commentary on women, with Richa calling for body-shaming to be given less attention and Katrina highlighting the importance of making personal choices without being influenced by social media criticism.

Australian freed from Iraq thanks family after landing in Ireland
- Published
Australian engineer Robert Pether has landed in Ireland after he was allowed to leave Iraq where he was arrested and detained five years ago.
The 51-year-old was jailed on fraud charges in 2021 alongside a colleague amid a contract dispute between the consulting firm he worked for and the Central Bank of Iraq.
The UN has said Pether's detention was illegal, and an international court has ruled his employer is not responsible for the business disagreement.
Shortly after arriving at Dublin Airport on Monday morning, local time, Pether was reunited with his family and thanked his wife and children who "have lived this every single day with me".
"Our children lost years with their dad," Pether, whose family lives in Ireland, said, fighting back tears.
"They watched their mum fight every day to try and bring me home. They grew up with uncertainty, fear and circumstances that no child should ever have to carry."
Describing his wife Desree as "incredible", Pether said her tireless years-long efforts to have him freed while also "holding our family together" had taken an "enormous toll on her too".
Hours after his release, Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong said it followed "many years of persistent advocacy" by Canberra and the Irish authorities.
"I spoke to Mr Pether shortly before his departure from Baghdad and am pleased he is now free to move forward with his life," she said.
"I'm hugely relieved," his wife Desree told the BBC in a statement before her husband landed.
"It's been an absolute nightmare, especially these last few months. So many obstacles and plot twists right up to the last minute."
Pether was conditionally released from prison in Iraq last year, but barred from leaving the country, with Canberra at the time saying he continued to face the prospect of more legal proceedings.
Pether worked in the Middle East for almost a decade before taking on a huge rebuild of the Central Bank of Iraq's Baghdad headquarters in 2015.
He was arrested alongside his CME Consulting colleague, Egyptian Khalid Radwan, after the bank accused the men of stealing money from the project.
After being held without charge for almost six months, and then subjected to a speedy trial, the two were each given a five-year jail sentence and a joint fine of $12m (A$18.4m, £8.8m). The BBC was unable to confirm whether Radwan was also released.
However, a 2022 report from the UN determined that the case contravened international law, and that Pether and Khalid had been subjected to "abusive and coercive" interrogations.
Iraq's government has previously denied allegations of ill treatment.
In 2023, the International Chamber of Commerce's (ICC) Court of Arbitration ruled that Iraq's central bank was at fault in the dispute with CME, and ordered it to pay $13m to the company.

Cornell bans all fraternity parties over gang sex assault allegations
- Published
Cornell University is banning all parties at fraternity houses as the school faces backlash over its handling of an alleged sexual assault on campus two years ago.
Last month, a woman known as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging she was plied with drugs and raped by several men in 2024 at a party at a Cornell fraternity house.
In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell's president, Michael Kotlikoff, announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including the end to fraternity parties for the rest of the school year.
"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," he said.
"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added.
Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals.
In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims".
"While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra.
Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended.
The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well.
Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault.
The president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus.
These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said.
Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations.
Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe.
State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case.
Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship".
He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.
