Everton up for sale again - so what next as owners TFG look for a way out?
- Published
When Everton's owners The Friedkin Group released a 170-word statement on Friday morning announcing they were effectively putting the club up for sale, it was as low-key and underwhelming as their tenure on Merseyside.
TFG, also owners of AS Roma in Italy's Serie A, paid more than £400m for a 99.5% share of Everton in December 2024, releasing the club from the financial crisis and toxicity that characterised the final days of Farhad Moshiri's chaotic regime.
It was meant to be the start of a bold new era for the club as they waited to move out of Goodison Park into a magnificent new stadium at Bramley Moore Dock.
Instead, TFG will now test the market, with football finance expert Kieran Maguire telling BBC Sport he expected them to seek a price between £750m and £800m for a complete sale, taking on current debts of around £468m.
In contrast to the high hopes and confidence that accompanied their arrival, TFG have effectively been absentee owners focusing their efforts on Roma - a stance illustrated by the fact chairman Dan Friedkin has never attended an Everton game or, even more startlingly, never spoken to manager David Moyes since he arrived back at the club in January 2025.
Moyes made that revelation in the aftermath of a botched summer transfer window that transformed the relationship between Everton's fans and TFG from cold acceptance to outright toxicity.
- Everton owners consider selling club two years after takeover 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Everton told to pay Burnley £35m over PSR breach 
  - Published10 June
Armstrong fiasco beginning of the end
The catalyst was TFG's attempt to sell teenager Harrison Armstrong, one of the finest products of Everton's Academy in recent years, to Nottingham Forest in a £40m deal.
The move was agreed by TFG until news leaked out, prompting loud threats of "a riot" from Everton fans during the game at Bournemouth later that day.
Such was the reaction, TFG went into damage limitation mode to block the deal for the 19-year-old midfielder, but it was little more than a face-saving PR exercise after a catastrophic decision that instantly alienated the fanbase.
Everton then sold Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65m and striker Beto - hardly elite but a recognised striker - to Fiorentina, before a move for Monaco forward Folarin Balogun collapsed with no time to seek alternatives.
It left Moyes a striker light and with only 18 senior outfield players. From that moment the credits were rolling for TFG, leading to the announcement they are looking to sell their stake in the club.
Why have TFG decided now is the time to sell?
Maguire said: "I think there are various factors at play. I suspect they were shocked by having to pay Burnley more than £35m for a breach of financial rules."
In 2024 Everton were found to have broken Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) over a three-year period. Burnley argued the breach had impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League in the 2021-22 season and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.
TFG injected £38m into the club to cover the cost, while Everton have subsequently appealed.
"I think that perhaps they thought English football was going to become as litigious as trying to operate in the United States," added Maguire. "This will not have appealed to them.
"It is also a good time to sell because it is such a buoyant market. The Americans will be interested. There are only 20 Premier League clubs you can buy. There are lots of potential buyers out there. There is that scarcity factor.
"I'd say TFG will look for £750m to £800m to sell. It can take 5 billion dollars or even more to buy a sporting franchise in the United States.
"I think they can see this as something they can flip - in other words, buy low and sell high."
What TFG have brought to Everton is a measure of financial stability following Moshiri's era of crisis, which Maguire believes will make them an attractive proposition to potential suitors.
"Everton have history and heritage," he said. They are Premier League perennials. They look like they will stay there and they have a passionate fanbase who fill a superb 50,000-plus stadium.
"You are not having to spend money on an upgrade of that stadium. I have a lot of respect for the finance people at the club. Unlike some of the chaos of Moshiri and what he left behind, you can lift up the carpet now at Everton and nothing unpleasant will come out.
"To paraphrase a former Prime Minister, you have got an 'over ready' football club coming on to the market. If you are an owner who wants to accelerate things at a football club, you have a starting point for that.
"And my start point for potential buyers would be the States."
There is no doubt, however, that Houston-based TFG's relationship with those back at base on Merseyside hinted at the dysfunctional.
The lack of a close relationship with manager Moyes was again emphasised when he admitted he only heard about Everton's potential sale at the same time as the wider public - only adding to the sense of disconnect between TFG and the club, compared to how they work at Roma.
Speaking at his press conference before Sunday's match away at Hull, Moyes said: "I'm disappointed that Evertonians have to go through another period of 'who are our owners?'
"I truly believed with new ownership we were in it completely. My ambition coming back was trying to get Everton back to the levels they have been in the past, and that is challenging for Europe more often.
"It has been a difficult summer for us. I only found out this morning. Maybe, I am a little bit surprised, but maybe I shouldn't be that surprised."
On TFG's approach, Maguire added: "They have not really engaged with the club or Liverpool as a city. Dan Friedkin has never been to an Everton game, which shows the difference.
"With Roma, they have got a club in the Champions League - with all that entails financially - and one with a far greater chance of being there on a regular basis which, and we are only stating a fact, is not the case with Everton."
How will TFG's tenure be remembered?
"With a mixture of disappointment and indifference," added Maguire. "I think they now have the right people at Everton, while I think under the Moshiri regime there were some there for decoration rather than substance."
TFG will hope to do a quick deal.
"Because so much due diligence has been done by the Friedkins themselves, all of the gremlins will have been highlighted and dealt with," said Maguire.
"It is now down to satisfying the Premier League's owners and directors' scenario. Are you a wrong 'un? Do you have the money? Can you prove where the money has come from - not just to buy the club but to run it?"
And Moyes is happy to give a reference as he added: "I'm looking forward to getting the right people in to take the club further forward.
"It's a great club. If anyone wants to speak to me then I will be the first person to let them know that it is certainly worth buying."

Martin Shkreli—the ex-pharmaceutical executive infamous for illegally hiking the price of a lifesaving anti-parasitic drug by more than 4,000 percent and getting a seven-year prison sentence for the fraudulent scheme he used to do it—has been under a lifetime ban from the pharmaceutical industry since 2022.
However, according to the Federal Trade Commission and the attorneys general of seven states, Shkreli has “flagrantly and repeatedly” violated that ban nearly the entire time—allegedly by trading stock in dozens of drug companies and discussing the industry during livestreams on social media.
On Tuesday, the FTC and the seven states asked a federal judge to hold Shkreli in contempt for the alleged violations. The states include New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Virginia—the same states that joined the FTC in suing Shkreli in 2020 over the “elaborate anticompetitive scheme” involving the anti-parasitic drug, Daraprim. The scheme raised the price from $17.50 per pill to $750 per pill virtually overnight, while blocking generic competitors from entering the market.
“Egregious” conduct
In 2022, the federal court recognized the “seriousness” of issuing such a lifetime industry ban, but ruled that “Shkreli’s egregious, deliberate, repetitive, long-running, and ultimately dangerous illegal conduct warrants imposition of an injunction of this scope.” The ban, among many things, “explicitly prohibits” Shkreli from owning stock in pharmaceutical companies and making public statements that could influence a pharmaceutical company’s business, according to the FTC and the states.
With the alleged violations, the FTC and the states are now seeking to force Shkreli to divest from all pharmaceutical companies and pay a fine equal to his profits from trading pharmaceutical company stocks. They also want the court to lay out “clear and escalating consequences” if Shkreli violates the ban in the future, including further financial penalties and incarceration.

A video showing a few men unloading garbage on the road is being shared with the claim that Municipal Corporation vehicles are littering the roads leading to Jantar Mantar before the student protests (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.

Fact: These visuals show sanitation workers in Panipat, Haryana, protesting by dumping garbage on the road at Samvidhan Chowk on GT Road in August 2026. According to these reports, sanitation workers in Panipat, Haryana, protested by dumping garbage on the road at Samvidhan Chowk on GT Road. The protest was part of their agitation over various pending demands, involving sanitation, sewer, and fire department workers.
Based on these reports, we geolocated the protest site to Samvidhan Chowk on GT Road in Panipat, Haryana. A comparison of the viral video with the geolocated location is shown below.
To sum up, this video shows sanitation workers’ protest in Panipat; It’s not related to the Delhi protest.

Honey bees are known to leave their stingers embedded in tender flesh once they sting you and fly away. Scientists have now determined that the stinger is able to continue pumping venom into its unfortunate victim even after the bee flies away, thanks to a unique double-piston pump-like mechanism, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Different species have evolved different mechanisms for delivering venom, which involves piercing the skin and then pumping venom from a gland or reservoir. Spiders, for instance, have muscles surrounding their venom glands, which contract and eject venom through hollow fangs. Bees, wasps, and ants deliver venom via their stingers, either by contracting muscles around the venom reservoir or through stiff elements called lancets working together to pump venom.
Honey bees (Apis mellifera) add a unique feature: Worker bees fly away after inserting their stingers in the target, leaving the stinger behind. The stinger continues to penetrate the tissue and pump venom on its own, a rare phenomenon known as autotomy. A honey bee’s stinger has three main interlocking elements that form the venom canal: a stylet that widens to form the main pumping chamber and two sharp-tipped lancets that slide back and forth, piercing the tissue and pumping venom into the target. But the precise mechanism by which the pumping action is achieved has never been directly observed.
The authors of this latest paper sought to capture the venom-pumping kinematics of honey bee stingers in order to identify the underlying biomechanics. They collected live worker bees and removed the stingers with forceps just prior to filming. Then they partially inserted those stingers into blocks of artificial gel and captured the pumping action using stereomicroscopy and high-speed color videography. This was followed by a frame-by-frame analysis to better track the movement, which is visible because the structures are semi-translucent.

Apple TV 4K 2022 vs. 2026: What's new and is it worth the $100 jump?
The 2026 model is faster and can hear you from afar, but the 2022 box gets Siri AI as well.
It's taken Apple four years to bring us a new version of the Apple TV 4K, and along with it comes a now all-too-familiar price rise. The fourth-gen box Apple announced today is $299, a $100 jump over the cheapest previous-gen model. The sticker price is actually more than twice what the 2022 version cost at the start of the year, before the summer price increase. It's set to be released on November 13 with a faster A19 chip and built-in mics for talking to Siri without the remote.
If you've already got the 2022 or short-lived 2021 model, there's some good news: Siri AI, the chattier assistant Apple has built this launch around, is coming to your box in an update. And the new remote, the one that's much harder to lose, supports older devices and is being sold on its own.
What's new for 2026?
Apple has swapped out the A15 Bionic chip from the 2022 model and replaced it with the A19, claiming that it's up to 50 percent faster at CPU tasks and twice as fast at graphics. In iPhone terms, it's like jumping from an iPhone 13 to an iPhone 17. The A19 also comes with double the RAM and a dedicated decoder for AV1, a newer video compression format that lets services stream at high quality over less bandwidth. Wireless networking has also seen a boost, with Wi-Fi 6 upgraded to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5 upgraded to Bluetooth 6. Thread support remains unchanged.
Away from the chip upgrades, three new mics are built into the box and can hear a Siri request over whatever's playing. In contrast, the 2022 box has no mics, and using Siri features requires holding a button on the remote and speaking to it. The remote for the fourth-gen also adds Precision Finding, which lets an iPhone lead you to wherever you've lost it, and can play a sound. That feature does need an iPhone 17 or later, an iPhone Air or an iPhone Duo, though. It doesn't work on the 17e. The new Siri remote costs $59 when purchased separately and supports all Apple TV 4K models plus the 2015 Apple TV HD.
For the first time, you can hook up four HomePods to work as a surround sound system, two in front and two behind. To do that though, you'll need the fourth-gen box and either HomePod mini 2 or second-gen HomePod speakers in matching pairs. Previously, you could only connect HomePods to an Apple TV 4K in a stereo pair.
What the extra $100 gets you
Apple refreshed the Apple TV 4K for Siri AI, but the fine print says the assistant is available on all Apple TV 4Ks from the second-gen onward. Old box or new, whoever is set as the home's owner needs an iPhone or iPad that supports Apple Intelligence, and at launch it works only in English across eight countries. The new Siri Remote works with the 2022 box too, but neither generation goes past 4K, and both handle Dolby Vision, HDR10+ and Dolby Atmos. A lack of AV1 hardware decoding has been a pain point for some Apple TV 4K users, especially when using platforms like YouTube, so that addition is welcome.
The 2022 Apple TV 4K came in two versions: a 64GB Wi-Fi model at $129 and a 128GB model with Ethernet at $149, until Apple raised them to $199 and $249 back in June, of course blaming AI data centers for a surge in memory and storage component demand. That increase alone had us questioning whether the Apple TV 4K was still worth buying after the price hike. The 2026 model comes one way only, with 128GB and Ethernet, for $299.
Essentially, you're getting double the storage, an Ethernet port, the A19, the new remote and those built-in mics for the extra $100 over the model it replaces. If you're comparing it to the 2022 Ethernet version, you're paying an extra $50 for the newer chip, remote and the mics.
Is it worth upgrading?
Both the 2022 and 2026 boxes are limited to 4K and 60 fps, so the A19 in the 2026 model will do little for you if all you're doing is streaming. Sure, hands-free Siri is convenient, but, at least on paper, there's nothing big to get your wallet out for. You'd mostly be paying $299 for a box with a faster chip and the convenience of talking to it.
If you regularly play games on Apple TV, or see yourself making use of Siri AI a lot, the equation may be different — we'll have to test just how much better the new hardware is at more complex tasks. The value proposition also changes if you're on the older Apple TV 4K or an Apple TV HD, because Apple's Siri AI isn't supported on those models.
We'll have a full review of the latest Apple TV 4K soon, which will answer the upgrade question with more than first impressions.

Duane (Keffe D) Davis gets 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating murder of Tupac Shakur
Shakur's killing 'devastating' to his family, siblings share in impact statements
An aging former gang leader was sentenced Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the 1996 drive-by shooting of rap icon Tupac Shakur near the Las Vegas Strip.
The killing, rooted in a long-running gang feud, had gone unsolved for decades — captivating the public and tormenting Shakur's loved ones — until Duane (Keffe D) Davis began speaking publicly about it in interviews and a memoir.
Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.
A former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, Davis stared blankly at Judge Carli Kierny as she imposed a sentence that, even with credit for time served, would not make him eligible for parole until he's at least 100.
Davis, whose lawyer said he will appeal his conviction, is the only person ever charged in Shakur's death. The late rapper's legend has only grown in the years since, and his songs continue to resonate with themes of hardship, love and Black struggle.
Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa (Set) Shakur, said it was hard to repeatedly hear Davis describe how he hunted and killed her brother, cutting him down at age 25, just as his popularity as a musician and actor was peaking.
Sekyiwa Shakur, a younger sister of Tupac, was one of two family members who shared impact statements during the sentencing hearing Tuesday in Las Vegas. (John Locher/The Associated Press)
Gentle and kind, Shakur was his family's protector, she said. Had he survived injuries that included the loss of a lung, he would have left rapping behind and turned to activism, following in the footsteps of luminaries such as Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr., and perhaps even entered politics, she said.
"This man's life mattered," Sekyiwa Shakur said as family members cried in the audience.
Shakur's brother, Maurice (Mopreme) Shakur, said the killing has been "devastating, heartbreaking and sad" for him, his family and Shakur's fans.
Fans of Tupac Shakur hold up a painted portrait of the late rapper and actor as they stand with others during a 2023 ceremony honouring him with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in Los Angeles. (Chris Pizzello/Invision/The Associated Press)
Unsolved for more than two decades
Davis spoke briefly in court, telling the judge he wanted pictures and other items that police took from his house. Asked if there was anything else he wanted to say, Davis said: "No, I'm good."
Davis was charged after giving interviews and publishing a tell-all memoir in 2019 detailing what he said was his role in the infamous shooting.
On the night of Sept. 7, 1996, Shakur was in the passenger seat of a black BMW with music mogul Marion (Suge) Knight when a white Cadillac pulled up at a red light. Shots were fired. Shakur was hit multiple times and died six days later, while Knight survived.
In his memoir, Davis said he was seeking retaliation after Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis' nephew hours before the shooting. He said he was in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed the gun to the backseat, where shots were fired.
Davis had spoken to detectives years earlier but avoided prosecution because of an agreement he had made with law enforcement.
Duane Davis arrives for a sentencing hearing in Las Vegas on Tuesday after his murder conviction in the death of Tupac Shakur. (John Locher/The Associated Press)
During the weekslong trial, prosecutors relied on Davis' own statements to law enforcement and documentarians. They argued Davis orchestrated the shooting and provided the gun used in Shakur's death, which they said stemmed from a rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru.
Davis' defence attorney pointed to a lack of physical evidence connecting his client to the nearly 30-year-old crime and portrayed Davis as a liar who was trying to make money.
After nine days of hearing testimony in August, the jury deliberated for three hours before turning over the guilty verdict.
Insufficient evidence to charge anyone else
The three other people allegedly in the Cadillac have died. They included Davis' nephew, Orlando (Baby Lane) Anderson, whom Davis said was the one who pulled the trigger.
Another name that has surfaced: Sean (Diddy) Combs. Witnesses testified at Davis' trial that the imprisoned music mogul used members of the South Side Compton Crips for security for his label, Bad Boy Records.
Davis alleged in his book and public statements that Combs offered him money to kill Shakur and Knight. Combs, who is serving a four-year prison sentence after being convicted of prostitution-related offences, has repeatedly denied any involvement in Shakur's death.
Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson has said his office doesn't have enough evidence to charge anyone else.
"But like any other case," he said after Davis' conviction, "if we come into more information, more evidence, we can always consider filing additional charges."

The death of actor Nana Patekar, 75, has drawn attention to coronary thrombosis, a condition in which a blood clot forms in an artery supplying the heart. What causes these clots, who is at risk, and how is the condition diagnosed and treated?
The story so far:
According to published accounts of the autopsy report, actor Nana Patekar died after a blood clot blocked the left main coronary artery, which supplies blood to a large part of the heart muscle. A blockage in this artery can severely restrict blood flow to the heart and cause a heart attack. The reported finding has drawn attention to coronary thrombosis, the formation of a blood clot within a coronary artery.
What is coronary thrombosis?
Coronary thrombosis occurs when a blood clot forms in one of the arteries that supply blood to the heart muscle. These arteries carry oxygen and nutrients that the heart needs to function. When a clot partly or completely blocks an artery, less blood reaches the heart muscle. If the blood supply is cut off for too long, the heart muscle can become damaged, leading to a heart attack. The severity depends on how much of the artery is blocked and how quickly blood flow is restored.
This form of thrombosis is often associated with atherosclerosis, in which fatty deposits, cholesterol and other substances build up in the artery walls. These deposits, called plaques, can remain unnoticed for years.
When a plaque ruptures or its surface is eroded, platelets gather at the site and a clot may form. The clot can then obstruct blood flow, sometimes suddenly. Damage to the inner surface of an artery can trigger the process of clot formation. Additionally, at rupture, the material beneath the plaque’s surface comes into contact with blood, prompting platelets to gather and the clotting process to begin. A clot may grow quickly and block the artery.
What are the warning signs?
A clot that significantly restricts blood flow through a coronary artery may cause chest discomfort, pressure or tightness. Pain may spread to the arms, shoulders, back, neck or jaw. Breathlessness, sweating, nausea, dizziness and unusual fatigue may also occur.
The symptoms depend on the artery affected and the extent of the blockage. Some people may have less typical symptoms or no obvious warning signs before the blockage becomes serious. Symptoms alone cannot confirm coronary thrombosis; medical assessment and investigations are needed.
Suspected coronary artery blockage accompanied by chest pain or breathlessness requires emergency medical attention.
Who is at risk?
People living with coronary artery disease are at greater risk of coronary thrombosis because fatty deposits can build up in their arteries and trigger clot formation if a deposit ruptures. Smoking, high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, diabetes, physical inactivity and an unhealthy diet can increase the risk of developing this artery disease.
In some cases, a clot may form in an artery affected by other conditions, including inflammation or injury to the blood vessel.
Older age and a family history of heart disease at a younger age are also risk factors. However it can occur even in people who have not been diagnosed with coronary artery disease. The underlying plaque build-up may have gone undetected until it triggers the formation of a clot.
How is this condition diagnosed?
Doctors assess symptoms and medical history and use tests to determine whether a coronary artery is blocked and whether the heart muscle has been damaged. An electrocardiogram (ECG) records the heart’s electrical activity, while blood tests measuring cardiac troponin can help identify damage to the heart muscle.
Coronary angiography uses a contrast dye and X-rays to show the coronary arteries and identify the location and extent of a blockage. This can help doctors decide how best to restore blood flow. Other tests may be used depending on the patient’s condition.
How is it treated?
Treatment aims to restore blood flow and prevent the clot from growing or new clots from forming. The approach depends on the location and severity of the blockage and the patient’s condition.
Angioplasty may be used to reopen the affected artery. A thin tube is guided to the blockage, where a small balloon is inflated to widen the artery. A stent, a small mesh tube, is often placed to help keep it open.
Doctors may also use antiplatelet medicines, which reduce the tendency of platelets to clump together, and anticoagulants, which interfere with the blood-clotting process. In selected cases, clot-dissolving medicines may be used. Coronary artery bypass surgery may be considered when the pattern of blockage makes it a more suitable option.
Preventing further clots involves managing the underlying risk factors and following the prescribed treatment plan. This may include controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar, stopping tobacco use, maintaining physical activity appropriate to the person’s condition and taking prescribed medicines.

Delhi Police detained journalists for a second consecutive day on Sunday, October 11, while they covered the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and Left-wing student outfits demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Journalists from mainstream outlets and independent houses were among those held, and several said they were detained even after showing press credentials. The detentions came on the same day the Supreme Court said lawyers, journalists and other professionals must not be hindered in their duties “in any manner whatsoever.”
Three journalists from Indian Express Hindi, Shashwat, Siya and Vijay, were among those detained. The organisation said on X that the three told police they were journalists doing their job but were forcibly put into a bus. It said Shashwat sent a video he recorded on his phone as the bus passed through Connaught Place, and that Siya’s phone was seized by police. The three were later released at Chhatrasal Stadium, the organisation said.

The Supreme Court’s Order
In a special hearing on Sunday morning, Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana sought responses from Union home secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi police commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro chief D Thara on a contempt petition alleging a prima facie violation of the court’s October 9 order against a complete shutdown of Metro and train services on Saturday. The court also asked for internet connectivity to be normalised and said there must be no illegal detentions, particularly of peaceful, unarmed gatherings beyond areas where Section 163 BNSS prohibitory orders are in force. It directed free movement in the city subject to law and order and traffic requirements, ordered the installation of barricades to be reviewed at once, and ordered prohibitory orders around the Supreme Court and other courts withdrawn. It also said lawyers, journalists and other professionals should not be hindered in discharging their professional duties.

Contempt Plea Filed
A contempt petition was filed in the Supreme Court on October 12 by Free Speech Collective over the alleged detention and forcible removal of journalists. The plea alleged wilful disobedience of the Court’s October 11, 2026 order directing that lawyers, journalists and other professionals must not be hindered in discharging their professional duties. It sought contempt action, identification of the police officers and supervising officials responsible, and disclosure of how the order was communicated to personnel on the ground.
According to the plea, journalists continued to be detained and removed from reporting locations, including R K Ashram Marg and Connaught Place, despite identifying themselves as members of the press.

The Spanish Springs shopping center in Sparks, Nevada, hosts many businesses, including a Spirit Halloween, a hearing aid supplier, and a Vietnamese restaurant. It’s also home to a consulting agency that’s received millions of dollars from one of the biggest pro-AI super PAC networks ahead of November’s midterm elections.
The problem is that the company—Lantern Production Consultants LLC—doesn’t seem to exist anywhere beyond a post office box in the Spanish Springs shopping complex.
Lantern Production Consultants has been paid around $20 million since last year by Think Big, part of a network of pro-AI super PACs funded by the Leading the Future PAC, for a wide array of services, including polling, digital advertising, research, and strategy, according to federal campaign finance records reviewed by WIRED. Backed by major AI investors, Leading the Future has taken a main role in supporting candidates who back what it calls “an AI innovation policy agenda.”
It is just one of four mysterious LLCs based out of Nevada that have received payments from super PACs in the Leading the Future PAC network, including Think Big and American Mission. The network, which is also based in Nevada, has raised over $140 million to influence political campaigns that align with AI-industry priorities in the midterms.
Summit Ridge Media Group LLC, which received around $13 million between December 2025 and September 2026 from American Mission, lists an address at a mail center in a Reno strip mall. Blue Horizon Compliance Consultants, which also appears in the filings, has its address listed as a Staples location in Reno. And Prusik Partners LLC’s listed address is at a strip mall in Henderson, Nevada, sharing a building with a chiropractor and a beauty salon.
Nevada’s secretary of state told WIRED that they were unable to locate any records for the businesses.

Election watchdogs argue that these LLCs are shell companies, designed to mask the identities of strategists, consultants, and production companies who are working with Leading the Future. “This is about hiding where the money is going,” claims Shanna Ports, senior legal counsel at the Campaign Legal Center.
In May, the Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC, which enforces campaign finance laws, alleging that Think Big and American Mission had broken federal law by using shell companies in this way. Specifically, lawyers with the Campaign Legal Center alleged that super PACs in the Leading the Future network had violated the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) by failing to disclose the actual recipients of their payments. The LLCs, they wrote in their complaint, “function as mere extensions of the super PACs they serve.”
In an emailed statement to WIRED, Leading the Future spokesperson Jesse Hunt wrote, “We comply with all applicable laws and this is merely a desperate ploy for attention from Public First, Anthropic, and the groups aligned with their outside organizations who see our message resonating with the public and policymakers.”
WIRED reached out to Anthropic and Public First—a pro-AI super PAC focused on transparency and safeguards that has significant backing from Anthropic leadership—to ask about Leading the Future’s charge. “I have no idea what they’re talking about,” said Public First spokesperson Anthony Rivera-Rodriguez. “We unequivocally had nothing to do with this complaint.” Anthropic did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The Campaign Legal Center said in a statement to WIRED that the suggestion they “filed this complaint at the direction of, on behalf of, or in consultation with any outside entity is absolutely false.”
The Campaign Legal Center doesn’t expect its case to be heard by the FEC anytime soon, given that the FEC is essentially toothless at the moment. The FEC has six commissioner seats, all presidential appointees. To make a decision on a legal complaint, the FEC needs a quorum of four commissioners, which it hasn’t had since May 2025. Meanwhile, Think Big and American Mission have continued to pour millions of dollars into the Nevada LLCs.
Leading the Future has piqued a lot of public interest, not just because it has the most cash of any pro-AI group—thanks to Silicon Valley bankrollers like billionaire Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman—but also because it funnels money into super PACs that support both Republicans and Democrats. Think Big overwhelmingly funds Democrats, and American Mission funds Republicans.
The fact that the Leading the Future network is playing both sides of the aisle, supporting AI-friendly Democrats and Republicans, has generated speculation from experts as to why it’s spending so much on shielded vendors. Typically, political strategists and consultants cater to Democrats or Republicans, not both. “If you’re running in a Democrat primary and Think Big comes to spend in your race, and they drop half a million on your congressional district doing positive ads while using Republican vendors and strategists—that’s news,” speculates Kyle Morse, deputy executive director of Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit advocacy group that’s critical of big tech.
There are plenty of reasons why a super PAC may want to hide its vendors, ranging from benign to nefarious. In this instance, it's possible businesses don’t want to be publicly associated with a pro-AI campaign. But with the FEC lacking a quorum for the foreseeable future, “We are not fundamentally equipped to figure out what’s happening here,” says Morse.
Leading the Future isn’t the only PAC accused of shielding vendors by using shell companies. Earlier this year, Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC against pro-gun YouTuber Brandon Herrera, who is running for Congress in Texas District 23, alleging that more than 99 percent of his campaign’s disbursements were funneled through Texas Strategy Group, which was, the complaint claimed, “being used as a shell entity.” When reached for comment, Herrera’s campaign directed WIRED to conservative personality Matt Braynard, who runs Texas Strategy Group. Braynard strongly denied the Campaign Legal Center’s accusations, calling the complaint “meritless” and “little more than a recycled legal theory from a partisan advocacy group.”
Campaign Legal Center also filed a complaint with the FEC against Lead Left PAC, a pop-up super PAC that was funded by Republican operatives while posing as a Democratic entity with the presumed goal of meddling in Democratic primaries. Campaign Legal Center accused it of paying shell companies to avoid being linked to Republican strategists.
Ports says that this marks a disturbing trend in campaign finance, at a time when dark money in politics already reigns. “There’s no way of tracing the source behind the money, and that’s bad enough on its own,” says Ports. “Now there’s this new component, where groups are playing games to hide where the money is being spent. As a result, voters really lack fundamental information about where the money is coming from and where it’s going.”

Doctors should exercise caution when using artificial intelligence (AI) tools to interpret medical images, as areas highlighted by AI models may not always align with those identified by radiologists, according to a study by researchers at the International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad (IIIT-H).
The study, conducted by the Language Technologies Research Centre (LTRC) at IIIT-H, examined four vision-language models for analysing chest X-rays and found discrepancies between the regions highlighted by the models and those identified by radiologists.
The findings underscore the need for doctors to independently assess AI-generated outputs rather than relying on them entirely for diagnosis.
The research team, led by Parameswari Krishnamurthy, sought to determine whether AI-generated heatmaps accurately represented the regions of an image that radiologists would identify as disease-related.
However, the researchers questioned whether these visual indicators necessarily reflected the models’ ability to identify the actual location of a disease.
“We essentially wanted to examine whether the heatmaps created by vision-language models actually correspond to where radiologists, who look at the image, would say the disease lies,” said Syed Faizan, principal investigator of the study titled “How Well Do Chest X-Ray VLM Attention Overlays Match Radiologist Boxes? A Cross-Model Audit and Radiologist Reader.”
The team evaluated four models, MAIRA-2, MedGemma-4B, LLaVA-Med-1.5, and LLaVA-1.5, against thousands of publicly available chest X-rays. Two radiologists also participated in the study to assess them, allowing the researchers to compare AI-generated highlights with human assessments.
The study, accepted at the International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) 2026, is to be presented at the iMIMIC Satellite Event in Strasbourg.
The researchers found that an AI model highlighting an apparently correct region of an X-ray did not necessarily mean that it had identified the disease in the same way as a radiologist.
Heatmaps based on diagnosis
According to Dr. Faizan, a model could arrive at a diagnosis first and then use that conclusion to determine where to place its heatmap, rather than independently identifying the affected region from the image.
To test this possibility, the team removed diagnostic information and examined how the models localised abnormalities. Their performance declined, suggesting that anatomical expectations associated with a diagnosis could influence the regions highlighted by the models.
The study also found a difference in the performance of these different models in the technical audit and radiologists’ assessments.
Dr. Faizan said this difference highlighted the importance of assessing AI tools from a clinical perspective. A model that focuses closely on a suspected abnormality may not provide all the information a radiologist needs, including how far a disease has spread to surrounding areas.
The gap that was addressed
The researchers said their work addressed a gap in the evaluation of medical AI systems, as earlier studies had largely focused on prediction and diagnostic accuracy rather than on whether AI-highlighted regions matched those identified by radiologists.
Study on paraphrase robustness
The LTRC is also investigating another potential weakness in vision-language models — their sensitivity to the wording of medical questions.
Doctors may phrase the same clinical query differently, for example, asking whether a chest X-ray shows pneumonia or whether pneumonia can be ruled out. They may also use technical terminology or more familiar expressions.
The researchers examined whether AI models responded consistently to medical questions worded differently in a study on paraphrase robustness.
The study explored how changes in the phrasing of medical questions affected the responses generated by vision-language models, raising questions about whether the systems genuinely understood the clinical query or depended excessively on the precise wording used.
Ms. Parameswari said the laboratory’s broader objective was to apply Natural Language Processing (NLP) to healthcare and use large language models and vision-language models to assist clinicians with tasks such as documentation, report writing and patient-doctor communication.
The aim was to reduce the time doctors spent on routine administrative work and enable them to devote more attention to clinical decision-making.
The researchers emphasised that the objective of medical AI research should be to support clinicians, not replace them, with human judgement remaining central to healthcare.

With just weeks to go until the midterms, election denial groups have found a new target: nursing homes.
The groups, led by the right-wing Election Integrity Network, have claimed without evidence that left-wing organizations are perpetrating voter fraud inside nursing homes, care homes, and assisted-living facilities. The network is now recruiting their followers to contact and question those facilities.
“These left-wing groups go into the nursing homes, and they go into the group homes, and they basically steal the votes of these most vulnerable,” Cleta Mitchell, the Election Integrity Network’s founder, said in a recent appearance on Steve Bannon’s War Room show.
As evidence, Mitchell referenced a case in Wisconsin from 2020 in which a sheriff alleged that eight residents in a care home had their votes filled out for them. The Wisconsin Election Commission rejected the claims. Mitchell told Bannon the case could have cost president Donald Trump the 2020 election, though that wouldn’t be possible: Trump lost Wisconsin in 2020 by over 20,000 votes.
Mitchell’s group has been urging followers to download a toolkit from the Election Integrity Network website and email and call nursing homes in their area. The group has also created multiple images for followers to share on social media which reinforce the idea of widespread voter fraud at nursing homes.
In one campaign, the network shared a series of posts that mapped residential care facilities in competitive congressional districts in states including Arizona, California, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Virginia. The posts identified “vulnerable residents” who “may become targets for political predators seeking easy access to ballots.”
Mitchell and the Election Integrity Network did not respond to requests for comment.
The effort is part of a much broader push by election deniers to undermine trust in the midterms. And just like the claims of noncitizen voting and widespread mail-in voter fraud, they have been supercharged by the Trump administration.
In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a memo that removed previous guidance on how staff at nursing homes could help residents to vote, such as assisting with mail-in voting or transporting residents to polling locations. The new memo replaced that guidance with threats of prosecution if staff “engage in inappropriate coercion or other violations of residents’ rights.”
The memo also claimed that the agency has “become aware of several allegations of instances in which resident rights were unlawfully violated.” However, the examples cited in the memo did not lead to any proven cases of voter fraud. CMS did not respond to a request for comment.
In August, senators led by Elizabeth Warren and Alex Padilla slammed the changes, writing in a letter to CMS that rather than protecting the country’s 2 million nursing home residents, the new rules would disenfranchise them.
“CMS issued a memo that appears to be an attempt to intimidate nursing home staff from assisting residents in the voting process,” the senators wrote in the letter, addressed to CMS administrator Mehmet Oz (who himself has flip-flopped on whether the 2020 election was rigged).
But now, with less than a month to go before the midterms, groups like the Election Integrity Network—which has close ties to the White House—are pushing the narrative that nursing homes are a hive of vote rigging activity.
Another election denial group, the New York–based Project Civicia, has launched a similar campaign, entitled “Adopt a Care Facility.” The group told WIRED that it could not share how many people were taking part in the campaign but repeated the claims made by CMS about voter fraud in Wisconsin, in addition to other allegations.
“We do not presume wrongdoing by a facility because its residents need voting assistance,” Kim Hermance, cofounder and president of Project Civica, tells WIRED. “There are other public cases of forged absentee applications and similar problems. Separately, in our own review of New York records, we noticed people over 85 who appeared to register and vote for the first time shortly before an election. That is not illegal by itself, but it raised a basic question about how facilities handle the process.”

Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
- Published
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.
The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.
Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.
The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Here's what we know.
Busisiwe Mahlangu
Case 1
Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.
Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.
Itumeleng Kekana
Case 2
Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.
The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.
No arrests have been made so far.
Nomfesane Mjobo
Case 3
Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.
Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.
No arrests have been made.
Unknown woman
Case 4
Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.
No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.
Gracious Nkomo
Case 5
Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.
Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.
Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo
Case 6
Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.
Unidentified woman
Case 7
Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.
No arrests have been made.
Dineo Motapane
Case 8
The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.
Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.
She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.
Jabulile Ntimba
Case 9
The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.
According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.
The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.
Ntombifuthi Nxumalo
Case 10
The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.
A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.
Unidentified woman
Case 11
The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.
The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.
The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.
No arrests have been made.
Boitumelo Gift Mashita
Case 12
Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.
Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.
Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.
While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.
The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.
It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.
Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners.
“Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together, in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi university, by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood, after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year old were also reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by the bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say that nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic underreporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and they could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi university, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country requires a deep societal shift where men no longer feel they have ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,’ she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women; as one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old a graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender-equality initiative, said she has experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before – but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago, but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe.’”
Many of the Delhi university students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
“Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades,” said Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for her masters in English at Delhi University. “It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said that it was no coincidence the protests took place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, which saw hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians take to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

Serum Institute of India’s recombinant Quadrivalent Human Papillomavirus vaccine (qHPV) vaccine Cervavac has received World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification.
The vaccine targets HPV types 6, 11, 16, and 18. It is indicated for girls and boys aged 9 through 26 years. Inclusion on the WHO list of prequalified vaccines allows Cervavac to be procured by United Nations agencies, Serum Institute said.
The vaccine was developed in collaboration with the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), along with the WHO-IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) and the Gates Foundation. It is the 32nd WHO prequalification for products/biologicals received by Serum Institute, the vaccine maker said.
“WHO prequalification of Cervavac is an important step in strengthening the global response to HPV. We are pleased to see this indigenously developed vaccine reach this achievement,” CEO Adar Poonawalla said.
Approved for use in India by DCGI
Cervavac has been approved for use in India by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI). The vaccine is administered for the prevention of diseases caused by the four HPV types — prevention of anal cancer in boys and young men, and cervical, vulvar, vaginal, and anal cancers in girls and young women. It is also indicated in preventing genital warts, as applicable to the indicated population.
The vaccine is administered intramuscularly and available in 1-dose vials of 0.5 ml and 2-dose vials of 1.0 ml presentations.

Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off the Falkland Islands.
With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war with Argentina in 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation.
A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated.
It is understood that the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working in the Falklands.
An oil project known as Sea Lion in the north Falklands basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors.
In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood.
Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.”
She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”
It is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character.
Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year.
The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.
The intensity of the Argentinian menace relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.
Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation.
Milei has initiated criminal proceedings against the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration, which are the core companies in the offshore Sea Lion project.
A draft national sovereignty introduced to Argentina’s congress would further expand the scope of sanctions to affiliates of those companies, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers.
The bill additionally contains clauses that could target those involved in the fishing industry in the Falklands, which makes up a large part of the islands’ economy. The archipelago is 300 miles (500km) east of the southern Patagonian coast of Argentina.
Workers in the oil and fisheries sectors on the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – are understood to be concerned that they could be targeted should they travel, particularly to South America where there is support for Buenos Aires’s sovereignty claim.
In a tandem move to kill off Sea Lion, Argentina is expected within 24 hours to escalate further its dispute with the UK by requesting arbitration under annexe VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (Unclos) over the oil project.
On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline to stop the project or face such a legal action. The deadline passed on Monday and Argentinian newspapers said an application for arbitration would follow.
Under it, Buenos Aires will claim that the UK is in breach of a UN resolution inviting the parties to negotiate over the sovereignty dispute and refrain from “unilateral modifications” to the situation. It will be seeking a binding ruling that the UK must stop the drilling. However, UK government sources are confident that Unclos will not wade into a sovereignty dispute.
At a public meeting on Monday evening, one of the Falkland Islands’ assembly members, Dean Dent, told constituents that the UK government was working hard on a tough response to the Argentinian Unclos threat.
“The UK government has assembled quite an in-depth team of legal advisers, KCs – that is the first step,” he said. “There have been four recent similar cases where a case of sovereignty has been taken to Unclos and all four were disregarded by the tribunal as all four cases were a sovereignty issue, not a maritime issue.”
The UK government is expected to be increasingly muscular in its approach to Argentina in the coming days. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Monday that he had raised the issue and “the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British” with the US president, Donald Trump.

GovTech and Google DeepMind developing real-time detection of AI scams on devices
Organisations will also receive funding through a new grant to protect against quantum threats.
SINGAPORE: The Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech) is collaborating with artificial intelligence research laboratory Google DeepMind to develop real-time detection of AI scams on devices, Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo said on Wednesday (Oct 14).
Mrs Teo, who is also the minister-in-charge of cybersecurity and smart nation group, said the collaboration could provide stronger protection while preserving privacy.
“If our devices can recognise signs of manipulation early, we can help potential victims avoid financial or credential loss, while keeping their personal messages on their devices,” she said.
Speaking at the Singapore International Cyber Week at the Sands Expo and Convention Centre, she said the fight against scams has become “harder to win” because of artificial intelligence.
“Our response should not be to turn away from AI because scammers misuse it. Instead, we must tune up our defences and make them better,” she said, adding that Singapore must coordinate its responses more tightly as scammers deploy their tactics across multiple systems.
A victim may first encounter a scam on social media, move to a messaging platform, receive a phone call and transfer money through a financial institution, said Mrs Teo. Each stage offers a chance to intervene, but no single defender sees the whole chain.
“It is therefore not enough to make every organisation better at stopping scams. We must also connect our defences so that a single signal detected on one part of the ecosystem can trigger action elsewhere.”
At the same time, AI can be used to detect threats at scale, she said. For example, the Scam Analytics and Tactical Intervention System by GovTech and the Singapore Police Force uses AI to scan and assess more than 600,000 websites every day, each in a matter of seconds.
It disrupts around 20,000 malicious websites every month, and has expanded to include mobile numbers and online platforms that are suspicious.
This allows Singapore to find and act on threats at a speed and scale that human effort alone cannot match, Mrs Teo said.
QUANTUM THREATS
Singapore should also pay close attention to quantum-related risks, said Mrs Teo.
Quantum computing uses the principles of quantum physics to solve complex problems. While it holds “enormous promise”, sufficiently powerful quantum computers could eventually break some of the cryptography protecting financial transactions, sensitive communications and digital systems, she said.
“We do not know when this will happen. But we know we must prepare for it. Bad actors are already motivated to steal sensitive encrypted data while waiting for quantum computers to decrypt them in future,” she said.
For larger organisations, migrating to quantum-safe solutions can take several years. They must assess risks, prioritise systems and data, and identify where current encryption can be broken.
They also need to work with technology suppliers, test alternative methods of encryption and progressively migrate their systems, she said.
In June, the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) issued guidance on migration milestones for owners of critical information infrastructure, or computer systems that provide essential services. They are expected to complete migration by 2031.
The agency previously identified energy, water, banking and finance, healthcare, transport, infocomm, media, security and emergency services, and government as sectors with such systems.
Mrs Teo said Singapore will issue guidance for other organisations to work towards quantum-safe migration by 2035. These include organisations whose exposure to the quantum threat could have serious consequences, she said.
For example, organisations that hold sensitive information that must remain confidential for many years, and those that provide critical services such as communications or digital transactions where maintaining integrity and confidentiality of information are essential.
A new quantum-safe kickstarter grant will also fund organisations to move from planning to implementation. The time-bound seed funding will help them identify implementation challenges, test quantum-safe solutions in real operating environments and build the experience needed for migration at scale.
The grant is open to all organisations, with priority for owners of critical information infrastructure systems. It will run from Nov 1 to Oct 31, 2027, with each funded pilot lasting up to six months.
Organisations may undertake pilots in-house or work with suitable solution providers, CSA said. Priority will go to use cases that address common migration challenges, including migrating an application or system from end to end and cryptographic discovery and inventory.
Mrs Teo said neither scams nor quantum threats can be solved by the government alone, or by any country on its own.
“Staying ahead depends not only on what we can build ourselves, but what we can pool together through mutual support,” she said.

Colombia's peace tribunal says former rebel leaders committed war crimes against Indigenous groups
Colombia’s transitional justice system has charged 10 former members of the rebel Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia with war crimes and crimes against humanity
BOGOTA, Colombia -- BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — Colombia’s transitional justice system Tuesday charged 10 former members of the rebel Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia with multiple war crimes and crimes against humanity, which it said were committed against five Indigenous groups.
In a news conference the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, or JEP, said that between 1996 and 2016 the suspects oversaw the torture, murder and forced displacement of Indigenous leaders. It said they also ordered their subordinates to place landmines in Indigenous territory and destroy ecosystems that tribes rely on for their survival.
“Today we are delivering justice to the most forgotten peoples of a segregated Colombia,” JEP magistrate Catalina Diaz said Tuesday. “These people have had their basic right to exist compromised.”
Three former members of the FARC’s last secretariat are among those charged with waging systematic attacks against tribes living in a remote area of southeast Colombia that is covered by rainforests and savannahs and where the FARC often exerted strict territorial control.
One of the suspects, Julian Gallo, served as a senator for eight years after the rebel group made a peace deal with Colombia’s government that gave its leadership 10 seats in Colombia’s congress.
Yhon Jairo Figueroa, a leader of the Koreguaje tribe attended Tuesday’s press conference and said he was thankful to the JEP for taking on the case.
“For the first time the Colombian state recognizes that (armed groups) did not just kill individuals,” he said. “But they attempted to kill the knowledge, the language, the territory” of Indigenous groups.
The special tribunal was established during the 2016 peace deal between the Colombian government and the FARC rebels with the aim of investigating crimes committed by both sides during decades of internal strife, and helping victims seek reparation and truth.
An independent truth commission that was also part of the 2016 peace agreement, found that at least 450,000 people were killed in the conflict, and 7 million were forced to leave their homes.
The former FARC leaders have 30 days to respond to the charges filed by the JEP.
The tribunal’s statutes indicate that if suspects accept charges and collaborate with investigations, they will not face time in prison. Instead they will have to provide reparations to victims and participate in truth and reconciliation schemes.
Suspects who do not accept charges and are found guilty of committing war crimes face up to 20 years in prison.

Singapore's economy grows 5.4% in Q3, down from 6.2% in previous quarter: Advance estimates
On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, Singapore's economy grew 1.1 per cent, compared to the 1.5 per cent growth in Q2.
SINGAPORE: Singapore’s economy grew 5.4 per cent in the third quarter of 2026, slightly slower than the 6.2 per cent reported in the second quarter of the year, according to advance estimates from the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) on Wednesday (Oct 14).
The manufacturing sector grew 7.5 per cent, slowing down from a 12.9 per cent expansion in Q2.
On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, Singapore’s economy grew 1.1 per cent, compared to the 1.5 per cent growth in Q2.
Advance estimates are largely computed from data in the first two months of the quarter, July and August in this case. They are intended as an early indicator and may be revised later when more data is available.
Growth in the manufacturing sector was driven by output expansions in the electronics, precision engineering, transport engineering and general manufacturing clusters, said METI in a media release on Wednesday.
This outweighed declines in output in the chemicals and biomedical manufacturing clusters, it added.
On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the manufacturing sector contracted 0.9 per cent, compared with the 6.3 per cent growth in Q2.
The construction sector grew 8.8 per cent in the third quarter, faster than the 6.1 per cent growth reported in Q2, as both public and private sector construction output increased, figures from METI showed.
On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the sector grew 3.4 per cent, turning around from the 2.7 per cent contraction in the previous quarter.

The number of Japanese municipalities whose foreign residents account for over 5% of the population climbed 2.5 times from 53 in 2020 to 132, according to 2025 census data released by the internal affairs ministry.
The data show increases in foreign populations not only in major cities and industrial districts but also in rural areas where the tourism and agricultural sectors thrive.
The number of foreign residents in Japan hit a record high of 3.84 million, or 3.1% of the country’s total population. The total rose roughly 40% from 2.74 million in the previous census in 2020.
The number of prefectures with municipalities where foreign nationals account for over 5% of the population increased from 17 to 27, with Miyagi and Hyogo among those that newly joined the list.
In the previous survey, such municipalities were mainly seen in large cities and areas with strong manufacturers, while in the latest survey, resort areas and regions where agriculture, forestry, and fisheries are the main industries were in the over 5% club.
In Hokkaido, the number of such municipalities jumped from five in 2020 to 22.
The rise marked in rural areas is believed to reflect growing employment of foreign workers amid severe labor shortages.
The highest proportion of foreign residents across Japan was 26.5% in the town of Kawakami, Nagano, where many foreign workers support the cultivation of lettuce, a local specialty. The proportion rose from 19.0% in 2020, when the town also held the top slot.
In the village of Shimukappu, Hokkaido, the share of foreign residents roughly doubled to 21.7%.
“The opening of a resort facility in 2017 led to increased hiring of foreigners to serve overseas visitors,” a village official said.
The proportion of foreign residents exceeded 10% in 21 municipalities, of which four topped 20%. This marks the first time a census has confirmed municipalities where foreign residents account for more than 20% of the population.
Of Japan’s 1,741 municipalities, 65 recorded increases in foreign residents that more than offset declines in their Japanese populations, resulting in overall population growth.
Such municipalities include Tokyo’s Nerima Ward, Urayasu in Chiba Prefecture and Higashihiroshima in Hiroshima Prefecture, which hosts a large number of foreign students.
The proportion of Chinese nationals in Japan fell to 24.0% from 28.5%, although they remained the largest foreign nationality group. Meanwhile, the share of residents from Southeast Asia, including Vietnam and Indonesia, increased.

Trump pick Zacharia gets off to bumpy start in unusual first press briefing: ‘My president, I mean my husband’
Newly-minted press secretary lasts less than 15 minutes in awkward debut before the White House press corps
