A judge blocks the government's tree-clearing spree at a municipal D.C. golf course
A federal judge has temporarily barred the Trump administration from cutting down additional trees at a D.C. municipal golf course, the latest example of a court intervening in the government's efforts to reshape pieces of the nation's capital.
The long-simmering fight over East Potomac Golf Links — which President Trump wants to redevelop into a championship-level course — erupted over the weekend, after the administration cut down hundreds of trees with little notice.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes had ordered the administration in May to get court approval before cutting down more than 10 trees at the golf course. Officials notified the court just before 5 p.m. on Friday of their plan to remove "up to 529 trees" in phases starting on Saturday — and had razed at least 430 by the end of the day, prompting Reyes to call an emergency hearing on Monday.
"What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility with me in this case," Reyes said during the nearly four-hour hearing, held via videoconference.
Reyes ordered a short-term stop to the tree-clearings, which she extended on Tuesday through Oct. 26. She warned Monday that "if that order is violated by two seconds, there are going to be contempt proceedings."
Reyes also ordered top officials from the Department of Interior and the National Park Service to testify at a hearing next Monday, to shed more light on the government's motivations and the future of the historic course.
"The questions go to whether or not I've been lied to," Reyes said. "Whether I've been lied to in declarations about the plans, whether or not I've been lied to about the timing of things, and whether I've been lied to about what kind of notice the court was going to receive."
East Potomac has emerged as another flashpoint in Trump's unilateral quest to remake D.C., and it's the subject of a lawsuit by critics who fear it could go the way of the now-lost White House East Wing unless a court intervenes. The D.C. Preservation League, along with two concerned residents, sued the government in February over what it calls an unlawful takeover.
"This is a tactic we're seen before from the Trump-Vance administration – act quickly to irrevocably alter a cherished national landmark, just to advance another one of President Trump's pet vanity projects," Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward — one of the firms involved in the lawsuit — said in a statement this weekend.
Perryman told NPR on Tuesday that the golf course is the latest in a pattern of the Trump administration "undermining the entire checks and balances process in this country, which includes undermining court proceedings."
Trump has long floated the idea of redeveloping East Potomac into a championship-caliber course and announced plans to do so earlier this year, though his target Sept. 1 start date has come and gone without a formal proposal.
The prospect — and the lack of clarity since — has raised alarm among locals concerned about losing access to the historically affordable course and to the surrounding recreational area, which is popular with cyclists, runners, fishers and picnickers.
Loading...
"This is a broader story than just about golf, especially when there's been this little transparency, … to say, 'Here's what the future of this little man-made peninsula is actually going to look like,'" Alex Rosen, a D.C.-based consultant who started the nonprofit Save East Po, told NPR in July.
A National Park Service official said in a Friday court filing that plans for renovations "remain in the conceptual stage." And the Interior Department told NPR in a statement on Tuesday that it is "committed to continuing the relationships we have built with the local golf communities to ensure these courses are safe, beautiful, open, affordable, enjoyable, accessible, and world-class."
But critics are growing increasingly concerned about the process itself. They worry the Trump administration is using so-called routine maintenance as a pretext to begin redevelopment without the proper authorization.
"You can't continuously say, 'There's no plan' … while you're clearly taking steps to effect a plan," Rosen, who is not involved in the lawsuit, told NPR after watching the hearing. "It's just frankly lying."
Why the rush? The court hopes for answers next week
At Monday's hearing, Reyes expressed regret that she hadn't issued a formal restraining order earlier, which she said was because "I have done everything humanly possible to give the government the benefit of the doubt in this case."
For example, after the administration quietly removed what it has since said were roughly 150 dying and invasive trees in late August, Reyes acknowledged that people were upset but declined to intervene: "I am not the Lorax," she said at an early September hearing.
By Monday, that benefit of the doubt was gone. When a government lawyer said they had done their best to notify the court, Reyes offered a sharp rebuke.
"You did not do your best," she said, voice raised. "You did your absolute worst."
Perryman, of Democracy Forward, said, "What was really remarkable about the hearing yesterday is that the government did not appear to have a defense for its failure to notify the court."
In Friday's court filing, National Mall and Memorial Parks Superintendent Kevin Griess described the tree-clearing as part of an effort "to address deferred maintenance needs and implement treatment recommendations to restore the cultural landscape."
Griess specifically cited a 2019 National Park Service report about D.C. municipal golf courses, which says several waves of tree planting at East Potomac over the last century have obscured views and changed the feel of the course from its original 1920s "links-style" design.
Griess said in his filing that NPS was able to act on the report because it had received a temporary surge of "approximately 20 to 50 trained personnel capable of performing labor-intensive grounds maintenance activities." Under questioning in court, he confirmed that surge was connected to the administration's 250th anniversary events, including the IndyCar race on the National Mall in August.
But critics are skeptical, given the president's public statements. Alex Dickson, one of the plaintiffs, said in a statement that "the administration is using a preservation report as cover to begin tearing out the course it was written to save."
Griess said he had gotten the green light last week from Frank Lands, the park service's deputy director of operations. At the judge's request, Lands then joined the hearing from his car in a parking lot. He said he had gotten the directive from Greg Wischer, deputy chief of staff to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.
Wischer was not reachable to join the hearing, despite Reyes' request that he do so. She has ordered Wischer and Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, to testify at another hearing next Monday.
The Interior Department didn't answer NPR's questions about the timeline and resources for the tree-clearing, but said in a statement that "President Donald J. Trump is fulfilling his commitment to make D.C. Safe and Beautiful as shown by the working fountains, clean parks and safe streets across the district for the first time in decades."
In granting the plaintiffs' request for an extended restraining order on Tuesday, Reyes wrote that they had "proven they will likely suffer irreparable harm absent injunctive relief." She also said the government must provide "three business days' written advance notice prior to making any irreparable modification" to the golf course.

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?
- Published
Imagine a world where Manchester City had not used "sham contracts" to build a team capable of winning three Premier League titles, one FA Cup and three EFL Cups.
If City were the winners, then there had to be losers.
Not just those teams who finished runners-up or lost cup finals.
The potential impact runs much deeper and includes missed Champions League qualification, relegation and Premier League prize money.
Thirty-five other teams played in the English top flight between 2009 and 2018.
And every one could in some way claim to have been left financially out of pocket.
City, of course, continue to deny any wrongdoing and they have appealed. But as it stands they are guilty of all charges related to inflating their sponsorship income to the tune of £830m, plus another £90m in expenses.
Strip that money out and it changes the whole complexion of the competition.
BBC Sport has crunched the numbers to assess the potential financial impact on the top flight.
How the figures are worked out
When Sheikh Mansour bought Manchester City in 2008 they were far removed from the club you see today.
Since finishing fifth in 1991-92, the last season before the formation of the Premier League, City's highest placing had been eighth in 2004-05.
The Abu Dhabi money poured in via what the Premier League's independent commission described as a "disguised funding scheme". It took the club's sponsorship revenues from being on a par with Stoke City in 2008-09 to eventually overtaking those of Manchester United.
City finished fifth in 2009-10. Since then, not once have they finished outside the top four in the Premier League.
Did this money deny other clubs a place in the competition, and other kinds of success?
This article is not trying to set out how much compensation a team might be able to claim.
Nor is it saying any one team would definitely have avoided relegation or reached the Champions League.
It is about chance, the possibility that a very different City team would have taken to the field without the hundreds of millions pumped in by the club's Abu Dhabi owners.
It has not considered potential future earnings from success, including sponsors' bonuses and further prize money.
Nor has it factored in players who may feel they have missed out on salary increases, or triggered payments, for how their club might have performed.
This is purely about domestic impact:
- Lost prize money by league placing
- Missed potential Champions League earnings
- Europa League payments
- Loss of Premier League status
- Impact of cup final defeats
- What Manchester's 'super-profit' deal with City owners has paid out so far 
  - Published8 hours ago
- Were any current Man City players signed during charges period? 
  - Published3 hours ago
How City gained £1.17bn, and others may have lost £844m
The full impact of City's behaviour on other clubs could be calculated at £844m.
- £188.2m in Premier League placing money
- £349.7m in relegation costs
- £217.8m in missed Champions League prize money
- £88.3m related to domestic cup competitions and the Europa League
We calculated these figures by taking published prize money from the relevant seasons.
For Premier League place money, each team that finished below City is considered to have potentially missed a payment for one place.
For relegation, this is the minimum value of being in the Premier League for the next season, minus the received parachute payment.
For the Champions League, we took City's earnings from the following seasons and deducted the impacted teams' Europa League prize money.
But City also earned prize money themselves during this period.
Across the competitions, City were paid £1.17bn:
- £812.3m from the Premier League - total income from prize money and broadcast revenues
- £363.4m via the Champions League
- £900,000 from the FA Cup victory
- £300,000 from the three EFL Cup victories
The most impacted: How Spurs could have missed out on £120m
"We have lived through a period of deception," former Tottenham Hotspur boss Mauricio Pochettino said last month.
"No type of punishment will make it possible to repair what was done."
You can see his point. Spurs finished one place outside the Champions League positions in four (although one only was under Pochettino) of the eight seasons in which City qualified for Europe's elite competition.
BBC Sport took City's earnings from the Champions League in the following season, and deducted Tottenham's Europa League prize money.
Over the four seasons Spurs missed out, Manchester City earned £148.2m from the Champions League, with Tottenham taking £29.9m from the Europa League.
The 2014-15 campaign led to the biggest deficit, as City finished second in the Premier League and Tottenham came fifth. City received £71.2m for reaching the Champions League semi-finals in the following season, but Spurs were only paid £17.7m from the Europa League - a difference of £53.5m.
Spurs also finished behind City in the Premier League table six times, with the cumulative prize money difference worth £6.6m.
The north Londoners did benefit in the 2013-14 season, as they only qualified for Europe because City beat Sunderland in the final of the EFL Cup.
Spurs gained £5.1m from their 2014-15 Europa League campaign which would not have been possible without City's success.
Taking into account all competitions, that produced a net financial loss for Spurs of £119.9m.
Did City's EFL Cup win cost Liverpool £37.8m?
The 2015-16 EFL Cup final proved to be decisive for Liverpool's hopes of European football.
Jurgen Klopp's men lost to City on penalties following a 1-1 draw. The Europa League place transferred to the league, and went to West Ham United.
Liverpool only finished eighth, which was not enough to qualify for Europe.
Had Liverpool won the final, they would have entered the Europa League, and this provides a key financial comparison.
Manchester United won the Europa League in 2016-17, receiving prize money of £37.8m. As part of that amount, the Red Devils' market pool payment, which is based upon the value of the television rights, was £26.6m.
While we cannot say for certain that Liverpool would have won the Europa League, they were a club of similar stature to Manchester United, which provides a comparison.
The market pool share may also have been slightly lower with both Liverpool and Manchester United involved.
Together with Premier League place money of £10.6m - Liverpool finished below City in all nine relevant seasons - the total financial impact on the Merseyside club was £52.3m.
As for the FA Cup, City won it just once in the period they were scrutinised over, beating Stoke in 2010-11. The difference in prize money was £900,000, with the runners-up going into the Europa League.
Everton were denied Europe five times
Everton missed out on the Champions League once, in 2013-14, and on four other occasions they finished one place below the final Europa League spot.
The Champions League place is calculated to be worth £32.6m - the £39m earned by Manchester City minus the Toffees' £6.4m winnings from the Europa League they competed in instead.
The combined impact on missing out on the Europa League four times is £23.2m.
Add on the £10.6m from Premier League prize money, and the total financial effect is £66.4m - making Everton the third-most impacted club.
Did two relegations cost Hull City £99m?
While parachute payments provide something of a cushion, relegation from the Premier League is still a considerable financial hit.
Could the teams who finished in 18th place, one spot from safety, argue that they might have stayed up but for City?
There are a couple of ways of looking at this.
Firstly, the results against City who took at least four points off every 18th-placed team other than Birmingham.
Secondly, the mere fact that City were able to assemble a squad far better than their finances should have allowed. Could they otherwise have been involved in relegation battles?
Again, this is not to say City would have been relegated. It is about chance.
BBC Sport has taken the total prize money earned by the team finishing in 20th in the following season. That suggests a minimum return for having stayed in the top flight.
Deducted from that is the first season of parachute payments to give a net amount.
Hull were relegated twice in the period, costing the Tigers £93.78m.
The Tigers finished below City in the table four times, adding £5.2m in place money to the sum.
It leaves the East Yorkshire club as the second-most impacted on £99m.
Swansea are fourth in the table with £63.1m. Of that total, £54m is from relegation and £9.1m in place money from the seven seasons the Swans were in the top flight.
Newcastle suffered relegation by finishing 18th in 2015-16, costing them a projected £60.4m, of which £7.9m was place money.
Norwich (£43.8m), Wigan (£39.6m), Burnley (£31.1m), Bolton (£26.4m) and Birmingham (£25.1m) also suffered relegations in 18th place.
The loss of Champions League money
Alongside Tottenham, four other teams missed out on Champions League football by one place across the eight seasons when City qualified.
The biggest impact was on Chelsea, who finished fifth in 2017-18.
City earned £79.2m from reaching the quarter-finals of the Champions League, with Chelsea getting £39.4m from winning the Europa League. That left Chelsea with a deficit of £39.8m.
Also just missing out on the Champions League were Everton (5th in 2013-14, £32.6m deficit), and Arsenal (5th in 2016-17, £22.1m deficit).
The only team not to experience much of a financial impact were Manchester United, who were fifth in 2015-16.
City got no further than the round of 16 in the Champions League, earning £42.6m, while United won the Europa League that season, receiving £37.8m. It left the Red Devils with a deficit of £4.8m.
The cumulative cost of league places
In the Premier League there is no specific prize pot for being crowned champions.
Broadcast revenue is allocated on a merit basis by final league position.
It is a 1+1 system, so the club in 20th get the base payment. Then the team in 19th get the base payment two times. For 18th, it is that base amount three times, and so on.
It means that the only financial difference, in prize money at least, for the team finishing runners-up in one of Manchester City's three title-winning seasons is one base payment.
Could any team claim they might have finished one place higher?
The value of a Premier League place rose sharply in line with the broadcast deals over the period of City's offences.
In 2010-11 it was £755,881 per place, and by 2016-17 it was up to £1.94m.
If any compensation were to be considered, Everton, Liverpool and Stoke City would have the biggest claim of £10.7m, having finished below City in all nine seasons.
West Brom and West Ham's total is £9.9m, with Swansea on £9.1m.
At the other end of the scale are the seven clubs who spent one season in the Premier League, including Blackpool (£756,756), Portsmouth (£800,424) and Huddersfield (£1.93m).

Ice cold: Even in Alaska, Trump can’t avoid being protested at rally — breaks out more ‘your mom’ shots
Trump fumed at a protester in Wasilla, Alaska, calling them a ‘spoiled child,’ among other insults, after they interrupted his stump speech for Republican Senate candidate Dan Sullivan

President Donald Trump can’t avoid being protested at his rallies as he campaigns for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections — including in red-leaning Alaska.
Amid record-low approval ratings, Trump is attempting to fire up his base to vote for members of his party as if he were on the ballot, as he often tells them to do. But the president has faced resistance from a series of lone protesters who have interrupted his rallies in Texas, Ohio and now Alaska.
What is Trump’s savvy retort? “Your mom” jokes.
Shortly after Trump took the stage in Wasilla, Alaska, at around 8:30 p.m. ET on Tuesday, a protester turned heads.
As the president was bashing his 2024 presidential opponent, former Vice President Kamala Harris, he stopped to call the demonstrator a “spoiled child.”
“Sounds like we have a spoiled child,” Trump said as his supporters booed at the protester and chanted “USA, USA, USA.”
As the protester, wearing a sweatshirt with a picture of a bald eagle carrying an American flag on it, was being escorted out, the president commended the “good law enforcement.”
“He’s now got the displeasure of going home to his mother and father, who both voted for me, by the way,” Trump said of the protester.
Alaskans have voted for the Republican presidential nominee since at least 1980, according to 270toWin. Trump won the vote with 51.3 percent support in 2016, 52.8 percent in 2020 and 54.5 percent in 2024.
Trump was in Youngstown, Ohio, last night, stumping for Sen. Jon Husted, who is running against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, and Vivek Ramaswamy, who ran against Trump for president in 2024 before endorsing him. Ramaswamy is running for governor in Ohio against Democrat Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health.
During last night’s rally, Trump gushed about how attractive and athletic Husted, a college football star, was, telling a crowd of his supporters, “I looked at his a**, and I looked at the whole, and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He's got these like claws.”
During one of two protests last night, Trump said the demonstrators “get paid by the lefties in order to destroy our country. They're scum.”
He then taunted the demonstrator currently causing a commotion, saying, “He's going back home to mom...He's got to go on a diet. He's a fat guy.”
“What he doesn't know is that his mother and father voted for me,” the president added, using a similar insult that he used against a protester in San Antonio, Texas, last week.
Wasilla was Trump’s latest stop as he vigorously campaigns in red states with the midterms right around the corner. The president is trying to boost Republican candidates’ chances as he struggles with his own image issues.
A whopping 65 percent of Americans disapproved of Trump’s job as president, while just 32 percent approved in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The Trump administration has been dogged by an unpopular war in Iran and stubborn inflation affecting Americans at the gas pump and grocery store.
While the party in power typically loses seats in the midterm elections, recent polling shows Democrats gaining ground in Senate races in states that Republicans would normally coast through.
Mary Peltola, a former Democratic congresswoman, is beating Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 7 percentage points, 50 to 43 percent, according to a New York Times/Siena University poll of likely voters in Alaska released earlier this month.
Peltola led by a slimmer margin in a poll recently released by Alaska Survey Research. The Democrat was just two percentage points ahead of Sullivan, 47 to 45 percent, among Alaska’s likely voters.

When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”
The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.
The point of the game was to stress-test the world’s response to a group of prospective technologies known collectively as solar radiation modification. These technologies promise to reverse global warming by reflecting away a portion of the sunlight reaching Earth, for example by spraying particles of sulphur dioxide or some other manufactured substance into the atmosphere. The cooling effect of this kind of solar geoengineering is widely accepted. It would mimic the well-known impacts of large volcanic eruptions, which temporarily cool the planet by half a degree or more. But the fallout is less certain—and less equal. Some regions will suffer: Models predict drying in sub-Saharan Africa and more intense tropical storms in the Atlantic. The cooling effect would also last only as long as the geoengineering continued; after that the global temperature could shoot back up with wild and hard-to-predict effects.
Until recently, the idea of solar radiation modification was a speculative niche of climate science. That has changed fast. Private firms are exploring solar geoengineering as a commercial opportunity: Last year, a US-Israeli startup called Stardust Solutions raised $60 million, and in May it released details of a suite of new inventions it claims would give humans the ability to dial down the global temperature as desired. In August, Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX might be a candidate for delivering geoengineering interventions, threw his voice behind solar geoengineering, writing on X: “Space satellites to control temperature and massive geo-engineering will be needed or it will be game over.”
The world is going to have to make decisions about how to govern this technology much sooner than most policymakers imagine, Cynthia Scharf, a former UN advisor, told WIRED. “It's not 15 years from now; it's in the next decade, easily.”
It was against this backdrop that Danielle Young, an assistant professor in international relations at Leeds University, arranged the war game. Its setting was a hastily convened UN committee charged with coordinating the international response to developments in solar geoengineering. The game unfolded over simulated meetings set at three points in time: the present, September 2027, and September 2028. Each step ratcheted up the stakes, with the game creators introducing new advances in sunlight-reflecting technology. As in real life, no one knew all the facts, and players had to respond to events that were bringing the world closer to a full-scale attempt at deploying solar geoengineering tech, even when they may not have a full picture of what had truly occurred—or what any of the others were up to.
The first session set the tone. Distrust and disinformation dominated. As participants discussed rules governing outdoor experiments in an attempt to agree an international deal, players representing both the US and China told the group they could not sign a deal that constrained their pursuit of research considered to be in their “national interest.” Nor could they accept a deal that would see their superpower rival taking the lead technologically. Speaking to WIRED, Jeffrey Nielsen, a major in the US Army who played the role of a US national security attaché, summarized the position as “worse than no deal at all is any deal that favors China.”
Tensions escalated when the team running the simulation handed the Russian delegates an “intelligence report” indicating they had found a plane near the Bering Strait believed to be involved in a US geoengineering research program. The US team—which was indeed flying research missions—accused Russia of disinformation.
Meanwhile, the US became convinced China was also conducting research and developing its own program. Beijing’s representatives had tried to insert language into a mooted deal that would ensure no retroactive punishment for past experiments. Then, China approached a player representing SpaceX to float the idea of a technology-sharing program. In a private discussion away from the group, the SpaceX player immediately reported the Chinese approach to the US team. The US demanded an international investigation. The finger-pointing continued, and countries abandoned the talks. The Canadian representative called it a “humiliating defeat.”
At the end of the session, Nielsen was pumped. He’d busted China and derailed any prospect of a global deal. In the context of the game, he told WIRED, it was a “humungous victory” for the Americans. But Young, the researcher who designed the scenario, said the Chinese were not, in fact, conducting experiments in the game. Mutual suspicion meant all parties left the room believing the others were moving as quickly as possible to build their own geoengineering capability.
What played out in the first session reflected “the likelihood, in my opinion, of the geoengineering arms race,” says Nielsen, who clarified he was speaking to WIRED in a private capacity and not representing the views of the actual US government. Most experts agree it would take a superpower’s reach to ensure the safe passage of planes needed to deliver payloads of dust to the stratosphere in a geoengineering exercise. But neither the US nor China would lightly cede control over the global thermostat, says Nielsen, and distrust and poor communication are a significant risk: “Any action related to the issue by one actor can be perceived as malintent by the other.”
The threat of falling behind a rival is “a very strong driver of research and development of capability,” a former British diplomat with a background in national security told WIRED. “But that's not at all the same thing as deployment.” There are similarities with nuclear arms dynamics—though solar radiation management, unlike nukes, has more obvious benefits as well as downsides, many of which are poorly understood. “There is an interdependence here,” says the former diplomat, who was not involved in the game and spoke on condition of anonymity to preserve relationships. “It's not an inherently zero-sum game.”
Scharf, who represented the US government alongside Nielsen in the game, told WIRED a “scientifically transparent international collaboration” between China and the US “might be the best we can do in terms of fending off a very dangerous competition between the two. But I certainly cannot imagine that happening under the Trump administration.”
Compounding the problem is a lack of information. Geoengineering has historically been viewed with suspicion and often ignored by the scientific mainstream. One researcher told WIRED he’d experienced ostracization and barriers to academic progression owing to his interest in the technology; he no longer works in the field.
This lack of scientific interest greatly frustrated Golja, who spent much of the game watching as a bystander while political posturing dominated. Given the low level of knowledge around solar radiation modification and its side effects, she was one of very few experts who could help the participants understand the climate impacts of what they were discussing—yet she was largely ignored.“I was just so surprised about how little anyone actually cared about the science,” she says.
In the next sessions, the organizers tried in vain to nudge the talks back toward the realities of climate change. The participants received frequent notifications of climate disasters. These barely registered. Golja had prepared an “emulator,” a real-world demonstration of the best available science on how solar radiation management might affect weather patterns in different regions. It was ignored. If country representatives asked her anything, it was usually a leading question looking for data that would serve their ends or frame a rival’s proposal as reckless.
Then, during the last day, players were trying to find a way to respond to reports that a major plume of aerosols had been detected. In the game, this had been caused by a joint US-Saudi test of Stardust’s technology, though not everyone knew this. Finally, scientific advice was at a premium. Countries needed to know how to establish a monitoring network of satellites and other observational tools in order to prevent tests like this from happening in secret. A player representing an NGO called the Climate Futures Cooperative approached Golja, offering her money to fund such a scheme.
“Great. Fabulous. Why wouldn't I do that?” she recalls thinking.
But it soon came out that the Climate Futures Cooperative was actually backed by the fossil fuel industry. The organizers had recognized that fossil fuel companies and major producing countries like the US and Saudi Arabia would have a clear interest in removing barriers from the development of a technology that could combat climate change without having to immediately stop burning coal, oil, and gas. The shadowy NGO spent the game subtly wrecking the vibe and carping about process—though mostly they just sat back and let it burn. Some players—Russia, the US, SpaceX and Stardust—figured out the CFC was not what it seemed, says Young. “But they assessed it was to their benefit and didn’t draw attention to it.” Then the CFC chose its moment to offer money to Golja, only to crater her credibility, isolating and fragmenting the voice of science in the room.
“It was a whole mess,” says Golja.
That final lesson in fossil fuel realpolitik was about all Golja could endure. By the end of the last day, she was in tears.
At no point did the countries in the game agree to a deal, despite multiple proposals being put forward. European countries and Canada tried to build support for safeguards and open scientific research, but the talks constantly got bogged down by delay tactics and veered into tense showdowns over duelling strategic interests. In their final report, the researchers running the simulation—whose work was sponsored by the UK government-funded Advanced Research and Invention Agency—concluded that “strategic competition and state sovereignty drove the simulations, not climate concerns.”
Simulations like this one are not supposed to predict the future. The outcomes depend on the design of the game and the relative personalities and experience of the players. Many of those in the room lacked first-hand diplomatic and national security experience. The UN forum, which organizers selected as the game’s setting, may also not be as effective as talks between smaller groups of major countries. But the experiment in London echoed and refracted through the real world, during and after the months it was running.
In March, two papers from conservative US think tanks urged the Trump administration to take the lead on solar radiation modification and counter China’s threat. One memorably invoked a new, MAGA-coded term: “Weather sovereignty.” This month, the Observer newspaper in London revealed that the UK Ministry of Defense had paid a deep tech security consultancy to conduct research into sunlight reflection. Then, last week, the British government released its first official policy paper on the field, backing further research but stating firmly that it did not support deployment and “does not plan to do so.” Stardust has continued its lobbying of the US and governments around the world; CEO Yanai Yedvab told WIRED its job was getting easier as, unlike before, “the majority of policymakers … are already aware of this technology.”
Stardust has always maintained that it will not conduct large-scale outdoor experiments, let alone full deployment, before global governance is in place. “We are developing a very powerful tool,” Yedvab says. “When you develop this kind of powerful technology—and you have many precedents—national interests will play out. We're not naive about it.”
Meanwhile, drivers of the climate crisis are intensifying. During the time span of the game, efforts to curtail the use of fossil fuels were being undermined by rising energy costs and political hostility. Week after week, an incredible summer of drought and heat pounded Europe. In the final week of August, the collapse of a glacier on the Tibet-Nepal border fulfilled the prophecies of decades of climate scientists, killing more than 1,450 people.
In the months since the simulation ended, Golja has reevaluated many things. On a corkboard behind her desk, she has pinned up a note to herself, laying out a vision for life in a world ruled by narrow geopolitical self-interest rather than science, evidence, and reason. Her answer: She plans to return to the small coastal town where she grew up in Connecticut and use her expertise to help local climate groups build the seawalls and coastal erosion buffers they will need to cope with the inevitable. “To try and make a difference where it feels like I actually have traction,” she says. After what she saw, pursuing science in the hope of informing global decisions no longer held as much appeal. “Now it feels a little bit more personal.”

Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay on Tuesday sought the release of more water from Andhra Pradesh to Chennai for drinking purposes, while the A.P. government gave no assurance in this regard, citing that it would consider the request depending on the water availability in the Krishna River and requirements of the State.
Mr. Vijay met Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu at the latter’s camp office in Vijayawada on Tuesday and discussed inter-State water issues, including the proposed Godavari-Cauvery river linkage and the supply of drinking water to Chennai.
Mr. Naidu said the Andhra Pradesh government was sympathetic to Chennai’s drinking water needs, despite a decline in Krishna River water availability due to the El Niño effect this year and the resulting water scarcity.
He informed Mr. Vijay that Andhra Pradesh had already released 4.08 TMC of water to Chennai.
“The Andhra Pradesh government will consider releasing additional water for Chennai, depending on the availability and requirements of the State,” Mr. Naidu told his Tamil Nadu counterpart.
Mr. Vijay, who arrived in the State to participate in the Vijayawada Utsav, was accorded a warm welcome by Mr. Naidu and HRD Minister Nara Lokesh. Both the Chief Ministers held discussions with officials on several issues of mutual interest.
During the meeting, Mr. Naidu explained the importance of linking the Godavari and Cauvery rivers, describing the interlinking of rivers as a permanent solution to drought.
Mr. Vijay, meanwhile, requested Andhra Pradesh to release additional drinking water for Chennai through the Telugu Ganga project to meet the requirements of the city.
Under the inter-State agreement signed in 1983, 15 TMC of the Krishna water is to be delivered annually at the Tamil Nadu border to cater to Chennai’s drinking water needs.
However, inadequate flood flows into the Krishna River at Srisailam and low storage in key reservoirs have complicated the prospects of meeting the demand in full.
The Andhra Pradesh government is understood to be examining the possibility of releasing a proportionate quantity from the available reserves at the Somasila and Kandaleru projects. A partial release of up to 5 TMC is likely to be a possible compromise, though a final government decision may be disclosed later.
“The Andhra Pradesh government cannot release the full quantity of water, given the water availability in the reservoirs. However, a proportionate release from the available storage at the Kandaleru and Somasila projects is likely to be considered,” sources said.
The Tuesday’s meeting brought back memories of January 12, 2017, when then Tamil Nadu Chief Minister O. Panneerselvam met Mr. Naidu and sought the release of the Krishna water for Chennai, which was facing an acute drinking water shortage.
Mr. Panneerselvam had written to Naidu on January 7, urging the immediate release of the agreed quantity from Kandaleru reservoir. During their meeting, he had explained the severity of the crisis and sought additional supplies.
Mr. Naidu had agreed in principle to a partial release, with the final quantity linked to water availability and Andhra Pradesh’s own requirements. Reports at the time said the two sides discussed a release of around 2.5 TMC.
Mr. Vijay’s visit marked his maiden trip to Andhra Pradesh after assuming office.

Minecraft Dungeons 2 is a substantial step forward for Mojang’s action-packed RPG. Surely it traded the original game’s disconnected missions for a sprawling world packed with dungeons, dangerous mobs, and mountains of loot. But that is precisely why I enjoyed taking on my own adventure through the Overworld and the vivid Sift dimension.
I had an absolute blast completing the main campaign, and I’m dying to try out the future DLCs planned for the game. So, before you purchase it, here’s a Minecraft Dungeons 2 review to help you.
Bye-Bye Menu Hopping: The Overworld Finally Grows Up
The original Minecraft Dungeons had a pretty straightforward structure: you select a mission, clear its objectives, collect loot, and return to the hub. While it worked, the world often felt more like a collection of disconnected dioramas. Thankfully, Minecraft Dungeons 2 finally gives the adventure aspect some room to breathe.
Although I had just visited the prequel recently to brush up on the lore and obtain the Hero Cape in Minecraft, the interconnected world is one of my favorite improvements. Instead of hopping between missions through a menu, you travel across distinct regions, stumbling into unexpected side quests, unearthing hidden dungeons, and crossing paths with some eccentric-looking NPCs.
While Brave Haven acts as the central operational hub, you can still explore other major biomes and perform all your enchanting, upgrading actions, purchasing new gear, or even teleporting elsewhere.
As you explore, rewards obtained from defeating the Minecraft Dungeons 2 enemies roaming all around feel organic. The side quests give you a legitimate reason to revisit the places even after the main story content.
Most importantly, the world feels alive, especially when an impromptu ambush completely derails your planned itinerary. Say I’m chasing a quest marker, but I get horribly sidetracked defeating a bunch of Royal Guards and Illagers. Although I could’ve used the fast travel stations to reach the nearest checkpoint, that’s exactly the chaos I’m looking for in a Minecraft ARPG game.
Welcome to Mojang’s Trippiest Dimension Yet – The Sift
If the Overworld sets up the structural bread and butter, The Sift is where Mojang brings out their fine China and shows what they’re capable of. The Sift in Minecraft Dungeons 2 is a surreal dimension, flexing wild biomes, bizarre alien fauna, and some lethal encounters.
I genuinely enjoyed exploring the aesthetic palette that broke away from the usual grass and stony blocks, giving the region its own charm. Discovering new enemies and bosses also makes discovering the hidden areas exciting, as it triggers that classic, “What on earth wrecked my health bar?” excitement.
It is also a massive narrative lore drop for the broader franchise, as Mojang has confirmed The Sift comes to Minecraft in 2027.
My main gripe? The game pulls you out far too soon. The Sift teases astronomical potential, and I just hoped that the main story was a bit more connected to exploring the secrets of this dimension.
Easy to Pick Up, Hard to Put Down, Buildcrafting Comes to Dungeons
On the surface, combat retains its signature pick-up-and-play grace. Light attacks, ranged shots, dodge rolls, jump smashes, Talisman passives, and a handful of Artifact abilities clear hordes of enemies before they turn your light-hearted adventure into a respawn speedrun.
The secret sauce is in the overhauled equipment system. While the original forces you into rigid, single-slot armor archetypes, the sequel throws open the workshop doors, allowing you to mix-and-match individual pieces with unique passive effects.
Whether you love to transform into a tanky build, become a self-healing wizard, wipe out the entire mob, or one-shot bosses with your ranged weapons, there are a ton of options for the best builds in Minecraft Dungeons 2.
Apart from buildcrafting, enchanting offers endless tinkering while an equipment upgrade system ensures that your prized Special and Unique weapons don’t turn out to be a paperweight. That feature eliminates the worst crime in loot games: watching your favorite weapon immediately become useless after five minutes of finding it.
The Story is Fun, but the Real Magic Happens in Co-Op
The Minecraft Dungeons 2 lore is a reliable excuse to start smashing things because the Illagers are up to no good. The narrative momentum moves at a solid pace, and the cinematic set-pieces pack in plenty of visual punch.
Minecraft Dungeons 2 probably will not win awards for the best storytelling, but I can assure you that you’ll definitely not rest until you’ve taken a hit at one of the High Council members.
The core gameplay loop rarely misses a beat. You cleave through enemy ambushes, chart through the unknown map of Minecraft Dungeons 2, and gradually turn your unarmored hero into a walking menace.
It shines the brightest when you play co-op in Minecraft Dungeons 2. If you’re not like me, having a ton of people around to try out the game, you’ll never want to head out on a solo adventure here. Whether your friends are seasoned dungeon crawlers or you’re introducing someone to the ARPG genre for the first time, the smooth mechanics and accessibility make it an effortless recommendation.
Performance: Stumbling Launch, Yet Smooth Sailing FPS
I tested Minecraft Dungeons 2 on a mid-range gaming laptop via Xbox Game Pass, and my personal run was smooth sailing. I managed to avoid the stability hiccups, FPS drops, and instant crashes reported by fellow community members on Steam. But if you know someone facing the same network problem, the Minecraft Dungeons 2 error code guide will surely help them out.

Although the launch week wasn’t quite as smooth across the broader community, Mojang moved fast and rolled out a hotfix update within days of launch. The patch targeted several client-side server crashes and bugs that would otherwise cause the bosses to show some unexpected behavior.
Verdict: Mojang Struck Diamond, but the Endgame Needs More Ore
Minecraft Dungeons 2 is a fantastic sequel that suffers from a bit of an identity crisis when the credits roll. If you’ve played the original Dungeons extensively, you should know how massive the replayability of the game was with each DLC.

A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?
- Published
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.
Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.
But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.
Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.
That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.
Morocco never found the requisite finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.
For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.
The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.
At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.
"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".
"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.
"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published8 hours ago
From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.
He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.
And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.
Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.
The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.
President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.
Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.
"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."
Why is Rwanda a controversial choice?
Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.
Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.
The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.
But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.
The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.
Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.
Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.
F1 is not blind to such issues. Its own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders to address any issues that arise.
It also says it focuses its efforts "in relation to those areas which are within our own direct influence".
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."

Liverpool's Wirtz problem - does he need to be dropped?
- Published
At the end of the 2024-25 season, Liverpool head coach Arne Slot flew to the south of France to honour talks with Rayan Cherki.
Cherki was on Liverpool's shortlist in their hunt for an attacking midfielder but the main target was Florian Wirtz - who was also wanted by Bayern Munich and Manchester City.
Once Wirtz said his preference was to move to Anfield and join the then-Premier League champions, the £116m deal became a formality.
At the time, his arrival felt like a quality acquisition for Liverpool, but more than a year on things are still not clicking.
The German has scored seven goals and provided 11 assists over 56 Reds appearances, but had no goal involvements against any of the top-10 teams in the Premier League last season.
This term, Wirtz has started every game in the league and Champions League so far - managing just one assist across seven matches.
Those struggles were summed up on Sunday against Manchester City when new Reds boss Andoni Iraola - who succeeded Slot in the summer - replaced Wirtz with Trey Nyoni in the 66th minute, shortly after Ryan Gravenberch was sent off and Erling Haaland broke the deadlock.
Wirtz is only 23 but so is Cherki, who put the icing on the cake in City's 3-0 win at Anfield with an exquisite goal - the kind we have become used to seeing since his £30m move from Lyon in June 2025.
Cherki cost less than a third of what Liverpool paid for Wirtz, but has already scored 16 goals and provided 18 assists in 65 City appearances.
The France attacker has also shown an ability to provide crucial game-changing moments. Liverpool fans haven't seen anywhere near enough of that from Wirtz yet.
"Wirtz has so much ability. I wish I had that ability because he just glides. He makes it look effortless - but he doesn't hurt teams," former Liverpool defender Steven Warnock told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"He doesn't impact the game enough. He drifts in and out of games. He's here for 10 or 20 seconds and then he disappears for five or 10 minutes and you think where is he now?"
After Liverpool's defeat by Man City, Jamie Carragher said it was time for Iraola to drop Wirtz.
"I think he needs to come out of the team, I said that last time out and I'm going to say it again," Carragher told Sky Sports.
"Liverpool played well [against Man City] for a lot of the game before the Gravenberch red card but they didn't create a chance, so they have a real problem with scoring goals and creating chances and that's what you got Wirtz for.
"He's not giving you anything defensively and he's not giving you anything going the other way. I don't want anyone to pile in on the lad but I think we're justified in saying we need more and we can't wait."
'Anyone who loves football can see Wirtz is outstanding'
Given that Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai are all currently sidelined, it would be a big call to drop Wirtz - but Liverpool have two games every week between now and the November international break.
With Gravenberch suspended for Saturday's trip to Brentford, Iraola will likely keep the Dutch midfielder in for Wednesday's Champions League game against LASK in Austria and give a start to Nyoni. More changes are expected from Sunday's defeat.
When it comes to the intensity of the top flight, Wirtz is still finding his feet, but his best performance this season came in the Champions League against Atletico Madrid and he was unlucky not to get an assist when Bradley Barcola fired wide.
Asked on Tuesday if Wirtz needed more time, Iraola defended his player and said: "The other day, he probably he didn't have his best game but he has had good games with us this season.
"Everyone starts looking for answers. He had some good performances in the national team - he scored one goal and he will have better or worse games.
"But I would like to look at it more collectively and more how they help us play and get results and after that I don't care who scores. I think it's a more collective thing."
Seeing Wirtz excel for Germany under Jurgen Klopp is proof - if it was needed - as to why he was seen as one of the hottest talents in world football when he joined Liverpool.
"Attacking players always need a functioning team that works well around them. Anyone who loves football can still see how outstanding Florian is as a player," Klopp said recently.
That is also a view shared by Steven Gerrard.
"I can just picture him beating himself up on how his Liverpool thing has started. This kid is a major talent in my opinion. I've seen enough to believe and give him a chance. I think he needs help and support now," Gerrard told The Overlap.
Wirtz created 95 chances from open play in all competitions last season - at least 27 more than any other Liverpool player - and his fizzing pass for Victor Munoz's equaliser against Nottingham Forest in August showed a glimpse of his class, but those moments have been few and far in between.
Against City at the weekend there was a moment at 0-0 when Wirtz hit an effort wide despite having Barcola and Milos Kerkez in space on his left. It was a poor decision from a man desperate for a big moment.
Back in August, Wirtz spoke candidly about how he felt "more ready" for his second season at Anfield. The physicality was a key aspect, with bulking up a big focus of his first campaign.
"I definitely learned a lot. I just learned how Premier League football is played and I think I am more ready for my second season because I know how it is now. I am really excited for my next season," Wirtz said then.
He impressed in pre-season but two months into the new campaign, Wirtz needs to start delivering sooner rather than later.
If not, then Iraola will be left with a tough decision to make.

On 10 October 2026, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) organised a major protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which protesters claim led to arbitrary voter deletions. In response to the demonstrations, authorities imposed a security crackdown, shutting down dozens of metro stations, cancelling trains, and enforcing prohibitory orders across the capital. Police have detained thousands of individuals, including political figures like Arvind Kejriwal, Pinarayi Vijayan and Mamata Banerjee, as well as CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who were later released.
Against this backdrop, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media with the claim that it shows protesters at Jantar Mantar demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing the October 10 CJP protest at Jantar Mantar, demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
Fact: The video was uploaded on 20 July 2026 and shows an earlier protest demanding Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation. It is unrelated to the October 10 CJP protest. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the same video (archive), uploaded to the Facebook page of Samar Moto Vlog on 20 July 2026. According to the post, the video shows a protest at Jantar Mantar on 20 July 2026, demanding the resignation of then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Delhi Police also stated that the video was an old one from July 2026 and urged users to refrain from spreading misinformation. We have previously debunked several old and unrelated visuals falsely linked to the October 10 protest.
To sum it up, a video from July 2026 is being falsely shared as footage of the October 10 CJP protest at Jantar Mantar.

Is Mini DisplayPort becoming obsolete?
How Thunderbolt and USB-C replaced the need for a dedicated video port.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
For a while, Mini DisplayPort was one of the main options for video output on smaller devices. Apple announced it in 2008 to replace interfaces like VGA and DVI with a single, slimmer connector. While it was seen on most Mac models for several years, it's since become difficult to find computers with Mini DisplayPort — even Apple has removed the port from Macs.
But does that mean it's obsolete? Not exactly, although you won't see it as often as you used to. The DisplayPort standard remains popular, especially among workstations and gaming monitors, so it's not as if the technology itself has become obsolete. But we now have another small port that's favored.
Why Mini DisplayPort faded out
Mini DisplayPort is called "mini" for a reason. The full-size version (simply called DisplayPort) supports the same core specifications, but with a larger connector. Apple always opted for the tiny version because it fits better on smaller computers like MacBooks and the Mac mini.
It doesn't matter whether you use DisplayPort (DP) or Mini DisplayPort — both can transmit video and audio through a single cable. Compared to older connectors like DVI and VGA, one of the main advantages of DisplayPort is that it offers much higher bandwidth. Depending on the generation, DP can handle resolutions up to 8K and beyond, at high frame rates (144+Hz) depending on the resolution. Meanwhile, older connectors struggle with anything above 1080p.
When the Thunderbolt standard emerged, its first two iterations used the Mini DisplayPort connector. While a standard Mini DP port only carries video and audio, Thunderbolt also supports high-speed data transfers. That meant the same connector could be used for video, audio and data — perfect for accessories like Apple's Cinema Display.
In late 2015 and 2016, the Thunderbolt 3 standard arrived and switched to the USB-C connector. Apple and other PC manufacturers quickly moved to USB-C or HDMI, leaving the Mini DisplayPort connector behind. These days, USB-C has become the standard for nearly everything. Not only can it support high-speed data transfer, but it can also handle video, audio and even the Thunderbolt protocol — all in a single, small reversible connector. Not every USB-C port can handle the same tasks, but you'll see some version of it on almost every device.
To further push Mini DisplayPort down, USB-C also supports DisplayPort Alternate Mode, meaning a compatible USB-C cable and ports can carry the same DisplayPort signal through the more modern cable. PC makers have no reason to have people buy a Mini DP-to-DP cable when they can simply buy a USB-C-to-DP cable.
Where DisplayPort still makes sense
That doesn't mean DisplayPort is gone. Of course, you may still find older hardware with Mini DisplayPort, like past laptops and graphics cards. If you still have one of these, you can buy a Mini DP-to-DP cable to connect them to a modern monitor. Since the protocol is the same, they'll communicate with each other just fine. New hardware also continues to use full-sized version of DisplayPort. It's still the standard for many high-end monitors and graphics cards.
HDMI has come a long way in recent years and can now transmit video at incredibly high resolutions. Still, DisplayPort remains the gold standard for absurdly high resolutions and refresh rates, such as 4K at 240Hz. For comparison, while HDMI 2.1 offers up to 48 Gbps of bandwidth, DisplayPort 2.1 can reach 80 Gbps. This makes a difference for those looking to get the most out of the hardware they have. HDMI 2.2 offers 96 Gbps bandwidth, which may even the field a bit once compatible devices are widely available.
Of course, when using older hardware, not everything may work as expected. VR headsets, for example, can be picky about their video signal, and they don't always play nice with Mini DisplayPort when you use an adapter. The same goes for the old Apple Cinema Display — Apple makes it clear that it doesn't work through a Thunderbolt adapter. Still, it doesn't hurt to try if you have the right cables on hand.

The Rejinagar and Nandigram by-elections in West Bengal concluded on October 9, Friday, with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) clinching victory in both seats. BJP’s Shankharavh Sarkar won in Rejinagar and Hasirani Rath won the Nandigram seat.
Polling in both the assemblies were, however, marred by allegations of electoral malpractices, with the Congress demanding repolling.
Amid these allegations, digital censorship emerged as another flashpoint, with social media content documenting alleged electoral malpractice and vote rigging being restricted in India. The restrictions also added to concerns over the growing suppression of online criticism of the ruling party. For the past couple of months, Alt News has reported extensively on this social media censorship frenzy in India.
On October 7, the Facebook page of the Murshidabad district wing of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress (@DCCMurshidabad) was restricted under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules. The page remains unavailable at the tome of this article being written.
